# Pitch

Autumn 1943. A man's body washes up on the breakwater at Coldwater Reach, a working fishing harbor on the Maine coast. He has no papers. He is not from the town. The Coast Guard removes him within the day and takes most of the official silence with it.

Three people in Coldwater Reach end up carrying the weight of that body, none of them by plan:

**Eira Bowman**, fifty-two, the town's harbormaster — the only woman in her position on the Maine coast, widowed eight years before when the previous harbormaster (her husband) drowned. She saw something on the dock the night before the body came in.

**Hannah Pfeiffer**, seventeen, inland on her family's dairy farm, where four German prisoners work the fields under armed escort. The youngest prisoner is from near where her father was born. Her parents have been disappearing, slowly, in different directions, since the war started.

**Marcus Klein**, forty-seven, Austrian-Jewish, who arrived in Coldwater in 1942 to teach German and Latin at the town high school after years of displacement across Paris, London, and a Canadian internment camp. He boards with the Black custodian Henry Crow and his wife Lillian — the only household in town that treats him as a guest rather than a curiosity.

None of the three meets the other two together. Their threads cross. The question of who the dead man was, and what happened that night, moves through all three of them across eighteen months, assembling in the reader before it assembles in any of the characters. The war ends in the background. Their resolutions are smaller and older than that.

# World

## Coldwater Reach, Maine — 1943–1945

Coldwater Reach is an invented coastal Maine town, positioned on a rocky tidal inlet south of Bangor, north of Portland — somewhere on the Penobscot Bay periphery, close enough to the sardine canneries and lobster wharves that its economy makes sense, far enough from the naval installations that it is not strategic, only adjacent. Population roughly 800. Not a summer colony. A working town.

The harbor is the organizing fact of Coldwater Reach. The breakwater runs two hundred feet out from the north shore, granite blocks laid in the 1890s, algae-striped from the waterline down. The tidal range is eleven feet. The fishing fleet — already shrunken by enlistments and fuel rationing — moors on the inside. The harbormaster's office occupies a cedar-shingled building at the foot of the commercial wharf, with a chart table, a tide log, a field telephone, and a kerosene stove.

## Physical texture

- **The harbor in November**: black water, spray over the breakwater, fog that sits in the channel until noon. The lobster smacks go out in the dark and come back in the dark. Diesel smoke and brine and the cold that is wet rather than dry.
- **The Pfeiffer farm**: three miles inland on Route 9, a working dairy operation. Red barn, icehouse beside it (now whitewashed inside and partitioned into a sleeping room for the prisoners). Twenty-two Holsteins. Corn stubble in October. The smell of silage. Stone walls the first Pfeiffers built in 1903.
- **The town itself**: one main street, a general store (Beal's), the post office, a Congregational church, a Legion hall that doubles as the rationing board offices, the school. The school is a WPA-era brick building; it handles grades one through twelve, a total enrollment of about 130 children.
- **Henry and Lillian Crow's house**: Elm Street, three blocks from the harbor, a white clapboard house with a good vegetable garden that Lillian tends. The house is warm, kept. Marcus rents the second bedroom. The kitchen is the social center.

## Historical layer

### The POW labor program
Under the Emergency Farm Labor program, German prisoners of war from the Houlton internment camp (Camp Houlton, a real and large facility in Aroostook County) were assigned to satellite work camps and individual farms to supply agricultural labor for the duration. The prisoners were housed under the Geneva Convention terms: adequate food, shelter, pay in scrip redeemable at the PX, and armed escort during work. The escort at the Pfeiffer farm is a single aging Coastal Patrol private, Lonzo Reed, who sits on a stool at the barn door with a Springfield rifle he has not fired in two years.

### Home-front rationing and communications
Ration books govern sugar, meat, coffee, fuel oil, rubber, and shoes. Fishermen receive a fuel-oil allocation; civilian vessels are prohibited from certain waters after dark. The Coastal Patrol (volunteers, mostly older men) patrols the beaches and harbor entrances for signs of enemy activity — their authority is real but their means are limited.

V-Mail (microfilmed letters photographed and printed at destination) is the dominant form of communication with men overseas. Casualty telegrams arrive at the Western Union office on Main Street; the Western Union clerk is Bertrand Hatch, seventy, who has delivered forty-three since December 1941 and has not gotten used to it.

The BC-1206 radio set is the standard wartime communications radio; civilian shortwave is restricted, but commercial broadcast (WLBZ out of Bangor) carries the nightly war news. Families gather at the kitchen radio at six o'clock.

### The U-boat context
By autumn 1943, the acute U-boat threat to the Maine coast that characterized 1942 has subsided (the Battle of the Atlantic having largely turned). Submarines are present in the Atlantic but are no longer surfacing near the coast or sinking tankers in visible range. The town remembers 1942 — the dim-outs, the floating debris, the one body that washed up at Pemaquid that summer — but 1943 is quieter. The body on the breakwater is not a U-boat story. The town will reach for that explanation first. It is wrong.

### German-American community
The Pfeiffers are not unique in coastal Maine; there were German-speaking communities throughout New England, established in the 19th-century waves of immigration. After Pearl Harbor and the subsequent declaration of war on Germany, these families occupied an uncomfortable national position. German-born noncitizens were classified as enemy aliens (required to register, restricted from coastal areas in some jurisdictions). The Pfeiffers are naturalized citizens; this protects them legally and does very little socially.

### Race in Coldwater Reach, 1943
Henry and Lillian Crow are Black Americans in a nearly all-white small Maine town. Henry's family came north from Norfolk, Virginia, in 1924 as part of the Great Migration's northern edge. He works as chief custodian of the school — a secure, respected, low-paying position that puts him in contact with almost everyone in town. The town's relationship to the Crows is specific: they are known, long-established, and still not quite unquestioned. The prose should render this without monologue.

## Seasonal arc

The story runs autumn 1943 through spring 1945:
- **Autumn 1943**: the body. The first accumulation of winter. Silage, deer hunting season.
- **Winter 1943–44**: the longest and most interior season. Ice on the harbor shallows. The school's furnace. Ration book renewal.
- **Spring 1944**: mud season. D-Day (June 6, 1944) falls within this narrative period — it arrives on the radio at Beal's store and at the Crows' kitchen.
- **Summer and autumn 1944**: the farm at full labor. The harvest. The war that seemed to be ending isn't ending yet.
- **Winter 1944–45**: Ardennes offensive (Battle of the Bulge, December 1944). The town loses two more men.
- **Spring 1945**: VE Day approaches. The story ends before it arrives.

## Tone

Not pastoral. Not elegiac as a sustained note — the prose does not linger for beauty. The world is cold and concrete: wood stoves, diesel, the particular smell of brine-soaked rope, the weight of a ledger that must balance. What is moving comes from specificity, not from atmosphere declared.

# Characters

## POV Characters

---

### Eira Bowman
**Age**: 52 in October 1943  
**Role**: Harbormaster, Coldwater Reach  
**Background**: Born in Coldwater, daughter of a lobsterman. Married Owen Bowman in 1913; they had no surviving children. Learned the harbor's rhythms as Owen's shadow, took the post formally after his death in November 1935 when the selectmen ran out of other options. Has held it for eight years. She is the only woman holding a harbormaster post on the Maine coast. Nobody mentions this to her face; everyone has an opinion about it.

**Drives**:
- Competence for its own sake. She does the job better than the men who might have done it, and she knows this with the dispassion of someone who has long since stopped needing to be told.
- Authority held at cost. The question beneath all of Eira's chapters: what does it cost to fill a role built for someone else's body, someone else's name? Not just gender — Owen's ghost is in the post itself.
- The body as professional problem and personal burden. She knows what she saw. She cannot unknow it. She has not decided what that knowledge obligates her to do.

**Voice and register**: Spare, procedural, observant in a working way. Sentences built for information transfer, not reflection. She thinks in tidal schedules, load limits, weather probability. Her grief — for Owen, for the accumulated missing of the war — does not announce itself; it appears in what she notices and when she notices it. Interior monologue is rare and tends to arrive disguised as professional observation. Dialogue is clipped, often interrogative.

**Physical**: Strong-handed, weathered, thick-coated. Not physically remarkable to herself. She dresses for weather and ignores the mirror.

**Key relationship**: Dead Owen, whose presence is structural throughout. The Coast Guard Lieutenant (a recurring contact, unnamed initially). Hannah's father Albrecht, who sometimes brings milk to the harbor store — one of the crossing points with that thread.

**Arc**: What it costs to hold a post built for someone else; whether authority exercised honestly is its own justification; whether she has the right to bury what she knows in order to keep the harbor running.

---

### Hannah Pfeiffer
**Age**: 17 in October 1943; turns 18 in March 1944  
**Role**: Daughter, student, farm laborer  
**Background**: Born in Maine, daughter of Bavarian immigrants. Speaks German at home and English everywhere else. Attends Coldwater High School, one of Marcus Klein's students in Latin and (unofficially) German. Works the farm every morning before school and every evening after.

**Drives**:
- Witness and accumulation. Hannah's chapters are the most porous — they take in what the others don't see or won't let themselves see. She is seventeen and still assembling the person she will be; the novel is about that assembly.
- Her parents' silence as weight. Albrecht's German-only household rule and Magda's deeper withdrawal are existential weather for Hannah. She does not understand them fully; she understands them acutely.
- Karl Reinmar. The youngest prisoner is from fifty kilometers from where her father was born. This is not a romance in the adult sense. It is something younger and more dangerous: recognition across a wall she was raised not to look over.

**Voice and register**: The most interior of the three POVs. Adolescent permission to follow a thought further than an adult would. German words and phrases surface at moments of high affect — her father's language bleeding through. The farm's seasons are her sensory world: calf smell, frozen ground, the particular silence of a snowed-in barn. Her prose has more movement than Eira's, more instability than Marcus's. She sees things the other two have learned to walk past.

**Physical**: Tall, practical-handed, Bavarian-fair. In winter she wears her father's old coat to the barn.

**Key relationships**: Albrecht Pfeiffer (father, receding); Magda Pfeiffer (mother, withdrawn); Karl Reinmar (prisoner, the thread she'll have to choose about); Marcus Klein (her teacher, one of the thread-crossings); Lonzo Reed (the guard she observes more carefully than he observes the prisoners).

**Arc**: The accumulation of small choices that constitutes adolescence; what she does with the permission — or the transgression — of crossing the lines her parents and the town have drawn; what she becomes on the other side of them.

---

### Marcus Klein
**Age**: 47 in October 1943  
**Role**: Latin and German instructor, Coldwater High School  
**Background**: Born in Vienna. Left Austria in 1936. Paris (1936–38), London (1938–39), Canada (interned at Sherbrooke, Quebec, 1939–41, under the British policy of interning "enemy aliens," including Jewish refugees). Released through the Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars. Cambridge, Massachusetts (1941–42), then hired by Coldwater High School when the previous instructor enlisted. He does not discuss Sherbrooke.

**Drives**:
- Displacement as condition, not event. Marcus does not wait to stop being displaced; he has learned, at cost, that the waiting itself is a trap. The question in his arc is different: what is left of a person, and what obligations survive, when the displacement has gone on long enough that there is nowhere else to return to?
- Language as survival instrument. He weighs every word for what it reveals about him. His formal, slightly overcorrect English is armor. Teaching language — the grammar and declension of it — is the one place he can be wholly competent.
- Henry and Lillian Crow. He recognizes a variant of his condition in theirs — not the same, not equivalent, but recognizable. The household is the one place he is not a specimen.
- The body on the breakwater intersects something in Marcus's past — not through plot-mechanics but through the kind of knowledge that accumulates in a man who has moved through wartime Europe: a certain type of person, a certain type of end.

**Voice and register**: Precise, slightly formal, with the characteristic careful pace of someone translating his thinking as it occurs. The academic's habit of measuring sentences. His narration has subordinate clauses that arrive to qualify or correct; he rarely commits to an absolute statement unless it concerns grammar or the calendar. His chapters sometimes have the quality of a letter written in a language not his own — not because his English is wrong, but because he is always slightly aware of the medium.

**Physical**: Slight, carefully dressed (the old European habit of dressing as a form of dignity). Wears a coat hat in autumn that looks distinctly not from Maine. Glasses. The Crows' house has the only room in town where he fully takes his coat off.

**Key relationships**: Henry Crow (landlord, recognition, something approaching friendship); Lillian Crow (who feeds him and asks him about Vienna); Hannah Pfeiffer (student, the site of one thread-crossing); the school board (threat, background pressure); Karl Reinmar (via Hannah, and via his own knowledge of what certain German boys' paths through the war look like).

**Arc**: Whether displacement ends, and if it does, what the displaced person becomes when the ground stops moving. Whether a man who has lost everything consecutive still has obligations to places, people, languages he no longer belongs to.

---

## Secondary and Supporting Characters

---

### Owen Bowman (deceased)
**Age at death**: approximately 47 (drowned November 1935)  
**Role**: Eira's husband; previous harbormaster  
**Background**: Fourth-generation Coldwater fisherman. Took the harbormaster post in the late 1920s. Drowned in the harbor during the November storm of 1935 — went out to secure a vessel that was breaking loose; was not found for three days. Eira found him.  
**Function**: Owen is structural throughout Eira's chapters — not as a ghost in the literary sense, but as the shape of the post she holds. The tools he used, the ledger in his handwriting, the men who still call the office "Owen's." He is the precedent she is always both following and revising.

---

### Albrecht Pfeiffer
**Age**: 56 in 1943  
**Role**: Hannah's father; dairy farmer  
**Background**: Born in Bavaria, near Nuremberg. Emigrated to Maine in 1922 with Magda. Naturalized citizen. He came to America wanting to leave Germany, and now Germany has followed him in a different form. Since the declaration of war he has retreated into German at home — not as defiance, but as a kind of grief. He does not speak of Bavaria specifically; what surfaces is the language, not the memory.  
**Voice**: His English is grammatically correct and formally old-fashioned. His German is the German of the region he left. The prose does not phonetically render either — it renders the fact of them.

---

### Magda Pfeiffer
**Age**: 53 in 1943  
**Role**: Hannah's mother  
**Background**: Also from Bavaria. Magda's withdrawal is more complete than Albrecht's retreat into German — she has gone quiet in ways that cannot be explained solely by the war. There is something older and more personal in her silence. She works the household, tends the kitchen garden, cooks. She does not speak much in any language. Hannah watches her.

---

### Karl Reinmar
**Age**: 19 in 1943  
**Role**: German POW, the youngest of four assigned to the Pfeiffer farm  
**Background**: Wehrmacht, captured in North Africa (Tunisia, spring 1943). From a town in Franconia, fifty kilometers from Albrecht Pfeiffer's birthplace. He is not ideological — at nineteen, drafted at seventeen, he has been a soldier long enough to have lost most of the beliefs the uniform was given with. He speaks a German that Albrecht recognizes down to the vowels. He is learning English from newspapers left in the icehouse.  
**Function**: The crossing point between Hannah's interior and the history she is surrounded by. His presence forces the question she cannot avoid: what side is she on, if sides are where the question lives.

---

### Lonzo Reed
**Age**: 63 in 1943  
**Role**: Coastal Patrol private, armed escort for the Pfeiffer farm POWs  
**Background**: From a Maine fishing family, too old for the regular service and assigned to the Coastal Patrol. He sits on his stool with the Springfield rifle, reads the Bangor Daily News, and pays attention to more than he shows. He is not unfriendly to the prisoners. He is not friendly either. He has a son in the Pacific who does not write often enough.  
**Function**: A dry, careful observer who occasionally appears as a perspective character in short interstitial sections if the structure calls for it. He knows more about what happens on the farm than anyone attributes to him.

---

### Henry Crow
**Age**: 51 in 1943  
**Role**: Chief custodian, Coldwater High School; Marcus's landlord  
**Background**: His family came north from Norfolk, Virginia, in 1924. Henry has been at the school for sixteen years. He knows every pipe, every furnace trick, every student by name. He is not a man to whom the town pays close attention. He notices this with the calm of someone long accustomed to being underestimated.  
**Voice**: Direct, warm at home, more reserved in public. He and Marcus have developed a friendship built on the recognition that both of them are in this town on sufferance — a recognition neither has stated directly.  
**Function**: The Crow household is the moral anchor of Marcus's chapters. Henry may carry a chapter or two from his own POV if the structure requires — his perspective on the school, the town, and Marcus's position is different from Marcus's own.

---

### Lillian Crow
**Age**: 48 in 1943  
**Role**: Henry's wife  
**Background**: Born in Maine (Waterville), one of the small number of Black families in the inland mill towns. She came to Coldwater Reach when she married Henry in 1924. She works some hours at the school as well (cleaning, cooking for events) though less formally than Henry.  
**Voice**: The warmest register in the novel. She asks Marcus about Vienna — actually wants to know. She has the quality of a person who has decided, actively, that the life available to her is worth inhabiting fully.  
**Function**: Grounds the Crow household in warmth rather than simply solidarity. Her relationship with Marcus is easy in a way that Coldwater Reach otherwise is not.

---

### The Body on the Breakwater (the unknown man)
No name is given in early chapters. Male, somewhere between 35 and 50. His clothing is unusual — not a fisherman's. His hands have calluses in the wrong places. The Coast Guard takes him. Official cause: drowning, storm exposure. The three POV characters accumulate understanding of who he might have been and how he came to be on that breakwater in ways that do not converge into a single clean answer before the book ends.

# Style

## POV and tense

Third-person limited past tense throughout. The narration is bound tightly to the chapter's POV character — the reader knows what that character knows, perceives what they perceive, and uses the vocabulary and conceptual frame they would use. The narrator does not editorialize independently of the POV. Free indirect discourse is the primary mode of interiority.

## Register: three voices, one restraint

All three POVs share a commitment to restraint — the prose trusts the reader to feel what is not said. But restraint applies differently in each voice:

**Eira's chapters**: The most compressed. Short declarative sentences. Professional vocabulary — tidal schedules, hull draft, load manifests, weather notation. Interior observation is disguised as external observation: what she notices and when and how long she looks are doing the work of interiority. She does not analyze her own emotions. They arrive as sudden physical facts (a cold that is not the wind; a weight in the hands that has nothing to do with the line she's coiling). Dialogue is clipped, often in shorthand; she says what is necessary and not the rest.

**Hannah's chapters**: The most porous. More interior consciousness than Eira's — adolescence permits it. Her sentences are longer and sometimes recursive; a thought can interrupt itself. German words and phrases surface under pressure (her father's language breaking through). The farm's sensory world is her primary anchor: her chapters ground quickly in physical sensation before moving inward. She is the character most willing to name her feelings, but only once — she does not rehearse them.

**Marcus's chapters**: Precise and slightly formal. The academic's habit of measurement: subordinate clauses that qualify, hedges that are grammatically precise. He is always slightly aware of the language he is writing in, as if English is a second home he keeps properly swept. His sentences tend to be longer than Eira's and more carefully constructed than Hannah's; he builds to his conclusions in a way that the other two do not. He occasionally catches himself in a formulation and revises mid-sentence.

## Sentence rhythm

- Average: 15–22 words (Marcus), 10–16 words (Eira), 12–20 words with more variance (Hannah)
- Eira's shortest declaratives can drop to 4–6 words at moments of extremity
- Marcus's longest sentences should not exceed 45 words; if they run longer, they should be doing complex grammatical work, not describing simple actions

## Dialogue

Dense enough to carry the story's social texture, but never decorative. No character explains what they mean. No character clarifies for the reader's benefit what they just said. Dialogue is where the constraint operates most visibly: what is not said in conversation has as much weight as what is.

- Eira's dialogue: imperative or interrogative; she does not explain.
- Hannah's dialogue: normal teenage speech in English, but registers differently in the few German exchanges.
- Marcus's dialogue: formal by one register above the conversation he is in, which he has learned to compensate for with attention to tone.

Tags are minimal. He said / she said is correct. Avoid "countered," "admitted," "declared."

## Interiority and indirect speech

Free indirect discourse carries the interior. "The body had been there since Wednesday, probably. Or Tuesday." is preferable to "She thought the body had been there since Wednesday, probably." The chapter's POV ownership is established at the opening; interior thinking flows without tag.

## Historical texture

Period-accurate language and objects are the story's floor. Do not modernize the idiom. Do not explain the period to the reader ("rationing, which was how the government controlled supplies during the war"). Use the period's terms and trust the reader. Specific names matter: the BC-1206, the V-Mail, the ration books, WLBZ, Camp Houlton, the Coastal Patrol.

## What the prose does not do

- Does not describe war heroism. The war is elsewhere. What reaches Coldwater Reach is loss (telegrams), constraint (rations), and the living displaced (Marcus, the prisoners).
- Does not make the sea romantic. The harbor is a workplace. Weather is a professional variable.
- Does not make the Germans — prisoner or parent — into symbols. Karl is nineteen and tired. Albrecht is a man who left one country and cannot fully leave it.
- Does not explain race. Henry and Lillian Crow are specific people living a specific life in a specific town. The prose renders this through what happens, what is said, what is not said.
- Does not reach for the lyric unless the POV earns it. Hannah is the character most likely to perceive something beautifully; even her prose earns that beauty through grounded sensory work first.

---

## Failure modes

The AI-author patterns most tempting in this story's register. The drafter should actively avoid these; the compression pass should cut them.

- **Post-scene subtext naming** — a paragraph after a scene names what the scene "was about." This story's whole contract is that the subtext stays subtext; the reader assembles meaning. Any sentence that functions as "which meant that..." or "the weight of that moment was..." should be cut.

- **Thesis restatement** — abstract sentence re-stating the chapter's or book's theme. The brief is explicit: "the story trusts the reader to feel what is not said." A sentence like "She understood then what it meant to hold a position built for another" is the failure mode, not the goal.

- **Sentence-after-the-sentence** — an image lands, and then the next sentence glosses it. Especially damaging in Eira's chapters, where compression is the register. The image should do its work alone. Exception: in Marcus's chapters, a qualifying sentence that adds precision (not emotion) is within register.

- **Emotional structural analysis** — "Her grief had the quality of..." "What she felt was not quite fear but a cousin of it..." This is not the register. Feelings arrive as physical fact or through what a character notices, not as taxonomized states.

- **Dialogue glosses** — "as if to say," "which meant he was asking," "the question beneath the question." The brief says the dialogue is where constraint operates most visibly. Interpretation of dialogue is the reader's work.

---

## Lean-into patterns

Patterns the drafter and editors should NOT treat as failures, because this register actively uses them.

- **Free indirect interiority that arrives quietly mid-scene** — a line that is clearly the character's interior thought, unmarked, embedded in external description. This is the mode. Do not tag it. Do not move it to a new paragraph unless the tonal shift needs marking.

- **Sentence fragments in Eira's chapters** — "November. The harbor quiet." These are correct; they are her perceptual rhythm. Not a failure of grammar.

- **German phrases in Hannah's chapters** — untranslated, in the flow of the sentence. The reader can feel the meaning from context. Not a failure of accessibility.

- **Marcus's qualifying subordinate clauses** — his narration builds to conclusions through subordinate structure. This is his register, not a verbosity failure. Cut only if the sentence collapses under its own weight.

- **Repetition of a word or phrase across a chapter** — this can be structural, not accidental. Eira's chapters may return to a specific technical term; Marcus's to a phrase he is interrogating; Hannah's to a word in two languages. Check before cutting a repeat.

# Continuity

Hard facts that must not change between chapters or drafts. Numbered for citation.

---

## Dates and timeline

1. The story opens in **October 1943** and closes in **spring 1945**, just before VE Day (May 8, 1945). Approximately eighteen months of narrative time.
2. The body washes up on the Coldwater Reach breakwater in **October 1943**, after a three-day blow.
3. Owen Bowman drowned in the **November storm of 1935**. He was the previous harbormaster. Eira found him after three days.
4. Eira has held the harbormaster post for **eight years** when the story opens (i.e., since approximately 1935).
5. Eira is **52** in October 1943.
6. Hannah turns **18 in March 1944** (she is 17 at story's opening in October 1943).
7. Marcus arrived in Coldwater Reach in **March 1942**.
8. Marcus is **47** in October 1943.
9. Marcus was on the Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars rolls **since autumn 1940**.
10. Marcus was interned at **Sherbrooke, Quebec** (a real Canadian internment camp for "enemy aliens," including Jewish refugees from Europe).
11. Marcus's path: **Vienna → Paris → London → Sherbrooke, Quebec → Cambridge, Massachusetts → Coldwater Reach**.
12. D-Day is **June 6, 1944** — within the narrative period. It arrives on the radio.
13. The **Battle of the Bulge** begins December 1944 — also within the narrative period. The town loses two more men.
14. The story ends **before VE Day**, not after it.

---

## Characters

15. Eira Bowman is **the only woman holding a harbormaster post on the Maine coast** in this period.
16. The Pfeiffer family (Albrecht and Magda) came to Maine from **Bavaria in 1922**. They are **naturalized U.S. citizens**.
17. Albrecht Pfeiffer is from a town **near Nuremberg**, Bavaria.
18. The Pfeiffer farm is **three miles inland from Coldwater Reach**, on Route 9.
19. Four German prisoners are assigned to the Pfeiffer farm. Karl Reinmar is the **youngest**, age 19.
20. Karl Reinmar was captured in **North Africa (Tunisia, spring 1943)**, following a Wehrmacht conscription at age 17.
21. Karl is from a town in **Franconia, approximately fifty kilometers from Albrecht Pfeiffer's birthplace**.
22. The armed escort at the Pfeiffer farm is **Lonzo Reed**, an aging Coastal Patrol private, age 63.
23. Marcus boards at **Henry and Lillian Crow's house on Elm Street**, three blocks from the harbor.
24. Henry Crow's family came north from **Norfolk, Virginia**, in **1924**. Henry is the school's **chief custodian**. He is 51 in 1943.
25. Lillian Crow is **48** in 1943. She is from Waterville, Maine.
26. Marcus teaches **German and Latin** at Coldwater High School. The previous instructor enlisted.
27. Marcus **does not discuss** his internment at Sherbrooke.

---

## The body on the breakwater

28. The body is male. Not from Coldwater. No papers found on the body.
29. The Coast Guard takes the body and handles the official response.
30. **Eira saw something on the dock the night before the body came in.** This is her load-bearing knowledge. It is not stated outright in any chapter's opening.
31. None of the three main POV characters ever possesses the complete picture of who the man was and what happened.
32. The body's identity is **not fully resolved** before the book ends. The three characters' relationships to it resolve; the underlying fact may remain in shadow.

---

## Setting and infrastructure

33. The Coldwater Reach breakwater is **granite blocks, laid in the 1890s**, approximately 200 feet long, running out from the north shore.
34. The tidal range in the harbor is **eleven feet**.
35. The harbormaster's office is at the **foot of the commercial wharf** — cedar-shingled building, chart table, tide log, field telephone, kerosene stove.
36. Coldwater High School is a **WPA-era brick building**, grades 1–12, approximately 130 students.
37. The German POWs are housed in the **renovated icehouse** on the Pfeiffer property.

---

## Structural rules

38. **The three POV characters never meet as a group of three.** Individual crossing points between pairs are allowed.
39. Eira, Hannah, and Marcus each have approximately **ten chapters** (~30 chapters total, distributed asymmetrically as the story requires).
40. Additional short chapters from **a fourth POV** (Henry Crow, Lonzo Reed, or Karl Reinmar) are permitted but exceptional — they supplement the main three, they do not rotate equally with them.
41. The three POVs have **distinct prose registers**: Eira's is spare and procedural; Hannah's is interior and porous, with German threading in; Marcus's is precise and formally constructed.
42. The ending's resolutions are **character-level, not war-level**. The war ending is background, not foreground.
43. **No spy thriller mechanics**: no coded messages, no submarine landings, no Nazi agents in Maine. The war is present through loss, constraint, and displacement — not through plot-machinery.

---

## Historical accuracy constraints

44. The POW labor program in Maine was real. Camp Houlton in Aroostook County was a real facility. Satellite farm placements were real.
45. The BC-1206 radio set is the correct period wartime radio reference.
46. V-Mail (microfilmed letter system) is the correct period communication reference.
47. By **autumn 1943**, the acute coastal U-boat threat of 1942 had substantially subsided. The body is not a U-boat story.
48. German-born noncitizens were classified as **enemy aliens** under wartime regulations. The Pfeiffers' naturalized citizen status protects them legally but not socially.
49. Race in 1943 coastal Maine is a fact of life rendered through specific behavior and specific silence — not through authorial monologue or lecture.

# Glossary

Terms, names, places, and objects for Coldwater Reach. Alphabetical. Downstream phases should add to this file as new terms are introduced.

---

**Albrecht Pfeiffer** — Hannah's father. Born in Bavaria near Nuremberg. Emigrated to Maine 1922. Naturalized citizen. Has reverted to speaking only German at home since the war began. Age 56 in 1943.

**Battle of the Bulge** — German Ardennes offensive, December 1944. Within the novel's narrative period. The town loses two more men.

**BC-1206** — The standard wartime radio communications set. Civilian shortwave use was restricted during the war.

**Beal's General Store** — Coldwater Reach's general store on Main Street. Where the radio is on June 6, 1944.

**Body on the Breakwater, the** — Unnamed male, not from Coldwater Reach, found on the breakwater after a three-day blow in October 1943. No papers. Coast Guard takes him. The spine object of the novel.

**Camp Houlton** — Real German POW internment camp in Aroostook County, Maine. Prisoners from Houlton were assigned to satellite farm-labor placements across the state under the Emergency Farm Labor program.

**Coldwater Reach** — Invented coastal Maine fishing town, the setting of the novel. On the Penobscot Bay periphery, south of Bangor, north of Portland. Population approximately 800.

**Coastal Patrol** — Wartime volunteer patrol organization, mostly older men. Responsible for watching Maine coastal beaches and harbor approaches. Lonzo Reed is a Coastal Patrol private.

**D-Day** — June 6, 1944. The Allied landings at Normandy. Within the novel's narrative period. Arrives on the kitchen radio.

**Eira Bowman** — Harbormaster of Coldwater Reach. Age 52 in 1943. Widow of Owen Bowman. The only woman in her post on the Maine coast. POV character.

**Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars** — Real American organization that helped displaced European academics find positions in U.S. institutions. Marcus Klein was on their rolls from autumn 1940.

**Emergency Farm Labor Program** — Federal program that assigned German POWs to agricultural labor to replace the wartime farm-labor shortage.

**Enemy alien** — Wartime classification for foreign-born nationals of Axis countries, including (unjustly) Jewish refugees. German-born noncitizens were required to register and faced movement restrictions. The Pfeiffers, as naturalized citizens, were not classified as enemy aliens, though the social weight of the designation still touched them.

**Hannah Pfeiffer** — Seventeen-year-old daughter of the Pfeiffer dairy farm family. POV character. Turns 18 in March 1944.

**Henry Crow** — Chief custodian, Coldwater High School. Age 51 in 1943. Marcus's landlord. Family came north from Norfolk, Virginia, in 1924. Black American. Not a POV character in the main rotation, but may carry occasional short chapters.

**Karl Reinmar** — Youngest of the four German POWs at the Pfeiffer farm. Age 19. From Franconia, approximately fifty kilometers from Albrecht Pfeiffer's birthplace. Captured in Tunisia, spring 1943.

**Lillian Crow** — Henry's wife. Age 48. From Waterville, Maine. Treats Marcus as a guest rather than a specimen. The warmest register in the novel.

**Lonzo Reed** — Coastal Patrol private. Age 63. Armed escort for the Pfeiffer farm POWs. Has a son in the Pacific. Pays more attention than he is attributed with. May carry occasional short chapters.

**Magda Pfeiffer** — Hannah's mother. Age 53. Born in Bavaria. Increasingly withdrawn. Not speaking much in any language.

**Marcus Klein** — Latin and German instructor, Coldwater High School. Age 47 in 1943. Viennese, Jewish, displaced through Paris, London, and the Sherbrooke internment camp. POV character.

**Owen Bowman (deceased)** — Eira's husband and previous harbormaster. Drowned November 1935 in a storm, securing a vessel that was breaking loose. Eira found him after three days.

**Ration book** — Government-issued booklet authorizing civilian purchase of rationed goods: sugar, meat, coffee, fuel oil, rubber, shoes. Renewed periodically at the rationing board (Legion hall in Coldwater Reach).

**Route 9** — The road on which the Pfeiffer farm sits, three miles inland from Coldwater Reach.

**Sherbrooke, Quebec** — Real Canadian city where an internment camp held "enemy aliens," including Jewish refugees from Europe, under British wartime emergency policy. Marcus was interned there 1939–1941. He does not discuss it.

**Springfield rifle** — The M1903 Springfield bolt-action rifle. Lonzo Reed's weapon of record while escorting the Pfeiffer farm POWs.

**V-Mail** — Victory Mail: the microfilm-based letter system used to communicate with U.S. servicemen overseas. Letters were photographed, the film transported, and prints made at the destination. The dominant form of communication between Coldwater residents and their men in service.

**VE Day** — Victory in Europe Day, May 8, 1945. The story ends before it arrives.

**WLBZ** — Real radio station out of Bangor, Maine. The source of the nightly war news in Coldwater Reach homes.

# Themes

## 1. Authority and its costs

What does it mean to hold a position built for someone else — someone else's body, someone else's name? Eira's chapters carry this question most directly, but it runs through the other two as well. Marcus occupies a teaching post that belongs to a man who enlisted; he exercises a scholar's authority over a language that is also a threat to his survival. Hannah inherits her father's language, his farm, his silences, the loyalties he brought from Bavaria — none of which she asked for. The theme is not about gender or displacement per se, but about the specific cost of living inside a role that was not designed for the person who holds it. The three of them never discuss this with each other. They do not need to. The story's structure makes the parallel visible to the reader.

## 2. Displacement and the question of home

Marcus's arc makes this question explicit; the story insists it also applies to the others. Displacement is not only geographic. Albrecht Pfeiffer has been in Maine for twenty years and still cannot fully leave Bavaria. Henry Crow's family came north in 1924 and has been not-quite-arriving ever since. The German prisoners are displaced in the most literal sense — harvesting corn in Maine because a war they participated in (some willingly, some not) stranded them there. Hannah is the only character who was born where she lives, and she feels the least at home in it. The theme asks not just where we belong but whether belonging is ever a settled question, or whether it is always a negotiation conducted under conditions we did not choose.

## 3. What we carry for the dead

Owen Bowman has been dead for eight years when the novel opens, but he is present on every page of Eira's chapters — in the post she holds, the tools she uses, the way the men speak about "Owen's office." The body on the breakwater is the novel's central dead weight: three living people carry knowledge of it, separately, without being able to set it down. The war produces its dead at a distance — the names on the telegrams that Bertrand Hatch delivers are boys who became data — but the novel is interested in the intimate dead: the ones who stay. The question the theme poses is whether carrying is obligation, love, or simply the unavoidable byproduct of having been present.

## 4. The limits of knowledge and what we do with them

None of the three characters ever sees the full picture of what happened on the dock and the breakwater in October 1943. The reader assembles more than any single character does, but the assembly is not complete. The novel proposes that this is not a tragedy but a condition. Eira works from the principle that you act on what you know and document what you cannot explain. Marcus's displacement has given him the particular knowledge of someone who has survived partial information — decisions made without full context, judgments rendered without appeal. Hannah is young enough to still believe that more information would resolve the question; her arc involves learning what adults already know: that sometimes the underlying fact stays in shadow, and the question is what you do with your piece of it.

# Drafter guidance — Coldwater Reach

## Voice register

This is literary adult fiction — the pipeline's native register. Restrained, precise, third-person limited past, trusting the reader. The closest shelf analogues are Elizabeth Strout's *Olive Kitteridge* (tightly bound multi-POV, coastal Maine, the weight of what is not said between people who share a small world) and Ron Hansen's *The Assassination of Jesse James* in its procedural calm — the world rendered through its work and its weather, not its feelings about itself. The prose earns its emotional weight through specificity, not declaration.

The critical drafter challenge here is not register — this is the default — it is **maintaining three distinct voices within that shared register**. Eira, Hannah, and Marcus must sound like themselves at the sentence level, not like variants of the same narrator. See details below.

## Sentence-length expectations

These vary by POV character:

**Eira**: 
- Average: 10–16 words
- Maximum: 28 words; anything longer is register drift
- Short declaratives (4–7 words) at moments of extremity are correct — do not pad them

**Hannah**:
- Average: 12–20 words with substantial variance
- Her sentences can be longer and can interrupt themselves; a clause that trails off or pivots is within register
- Maximum: 35 words; her interiority is allowed but not sprawling

**Marcus**:
- Average: 15–22 words
- Subordinate clauses and careful qualification are correct; they are his register
- Maximum: 45 words; if longer, the sentence must be doing grammatical work, not simply being verbose

## Chapter-opening conventions

Establish which POV character you are in within the first sentence. Drop into their world immediately — sensory or professional, not abstract. 

- **Eira's chapters** should open on work or observation: tide log, the harbor, weather, the specific task of the morning. No meditation in the first paragraph. She is already doing something when we meet her.
- **Hannah's chapters** may open on sensation or domestic detail (the cold of the barn, the smell of silage, the sound of her father's German from the kitchen), then move inward. Adolescent interiority is permitted, but establish the physical world first.
- **Marcus's chapters** may open mid-observation or mid-thought, but the thought should be grounded in something specific: a class he is teaching, a student's face, the walk to school, something Henry said. Not in abstract rumination.

Do not open any chapter with weather description as scene-setting. Weather belongs inside a scene, noticed by a character who has a professional or practical reason to notice it.

## Chapter-ending conventions

This register leans heavily toward literary endings: **literary-fade**, **resolved-beat**, **turn**, and **coda**. Cliffhangers and mid-action cuts are rare and should be used deliberately, not as defaults.

For 30 chapters, a rough distribution:
- Literary-fade: ~10 chapters (especially Eira's)
- Resolved-beat: ~8 chapters
- Turn (reveal or pivot): ~5 chapters (sparingly; used when a POV's knowledge shifts)
- Coda: ~4 chapters (the brief aftermath-beat)
- Cliffhanger or mid-action: 2–3 chapters maximum (and these should feel earned, not genre-default)

Do not end consecutive chapters the same way. Check the craft log.

## POV strategy

Three co-leads with roughly equal weight (~10 chapters each). The rotation is **asymmetric** — do not mechanically alternate. Follow the story's logic: if Eira's thread has momentum, two consecutive Eira chapters is correct. If Marcus needs a long development, give it to him.

The **three leads never appear in the same scene simultaneously**. They cross in pairs (Eira and Marcus may speak; Marcus and Hannah have the teacher-student channel; Eira and Albrecht have the milk-delivery contact) but never as a trio.

Occasional **fourth-POV chapters** (Henry Crow, Lonzo Reed, or Karl Reinmar) are permitted but should be exceptional — use them when a piece of the breakwater mystery or a piece of the thematic weight is only visible from outside the main three. These chapters should be noticeably shorter than the main-POV chapters. Do not use them to resolve plot questions that the main three cannot see — use them to reframe a question the main three are already carrying.

## Dialogue density

Dialogue carries social texture and subtext, not exposition. A chapter's dialogue load should feel natural to the setting: the harbormaster's office has different rhythms than the school or the Crow kitchen. Hannah's chapters may have less dialogue (more interior), Eira's more (she transacts with people), Marcus's is mid-range.

Rules:
- No character explains what they mean for the reader's benefit.
- No character repeats information the POV character already knows.
- Tags: "said" and "asked" are correct. Avoid "countered," "admitted," "ventured," and all other gloss-tags.
- Do not follow a line of dialogue with a sentence explaining what the speaker meant by it (dialogue gloss failure mode).

**German in Hannah's chapters**: when Albrecht speaks to Hannah in German, or when a German phrase surfaces in Hannah's interior, render it in German without translation. The meaning should be inferable from context. Do not supply the English in brackets or in a following clause.

**Marcus's English**: formally correct, one register above the conversation he is in. He does not use contractions freely; he chooses his words deliberately. This should feel natural by the middle of his first chapter, not like a speech impediment.

## Comic timing and tonal balance

This is not a comic register. The tonal signature is gravity: the weight of loss, of partial knowledge, of lives proceeding under constraint. There is warmth (especially in the Crow household scenes) and there is dry observation (especially in Eira's narration of the town's behavior toward her), but these are within a serious frame. Do not deflect serious scenes with humor. Do not deflect humor with sentimentality.

The closest thing to comic timing in this novel is **Eira's dry observational mode** — her narration of what the town thinks about her, what the Coast Guard lieutenant does not ask, what the ledger records and what it does not. This is wry, not comic. It is the humor of competence in an incompetent situation.

## The breakwater mystery: structural, not genre

The body on the breakwater is a structural spine — it is what the three characters separately carry, what orients each arc, what the reader uses to track how the three threads relate. It is **not a mystery novel**. The drafter must not let it generate genre-mechanical scenes: no interrogation sequences, no code-breaking, no chapter that reads as investigation. 

What is correct:
- A character notices something that recontextualizes what we already know
- A character is forced to act (or not act) on their piece of knowledge
- Two characters' knowledge proximity is almost visible to us but not to them

What is wrong:
- A character actively investigates (goes to the Coast Guard, asks around town)
- The mystery is "solved" mid-novel
- Any chapter whose function is primarily exposition of the mystery

## Anti-defaults

Because this is the pipeline's native register, the usual anti-drift warnings don't apply. The specific drift risks for this book are:

1. **Voice homogenization**: Eira, Hannah, and Marcus all running in the same prose register — spare literary — without the specific differentiation the brief demands. Check: does Eira's chapter have the short declarative rhythm? Does Marcus have the subordinate clause pattern? Does Hannah have German vocabulary and internal interruption?

2. **The mystery becoming a plot**: Any scene that functions as "investigation" rather than "character in their world encountering their piece of what happened" is drift. The body is a load the characters carry; it does not drive their actions.

3. **The war becoming foreground**: Radio news, casualty telegrams, D-Day — these should arrive as weather, not as event. A sentence, not a scene. The characters' responses to them are interior (usually) or brief external (Eira, who notes things in ledgers).

4. **Period texture as set decoration**: Ration books and V-Mail should not appear as atmospheric props. They should appear because a character needs them, waits for them, is angered or relieved by them. If a period detail has no function in the POV character's immediate life, cut it.

5. **The body becoming a symbol**: The unknown man on the breakwater is a dead person. He is not a symbol of the war, or of displacement, or of anything else. The themes arise from the characters' lives — not from the body as symbol. Let him be a dead man.

# Plotter guidance — Coldwater Reach

## POV count and rotation

Three primary POV characters: Eira Bowman, Hannah Pfeiffer, Marcus Klein. Each carries approximately 10 chapters. The rotation is **asymmetric** — it follows narrative necessity, not a mechanical cycle. When one thread has momentum, two or three consecutive chapters in that POV is correct. When a thread needs space to develop before the next confrontation with its stakes, that POV may go quiet for several chapters.

Rules:
- Do not mechanically alternate (Eira, Hannah, Marcus, Eira, Hannah, Marcus).
- Do not allow any primary POV to go more than 4–5 consecutive chapters without an appearance.
- The opening chapter should be Eira's — she holds the inciting object (she was at the dock the night before the body came in).
- The closing chapter should also be Eira's, or a chapter that ends in her register.

**Fourth-POV chapters** (Henry Crow, Lonzo Reed, or Karl Reinmar) may be used 2–3 times across the manuscript. They should be shorter than main POV chapters (~1,500–2,000 words vs. ~2,500–3,000 for primary POVs). Assign them where:
- The reader needs information or a vantage point that the main three genuinely cannot provide
- A thematic echo needs to land from outside the main three's perspective

Suggested fourth-POV placements:
- One Lonzo Reed chapter, perhaps mid-novel, showing what the farm looks like from the outside of Hannah's interiority
- One Henry Crow chapter, late in the novel, showing what Marcus's displacement looks like to the man who has housed him
- Karl Reinmar if the structure calls for it, but use sparingly — his interiority is culturally remote and should not be over-explained

## Chapter-shape preferences

Standard shape for this novel: a chapter follows one POV character through a unit of time (typically a day or a portion of a day) in which something shifts — an external event, a new piece of knowledge, a decision made or not made, a relationship that changes by one degree. The shift does not need to be dramatic. Accumulation is the structural method.

**Single-scene chapters** (one continuous scene) are appropriate for high-pressure moments: Eira finding the body, a confrontation between Hannah and her father, a scene between Marcus and the school board. Use them for the chapters where compression and intensity are needed.

**Multi-beat chapters** (two or three short scenes in the same POV, same day or across a short span) are the novel's workhorse. They allow the POV character's day to cover more ground and let the mystery-pieces assemble gradually.

**Interiority-heavy chapters** are correct for this register and should appear regularly — especially in Marcus's and Hannah's chapters. These are not slow; they are the novel's mode of action. A chapter in which Marcus works through a piece of knowledge across a long walk home is not an "interior chapter" as a failure mode; it is a chapter.

**Short interstitial chapters** (fourth-POV) function as reframing devices. They should not advance plot mechanically but should shift how the reader understands what has already happened or what is about to happen.

## Episode-vs-arc structure

This is an **arc structure**, not episodic. Chapters do not resolve into self-contained units. The accumulation of what each character knows and carries is the structure — each chapter adds a weight, adjusts a relationship, or shifts the angle of a question. The three arcs are:

- **Eira**: authority and its costs → what obligation her knowledge of that night creates → a resolution that is hers alone, not the war's
- **Hannah**: accumulation of small choices → the choice about Karl Reinmar and what it means → what she is becoming on the other side of it
- **Marcus**: whether displacement ends → what the displaced person becomes when the ground stops moving → the Crow household as its own answer

The mystery of the body threads through all three arcs without resolving them. None of the three arcs concludes **because** the mystery is solved. They conclude because the characters have changed.

## Ending-mode distribution

For 30 chapters, target this approximate distribution:

- **Literary-fade** (quiet sensory or atmospheric close, no action resolution): 10 chapters
- **Resolved-beat** (the chapter's central question or pressure resolves): 7 chapters
- **Turn** (reveal or pivot that recontextualizes): 5 chapters (used at genuine inflection points — not as default tension)
- **Coda** (brief aftermath or reflective beat after main close): 4 chapters
- **Cliffhanger or mid-action**: 2–3 chapters (maximum; used with intention)
- **Elliptical** (deliberate ambiguity, open question): 1–2 chapters (especially useful at the end)

**Distribution rules**:
- No more than 2 consecutive chapters with the same ending mode
- Cliffhangers are not the default for mid-novel momentum; literary-fade or turn are
- The final chapter should end elliptically or with coda — the story ends before VE Day, in the register of lives that have shifted but not concluded

## Chapter target words

Primary POV chapters: **~2,500–3,200 words** (approximately 8–10 pages). The variance is intentional — high-pressure chapters may compress to 2,000; set-piece chapters may run to 3,500.

Fourth-POV chapters: **~1,500–2,000 words**. Shorter by design — these are lenses, not arcs.

Total target: ~80,000 words across 30 chapters. With ~27 primary-POV chapters averaging ~2,700 words plus ~3 fourth-POV chapters averaging ~1,700 words: ~77,900 words. The math works with normal variance.

## Genre-specific structural conventions

This is not a genre mystery, but the mystery of the body provides structural spine. These structural requirements follow from the brief:

1. **The body arrives in Chapter 1 or 2** — Eira finds it (or hears about it; she saw the dock the night before). This is the inciting object. Delay weakens the structure.

2. **Each POV character's relationship to the body must be established in their first chapter** — not through their explicit awareness of the mystery, but through the fact that they hold a piece of it, even if they don't know it yet.

3. **The reader's knowledge of the full picture should assemble across the middle third** of the novel — chapters 10–20 — through juxtaposition of the three POVs, not through any single character's investigation.

4. **The body is not resolved with a clean answer**. By the novel's end, the reader should have a probable picture of who the man was and what happened, assembled from the three partial views. But this is implied, not announced. The final chapter does not explain.

5. **D-Day (chapter ~20, roughly)** should arrive as a chapter-beat — the kitchen radio, the school, the harbor — and mark the turn toward the novel's final third without redirecting any of the three arcs toward war-drama.

6. **The three characters must never be in a scene together**. Plot crossings are pairwise only. If the outline ever places all three in one location at one time, that is a structural error.

7. **At least one thread should be deliberately unresolved at novel's close**. The breakwater question itself is the primary candidate. The characters' relationships to it should resolve; the underlying fact may stay in shadow.

8. **No chapter should function as spy-thriller mechanics**: no coded messages, no submarine landings, no chapter driven by the question "who is the enemy." The war is background. The body is a human mystery, not a national-security mystery.

# Reader guidance — Coldwater Reach

## Intended audience

Adult readers of literary fiction with patience for accumulation and restraint. The shelf comps are Strout (*Olive Kitteridge*, *Olive, Again*), Richard Russo (*Empire Falls*), and Ron Hansen — multi-character American novels set in specific communities where the weight of a place and a period is the subject as much as any individual arc. Readers who expect plot-driven mysteries should be warned early; this is not that book. Readers who trust restrained, precise prose to carry emotional weight without declaration will be rewarded.

Secondary audience: readers of WWII home-front fiction (Susan Choi's *American Woman*, Jesmyn Ward's *Sing, Unburied, Sing* in its temporal weight, Ian MacEwan's *Atonement* in its partial-information structure) — readers who want the war as texture and pressure, not as event.

---

## Brief-adherence checks to perform

These are the yes/no questions the Reader must answer for this manuscript, beyond general craft review:

1. **Are all three POV voices distinct at the sentence level?** Eira's chapters should have short declaratives and professional vocabulary. Hannah's should have interior permission and German threading. Marcus's should have formal precision and subordinate qualification. If all three sound like the same narrator, this is a critical failure.

2. **Does any chapter behave like a genre mystery?** (Investigation scenes, code-breaking, the protagonist "digging into" the body's identity as if running a plot.) If yes, flag it — this is structural drift from the brief's explicit constraint.

3. **Does the war appear as foreground in any chapter?** (A chapter whose dramatic center is a war event rather than a character's life.) D-Day and the Bulge may appear as chapter-beats; they must not be chapter-centers.

4. **Does the body on the breakwater resolve too cleanly?** The brief requires the breakwater question to stay at least partially in shadow. A chapter or ending that provides a clear, explained answer is a breach of the brief's explicit instruction.

5. **Do the three POV characters ever appear in the same scene together?** This is a hard structural rule. If it happens, it must be flagged as a critical error.

6. **Is the historical texture embedded or decorative?** Period-accurate terms (V-Mail, ration books, BC-1206) should appear because characters need them, not as atmospheric props. If a chapter reads like a period-detail insertion pass, flag it.

7. **Is race a fact of life, rendered specifically, not lectured?** Henry and Lillian Crow should be specific people whose specific lives in 1943 coastal Maine are rendered through behavior and silence. Any passage that reads as the author explaining race relations to the reader is a breach of the brief.

8. **Do the three individual arcs (Eira/authority, Hannah/becoming, Marcus/displacement) each reach their own resolution** that is independent of whether the mystery resolves? The brief requires these to be character resolutions, not mystery-plot resolutions.

9. **Does the ending arrive before VE Day?** The story closes in spring 1945, before May 8. Any chapter that describes VE Day itself has overrun the ending.

10. **Is the dialect handling restrained?** Albrecht's English should not be phonetically rendered as stage-German. Marcus's English should feel formally overcorrect without being burlesqued. German phrases in Hannah's chapters should be untranslated. If any of this has become caricature, flag it.

---

## What "good" looks like for this book

A good chapter in this manuscript:
- Establishes its POV within the first sentence through vocabulary and perceptual mode (Eira notices the tide; Hannah notices the cold in her father's voice; Marcus notices the grammar of a student's mistake)
- Advances its character's internal arc by one small increment without announcing the advancement
- Contains at least one moment where the reader understands more than the POV character — because of the juxtaposition with another chapter, or because the POV character's language reveals what they are not letting themselves think
- Ends in a way that does not require the next chapter to recap it

A good Eira chapter has the compression and procedural calm of a harbormaster's log that turns out to be a grief document.

A good Hannah chapter has the quality of a seventeen-year-old's awareness — acutely observant, slightly more honest than an adult would allow, and willing to follow a thought further than it's comfortable to follow.

A good Marcus chapter has the quality of a letter in a second language by someone who is very good at it — but the reader can see, under the precision, what the writer is working not to say.

---

## What to flag explicitly if the manuscript drifts

**Voice homogenization**: If Eira, Hannah, and Marcus sound like the same careful literary narrator, name it explicitly and cite examples from each POV. This is the primary drift risk for this register. The brief specifies three different prose registers; if they have converged, the drafter has defaulted to a single literary voice.

**Mystery-genre drift**: If any chapter reads like an investigation, a thriller scene, or a plot-driven mystery (protagonist searches for information, information reveals a key clue, momentum is driven by "what happened"), name it explicitly. The brief prohibits spy-thriller mechanics. A chapter that functions as investigation has misread the brief, even if the prose is excellent.

**The body as symbol**: If any chapter or passage treats the unknown man as a symbol of the war, of displacement, or of any theme (rather than as a dead human being), flag it. The brief is explicit that the body is not symbolic machinery.

**Period-lecture**: If a character explains what ration books are, or the novel pauses to describe the V-Mail system as if the reader needs orientation, flag it as register failure. The period texture should be invisible infrastructure, not taught content.

**Over-articulated emotion**: If a passage explicitly names the architecture of a character's feeling ("Her grief had the quality of..."; "What he felt was not quite fear but..."), flag it. The brief's register carries feeling through what characters notice and do, not through taxonomy of states.

**The war as drama**: If D-Day or the Bulge are staged as dramatic scenes (the town gathers, characters emote, the chapter turns on the event), flag it. These should arrive as weather — a sentence, a paragraph at most, then the character's ordinary life continues under new pressure.

---

## What to applaud

**When the three POV voices are genuinely distinct**: Eira's short declaratives, Hannah's German threading and interior recursion, Marcus's formal precision — if these are working at the sentence level throughout, this is the book's central craft achievement and should be named and celebrated. Do not flatten it in editorial notes.

**When the mystery assembles without announcing itself**: The best moments in this manuscript will be chapters where the reader's picture of what happened on the breakwater shifts without any character investigating anything — because a detail in Eira's professional log intersects with something Hannah noticed at the farm, or because Marcus's knowledge of a certain type of displacement gives a name to something Eira won't let herself name. When this works, defend it. Do not suggest the author "clarify" connections the reader should assemble themselves.

**When Henry and Lillian Crow are fully present without the prose explaining them**: When the Crow household scenes carry their full social weight through dialogue, domestic detail, and the texture of a warm kitchen in a cold-to-them town — without the narrator stepping in to contextualize — that is the brief being honored. Defend those scenes.

**When a chapter earns its emotion through specificity**: A chapter that makes the reader feel something through a specific tool (the harbormaster's log entry, the German word that surfaces in Hannah's interior, the sentence Marcus almost-writes and doesn't) should be identified and defended, not subjected to "more emotion" suggestions.

facts: Eira Bowman, 52 in October 1943, is harbormaster of Coldwater Reach — the only woman holding a harbormaster post on the Maine coast. She was widowed when her husband Owen drowned in November 1935 and has held the post for eight years.

An unidentified man's body (no papers, not from Coldwater) washes up on the Coldwater breakwater in October 1943 after a three-day blow. Eira saw something on the dock the night before the body came in. The Coast Guard takes the body and the official silence.

Hannah Pfeiffer is 17 in October 1943 (turns 18 in March 1944). Her family's dairy farm three miles inland on Route 9 houses four German POWs in the renovated icehouse under the Emergency Farm Labor program. Karl Reinmar, 19, is the youngest; he is from Franconia, approximately fifty km from where Hannah's father Albrecht was born.

Marcus Klein, 47, is a Viennese Jewish displaced scholar who arrived in Coldwater Reach in March 1942 to teach German and Latin. His path: Vienna → Paris → London → Sherbrooke internment camp (Quebec) → Cambridge → Coldwater. He does not discuss Sherbrooke. He boards with Black custodian Henry Crow (51) and his wife Lillian (48) at Elm Street.

The three POV characters (Eira, Hannah, Marcus) never appear in a scene together as a group of three. The narrative rotates asymmetrically across approximately 10 chapters each, for 30 total chapters, targeting ~80,000 words.

The story runs October 1943 to spring 1945, ending before VE Day (May 8, 1945). D-Day (June 6, 1944) and the Battle of the Bulge (December 1944) fall within the narrative period and arrive as background weather, not as chapter-center events.

The mystery of the body on the breakwater is not fully resolved before the novel ends. None of the three POV characters ever possesses the complete picture. The three characters' relationships to the mystery resolve; the underlying facts may remain in shadow.

There are no spy-thriller mechanics in this novel: no coded messages, no submarine landings, no Nazi agents in Maine. The war is present through loss (casualty telegrams), constraint (rationing), and displacement (Marcus, the prisoners) — not through plot machinery.

The Pfeiffer family (Albrecht and Magda) are naturalized U.S. citizens who came from Bavaria in 1922. Albrecht has stopped speaking English at home; Magda has effectively stopped speaking. German-born noncitizens were classified as enemy aliens; the Pfeiffers' citizenship protects them legally but not socially.

Race is rendered as specific fact through behavior and silence — not through authorial lecture. Henry and Lillian Crow are specific people living a specific life in 1943 coastal Maine. The prose does not explain their situation to the reader; it shows it.
