input.content:
# The Gift

The cold in her room was the March kind — not the dead weight of winter that had been sitting in the walls since December, but something different now, thinner at the edges, the light coming in gray at the window with a quality it hadn't had last week. She lay still for a moment. Eighteen. The word arrived, turned itself over once, and went quiet. The barn would want the same morning she had given it every morning.

She dressed and went downstairs.

She had milked before full light, as she had most mornings since she turned fourteen and her father's back started. The Holsteins in the dark, their breathing, the pail going full in the silence, the cold that was barn-cold now rather than outside-cold. By the time she came back inside and washed, the kitchen windows were beginning to show the gray-white of early morning. She went upstairs to change out of the barn clothes. There was no school until nine.

The smell reached her from the stairwell.

Butter, going warm in a pan. And underneath it — flour, eggs, the particular rich complexity that was not bread and not anything else, that she had not smelled on an ordinary morning since November, since the last time she had asked directly and her mother had made them and not looked up from the bowl the whole time.

This time she had not asked.

She stopped at the bottom of the stairs.

Her mother was at the stove. Not at the table with her coffee, not standing at the window the way she had been standing most mornings for four months, but at the stove with the mixing bowl on the counter and the iron pan already going and her back to the room in the angle that meant she was paying attention to something in front of her. She had braided her hair. Hannah had not noticed this until now — the dark braid with its gray at the temples, pinned at the neck, the straight line of her mother's shoulders, occupied.

The coffeepot was on the back element. The stove was hot.

Hannah came in and sat down at the table.

Her father came in from the barn five minutes later, the cold still on his coat. He looked at the stove, then at Hannah. *Herzlichen Glückwunsch*, he said — she would hear it all day at school from Ruth and the others, in English, but here it was in German, the way her father said anything that mattered — and he set one hand briefly on her shoulder, then was pulling out his chair and reaching for the coffee.

Magda brought the pancakes to the table in two batches. On Hannah's plate she put two extra without speaking and went back to the stove for the coffeepot. She did not look at Hannah when she set the plate down. She was already turning.

They ate. Her father ate with the focused quiet he brought to early mornings — contained, his attention on the food and the sounds of the farm coming through the window: one of the Holsteins shifting in the far stall, the drip from the barn roof where the frost was already lifting. Hannah ate her pancakes and the two extra ones and drank her coffee. The plates were the German ones with the blue border that her mother had wrapped in her good dresses to cross the Atlantic and that had not, in twenty-one years on this table, developed a single crack.

She was aware of her mother at the stove, moving between the pan and the counter, then standing still. The way she was aware of the drip from the barn roof — something present, something that had not been there before, or had been but differently.

After breakfast she washed the dishes. Pan, mixing bowl, the plates, her father's cup, her own. Water from the pot she had put on before they ate. She set the dishes in the rack and dried her hands on the towel beside the sink.

She did not say anything about the pancakes.

---

The south fence post had been heaving since February — the frost and thaw cycling it out of true until there was daylight between the post and the stone wall on the east side, the wire gone slack on three runs. She took the bar and the wire gauge and went out in the late morning, after the frost had lifted enough to work with.

The south field still had some gray in it at the far end, but the stone walls were clear at the tops now, the snow gone in the last week, the first bare stone of the year coming back. The mud smell was in everything: the field, the yard, the air itself, the particular March smell that was cold and damp and carried something green underneath it that wasn't visible yet but was there.

The prisoners were at the north fence line. She could see them from across the farm — four figures at the far end, two with the manure spreader and two working the stone. Lonzo was at the gate with the Springfield and the Bangor Daily News across his knee.

She worked the corner post back into true. The ground took the bar at the surface and resisted six inches down — the March ground, the winter still in it underneath. She leaned into the reset and felt the post come level, drove the brace pin, tested it with her hand. Then she went along the fence checking the wire, running the gauge along each strand: first run, second run, third. The work was clean — her hands, the bar, the gauge, the wire. The Holsteins were out in the south field behind her now, moving in the slow good-tempered way they had when there was some warmth in the air.

The east face of the corner wall had heaved at the top, the frost lifting the stones until a narrow shelf opened in the shadow between the wall and the fence post. She was running the gauge along the base when she saw it.

It was back in the shadow where the heaved stone made the shelf. Not visible from the house. Not visible from the gate where Lonzo sat. You would not find it unless you were working this exact section, on this side of the fence, at this height.

She reached in and took it out.

Birch — pale, the bark stripped, the surface worked smooth with a small blade. About the length of her longest finger. A bird, clearly: the head angled slightly down, the wings folded close to the sides, the tail cut to a clean notch. Not fine work — the grain of the wood showed through, and there was a place on the breast where the blade had gone slightly wrong and been corrected rather than hidden, a faint ridge you could feel with your thumb. But the shape was right. The angle of the head was right. Someone had taken time with it, had come back to it more than once; you could tell where the work had continued past what the shape strictly required.

She knew whose hands had made it before she had finished the thought.

She looked up. Lonzo was at the gate with his back to her, the newspaper across his knee. The figures at the far end of the farm were the figures at the far end of the farm.

She put the bird in her coat pocket.

It fit against her palm when she closed her hand — the notched tail at the base of her thumb, the smooth birch against her fingers, the small weight of it. She stood with her hand in her pocket. The mud smell was in the air. The Holsteins moved behind her.

Then she went back to checking the wire.

---

Ruth met her at the corner of Bridge Street with things to say about Mabel Pearce's birthday last Saturday and the ration allocation at Beal's and a question about the Latin for Tuesday's quiz. Hannah answered the question about the Latin. The bird was in her coat pocket and she was aware of it against her palm the whole walk over — the notched tail, the corrected place on the breast.

She had not told Ruth.

In Latin, Marcus was explaining the ablative absolute for the third day running. He had written it on the board in his precise handwriting — letters close together, almost no slant — and was going through the same example sentence: *the city having been taken, the soldiers returned*. Hannah had understood the ablative absolute since October; he had explained it well the first time and she had carried it away whole. She watched him work through the parsing now. Half the class was still doing it the long way, treating every absolute construction as a subordinate clause, arriving at the same place by a harder route. She understood why he kept returning. He was patient in a way that was not exactly kind — more like precision, the kind that does not give up on a problem until it is fully solved.

The bird was in her coat on the hook in the hallway.

Karl's hands had made this. The thought was already there when she looked for it, the way the pancakes had been already on the plate that morning. It sat in her coat pocket and did not ask what she meant to do with it. She was eighteen today; this was the fact of the morning, and the pancakes, and this, and none of them was the same fact but they were all here in the same day.

She thought: it is not wrong to keep something that was left for you.

She held this for the rest of Latin and into the German period, where Marcus had them reading a passage from a short novel about a family in Swabia. She read her passage aloud when called on and Marcus nodded. The German was easy — easier than the Latin, always, though she would not have said so in this room.

During study hall she went out to the hallway for her Latin notes and found the bird instead. She stood in the empty hall and held it a moment in her closed hand: the notched tail, the corrected breast, the small smooth weight of it. Then she found her Latin notes and went back to her desk and put her hand flat on the desk.

She did not take the bird out again. She did not show it to Ruth. She did not mention it to Marcus after class, when Ruth stayed behind to ask about the quiz. She walked home alone — her right hand in her coat pocket, the bird against her palm — and she did not take it out on the walk either.

It was hers. She had not decided this; she had arrived at it, the way you arrived at things you had already decided without knowing you had.

---

The evening milking ran late — the cows had been outside all afternoon and were slow to come in, and she worked down the line in the good kerosene light. The barn smelled of warm animal and mud tracked in from the field and the milk going into the pails. The Holsteins were settled now, the quiet they had after a day with some warmth in it, their bodies turned into the stalls, the near ones watching her move past with the mild attention of animals who knew the order of things and found it sufficient.

From the barn door she could see the light in the icehouse window. A yellow rectangle in the dark fifty yards off, the curtain drawn, the light behind it steady. The prisoners would have been in since five, when Lonzo brought them in and locked the door and filled out his report and drove off down Route 9.

She stood in the doorway with her hands on the frame. The mud smell was in the air, sharp and cold both, the March smell at dusk. The early dark had come on, the sky to the west still holding a gray-blue line above the treeline, everything else already black. Karl was in there, in the icehouse, which was fifty yards off and was where he would be until morning.

She went back in and finished the milking. Twenty-two cows, number fifteen slow as always. Hannah sat with her and was patient. She brought the milk cans to the cooling room and covered them and washed the equipment and came back through the barn to check the doors.

She came into the house and hung her coat on the hook by the door. Her mother was at the stove; her father was at the table with the farm account book, making his entries. Hannah took off her boots and washed her hands at the sink.

The kitchen was warm. Outside, the dark had come on fully now, the frost already returning to the ground, the mud smell going quiet under it. The thaw smell would be there again tomorrow, and the frost again tomorrow night, back and forth until the weather finally settled on one or the other — a few more weeks of this.

The coat was on the hook.

The bird was in the pocket.

She set the table for supper.

She did not tell anyone — not Ruth, not Marcus. This is her first deliberate secret about Karl Reinmar, actively chosen rather than accidental.

# The Unregistered Boat

The spring mooring assignments ran fourteen pages in the ledger that year — more changes than any season since she had taken the post. She worked them in order, north dock first, going south. The order was Owen's. He had invented it in his first year and she had inherited it with the ledger, and she saw no reason to alter a system that worked.

April fourteenth. Cold still, but a different cold — the active kind, the kind that came with the smell of the water back in it. The harbor had been open since mid-March, the inner-cove ice gone in the second week, and the fleet was returning from the winter moorings and the drydock yards and in some cases from the decisions made over the winter about whether to return at all.

This season she had two deletions.

Robert Cates, berth fourteen. His boat the *Idabelle* had been registered at fourteen since the summer of 1938. He had shipped as mate on a merchant vessel the previous September — she had the letter from the company, which was the way it was done, the company notifying the harbor office as a matter of form. His wife had written separately in February to say the berth could go. Eira had kept it open through the winter. She did that when a man left: hold through the season, then decide. Now it was April and she reassigned berth fourteen to Archie Lunt of Tenants Harbor, one of two men who had come down from Tenants Harbor when the Price fish house folded in February.

Harold Vose, berth nine. She had processed his papers in December and mailed the original registration certificate back to his mother in Searsport, because his mother was the named next of kin and there was no wife and no partner and no one else on the form. She had held berth nine empty through the winter. She marked it available and did not reassign it yet. She would hold it through the spring in case a buyer materialized.

The three additions: Archie Lunt, Eddie Lunt his brother — no relation to the Lunts from Port Clyde — and Roy Tremblay from Spruce Head, vouched for by Elias Hollis, whose judgment she trusted for this purpose. Tremblay would have berth nine provisionally; she would do the hull inspection on the fifteenth.

She finished the mooring assignments by half past eight.

Then the depth soundings. The District office had sent the winter survey in February, three corrections noted. A shoal building at the south entrance, up two feet since the 1942 survey. A reduction in clearance off the breakwater where silt deposit had settled. An improvement in the north channel where the winter storms had scoured the bottom. She went through each correction against her working chart, marked them in pencil, entered them in the tide log with the survey date and District reference number. The shoal at the south entrance would affect approach draft on anything over eight feet — she noted it in the mooring assignment column for the south entrance berths and put a penciled flag on the chart.

She worked until ten, then took her coat and walked the dock.

She did this most mornings — the north berths and then south along the commercial wharf, the whole fleet in order. The harbor in April had a specific quality she had been noticing for eight years: the cold and the activity at once, the season not yet settled, the fleet reassembling itself after the long quiet. Today there was a supply tender at the outer dock and the Lunt boats rigging at the far berths and someone on the commercial wharf with a hand truck. She walked through it without hurrying.

She knew every registered boat in the harbor by sight. She could name each one going along the dock — by hull shape, by waterline, by the way it sat when loaded or empty, by the specific shade of the topsides after years of paint and weather. She had learned this from Owen and she had learned it again through her own watching. It was not a remarkable skill. It was what you knew when you had been looking at the same fleet long enough.

---

At dock post seven, which she had left open pending reassignment, there was a lobster boat she did not know.

She stopped and looked at it. Small — twenty-six feet, perhaps twenty-seven. An older hull, the topsides faded from something that had been red, a standard work design, the lines of nothing particular. The kind of hull you saw from one end of the coast to the other without being able to place the builder. It sat at the post with its lines double-tied, which meant someone had secured it properly and not simply run a line through and walked away.

She went to the stern and read the registration number.

She went back to the office and looked it up. The Maine registry — main volume, then the 1944 supplement. Not there.

She went back to the dock.

Hector Brann was at berth twelve, coiling line. He had been the one to find the body on the breakwater in October — she had thought about that the first time she'd renewed his berth since, and not since. He was a steady tenant and he didn't ask questions about what wasn't his business.

She asked him whose boat was at seven.

He straightened and looked down the dock. "Think it's someone from Owls Head," he said. "Been there a few days."

She thanked him.

Back in the office she opened the second drawer and found the Owls Head harbor contact list. She kept lists from four coastal offices — Knox County, the Owls Head harbor, Rockland, Vinalhaven — a practice Owen had started and she had maintained, updating when the offices changed personnel or the phone numbers changed. The Owls Head list ran three typewritten pages, alphabetical by registration number. She went through it twice.

Not there.

She took out the tide log.

*Unregistered vessel, dock 7. First observed morning of 14 April 1944. Registration number not in Maine registry (main volume or 1944 supplement) or Owls Head harbor contact list. Inquiry to be sent to District office, Portland. —E.B.*

She put the tide log back on the desk and drafted the inquiry: two paragraphs, the registration number, the date of first observation, the dock location, a request for identification or nearest-office follow-up. She sealed it in an official envelope and put it in the mail pouch for the three-o'clock run to the Birch Street post office.

In the afternoon she did the hull inspection on Tremblay's boat. Registration in order, hull sound, some cosmetic work needed on the topsides but nothing structural. She countersigned his certificate and filed the copy.

On the morning of April sixteenth she walked the fleet.

Dock post seven was empty.

The double-tied lines were gone with the boat. She stood at the post for a moment. The water under it was the same harbor water it had been yesterday and the day before. No mark on the post that would last beyond the week.

She went back to the office.

*Unregistered vessel, dock 7. Departed approximately April 15 or 16, unseen. Inquiry to District office posted April 14. No response received.*

She did not expect a response before May. Possibly June. An unregistered lobster boat at a Maine dock for two days was not, in April of 1944, the most urgent item in anyone's mail.

She noted it and turned to the day's other work.

---

The official mail came on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, dropped by the post office boy who had been doing the harbor rounds since before the war. It came on April sixteenth while the tide log was still open on her desk.

Four items: the weekly District bulletin, a supply order confirmation, the spring fuel allocation form, and a letter from the Coast Guard regional office in Portland.

She set the bulletin and the form on the left side of the desk. She opened the supply confirmation and checked it against the pending order list. She opened the Portland letter last.

Two paragraphs on official stationery. Dated April 12. Addressed to the Harbormaster's Office, Coldwater Reach, Maine, attention Harbormaster.

*In re: October 1943 recovered remains — Coldwater Reach harbor, follow-up communication.*

She read it through.

*Through liaison with Allied civilian records, this office has received identification of the remains recovered October 28, 1943. The individual has been identified as Jan Václav Horak, Czechoslovak national, status: displaced person. Last known location: Halifax, Nova Scotia, October 1942. No next of kin information is available through current records. The official record is herewith amended to reflect this identification. The classification of cause of death is unchanged: accidental drowning consistent with storm exposure. No further investigation is anticipated at this time. This communication is for your records.*

She read it again.

Jan Václav Horak.

She folded the letter and set it on the chart table and sat down.

Czech. In Halifax in October of 1942. On the Coldwater breakwater in October of 1943. Between those two facts there was a year of movement that the letter did not account for and that she had no account of from any other source. Halifax to the coast of Maine was not a straight line. It was a year of intermediate stops that the two paragraphs on official stationery had left blank.

The office was quiet. The stove had burned down while she was at the desk — she could hear that it had gone quiet, the iron no longer ticking — but she did not get up. Outside, the harbor was going about its midmorning work. Someone at the outer dock. The Lunt boats coming in early from the south. The tide log open to April 16 on the desk.

She knew his hands. She had been at the dock that morning in October when the Coast Guard lieutenant had done the inventory — everything that was on the body and everything that wasn't — and she had looked at the hands because that was one of the things you looked at, if you were trying to understand what kind of man you were dealing with. The calluses were in the centers of the palms, not at the base of the fingers. Not a fisherman's hands. Not a farmer's or a cannery man's. She had noted the coat he wore, the European cut of it, the quality of the wool, the way it was not built for this water or this cold. She had noted the several days' growth of beard.

She had known he was not from anywhere near Coldwater Reach.

She had his name now.

Jan Václav Horak. Czechoslovak national. Halifax in October 1942.

Halifax was a port. You could come into Halifax by certain routes — without the right papers, or with papers that weren't quite right, or with the kind of contacts that didn't appear in any official record — and from Halifax you could move south along the coast by routes that had no file in any District office. She knew this from Varnum. Last December, at the quarterly meeting in Portland, after the fuel allocation was settled and the room had relaxed: Varnum had used the phrase *refugee crossings*. Not a common category on this coast, he had said. Known, though. A kind of thing that happened.

She had driven back to Coldwater on Route 1 in the dark with that phrase and the approved fuel figures and two cups of coffee. She had held the phrase beside what she had seen on the dock on the night of October twenty-sixth: the man at the far bollard, eleven in the evening, a second figure in the shadow between the fish house and the net shed. She had stood for a moment at the dock head and looked, and then she had gone back to the office and written in the log: *2300: mooring check completed, fleet secure.*

She had not entered the man. She had not entered the second figure. She had not entered what the two of them had appeared to be doing at the far bollard at that hour, or what the shape of it had looked like in the dark.

Jan Václav Horak. She had not known his name when she wrote that entry, and she had not gone back to annotate it, and now the Coast Guard regional office had sent her two paragraphs of official stationery and she had his name, and the log still read *fleet secure*.

She looked at the letter on the chart table.

No next of kin. She turned that over. His name had been in the records somewhere — in some Allied civilian file, in some registry of displaced persons that someone in some office had access to, because they had found it and sent her this letter in April of 1944, and the name was here now. But no next of kin. No one the Allied civilian records had associated with him. He had moved through the records without leaving a person who would be notified.

He had been a displaced person. That was the status the letter gave him. Displaced from where to what, it did not say.

She tried to trace the year between Halifax and this breakwater. The ports where you could stop, moving south. The Bay of Fundy, the Passamaquoddy coast, the islands — she knew them all as harbors, as navigational facts, as names on the chart she looked at every working day. She could see the route in theory. She could not see who would have been helping him along it, or whether anyone had been, or what it had cost him and whoever was in that shadow at the far bollard to move him to this dock and to what happened after.

She had seen enough, that October night, to have entered something. She had not entered it.

Owen had left a gap in 1934 and named it. He had written *not entered at time; entering here as complete account* and he had made the record complete. She had thought about that in January, standing at the chart table with his 1934 log and her 1943 log open side by side, his October pages and her October pages. She had thought about the distinction between a deferred entry and an absent one. She had closed the 1943 log and not returned to it.

Jan Václav Horak.

Czech. Halifax. Displaced. No next of kin. Dead on this breakwater at the end of October, in the water twelve to thirty-six hours before Hector Brann found him on the granite seam on the ocean side. That was what the Coast Guard had said: twelve to thirty-six hours in the water. She had done the arithmetic at the time, standing in the dock office with the lieutenant's report in front of her, and the window had put him in the water between midnight and two in the morning on October 27, 1943. The night after she had seen him at the dock.

She knew more now than she had known in October. In December. She knew his name and his country and the city where he had last been registered, a year before she had seen him at the far bollard with whatever papers he did not have on him when the Coast Guard lieutenant turned out his pockets.

She did not know what he had been moving toward. She did not know what he had been running from. She did not know whose hands had put him in the water or whether his had been the only ones.

She had a name.

The chart table under her hands was Owen's — the same one he had worked at, the surface worn at the corners where you rested your forearms when you leaned over the charts. Outside the window the harbor was going about the business of mid-April. The fleet resuming. The season coming back.

She looked at the letter.

Jan Václav Horak.

She was sitting at the chart table.

# Franconian

The building had been mostly empty for an hour. He could hear the custodian's cart somewhere down the east corridor — the particular sound of a bucket set down and not yet retrieved — and the last of the afternoon light came through the west windows at a low angle, illuminating the chalkboard's residue in a way that was not visible during lessons. The third declension. A tense paradigm. He had been trying to erase the board to something approaching clean when Hannah Pfeiffer knocked and came in.

She was carrying her Latin textbook and, under it, the German grammar she had been borrowing and returning in alternation since January, as if she were not quite ready to possess it and not quite ready to relinquish it. She set it on the nearest desk and did not sit.

"I heard something," she said. "One of the prisoners — Karl — he was talking to someone through the icehouse window. I was at the south fence, and I wasn't listening on purpose. I was there to reset a post."

He put the eraser down.

"A phrase," she said. "About the harvest. I'm going to try to say it right."

She gave it to him.

Her German was her father's German, fundamentally — the vowels slightly flattened in the Bavarian way, the consonants not quite Munich and not quite rural. For a girl who had spoken it since before she spoke English, she had the unselfconsciousness of a native and the slight displacement of someone who had learned it in translation, in a country where it was not the native tongue. She was trying to reproduce what she had heard, and what she had heard was not her father's dialect.

He received the phrase as two things simultaneously. As a linguistic object, first — the particular rounding of the *a*, the contraction that shifted stress from the first syllable to the second. As a problem, second. He had been aware of the problem for some months without committing to its full assembly; the phrase she had given him was the kind of precision that made assembly unavoidable.

"That is a harvest idiom," he said. "An Upper Franconian form. Not Bavarian. Not standard German." He came away from the board and sat at the teacher's desk. The chair was the school's regulation chair, wooden, the finish gone from the arms. He had been sitting in it for two years and had stopped noticing it. "The idiom comes from the communities along the Upper Main River. The country between Nuremberg and the Czech border."

Hannah was quiet. She had the quality — he had observed it across several months of watching her in Latin, and on the few occasions their other conversations had warranted this kind of attention — of hearing things completely before she responded. She did not interrupt. She waited until she had understood.

"He grew up hearing that dialect," Marcus said. "The phrase, at minimum, belongs to someone who learned it at home. It is not something you acquire as an adult."

"Where in Franconia?" she said.

"Where in Franconia is he from?"

"I think Ansbach. Someone said Ansbach."

Ansbach was Middle Franconia — the flat country west of Nuremberg, the agricultural plain, the market town that had been a regional center for several centuries without being particularly close to anything. The speech there was recognizably related to what she had given him. It was not identical. The stress pattern she had reproduced was not the Ansbach form.

"The phrase is from further east than Ansbach," he said. "Twenty, perhaps thirty kilometers east of there. The valley between Feuchtwangen and Dinkelsbühl, or the villages east of Dinkelsbühl toward the Bohemian hills."

She looked at him.

"That's where my father is from," she said.

"Yes," Marcus said.

There was a pause. Outside the window the afternoon went on being April — the specific quality of late light in a month where the cold was not yet gone but the angle of the sun had changed, so that the warmth and the cold arrived on different sides of the same air. He had found April in coastal Maine stranger than November. November he had understood immediately. April was something he was still learning.

"Thank you," Hannah said. She picked up her Latin textbook. The German grammar she left on the desk.

"The translation," she said from the doorway.

He had been waiting to see if she would ask. "The field takes what it is owed, and the man who worked it walks home lighter." He paused. "More or less. Some things do not translate exactly."

She nodded. He heard her footsteps recede down the corridor.

---

He sat for some time in the teacher's chair.

The precise measure of the phrase's origin — Feuchtwangen and eastward, toward the Czech border — was not information he had possessed before. He had possessed the general geography: Karl Reinmar was from Franconia, Hannah had established that much at the fence in October, and Albrecht Pfeiffer was from Feuchtwangen, which was in the same county. Fifty kilometers between them, approximately, which had been the phrase Hannah had brought to him in November with the word *Landsmann* — a word he had translated precisely, and had declined, at the time, to follow to its geographic conclusion.

Now the phrase she had given him placed Karl's origin not at the fifty-kilometer distance from Albrecht's birthplace but in the same specific valley, or very close to it. The Feuchtwangen-Dinkelsbühl corridor, the communities running east toward the Franconian Heights, toward the Bohemian Forest, toward the border that the maps had marked and the communities on either side had spent several centuries treating as somewhat negotiable.

The Czech border. He stood and went to the window.

He had heard the name Horak in late April — it had come into the school the way things came into the school from the official mail, which was to say through the post office and Beal's general store and by the end of the week through three different conversations he had not sought. Jan Václav Horak. Czech national. Displaced person. Halifax, 1942. He had heard it and had not needed to ask any follow-up questions, because he knew what the category meant.

He was perhaps the only person in Coldwater Reach who knew from the inside what the category meant. That was not a distinction he had sought. He had simply been, for a period of years, a person who moved through the administrative machinery of displacement — the waiting rooms, the transit papers, the offices that determined your right to remain in a given place — and the movement had given him a specific kind of knowledge. The kind that was not listed in a record but was present in the body, in the acquired habits of a person who had learned when to move quickly, when to move quietly, and how to read the room before committing to any action that might require the room's cooperation.

He knew what a displaced Czech national in Halifax in 1942 was. Not Jan Václav Horak specifically — he had not known the man — but the category of person. The category meant you were moving along routes that did not appear in any official file. It meant the people who moved you along those routes were people who had their own reasons for keeping their names out of the record. It meant your next station was reached through someone who knew someone who knew someone — a chain of connection that ran through origin, through language, through the specific geography of shared community.

Halifax was a port. From Halifax, moving south along the coast toward Maine, you would look for the contacts you could authenticate by origin. Not German-Americans generally. The German-American population along the Maine coast was not organized into a network of this kind, and a Czech displaced person would have no particular reason to seek it. What he would seek — what anyone in that position would seek, in Marcus's experience — was the specific German-Americans from the borderland communities, the families who had come from the country where the German and Czech populations had lived alongside each other for centuries, where the dialects carried inflections from both sides, where the family names crossed the border in both directions without particular comment, where you could authenticate a contact not by documentation but by the sounds of the dialect they had grown up in.

He was constructing this. He was aware that he was constructing it. The distinction between recognizing a shape and inventing one was not always as clear as he would have preferred — he had learned this too, in the waiting rooms and the transit offices, where constructed pictures sometimes replaced available facts because the available facts were insufficient and the constructed picture was more tolerable. He had seen what happened to people who committed to a constructed picture before the evidence warranted it. On several occasions he had been the subject of such a commitment.

He would not do that here.

And yet the shape was there regardless. A Czech displaced person, moving south from Halifax along the coastal routes. Reaching, at some point in the year between October 1942 and October 1943, the coast of Maine. Seeking a contact he had been given — a farm name, a family name, an address on a route that ran through the Franconian-Czech émigré network and terminated, if the network ran as such networks ran, at the one farm in the area whose owners came from exactly that borderland country.

The Pfeiffer farm. Three miles inland on Route 9. Albrecht Pfeiffer, from Feuchtwangen, who had paused for two seconds in October when a prisoner in his field used the vowels of his home country's dialect — and who had been speaking German at home, only German, since the declaration of war, as if the language were a room he was withdrawing into.

Marcus did not conclude that Albrecht Pfeiffer had known Jan Václav Horak. He had no evidence for that. He had no evidence for any of it, strictly speaking — what he had was the structure of a probable picture, assembled from a phrase a girl had reproduced at the end of a school day and from a year of not-quite-looking at the question the phrase had now made unavoidable.

He moved to the window and looked at the street below. The elm branches had their April leaves — pale green, tentative, the color that lasted only a week or two before deepening. Henry had been remarking on the elms since March, watching for the first leaves the way a man watches for something he has been waiting on. He had been at the school sixteen years; he knew the elms' schedule.

The harbormaster would have the same letter he had heard about. The identification of the body — Jan Václav Horak, the Czech national, the displaced person — would have come to her office first, officially, and she had been holding whatever she held about the night of October twenty-sixth since October. He was certain now that she had been at the dock. He had been certain of this since September, when he had met her at the breakwater and recognized in the particular quality of her compression — her professional exactness, the way she answered the question she had decided to answer — the same instrument he used about Sherbrooke and Vienna. The instrument of someone who had made a decision about what to account for and what to hold.

She would have heard the name Horak. She would have done the same arithmetic he was doing now — Czech national, Halifax, the year between — and she would have reached a different set of probable pictures, because she had a different set of pieces. She had seen the dock. She had seen the second figure, if there had been one. She knew the harbor in the way that a harbormaster knew a harbor, which was to say she knew every boat and every post and every registered approach, and she would know, with precision, what was not in the record of that night.

He did not know if she had assembled what he had assembled. He did not know if she would want to.

He went back to the desk. His lesson book was open to the ablative notes — the third iteration, because the ablative absolute did not stay with students until it had been approached from three different directions, and he had not yet found the third direction. He closed the lesson book.

The German grammar Hannah had left was on the corner of the front desk. She had been doing this since January — leaving it as a placeholder, or a promise, or simply as evidence that she intended to return. He straightened it and set it where students left things for him. She would be back on Friday for Latin. Whether she came back for the grammar was her decision.

He took his coat from the hook by the door.

He did not know what had happened at the dock on the night of October twenty-sixth. He did not know whether the man who had come south from Halifax across the year had found what he was looking for when he found the Coldwater Reach commercial wharf, or whether he had arrived at the right address too late, or whether the address had been wrong from the start, or whether the Pfeiffer farm had nothing to do with it and the shape he had assembled was wrong in some fundamental way.

He put on his coat. He took his hat from the hook.

What he had was the phrase from the valley east of Feuchtwangen, reproduced in a girl's voice, and the name of a dead man who had been Czech and displaced and a year unaccounted for between Halifax and this breakwater. What he had was the shape of it. He knew what such shapes usually were, when the pieces fit as these pieces fit.

He pulled the door until the latch caught. Down the east corridor the custodian's cart was still.

He went down the stairs and out into the April air, which was cold on the shaded side of the building and not cold at all on the other.

# Albrecht and Karl

The fence post she wanted was at the north corner, where the property line turned and the drainage from the upper field ran along the stone wall. She had taken the ratchet and a coil of wire from the hook in the barn, in case the staples had pulled through, and was walking the fence line in the gray of the morning before the full light came over the maple ridge to the east. The frost was gone from the ground by the second week of April but the posts were still working themselves in places — she had found three heaved since March, one of them badly enough that the cedar had split at the base, and she had replaced it herself on a Saturday while her father was in the south field. This section was the last one she hadn't walked since the thaw.

May. The smell of the turned earth was in everything — in the air, in her coat, in the fold of her scarf. Albrecht had been plowing the north field since Monday, the team working east to west across the upper slope and stopping at the drainage dip, working around the low place where the clay held snowmelt into the third week of spring. She could see the rows from the lane, the dark parallel cuts going nearly black where the soil was wet, the topsoil thin over the clay subsoil in the north corner and impossible to do much about except build the planted rows higher, above where the water sat. Her father had done it this way every spring she had been old enough to watch.

She walked the fence line. The cedar posts were still holding in the upper section; she pressed each one with her shoulder and found them true. At the north corner she crouched to look at the bottom wire where the stone wall met the post — the junction was always where the frost pushed hardest, lifting the base of the stone and tilting the post with it — and found it solid. She ran her hand along the staples anyway. The wire was tight.

She heard voices before she stood up.

German.

Her father's voice was the lower one, and she knew it immediately — the register of it, the particular quality of how he shaped a sentence in his first language, which was different from his English in a way she had always felt rather than been able to name. As if German were where the sentence went when it was finished; as if English was where it went when it was only getting somewhere. She stayed crouched at the fence post. She did not move.

The voices were coming from the other side of the barn, around the corner where the field fence ran along the east wall. She had heard them from thirty feet away, which meant they were not being quiet. Two men in the morning, talking about the work.

She straightened slowly and walked back along the fence line toward the barn. At the corner there was a gap where two boards had been replaced after the ice damage the previous winter, the new planking not quite flush with the old, and through the gap she could see a section of the field fence and beyond it the near plot, the dark rows her father had turned. Her father was at the fence with his hands on the top rail. Karl was on the field side of it, perhaps three feet away.

She stopped.

They were speaking the same German. That was what struck her first — not that they were speaking, but that the language was the same in the way that mattered, the way that two instruments tuned to each other were the same. Her father's dialect had always been the particular German of home, of the kitchen and the dinner table, and she had never heard it exactly replicated outside those walls. Now it was coming from both sides of the fence rail. The vowels deep and rounded in the same places. The way the final consonants were handled. She could not have described it in linguistic terms the way Marcus could, but she could feel it — the fit between the two voices, the way they were working in the same grammar.

Karl was speaking. She caught: *der Boden* — the soil — and then *Wasser*, water, and *zu nass*, too wet. Her father said something she couldn't make out because he was turned partly away from her. She could see the profile of him, the set of his shoulders. He was listening with the quality she had learned to read: fully, without interrupting, turning the information over.

Karl crouched and picked up a handful of the field earth and held it out on his palm so her father could see the color, the clot of it, the way it kept its shape when the pressure eased. Not offered — just shown. Her father looked at it.

Karl spoke again. She caught *die Rücken* — the ridges — and watched him make a gesture with his free hand, the palm cutting flat through the air at an angle. The same gesture repeated with the hand tilted higher. She understood it without needing the German. She had watched her father work the north-corner rows since she was six, building the planted beds up with the hoe so the roots would sit above where the water sat in the clay. Karl was describing the same thing — the same problem, the same solution, something he had learned in a field in Franconia. He set the earth back down on the fence post. He said something more, and she caught *bei uns* — with us, where we come from — and *der Frühling*, spring, and a phrase about the timing of it, the March ground. How early you could start, if the clay was this kind of clay. What you watched for.

Her father was nodding slowly.

They went on like that for a few minutes — she couldn't have said exactly how long, because she had stopped thinking about time and was only watching the way two men talked when they were talking about something they both knew from the ground up. Karl asked a question; her father answered. Her father pointed toward the north end of the near field, the worst of the drainage dip, and Karl looked where he was pointing. There was something easy in it that she did not have a word for. Not friendship — she had seen her father with friends, with the neighbors at the feed cooperative meetings, with the men from church who came sometimes in summer. This was not that. It was the ease of two people who had the same information in their hands and were exchanging it without having to explain where the information came from.

Then Karl said something that included a place name.

Two syllables. A proper noun — she could tell by the shape it made in the sentence, the way it stood apart from the words around it. She didn't know it. She had learned, since October, the few Franconian place names she could attach to what she knew about her father's first country — Feuchtwangen, Ansbach, Dinkelsbühl, names she had pulled from the grammar and the atlas in the school library. This was not one of them.

Her father let go of the fence rail.

He didn't step back. He simply released the rail, slowly, and put both hands into his coat pockets. He looked at Karl. Not the sharp stop of October, not the mid-swing pause she had counted to two seconds and not been able to forget. This was a slower stillness. The kind that came from hearing something you had not expected and then, in the moment of hearing it, recognizing that in some other part of yourself you had expected exactly this.

He said something very quietly. She could not hear what. Just the register of it — low, almost flat, the tone that her father used when he was stating a fact that had already been established.

Karl nodded once.

They stood at the fence. Ten seconds, no more. Then her father looked back toward the field and said something that was probably about the drainage, something practical, returning the conversation to the ground. Karl went back to his row. Her father walked toward the far end of the north plot without looking back.

She waited at the barn wall until she could no longer hear either of them moving. Then she went back the way she had come.

---

The milking took until a quarter to seven. Twenty-two cows, the same twenty-two, and she knew every one of them — knew which would shift when she came up on the left side and which needed a hand on the flank before she could start, knew the sounds each one made in the sequence of filling the pail. She worked from right to left along the row, same as always, the pail moving, the smell of the warm animals around her.

She thought about her father's hands leaving the fence rail.

She had been watching her father for two years with a particular attention — not deliberately, always, but the way you watched something that had become weather, that told you things about what was coming whether you chose to read it or not. She had come to know the quality of his attention when he was receiving news he had already partly assembled. It was different from the quality of his attention when something was genuinely new. New things made him slower, more careful, the way he was with unfamiliar equipment. Already-assembled things made him still in a different way. He absorbed them into what he already had; the stillness was the sound of the pieces finding their places.

The stillness at the fence had been the second kind.

Karl had named a place and her father had gone still in the way that said: I know this already, or I have been waiting for it, or it is the thing that connects what I knew to what I now cannot pretend not to know. She had felt that stillness herself, in Marcus's classroom, in April, when he had said the valley east of Feuchtwangen toward the Bohemian hills, and the geography of her father's country had suddenly become a specific shape she had not known she was standing inside.

Her father knew exactly where Karl was from.

Not Franconia in the general way that she had understood since October, since the phrase that stopped him mid-swing in the field and the fifty kilometers she had mapped in her head afterward. More specific than that. The town Karl had named — the two syllables she didn't know — had a meaning to her father that showed in his hands leaving the fence rail, in the particular quiet of what he had said. He had the name already. He had been living alongside this knowledge since October, or longer, and what Karl had given him at the fence this morning was not new information but the piece that completed a shape he had been carrying.

She didn't know what that shape was. She had pieces of it — the same pieces she had been accumulating since October, since the first *Danke* through the fence in the fall, since the mid-swing pause, since the bird in her coat pocket. She had the shape of something, outlined by what she couldn't see rather than by what she could. She was learning, slowly, that this was how her father's knowledge worked: present in the outline it cast, absent in its center.

*Die Erde hier ist schwer.*

The phrase came up again, the way it kept doing. She had stopped being able to place it exactly — had lost the seam between the first time she'd thought it and all the times since. It was in the grammar from Bavaria, she thought. One of the field-prayers in the back pages, the ones she'd never asked her father to explain because she didn't know if they were prayers or something else. The earth here is heavy. The clay in the low places, going dark after rain, keeping its cold into May. The rows Karl had been showing her father how to build — the raised beds, the same technique her father had been using in the north corner for as long as she could remember, the technique that turned out to have a name in the same language as the soil it was meant to answer.

She worked along the row. The pail rang against the stanchion where the fourth cow shifted.

She thought: her father has something in common with Karl Reinmar that he has not told her. He has not told her because it is his to keep. She did not know what to do with this — whether to want to know, whether the wanting to know was the thing she needed to examine more carefully than the knowledge itself. She had been taught, more by weather than by instruction, that there were things her parents carried that were not hers to enter. The weight of the first country. The particular sorrow that had no name in English and that her father did not name in German either, in front of her, because it was his to carry in whatever room of himself he kept it.

She moved to the last cow. Outside the barn the light had gone from gray to pale gold.

---

When she came back across the yard, pails in hand, she looked up at the kitchen window.

Magda was there.

Standing at the window with a dishcloth in her hands — not drying anything, just holding it — and looking out toward the field. Not toward the yard, not toward Hannah coming across with the milk, but toward the far end of the north plot, where her father was working the second pass of the plow. Hannah stopped in the yard. She could see the side of her mother's face: the stillness of it, the quality of attention she had turned toward the field.

She couldn't tell if Magda had been at the window since before the gray light came, if she had seen the conversation at the fence, if she was standing there now because of what she had seen or because she had not seen it and didn't know. She couldn't tell if the dishcloth in her mother's hands was the evidence of something interrupted or something never started. She couldn't read Magda's face from here, at this distance — the face her mother wore in the kitchen, the one she could sometimes read, was not available to her from the yard.

Magda looked down at the cloth. Then she turned from the window and was gone back inside.

Hannah stood in the yard for a moment. Then she went to the pump to wash her hands and brought the milk in.

---

Lonzo came at seven, the green truck up Route 9 in the morning light, the Springfield in the rack behind his seat, the paper folded on the dash. He came across the yard at his usual pace and tipped his chin at Hannah. She said morning. He said morning.

He looked at the field, where her father was turning at the far end. She watched him look. There was nothing in his face that told her what he had seen or when he had arrived; he had the quality, she had noticed over many months, of a man who took in information the way a tide gauge took in water — registering, marking, not commenting. He went and retrieved his stool from the barn and set it at the gate and opened his paper. The prisoners were coming out of the icehouse — the three older ones first, then Karl behind them, Karl with his collar up and his hands still in his coat pockets though the morning was warming.

Lonzo watched them cross the yard the way he always watched: the count that wasn't counting, the assessment that looked like morning habit.

Hannah watched him for a moment and then stopped. She didn't know what she wanted to know. Whether he had been there early enough to see. Whether it mattered if he had. Whether anything about the morning at the fence had been the kind of thing Lonzo put in a report, or the kind of thing he had decided, months ago, was not that kind of thing.

She went inside to change her boots.

---

She walked the road to school with mud on her boots, the same clay mud from the north field, dark and dense, the kind that held its shape. The air had the particular quality of a May morning that was not yet sure of itself — cool still in the shade of the maples along the road, warmer in the open stretches where the sun had been working since first light. She walked past the south field where the Holsteins were grazing along the fence line, their brown eyes following her with the patient indifference of animals who had learned that she came and went and always came back.

She was thinking about the conversation at the fence. Not thinking, exactly — turning it in her hands the way you turned something in the dark to understand its shape. Her father and Karl had talked about the soil. About the drainage, the clay, the ridges you built to keep the roots out of what the ground kept. They had talked about it in the same language, with the same grammar, from the same landscape — the Franconian valley where the soil went heavy in the spring, where the farmers had learned what to do with early-wet ground the same way her father had learned it, before he came to Maine and found the same problem waiting for him.

Her father had heard a town name and gone still.

She didn't have the rest of it. She had the shape of the silence, the ten seconds at the fence, the hands going into the coat pockets, the quiet sentence she hadn't been able to hear. She had Magda at the kitchen window, looking toward the field. She had twenty-two cows and a school a quarter-mile down the road and mud on her boots from a field two men had just compared to a field in Franconia thirty years and thirty-five hundred miles away.

The morning opened around her. The crossroads, the church, the school building ahead where Marcus would be unlocking the door at this hour, the same hour he unlocked it every morning. The ordinary hours of the ordinary day proceeding through themselves, her father at his second pass in the north field, Karl in the far rows, Lonzo at the gate with his paper, Magda somewhere in the house with her dishcloth and her window.

The light on the road was the light of a morning that was going to be warm by noon, that was going to smell like turned earth and new growth all the way to the harbor and back. *Die Erde hier ist schwer.* The earth here is heavy; she carried a little of it on her boots, going to school.

She went on.

# Mr. Klein's Room

He left at a quarter to seven. The walk was three blocks — Elm Street north to the school — and he had been making it for sixteen years.

The May morning was the best morning of the year in Maine. Cold still in the shadow of the houses, the sun coming over the ridge to the east, the light flat and clean in a way it had not been since October. He knew every house on his route — the Peabody porch board that had needed painting since 1939, the forsythia at the corner that came back the same width every spring regardless of how far it was cut in April, the fence at the white house that had lost two boards in the January ice and still needed replacing. He knew which yards the low-tide smell reached on a southeast wind and which ones the lilacs got to first. Sixteen years of the same route, the same details accumulating, the town showing him the same face every morning as he walked past it going north toward the school.

Going the other way, as he turned onto the main road, the fishermen were heading down to the harbor — two of them that he could see, in their oilskins, carrying their gear. He nodded. They nodded. They had been passing each other at this corner, going opposite directions, for as long as he had been in Coldwater, and the nod had never changed.

At number 14, the curtain moved.

The woman at that window was always there when he passed. He had considered this, years ago — whether she was always at her window or whether something about the sound of his step on the road brought her to it — and then let the question go. He nodded toward the curtain. The shape behind it nodded back. They had been exchanging this nod since the spring of 1936, when he had first noticed her there and decided to acknowledge rather than ignore. It had not changed since. He could not have said what it meant, exactly. He understood it was not unfriendly.

He walked on.

The town had known him for twenty years. His father had brought the family north from Norfolk in 1924 — a sound decision, given what his father knew about Norfolk and what he had been told about Maine. He had found work at the school within the first two years, when the previous custodian left for Bangor, and he had been there since. He knew the town's face now: not the face it showed to strangers but the one it wore in the moment before deciding whether to grant you the ordinary courtesies without having to think about them first. Coldwater Reach was not unkind, as a rule. Not unkind in the way a person is not unkind when they have been polite long enough that the politeness runs on its own, without decision. You did not mistake that for something else. You did not have to, after twenty years. The patience had been in him long enough that it had become its own form of knowing, and the knowing was his.

He turned the last corner before the school.

---

He opened the building at seven. The key was on the ring with eleven others; he never confused it because the shaft was bent at the top from the time he'd used it to pry open a stuck gutter coupling in 1937 and had never gotten it straightened. He let himself in through the east door and stood for a moment in the hallway. The air inside was cooler than outside — furnaces banked overnight — and the smell was chalk dust, the sourness of the mop water that never quite left the floor, and the first warmth working in through the south-facing windows.

He did the east furnace first.

He had been managing the east wing's flue since November. A baffle plate sitting wrong in the air-change fitting had restricted the draw on cold mornings; he had shimmed it in December and adjusted the damper morning by morning since then, reading the stack draft by the sound of it and the gauge reading together. In May he could bank it down to almost nothing — the radiators in the east wing were warm but not needed — and this itself was a relief, the easing of a piece of equipment he had been watching all winter. He bled the pressure valve and recorded the gauge in the log: thirty-eight pounds, which was right. He checked the firebox, cleared the grate, made the entry in the maintenance book. Same for the west furnace, which had been easier all winter; the boiler there was newer, installed in 1938, and the system ran clean.

He did the hallways. He had mopped them the afternoon before and they were dry; he walked each corridor checking for what had come in overnight, because the east door seal let in leaves in any wind, and found nothing. He checked the lavatory fixtures on both sides of the ground floor. He oiled the gymnasium door hinge that had been dry since January and that he had been getting to for two months. He was working his way down the second-floor corridor when he came to the classroom at the end.

He had left the door standing open six inches the previous afternoon, because the window latch on the south side had been sticking since March and he had meant to come back to it. He pushed the door open now and went to the window.

The latch had freed itself. The warmth of the last few weeks had broken the paint seal and the swivel pin was seated properly; when he closed the window and opened it again it moved without resistance. He checked it twice. He opened the window four inches, because the morning warranted it, and looked out at the yard below.

Then he turned and looked at the room.

It was Marcus's room — he never thought of it as the Latin room or the German room, though it was both. Twenty student desks in four rows, eleven of them with names carved into the wood because this school had been here long enough for that. The blackboard with tomorrow's date in the upper right corner, where Marcus put it at the end of every class so the students could see it when they came in. The shelf behind the desk: the Latin dictionary, the mark book in its green cover, the spare chalk box.

The German grammar was not on the shelf.

All winter it had been there — spine out, between the dictionary and the mark book, and he had dusted around it every week since October. It was on the desk now. Cover up, in the working space, next to a composition book with student names written across the front in various hands, a different student's name in the corner of each page where a page corner was turned. And a pencil, short now — four inches at most — the tip broken off and not yet resharpened.

He stood at the door for a moment.

Then he went out and pulled the door back to six inches and continued his rounds.

---

He had been watching Marcus change since the school board meeting in December.

He did not try to name what he was watching in precise terms. Precision was the instrument he used for pipe fittings and furnace draws and joist tolerances, not for people. People he observed and understood by the slow accumulation of what he saw, and named what he saw when a name was useful, which was not always.

What he had been seeing: since December, Marcus had stopped holding himself quite so far from the door.

He'd had a quality, when he arrived in '42 and for the first year and more after that, of a man whose coat was not fully off. Not literally — Marcus was particular about his coat, hung it on the hook when he came into the house, kept it brushed. Something else. The quality of a man still working out whether this was the place where the coat came off and nothing happened. Of a man for whom *I am here* was still a provisional sentence, held out like a question rather than set down like a fact. He had recognized this quality when he first saw it because he knew it from the inside — from his own first years in Coldwater, before he had gotten to the provisional sentence himself. He had not thought about it in these terms at the time; he had simply recognized the quality in Marcus and noted it without speaking.

After December, it was different. Not that the man was careless — Marcus was never careless, and the particular quality of attention he gave to everything had not changed. The grammar was on the desk. The window was open in the mornings when the weather allowed. The chalk went onto the blackboard in longer strokes, the kind a person made when they were comfortable with the room they were working in. Henry saw these things on his rounds because he was in those rooms every morning, and his job required him to know exactly what was in them.

He had sat in the Legion hall in December, along the left wall in the extra chairs the Legion kept for when the membership room was being used for other business, while three men he had known for sixteen years decided something about a man he lived with. He had sat in rooms along the wall before, for different reasons, with different people at the table, and he knew how those rooms felt from that position — what it cost to be in the chair in front, what it cost to be at the wall, and that these costs were not the same cost. He had watched Marcus sit in the chair before the table and use the voice a man used when he had used it before, in other rooms, and had learned exactly how to use it. That was a specific kind of knowing: how you held your shoulders, how you waited for the next question, what you did not answer when it had not been asked. He knew it from his own practice. He did not know whether Marcus had it from the same place or a different one; that was not his to assume.

He had said *I have too*, walking out. Not because Marcus needed to hear it — or maybe he did; he couldn't say — but because it was true, and he had been careful, for some years, about leaving true things entirely unsaid.

What he had not said, and did not say now, and was not inclined to say: the two things were not the same. His twenty years here and Marcus's three were not the same condition with different names attached. They rhymed — he had seen the rhyme since the first months, seen it clearly and without needing anyone to point it out to him — but a rhyme was not a claim of equivalence, and the specific nature of what each of them had put down in this town, what it had cost each of them, what each of them had left in order to be putting anything down here at all, was not the same. He had been careful about this. He intended to remain so.

He was also glad Marcus was here. He was glad the grammar was on the desk.

He said none of this, because no one had asked him. His observations had a way of becoming invisible to the people who benefited from them, and over time he had learned to hold them. This was not the same as suppression. It was a skill — the skill of a man who had been watching long enough that the watching was its own kind of work, precise and complete and done for its own sake, not for the record.

---

The last item on the morning rounds was the south radiator in the main corridor.

It had been slow all winter — a fitting on the feed line that he had suspected was admitting air into the circuit, starving the pressure and keeping the radiator from reaching full heat on cold mornings. He had worked around it all season, balancing the other radiators on the circuit, and it had never been serious enough to pull the fitting during the heating season. Now it was May. He got his wrench from the furnace room, bled the fitting, and ran it until it was clear: eight seconds of air before the water came. He tightened the fitting and tagged it with a strip of red tape — his notation for the summer work order. He made the entry in the maintenance book: *South corridor, main feed, air in fitting. Bled and tagged, summer priority*.

He put the wrench away. He washed his hands at the utility sink. He could hear, out in the corridor, the east door opening — the first teacher arriving, footsteps on the floor he had mopped the afternoon before, the ordinary sound of the building coming on.

He went and got his coffee from the thermos on the shelf in the furnace room, the same shelf where Lillian packed it every morning and where it had been every morning for sixteen years.

His rounds were done.
