# The Half-Question

The conjugation *fero, ferre, tuli, latum* was on the board in his handwriting, which was smaller than the board required and which he had been compensating for, with limited success, since his first day at the school in March of the previous year. Third-period Latin, third-year students, eleven-thirty in the morning. The furnaces were working at full effort and losing to the cold that had flattened itself against the building sometime overnight. The panes fogged from the inside — not ice, not yet — but the thick condensation of two temperatures meeting each other at the glass. Through the clear portion at the upper edges of the nearest window, the schoolyard was grey and approximate, the far spruce a dark shape against a sky that had committed to nothing.

He went through the conjugation with the class. *Fero, ferre* — the shift from the root *fer-* to *tul-* in the perfect that required what he had come to think of, privately, as an act of trust: the language had been that particular way for long enough that arguing with it was beside the point. The passive forms were further difficulty. Michael Bates, third row from the left, had been having trouble with *fertur* since the Tuesday of the previous week — the same slight adjustment before the word arrived, as if it were sitting half a degree off-center in his mouth and needed correcting before it could be produced. Marcus had not mentioned this yet. He had been watching the gap narrow on its own.

"Bates," he said. "Once more."

"*Fertur*." A half-second. "Is carried."

"Again."

Bates said it without the gap this time. Marcus noted this without comment and moved on.

The exercises occupied the rest of the period. He moved between the rows as the class worked, pausing to confirm a form here or redirect an error there. Clara Walsh had finished early and was reviewing her answers with the composed efficiency of someone who was not checking her conclusions so much as reacquainting herself with them. In the back half of the room, the work was slower, more visible — the pencils pausing, the pages turned back. *Arma ferenda sunt.* Weapons must be carried. He looked at it on Donna Packard's paper and thought, not for the first time, that the textbook's choice of example sentences had a certain bluntness to it that the writers probably had not considered before 1941.

The bell. The chairs.

---

He was collecting the exercise papers from the desks when Hannah Pfeiffer came up.

She stayed after class with some regularity — not every week but with a consistency that established it as a pattern rather than an exception. Latin questions most often; German questions occasionally; sometimes both, when she was working through a construction that her two languages were resolving in conflicting ways. She had been in his courses since September of last year, and he had formed the opinion early and not revised it: she approached language as a system of logic rather than a series of items to be memorized, which was the quality that made the work interesting. He had noted this about her and considered the noting sufficient.

She set her notebook on the nearest desk and did not open it. Not a Latin question.

He waited.

"What does *Landsman* mean?" she said. "I think I have the German approximately right — *Landsmann*. Or is it —"

"*Landsmann*," he said. "The plural would be *Landsmänner*, yes." He looked up from the folder. "Where did you hear it?"

She considered for a moment. "One of the men at our farm. I think he said it to himself."

He placed the remaining exercise papers in the folder and closed it. He did this without hurrying.

"The word," he said, "is a term of affiliation. Literally: a person from the same land, the same region. It is not a synonym for *Landsleute* — for countrymen in the national sense — though it can be used loosely that way. Used precisely, it implies a shared *Gegend*." He paused. "Do you know the word?"

"Home district," she said. "Home ground."

"Near enough. It names a specific common origin — not *I am German and you are German*, which is nationality, but *we come from the same part of the world*, which is something more particular. A man from Munich would not naturally call a man from Hamburg his *Landsmann*, or not with any content to it. The word belongs to a smaller geography than the nation."

She was listening with the posture he had identified as her taking-in posture — not yet assembling, simply receiving. He waited to see what she would do with it.

"I see," she said.

"Said it to himself," he said. "Or to someone?"

"I don't — I'm not sure." A small motion of her hand on the notebook cover. "Maybe to someone. I wasn't close."

"Which farm?"

"Pfeiffer." Stated as something she expected him to be able to place, which he was. He knew the Pfeiffer farm the way he knew most things about Coldwater Reach — indirectly, through accumulation, through the town's habit of circulating information about itself through every available channel. The German family on Route 9. The dairy farm, the milk that Lillian picked up Tuesday mornings when the week permitted. The prisoners placed there in October, under the Houlton program — he had heard this at Beal's, at the school, without seeking it.

"It is an interesting word to use in that context," Marcus said.

He did not elaborate. There was more to elaborate on — rather a lot more, in fact — and he set all of it aside, on the other side of the sentence, where it would wait. The word was doing its work without his assistance. Hannah Pfeiffer was seventeen years old and one of his better students and she had asked what was, for her, a vocabulary question, and he had answered it accurately, and that was the scope of what had happened here.

She looked at him for a moment. Waiting for further, calculating whether it was coming.

"He's from Franconia," she said. She said it in the tone of a person setting down a piece of information that had taken some effort to acquire, and watching to see what it landed on.

"I see," Marcus said.

He did.

She gathered her notebook and her coat from the back chair. "Thank you, Mr. Klein."

"Fräulein Pfeiffer."

She went out.

---

He stood by the window.

The schoolyard was grey and still. A line of dead leaves at the east fence. The spruce boughs bending under nothing in particular — the cold air held enough moisture to make the light heavy. Two boys on the stone wall at the far end of the yard, small from this distance, doing something that did not require motion. He looked at the spruce, the boys, the fence, the flat grey sky above the roof of the woodshop, and registered none of it with any precision, which he recognized as a sign that he was looking at something else instead.

He had been not thinking about something for three weeks.

The body had been found in the last days of October — the storm, the breakwater, Hector Brann's boat coming in with the discovery. The town had settled quickly on its preferred account. U-boat, or something connected to submarines, or the relevant period of submarine activity along this coast and what it might have left behind — the exact theory had softened with each retelling until what circulated was a general agreement that this was a wartime thing and the proper people had addressed it. Parsons had come and gone. The record was presumably closed.

Marcus had not offered his version of events. He had been careful, in fact, not to develop his version to the point at which it would require offering, which was a more precise operation than simply keeping quiet.

The detail about the calluses had reached him through Edna Price and then through one of the fishermen at the counter at Beal's — centers of the palms, she had said, though by the time it had moved through two or three people the precision had softened somewhat. He had filed the softened version alongside the version he held, which was somewhat more specific and which had arrived in his mind fully formed and unwanted approximately three days after the body was found: a man in European civilian clothes with palm-center calluses and no papers was not a military operative. Military operatives had documentation, or the specific absence of documentation that constituted its own kind of record. What this man had was no papers — which was a different category entirely, not the no papers of a spy but the no papers of a person who had been traveling by means that did not generate documentation, which was to say by means available to people for whom the documented means were not available.

He had known this since October. He had spent November not following the thought further.

The reason had to do with what following it required.

He knew the logic of wartime displacement from the inside — not from study, not from the reports and lectures that circulated through refugee-aid organizations and emergency committees, but from the specific, physical experience of having been a person who moved through it. His passage from London to Sherbrooke in the summer of 1939 had involved, among other things, arrangements of the unofficial kind: a contact in a city he did not name, a boat that did not advertise its route, a farm somewhere in maritime Canada where he had spent two days in a room he was not registered as occupying. The people who had made these arrangements had not made them for personal advantage. They had made them because the official channels had stopped working for people in his category, and they understood this, and they had built something that worked in the spaces the official channels left empty. He had been grateful. He was still grateful. He had not discussed any of it since, partly from caution and partly because the people who had helped him had helped him in order to get him somewhere, not in order to become part of a story he told at dinner tables in coastal Maine.

He had spent two years in this town working at the project of being a different kind of person: one who taught Latin and German irregular verbs and walked the same three blocks to Elm Street every school day and told Lillian Crow about the Prater in October, a piece at a time, and ate fish chowder at a kitchen table that was warm enough to stay in for as long as the evening allowed. This was not a performance or a disguise. It was where he had arrived after everything that came before it. He valued it, and he had been, since the end of October, protecting it from the question that was waiting for him at the window.

A German prisoner from Franconia.

On the Maine coast. On a farm owned by a family from Feuchtwangen, Bavaria, which was Franconia — the same region, the same regional dialect, the specific vowels that would make a man use the word *Landsmann* and mean it precisely, in the sense of the same ground, the same particular piece of the world, down to a day's walk.

And a body on the breakwater in European civilian clothes with palm-center calluses and no papers, deposited by a three-day blow.

He was not forming an argument. He wanted to be careful with himself about this: what he had was a probable shape, assembled from inadequate evidence, which was not the same as a conclusion, and he was aware of the distinction. The shape suggested — not a spy operation, not the machinery of military intelligence, nothing of that genre — a different logic. The logic of a long chain of people trying to reach people, across distances that were not primarily geographical. A Czech man in transit — he held *Czech* as inference, not fact; the clothing, the route, the kind of person who was still in irregular motion across the Atlantic in the autumn of 1943 — who had known someone, and that someone had known of a farm on the Maine coast where a Bavarian family had come from the right general region of Europe, a family that might have been known to someone somewhere along the chain, or known of, or simply represented a recognizable kind of contact: the immigrant family with the old country still in them, in the right place at the right time, with a farm and a fence and the cold New England distance from official scrutiny.

Not spies. Refugees. The long effort of people who were trying not to be lost.

He did not know this. What he had was the probable shape of it, and the fact that a seventeen-year-old girl asking about a vocabulary word had made the shape visible to him in a way that three weeks of deliberate not-looking had not. He had no obligation to pursue it. He had no means to pursue it and no standing to pursue it and the official record was, by all accounts, closed. He was a man who taught Latin and German at a school in a coastal Maine town and who had been, for two years, the person this particular version of himself required him to be.

He turned away from the window.

The exercise papers were in the folder. Bates's *fertur* was in there, finally said without the gap. He had the afternoon.

---

Ralph Garland was at the table in the teachers' room with the Bangor Daily opened to the sports section. Edna Price was marking tests, red pencil, the focused efficiency she brought to everything she put the pencil to. The gas ring had been on since before seven o'clock that morning and the coffee in the pot had arrived at the particular density of late-session conviction.

Marcus rinsed his cup at the small sink, dried it once on the dish towel, filled it at the pot. He stood by the counter.

Ralph said, without looking up: "Cold today."

"Yes," Marcus said.

It was cold in the particular way of a Maine November that had decided, against no significant opposition, to simply be November. He had experienced two of them now in this town and had not yet entirely habituated to the quality of this cold — the moisture in it, the way it pressed flat against everything and found the gaps in the insulation. He expected this would normalize eventually. Most things did, given sufficient time and insufficient alternative.

He stood by the counter and drank the coffee and thought about the gerundive of obligation, which was the afternoon's subject. *Legendum est.* It must be read. Needing to be read. The construction in which a thing's necessity was built into its grammatical form, inseparable from the name of the thing itself. He thought about how to present this. The passive periphrastic, which was the technical name for the construction, was not a phrase he would open with; he would arrive at the name after the students had the feel of the form, which was the order that worked best. He had the afternoon's preparation in the folder with the exercise papers. He would look at it before the period began.

Edna made a mark on her test and turned to the next one. Ralph turned a page. The gas ring made its small continuous sound.

Marcus finished the coffee and rinsed the cup. He retrieved the folder from the shelf, opened it to the afternoon's notes. *Legendum, legenda, legendum.* The thing that must be done. He read through what he had written on the walk in this morning and made one small change in the margin, a different example sentence, something with less bluntness to it.

The question at the window was still there. He was aware of this in the way you are aware of the contents of a drawer you have just opened and then closed again — it did not require anything of him yet, and there was work to do.

He put on his coat. The afternoon was waiting.

# The School Board

Henry had told him on a Monday, at supper. Someone had filed a question with the selectmen — *question* was the word Henry used, and Marcus registered both the accuracy and the careful choice — about the German-language instructor at the school, and the selectmen had passed it to the school board. The board would address it at the February meeting. Three members would be present, not the full board: Dwight Hatch, Agnes Vane, Gordon Sears. Marcus knew Hatch by sight and Vane by name. He had not encountered Sears.

Henry said: "Your credentials are on file."

Marcus said: "Yes."

He had gone upstairs after supper and opened the bottom drawer of the chest. The file had been with him since Cambridge — since before Cambridge, since London, some of it dated from the years between Vienna and Paris when there had still been institutions willing to put letterheads on things. He laid the papers on the desk and went through them. Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars, dated November 1940, signed by Harrington, Whitmore's predecessor. His Vienna university credentials: the teaching certification, the faculty appointment letter. These were dated 1934. The letterhead was the university's, as it had existed before the annexation — the institution itself, its seal, its address, the name of the rector who had signed. He was aware that the letterhead cut two ways. The same date that documented his legitimate academic standing also marked it as belonging to an institution that no longer functioned as it had, in a country no longer sovereign. A board member predisposed to suspicion could read the letterhead as easily as one predisposed to fairness.

He included the documents anyway. A man who withheld his best evidence because the evidence had a complicated history was not a man who would be persuasive. The Cambridge letter. His Maine teaching certificate, issued in the spring of 1942 after the state board had reviewed his credentials and satisfied itself that a man with his qualifications could instruct the children of Maine in the German language. He thought briefly about the draftsmanship of that particular irony and put it aside.

He arranged the papers in order of probable utility. Emergency Committee letter first — it was the document most legible to an American institutional mind, because it was American, and because it named what he was: a scholar displaced by circumstances the Committee had determined to be genuine. His credentials after that. The outcomes list at the end, because the outcomes list was the argument that would land with a school board, and it should arrive last.

He spent the next day as he spent most Tuesday afternoons: teaching the Latin third-year through the gerundive, then the German second-year through the passive voice, then correcting the third-year examination papers in the empty classroom while the building went quiet around him. He had considered the probable objections while walking the three blocks home. Agnes Vane would raise something articulate; she had the reputation of a woman who chose her concerns precisely. Gordon Sears would raise something direct. Hatch, who organized such meetings, would say the least and carry the most weight.

He thought about what Vane might mean by *articulate but not specific*, which was the phrase Henry had used. He had encountered this category before. It was more resistant than outright hostility, because outright hostility could be countered with evidence, and this other thing — the concern that takes care to avoid stating itself as prejudice while remaining, at its foundation, exactly that — could not be countered by the same instruments. It required a different approach. Not engagement on its terms, but refusal to engage on its terms while appearing to engage. He had made an art of this, over the years, in several languages.

Henry had said: "I'll be there." And Marcus had said he didn't need a witness; Henry had said he knew; and without either of them elaborating further Marcus had understood that Henry would come anyway, and that this was, for Henry, a different decision than it might look like from outside.

---

The Legion hall on February evenings had the quality of a room borrowed from its proper use. The rationing board used it from nine to four on weekdays; the folding tables were still arranged in that configuration — two parallel rows facing the front — and the school board had simply relocated the chairs and positioned a single additional chair, unambiguously solitary, before the table. The American Legion banner ran the width of the back wall, its gold fringe losing color at the folds. The electric light was two bulbs in ceiling fixtures and was adequate and no more. The windows on the north side showed the street: black, empty, the temperature below ten and still dropping. It was seven twenty-two.

Marcus was early. He had learned this from experience in rooms not unlike this one — preferred the physical fact before the people arrived, preferred to know where the door was, where his chair sat in relation to theirs, how the light fell across the table, whether there was anything in the room that would require management. The preference was not anxiety. It was preparation in the same register as the document ordering, as the probable-objection work. He had done it in Vienna before the meeting where they had informed him that his faculty position would need to be reviewed in light of recent developments. In Paris before two consular appointments. In London at the Home Office. In Sherbrooke — not preparation, there, because in Sherbrooke one arrived as instructed rather than early, but in the waiting rooms at Sherbrooke he had learned what the same instinct looked like when it had no purchase on the room. In Cambridge, twice. In Coldwater Reach, in March 1942, before the school board had offered him the appointment.

He straightened his documents once and did not touch them again.

Henry came in at twenty past. He crossed directly to the chair along the right wall — not at the table, not at Marcus's chair — settled into it, and opened the Bangor Daily News he had folded under his arm. He did not look at Marcus; he gave his attention to the newspaper with the ease of a man who had arranged himself exactly where he meant to be and saw no reason to comment on it.

The positioning was correct. Henry knew it was correct, and Marcus knew it, and there was nothing to say about it. The one wrong thing would have been to acknowledge it. He kept his eyes on the table.

Hatch came in at twenty-eight minutes past, followed by Vane and then Sears. They were carrying their coats — they had not been here long enough to have hung them anywhere — and they settled into their chairs with the efficiency of people who had occupied positions at this table before and had no need to establish the configuration. Hatch had a yellow legal pad and a pen. Vane had a folder.

Sears had nothing. He folded his hands on the table and looked at Marcus with the directness of a man who found the whole proceeding tiresome in ways he was not at leisure to say.

---

"We've had some concerns raised," Hatch began, with the tone of a man measuring how much weight to give the word. "From parents. About the, ah — the current situation. Whether it's appropriate to have a German-language instructor at the school, given the national circumstances."

"The national circumstances," Marcus said.

"The country of the instructor's birth being currently at war with this country."

"I was born in Austria," Marcus said. "Which was annexed by Germany in March 1938, against the will of its government, and which I departed in 1936 — two years before that annexation — for reasons that I can detail for the board if it wishes." He moved the Emergency Committee letter across the table. "I have been on the rolls of the Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars since November 1940. I was hired by Coldwater High School in March 1942. I have been teaching here for twenty-three months."

He laid the outcomes list on the table. Examination results, progression rates, the comparative data from the three years prior to his hire when the German course enrollment had been running at a different level. The numbers were legible. He had prepared them to be legible to a school board, which was different from preparing them to be legible to a faculty committee — less subordinate structure, more column alignment — and he had done it without particular satisfaction but with the same care he brought to anything that was worth doing correctly.

Hatch read the Emergency Committee letter. Vane opened her folder and produced a copy of something — Marcus could see from across the table it was his teaching certificate, already on file as Henry had said. She compared it to the document in front of her, set both on the table, and looked at him.

Agnes Vane was a composed woman. She had the specific composure of someone who had been in rooms where things were decided, who had learned that the most effective way to carry weight was not to display it. She said: "We understand your history, Mr. Klein. The concern that was brought forward has to do, specifically, with —" She paused. She was, he thought, genuinely searching for a formulation. "The language itself. At this particular time."

Marcus waited.

She let the sentence end where it was.

"I teach German," Marcus said, "to American students who may need to speak it. In a military capacity, in an administrative capacity — in whatever capacity the period following this war creates a need for Americans who can speak German to German-speaking people. The utility of that instruction does not diminish because the language is currently spoken by an enemy government. It increases, if we are thinking about the war's conclusion and what follows it."

"That's a long view," Vane said.

"The instruction of languages generally requires a long view," Marcus said. "One does not teach a child the subjunctive for immediate tactical deployment."

Something crossed Vane's face that was not quite a reaction and was not quite suppressed. She looked down at her folder.

"The thing I don't see," Sears said — he had been watching Marcus throughout with the patient expression of a man waiting for the moment when the real question became available — "is why we need it at all. German. I don't see that the school was worse off before we had a German-language course."

"The school had a German-language course before I arrived," Marcus said. "I replaced the previous instructor when he enlisted."

Sears considered this. "Well, I know that." He appeared to feel this was a beside-the-point correction. "What I mean is, why should we have one now. Given everything."

"Because the language does not belong to the government using it," Marcus said. "And because the students in my classroom will live through whatever comes after this war, and they will find the capacity to speak German more useful then than it has been in the last two years."

Sears looked at him for a long moment. His expression was the expression of a man who understood perfectly well that the person in front of him had the better argument and who had not yet decided whether the better argument was sufficient.

"You understand our position," Sears said.

"I understand it perfectly," Marcus said.

There was a pause in which the room was very quiet. Outside one of the north windows a car passed on the street — the only vehicle Marcus had heard in the twenty minutes since he arrived. Then it was quiet again.

Hatch cleared his throat. "I think we have what we need here." He looked at Vane, who nodded. He looked at Sears, who held Marcus's gaze for another half-second before he looked down at the table and nodded as well. "The board votes to continue Mr. Klein's appointment. Unanimous." He made a notation on his yellow legal pad. "We'll note in the record that a formal review was conducted and the appointment confirmed."

Marcus gathered his documents. The Emergency Committee letter, the credentials, the outcomes list, back into the file in the order he had removed them. He was aware, as he did this, of the quality of the action — the same action he had performed at the end of several other meetings of this kind, the returning of papers to the file that had accompanied him through too many such rooms, and the specific texture of collecting those papers from a table where they had been sufficient for the purpose. Not triumph. Not relief, precisely. Something closer to the completion of a task that one had known would be completed, but had not been able to assume would be completed until it was.

The meeting had lasted thirty-eight minutes.

---

Outside, the night was clear and cold in the particular way of a February in coastal Maine — the cold not heavy or wet, as it was in a storm, but dry and still and absolute, the kind that entered the collar and the cuffs and made the walk home a matter of economy: the fewest unnecessary motions, the steadiest pace, the breath that went out and came back cold and went out again.

The street was empty. Coldwater Reach cleared itself by seven on nights like this; the residents who were inside were inside and the ones who had gone out had already returned. The door of the Legion hall closed behind them, and the sound of it carried in the cold air farther than the same door would have carried in any other season.

They walked without speaking. Down to the corner of Bridge Street, left toward the harbor road. This was not the most direct route and Marcus was aware that he had not chosen it, had simply found himself beside Henry on this bearing without registering the decision. The harbor in February showed itself as it did in January — the dark water, the moored boats, the lights on the commercial wharf, the breakwater running out from the north shore, the algae line black at the waterline. The cold sat on the surface of the water without disturbing it. Very still.

They turned onto Birch Street. They turned onto Elm.

Three blocks from the Legion hall Henry said: "You were very calm."

"I have had some practice," Marcus said.

"I know," Henry said.

They walked.

The footsteps on the cold pavement were the only sound between the buildings. Marcus watched the light in the kitchen window of the house ahead — it was their house, theirs, a fact that had taken him longer than it should have to accept as simply a fact — and did not look away from it.

"I have too," Henry said.

Marcus did not answer. There were statements that completed themselves, that required nothing added, whose meaning lay in having been said and left precisely where they were. Any word he offered would diminish what Henry had said by appearing to receive it, to acknowledge it, to bring it into the category of things that had been discussed. Henry knew this. Marcus knew it. They both knew it for the same reason, which neither of them named.

They walked the rest of the way home in silence.

---

The house on Elm Street had a light in the kitchen window and the quality of the light was warm — the particular quality that distinguished a lit window from a lit-and-heated window, something in the color of it, in the depth, that Marcus had learned to read from the outside as he learned to read the inside of the house itself. Lillian had left the stove going. She was not in the kitchen — he could see through the glass that the kitchen was empty — but the pot was on the back element and the room was warm.

Henry hung his coat on the hook inside the door and went to the sink to fill the kettle without discussing it.

Marcus sat down at the kitchen table. He set his file folder on the chair beside him. The table was pine, the surface marked with years of use — the rings from cups and glasses, a long pale scratch across one corner from something Lillian used the table for that he had never identified, the general worn smoothness that accumulated in things that were used and attended to and neither replaced nor preserved. He put his hands flat on it.

The stove ticked. Henry filled the kettle.

Outside, February continued: the cold still, the street empty, the harbor somewhere below the last rise with its winter shape in the dark. He had his documents in the file. He had his classroom tomorrow, the Latin third-year in the first period, the German second-year in the third. In the morning he would walk the three blocks from Elm Street to the school with his paper bag of tea in his coat pocket and the grammar book on its shelf where it always was, and the classroom would be the classroom, the students the students, the ablative case still the ablative case regardless of what any board of selectmen had to say about it.

The kettle began to warm.

He had had some practice. He was aware of what that practice had cost him, and he was aware — sitting here, his hands on the table, the stove going — that the cost was not the only thing it had been.

# The Unregistered Boat

The spring mooring assignments ran fourteen pages in the ledger that year — more changes than any season since she had taken the post. She worked them in order, north dock first, going south. The order was Owen's. He had invented it in his first year and she had inherited it with the ledger, and she saw no reason to alter a system that worked.

April fourteenth. Cold still, but a different cold — the active kind, the kind that came with the smell of the water back in it. The harbor had been open since mid-March, the inner-cove ice gone in the second week, and the fleet was returning from the winter moorings and the drydock yards and in some cases from the decisions made over the winter about whether to return at all.

This season she had two deletions.

Robert Cates, berth fourteen. His boat the *Idabelle* had been registered at fourteen since the summer of 1938. He had shipped as mate on a merchant vessel the previous September — she had the letter from the company, which was the way it was done, the company notifying the harbor office as a matter of form. His wife had written separately in February to say the berth could go. Eira had kept it open through the winter. She did that when a man left: hold through the season, then decide. Now it was April and she reassigned berth fourteen to Archie Lunt of Tenants Harbor, one of two men who had come down from Tenants Harbor when the Price fish house folded in February.

Harold Vose, berth nine. She had processed his papers in December and mailed the original registration certificate back to his mother in Searsport, because his mother was the named next of kin and there was no wife and no partner and no one else on the form. She had held berth nine empty through the winter. She marked it available and did not reassign it yet. She would hold it through the spring in case a buyer materialized.

The three additions: Archie Lunt, Eddie Lunt his brother — no relation to the Lunts from Port Clyde — and Roy Tremblay from Spruce Head, vouched for by Elias Hollis, whose judgment she trusted for this purpose. Tremblay would have berth nine provisionally; she would do the hull inspection on the fifteenth.

She finished the mooring assignments by half past eight.

Then the depth soundings. The District office had sent the winter survey in February, three corrections noted. A shoal building at the south entrance, up two feet since the 1942 survey. A reduction in clearance off the breakwater where silt deposit had settled. An improvement in the north channel where the winter storms had scoured the bottom. She went through each correction against her working chart, marked them in pencil, entered them in the tide log with the survey date and District reference number. The shoal at the south entrance would affect approach draft on anything over eight feet — she noted it in the mooring assignment column for the south entrance berths and put a penciled flag on the chart.

She worked until ten, then took her coat and walked the dock.

She did this most mornings — the north berths and then south along the commercial wharf, the whole fleet in order. The harbor in April had a specific quality she had been noticing for eight years: the cold and the activity at once, the season not yet settled, the fleet reassembling itself after the long quiet. Today there was a supply tender at the outer dock and the Lunt boats rigging at the far berths and someone on the commercial wharf with a hand truck. She walked through it without hurrying.

She knew every registered boat in the harbor by sight. She could name each one going along the dock — by hull shape, by waterline, by the way it sat when loaded or empty, by the specific shade of the topsides after years of paint and weather. She had learned this from Owen and she had learned it again through her own watching. It was not a remarkable skill. It was what you knew when you had been looking at the same fleet long enough.

---

At dock post seven, which she had left open pending reassignment, there was a lobster boat she did not know.

She stopped and looked at it. Small — twenty-six feet, perhaps twenty-seven. An older hull, the topsides faded from something that had been red, a standard work design, the lines of nothing particular. The kind of hull you saw from one end of the coast to the other without being able to place the builder. It sat at the post with its lines double-tied, which meant someone had secured it properly and not simply run a line through and walked away.

She went to the stern and read the registration number.

She went back to the office and looked it up. The Maine registry — main volume, then the 1944 supplement. Not there.

She went back to the dock.

Hector Brann was at berth twelve, coiling line. He had been the one to find the body on the breakwater in October — she had thought about that the first time she'd renewed his berth since, and not since. He was a steady tenant and he didn't ask questions about what wasn't his business.

She asked him whose boat was at seven.

He straightened and looked down the dock. "Think it's someone from Owls Head," he said. "Been there a few days."

She thanked him.

Back in the office she opened the second drawer and found the Owls Head harbor contact list. She kept lists from four coastal offices — Knox County, the Owls Head harbor, Rockland, Vinalhaven — a practice Owen had started and she had maintained, updating when the offices changed personnel or the phone numbers changed. The Owls Head list ran three typewritten pages, alphabetical by registration number. She went through it twice.

Not there.

She took out the tide log.

*Unregistered vessel, dock 7. First observed morning of 14 April 1944. Registration number not in Maine registry (main volume or 1944 supplement) or Owls Head harbor contact list. Inquiry to be sent to District office, Portland. —E.B.*

She put the tide log back on the desk and drafted the inquiry: two paragraphs, the registration number, the date of first observation, the dock location, a request for identification or nearest-office follow-up. She sealed it in an official envelope and put it in the mail pouch for the three-o'clock run to the Birch Street post office.

In the afternoon she did the hull inspection on Tremblay's boat. Registration in order, hull sound, some cosmetic work needed on the topsides but nothing structural. She countersigned his certificate and filed the copy.

On the morning of April sixteenth she walked the fleet.

Dock post seven was empty.

The double-tied lines were gone with the boat. She stood at the post for a moment. The water under it was the same harbor water it had been yesterday and the day before. No mark on the post that would last beyond the week.

She went back to the office.

*Unregistered vessel, dock 7. Departed approximately April 15 or 16, unseen. Inquiry to District office posted April 14. No response received.*

She did not expect a response before May. Possibly June. An unregistered lobster boat at a Maine dock for two days was not, in April of 1944, the most urgent item in anyone's mail.

She noted it and turned to the day's other work.

---

The official mail came on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, dropped by the post office boy who had been doing the harbor rounds since before the war. It came on April sixteenth while the tide log was still open on her desk.

Four items: the weekly District bulletin, a supply order confirmation, the spring fuel allocation form, and a letter from the Coast Guard regional office in Portland.

She set the bulletin and the form on the left side of the desk. She opened the supply confirmation and checked it against the pending order list. She opened the Portland letter last.

Two paragraphs on official stationery. Dated April 12. Addressed to the Harbormaster's Office, Coldwater Reach, Maine, attention Harbormaster.

*In re: October 1943 recovered remains — Coldwater Reach harbor, follow-up communication.*

She read it through.

*Through liaison with Allied civilian records, this office has received identification of the remains recovered October 28, 1943. The individual has been identified as Jan Václav Horak, Czechoslovak national, status: displaced person. Last known location: Halifax, Nova Scotia, October 1942. No next of kin information is available through current records. The official record is herewith amended to reflect this identification. The classification of cause of death is unchanged: accidental drowning consistent with storm exposure. No further investigation is anticipated at this time. This communication is for your records.*

She read it again.

Jan Václav Horak.

She folded the letter and set it on the chart table and sat down.

Czech. In Halifax in October of 1942. On the Coldwater breakwater in October of 1943. Between those two facts there was a year of movement that the letter did not account for and that she had no account of from any other source. Halifax to the coast of Maine was not a straight line. It was a year of intermediate stops that the two paragraphs on official stationery had left blank.

The office was quiet. The stove had burned down while she was at the desk — she could hear that it had gone quiet, the iron no longer ticking — but she did not get up. Outside, the harbor was going about its midmorning work. Someone at the outer dock. The Lunt boats coming in early from the south. The tide log open to April 16 on the desk.

She knew his hands. She had been at the dock that morning in October when the Coast Guard lieutenant had done the inventory — everything that was on the body and everything that wasn't — and she had looked at the hands because that was one of the things you looked at, if you were trying to understand what kind of man you were dealing with. The calluses were in the centers of the palms, not at the base of the fingers. Not a fisherman's hands. Not a farmer's or a cannery man's. She had noted the coat he wore, the European cut of it, the quality of the wool, the way it was not built for this water or this cold. She had noted the several days' growth of beard.

She had known he was not from anywhere near Coldwater Reach.

She had his name now.

Jan Václav Horak. Czechoslovak national. Halifax in October 1942.

Halifax was a port. You could come into Halifax by certain routes — without the right papers, or with papers that weren't quite right, or with the kind of contacts that didn't appear in any official record — and from Halifax you could move south along the coast by routes that had no file in any District office. She knew this from Varnum. Last December, at the quarterly meeting in Portland, after the fuel allocation was settled and the room had relaxed: Varnum had used the phrase *refugee crossings*. More of it than people thought, he had said. Known, though. A kind of thing that happened.

She had ridden back to Coldwater along Route 1 in the dark with that phrase and the approved fuel figures and two cups of coffee. She had held the phrase beside what she had seen on the dock on the night of October twenty-sixth: the man at the far bollard, eleven in the evening, a second figure in the shadow between the fish house and the net shed. She had stood for a moment at the dock head and looked, and then she had gone back to the office and written in the log: *2300: mooring check completed, fleet secure.*

She had not entered the man. She had not entered the second figure. She had not entered what the two of them had appeared to be doing at the far bollard at that hour, or what the shape of it had looked like in the dark.

Jan Václav Horak. She had not known his name when she wrote that entry, and she had not gone back to annotate it, and now the Coast Guard regional office had sent her two paragraphs of official stationery and she had his name, and the log still read *fleet secure*.

She looked at the letter on the chart table.

No next of kin. She turned that over. His name had been in the records somewhere — in some Allied civilian file, in some registry of displaced persons that someone in some office had access to, because they had found it and sent her this letter in April of 1944, and the name was here now. But no next of kin. No one the Allied civilian records had associated with him. He had moved through the records without leaving a person who would be notified.

He had been a displaced person. That was the status the letter gave him. Displaced from where to what, it did not say.

She tried to trace the year between Halifax and this breakwater. The ports where you could stop, moving south. The Bay of Fundy, the Passamaquoddy coast, the islands — she knew them all as harbors, as navigational facts, as names on the chart she looked at every working day. She could see the route in theory. She could not see who would have been helping him along it, or whether anyone had been, or what it had cost him and whoever was in that shadow at the far bollard to move him to this dock and to what happened after.

She had seen enough, that October night, to have entered something. She had not entered it.

Owen had left a gap in 1934 and named it. He had written *not entered at time; entering here as complete account* and he had made the record complete. She had thought about that in January, standing at the chart table with his 1934 log and her 1943 log open side by side, his October pages and her October pages. She had thought about the distinction between a deferred entry and an absent one. She had closed the 1943 log and not returned to it.

Jan Václav Horak.

Czech. Halifax. Displaced. No next of kin. Dead on this breakwater at the end of October, in the water twelve to thirty-six hours before Hector Brann found him on the granite seam on the ocean side. That was what the Coast Guard had said: twelve to thirty-six hours in the water. She had done the arithmetic at the time, standing in the dock office with the lieutenant's report in front of her, and the window had put him in the water between midnight and two in the morning on October 27, 1943. The night after she had seen him at the dock.

She knew more now than she had known in October. In December. She knew his name and his country and the city where he had last been registered, a year before she had seen him at the far bollard with whatever papers he did not have on him when the Coast Guard lieutenant turned out his pockets.

She did not know what he had been moving toward. She did not know what he had been running from. She did not know whose hands had put him in the water or whether his had been the only ones.

She had a name.

The chart table under her hands was Owen's — the same one he had worked at, the surface worn at the corners where you rested your forearms when you leaned over the charts. Outside the window the harbor was going about the business of mid-April. The fleet resuming. The season coming back.

She looked at the letter.

Jan Václav Horak.

She was sitting at the chart table.

# Franconian

The building had been mostly empty for an hour. He could hear the custodian's cart somewhere down the east corridor — the particular sound of a bucket set down and not yet retrieved — and the last of the afternoon light came through the west windows at a low angle, illuminating the chalkboard's residue in a way that was not visible during lessons. The third declension. A tense paradigm. He had been trying to erase the board to something approaching clean when Hannah Pfeiffer knocked and came in.

She was carrying her Latin textbook and, under it, the German grammar she had been borrowing and returning in alternation since January, as if she were not quite ready to possess it and not quite ready to relinquish it. She set it on the nearest desk and did not sit.

"I heard something," she said. "One of the prisoners — Karl — he was talking to someone through the icehouse window. I was at the south fence, and I wasn't listening on purpose. I was there to reset a post."

He put the eraser down.

"A phrase," she said. "About the harvest. I'm going to try to say it right."

She gave it to him.

Her German was her father's German, fundamentally — the vowels slightly flattened in the Bavarian way, the consonants not quite Munich and not quite rural. For a girl who had spoken it since before she spoke English, she had the unselfconsciousness of a native and the slight displacement of someone who had learned it in translation, in a country where it was not the native tongue. She was trying to reproduce what she had heard, and what she had heard was not her father's dialect.

He received the phrase as two things simultaneously. As a linguistic object, first — the particular rounding of the *a*, the contraction that shifted stress from the first syllable to the second. As a problem, second. He had been aware of the problem for some months without committing to its full assembly; the phrase she had given him was the kind of precision that made assembly unavoidable.

"That is a harvest idiom," he said. "An Upper Franconian form. Not Bavarian. Not standard German." He came away from the board and sat at the teacher's desk. The chair was the school's regulation chair, wooden, the finish gone from the arms. He had been sitting in it for two years and had stopped noticing it. "The idiom comes from the communities along the Upper Main River. The country between Nuremberg and the Czech border."

Hannah was quiet. She had the quality — he had observed it across several months of watching her in Latin, and on the few occasions their other conversations had warranted this kind of attention — of hearing things completely before she responded. She did not interrupt. She waited until she had understood.

"He grew up hearing that dialect," Marcus said. "The phrase, at minimum, belongs to someone who learned it at home. It is not something you acquire as an adult."

"Where in Franconia?" she said.

"Where in Franconia is he from?"

"I think Ansbach. Someone said Ansbach."

Ansbach was Middle Franconia — the flat country west of Nuremberg, the agricultural plain, the market town that had been a regional center for several centuries without being particularly close to anything. The speech there was recognizably related to what she had given him. It was not identical. The stress pattern she had reproduced was not the Ansbach form.

"The phrase is from further east than Ansbach," he said. "Twenty, perhaps thirty kilometers east of there. The valley between Feuchtwangen and Dinkelsbühl, or the villages east of Dinkelsbühl toward the Bohemian hills."

She looked at him.

"That's where my father is from," she said.

"Yes," Marcus said.

There was a pause. Outside the window the afternoon went on being April — the specific quality of late light in a month where the cold was not yet gone but the angle of the sun had changed, so that the warmth and the cold arrived on different sides of the same air. He had found April in coastal Maine stranger than November. November he had understood immediately. April was something he was still learning.

"Thank you," Hannah said. She picked up her Latin textbook. The German grammar she left on the desk.

"The translation," she said from the doorway.

He had been waiting to see if she would ask. "The field takes what it is owed, and the man who worked it walks home lighter." He paused. "More or less. Some things do not translate exactly."

She nodded. He heard her footsteps recede down the corridor.

---

He sat for some time in the teacher's chair.

The precise measure of the phrase's origin — Feuchtwangen and eastward, toward the Czech border — was not information he had possessed before. He had possessed the general geography: Karl Reinmar was from Franconia, Hannah had established that much at the fence in October, and Albrecht Pfeiffer was from Feuchtwangen, which was in the same county. Fifty kilometers between them, approximately, which had been the phrase Hannah had brought to him in November with the word *Landsmann* — a word he had translated precisely, and had declined, at the time, to follow to its geographic conclusion.

Now the phrase she had given him resolved the fifty-kilometer estimate into a specific corridor. Not the broad territory of Franconia but the particular landscape east of Feuchtwangen — the country running toward the Franconian Heights, toward the Bohemian Forest, toward the border that the maps had marked and the communities on either side had spent several centuries treating as somewhat negotiable.

The Czech border. He stood and went to the window.

He had heard the name Horak in late April — it had come into the school the way things came into the school from the official mail, which was to say through the post office and Beal's general store and by the end of the week through three different conversations he had not sought. Jan Václav Horak. Czech national. Displaced person. Halifax, 1942. He had heard it and had not needed to ask any follow-up questions, because he knew what the category meant.

He was perhaps the only person in Coldwater Reach who knew from the inside what the category meant. That was not a distinction he had sought. He had simply been, for a period of years, a person who moved through the administrative machinery of displacement — the waiting rooms, the transit papers, the offices that determined your right to remain in a given place — and the movement had given him a specific kind of knowledge. The kind that was not listed in a record but was present in the body, in the acquired habits of a person who had learned when to move quickly, when to move quietly, and how to read the room before committing to any action that might require the room's cooperation.

He knew what a displaced Czech national in Halifax in 1942 was. Not Jan Václav Horak specifically — he had not known the man — but the category of person. The category meant you were moving along routes that did not appear in any official file. It meant the people who moved you along those routes were people who had their own reasons for keeping their names out of the record. It meant your next station was reached through someone who knew someone who knew someone — a chain of connection that ran through origin, through language, through the specific geography of shared community.

Halifax was a port. From Halifax, moving south along the coast toward Maine, you would look for the contacts you could authenticate by origin. Not German-Americans generally. The German-American population along the Maine coast was not organized into a network of this kind, and a Czech displaced person would have no particular reason to seek it. What he would seek — what anyone in that position would seek, in Marcus's experience — was the specific German-Americans from the borderland communities, the families who had come from the country where the German and Czech populations had lived alongside each other for centuries, where the dialects carried inflections from both sides, where the family names crossed the border in both directions without particular comment, where you could authenticate a contact not by documentation but by the sounds of the dialect they had grown up in.

He was constructing this. He was aware that he was constructing it. The distinction between recognizing a shape and inventing one was not always as clear as he would have preferred — he had learned this too, in the waiting rooms and the transit offices, where constructed pictures sometimes replaced available facts because the available facts were insufficient and the constructed picture was more tolerable. He had seen what happened to people who committed to a constructed picture before the evidence warranted it. On several occasions he had been the subject of such a commitment.

He would not do that here.

And yet the shape was there regardless. A Czech displaced person, moving south from Halifax along the coastal routes. Reaching, at some point in the year between October 1942 and October 1943, the coast of Maine. Seeking a contact he had been given — a farm name, a family name, an address on a route that ran through the Franconian-Czech émigré network and terminated, if the network ran as such networks ran, at the one farm in the area whose owners came from exactly that borderland country.

The Pfeiffer farm. Three miles inland on Route 9. Albrecht Pfeiffer, from Feuchtwangen, who had paused for two seconds in October when a prisoner in his field used the vowels of his home country's dialect — and who had been speaking German at home, only German, since the declaration of war, as if the language were a room he was withdrawing into.

Marcus did not conclude that Albrecht Pfeiffer had known Jan Václav Horak. He had no evidence for that. He had no evidence for any of it, strictly speaking — what he had was the structure of a probable picture, assembled from a phrase a girl had reproduced at the end of a school day and from a year of not-quite-looking at the question the phrase had now made unavoidable.

He moved to the window and looked at the street below. The elm branches had their April leaves — pale green, tentative, the color that lasted only a week or two before deepening. Henry had been remarking on the elms since March, watching for the first leaves the way a man watches for something he has been waiting on. He had been at the school sixteen years; he knew the elms' schedule.

The harbormaster would have the same letter he had heard about. The identification of the body — Jan Václav Horak, the Czech national, the displaced person — would have come to her office first, officially, and she had been holding whatever she held about the night of October twenty-sixth since October. He was certain now that she had been at the dock. He had been certain of this since December, when he had met her at the breakwater and recognized in the particular quality of her compression — her professional exactness, the way she answered the question she had decided to answer — the same instrument he used about Sherbrooke and Vienna. The instrument of someone who had made a decision about what to account for and what to hold.

She would have heard the name Horak. She would have done the same arithmetic he was doing now — Czech national, Halifax, the year between — and she would have reached a different set of probable pictures, because she had a different set of pieces. She had seen the dock. She had seen the second figure, if there had been one. She knew the harbor in the way that a harbormaster knew a harbor, which was to say she knew every boat and every post and every registered approach, and she would know, with precision, what was not in the record of that night.

He did not know if she had assembled what he had assembled. He did not know if she would want to.

He went back to the desk. His lesson book was open to the ablative notes — the third iteration, because the ablative absolute did not stay with students until it had been approached from three different directions, and he had not yet found the third direction. He closed the lesson book.

The German grammar Hannah had left was on the corner of the front desk. She had been doing this since January — leaving it as a placeholder, or a promise, or simply as evidence that she intended to return. He straightened it and set it where students left things for him. She would be back on Friday for Latin. Whether she came back for the grammar was her decision.

He took his coat from the hook by the door.

He did not know what had happened at the dock on the night of October twenty-sixth. He did not know whether the man who had come south from Halifax across the year had found what he was looking for when he found the Coldwater Reach commercial wharf, or whether he had arrived at the right address too late, or whether the address had been wrong from the start, or whether the Pfeiffer farm had nothing to do with it and the shape he had assembled was wrong in some fundamental way.

He put on his coat. He took his hat from the hook.

What he had was the phrase from the valley east of Feuchtwangen, reproduced in a girl's voice, and the name of a dead man who had been Czech and displaced and a year unaccounted for between Halifax and this breakwater. What he had was the shape of it. He knew what such shapes usually were, when the pieces fit as these pieces fit.

He pulled the door until the latch caught. Down the east corridor the custodian's cart was still.

He went down the stairs and out into the April air, which was cold on the shaded side of the building and not cold at all on the other.

# Mr. Klein's Room

He left at a quarter to seven. The walk was three blocks — Elm Street north to the school — and he had been making it for eighteen years.

The May morning was the best morning of the year in Maine. Cold still in the shadow of the houses, the sun coming over the ridge to the east, the light flat and clean in a way it had not been since October. He knew every house on his route — the Peabody porch board that had needed painting since 1939, the forsythia at the corner that came back the same width every spring regardless of how far it was cut in April, the fence at the white house that had lost two boards in the January ice and still needed replacing. He knew which yards the low-tide smell reached on a southeast wind and which ones the lilacs got to first. Eighteen years of the same route, the same details accumulating, the town showing him the same face every morning as he walked past it going north toward the school.

Going the other way, as he turned onto the main road, the fishermen were heading down to the harbor — two of them that he could see, in their oilskins, carrying their gear. He nodded. They nodded. They had been passing each other at this corner, going opposite directions, for as long as he had been in Coldwater, and the nod had never changed.

At number 14, the curtain moved.

The woman at that window was always there when he passed. He had considered this, years ago — whether she was always at her window or whether something about the sound of his step on the road brought her to it — and then let the question go. He nodded toward the curtain. The shape behind it nodded back. They had been exchanging this nod since the spring of 1936, when he had first noticed her there and decided to acknowledge rather than ignore. It had not changed since. He could not have said what it meant, exactly. He understood it was not unfriendly.

He walked on.

The town had known him for twenty years. His father had brought the family north from Norfolk in 1924 — a sound decision, given what his father knew about Norfolk and what he had been told about Maine. He had found work at the school within the first two years, when the previous custodian left for Bangor, and he had been there since. He knew the town's face now: not the face it showed to strangers but the one it wore in the moment before deciding whether to grant you the ordinary courtesies without having to think about them first. Coldwater Reach was not unkind, as a rule. Not unkind in the way a person is not unkind when they have been polite long enough that the politeness runs on its own, without decision. You did not mistake that for something else. You did not have to, after twenty years. The patience had been in him long enough that it had become its own form of knowing, and the knowing was his.

He turned the last corner before the school.

---

He opened the building at seven. The key was on the ring with eleven others; he never confused it because the shaft was bent at the top from the time he'd used it to pry open a stuck gutter coupling in 1937 and had never gotten it straightened. He let himself in through the east door and stood for a moment in the hallway. The air inside was cooler than outside — furnaces banked overnight — and the smell was chalk dust, the sourness of the mop water that never quite left the floor, and the first warmth working in through the south-facing windows.

He did the east furnace first.

He had been managing the east wing's flue since November. A baffle plate sitting wrong in the air-change fitting had restricted the draw on cold mornings; he had shimmed it in December and adjusted the damper morning by morning since then, reading the stack draft by the sound of it and the gauge reading together. In May he could bank it down to almost nothing — the radiators in the east wing were warm but not needed — and this itself was a relief, the easing of a piece of equipment he had been watching all winter. He bled the pressure valve and recorded the gauge in the log: thirty-eight pounds, which was right. He checked the firebox, cleared the grate, made the entry in the maintenance book. Same for the west furnace, which had been easier all winter; the boiler there was newer, installed in 1938, and the system ran clean.

He did the hallways. He had mopped them the afternoon before and they were dry; he walked each corridor checking for what had come in overnight, because the east door seal let in leaves in any wind, and found nothing. He checked the lavatory fixtures on both sides of the ground floor. He oiled the gymnasium door hinge that had been dry since January and that he had been getting to for two months. He was working his way down the second-floor corridor when he came to the classroom at the end.

He had left the door standing open six inches the previous afternoon, because the window latch on the south side had been sticking since March and he had meant to come back to it. He pushed the door open now and went to the window.

The latch had freed itself. The warmth of the last few weeks had broken the paint seal and the swivel pin was seated properly; when he closed the window and opened it again it moved without resistance. He checked it twice. He opened the window four inches, because the morning warranted it, and looked out at the yard below.

Then he turned and looked at the room.

It was Marcus's room — he never thought of it as the Latin room or the German room, though it was both. Twenty student desks in four rows, eleven of them with names carved into the wood because this school had been here long enough for that. The blackboard with tomorrow's date in the upper right corner, where Marcus put it at the end of every class so the students could see it when they came in. The shelf behind the desk: the Latin dictionary, the mark book in its green cover, the spare chalk box.

The German grammar was not on the shelf.

All winter it had been there — spine out, between the dictionary and the mark book, and he had dusted around it every week since October. It was on the desk now. Cover up, in the working space, next to a composition book with student names written across the front in various hands, a different student's name in the corner of each page where a page corner was turned. And a pencil, short now — four inches at most — the tip broken off and not yet resharpened.

He stood at the door for a moment.

Then he went out and pulled the door back to six inches and continued his rounds.

---

He had been watching Marcus change since the school board meeting in February.

He did not try to name what he was watching in precise terms. Precision was the instrument he used for pipe fittings and furnace draws and joist tolerances, not for people. People he observed and understood by the slow accumulation of what he saw, and named what he saw when a name was useful, which was not always.

What he had been seeing: since February, Marcus had stopped holding himself quite so far from the door.

He'd had a quality, when he arrived in '42 and for the first year and more after that, of a man whose coat was not fully off. Not literally — Marcus was particular about his coat, hung it on the hook when he came into the house, kept it brushed. Something else. The quality of a man still working out whether this was the place where the coat came off and nothing happened. Of a man for whom *I am here* was still a provisional sentence, held out like a question rather than set down like a fact. He had recognized this quality when he first saw it because he knew it from the inside — from his own first years in Coldwater, before he had gotten to the provisional sentence himself. He had not thought about it in these terms at the time; he had simply recognized the quality in Marcus and noted it without speaking.

After February, it was different. Not that the man was careless — Marcus was never careless, and the particular quality of attention he gave to everything had not changed. The grammar was on the desk. The window was open in the mornings when the weather allowed. The chalk went onto the blackboard in longer strokes, the kind a person made when they were comfortable with the room they were working in. Henry saw these things on his rounds because he was in those rooms every morning, and his job required him to know exactly what was in them.

He had sat in the Legion hall in February, along the left wall in the extra chairs the Legion kept for when the membership room was being used for other business, while three men he had known for sixteen years decided something about a man he lived with. He had sat in rooms along the wall before, for different reasons, with different people at the table, and he knew how those rooms felt from that position — what it cost to be in the chair in front, what it cost to be at the wall, and that these costs were not the same cost. He had watched Marcus sit in the chair before the table and use the voice a man used when he had used it before, in other rooms, and had learned exactly how to use it. That was a specific kind of knowing: how you held your shoulders, how you waited for the next question, what you did not answer when it had not been asked. He knew it from his own practice. He did not know whether Marcus had it from the same place or a different one; that was not his to assume.

He had said *I have too*, walking out. Not because Marcus needed to hear it — or maybe he did; he couldn't say — but because it was true, and he had been careful, for some years, about leaving true things entirely unsaid.

What he had not said, and did not say now, and was not inclined to say: the two things were not the same. His twenty years here and Marcus's two were not the same condition with different names attached. They rhymed — he had seen the rhyme since the first months, seen it clearly and without needing anyone to point it out to him — but a rhyme was not a claim of equivalence, and the specific nature of what each of them had put down in this town, what it had cost each of them, what each of them had left in order to be putting anything down here at all, was not the same. He had been careful about this. He intended to remain so.

He was also glad Marcus was here. He was glad the grammar was on the desk.

He said none of this, because no one had asked him. His observations had a way of becoming invisible to the people who benefited from them, and over time he had learned to hold them. This was not the same as suppression. It was a skill — the skill of a man who had been watching long enough that the watching was its own kind of work, precise and complete and done for its own sake, not for the record.

---

The last item on the morning rounds was the south radiator in the main corridor.

It had been slow all winter — a fitting on the feed line that he had suspected was admitting air into the circuit, starving the pressure and keeping the radiator from reaching full heat on cold mornings. He had worked around it all season, balancing the other radiators on the circuit, and it had never been serious enough to pull the fitting during the heating season. Now it was May. He got his wrench from the furnace room, bled the fitting, and ran it until it was clear: eight seconds of air before the water came. He tightened the fitting and tagged it with a strip of red tape — his notation for the summer work order. He made the entry in the maintenance book: *South corridor, main feed, air in fitting. Bled and tagged, summer priority*.

He put the wrench away. He washed his hands at the utility sink. He could hear, out in the corridor, the east door opening — the first teacher arriving, footsteps on the floor he had mopped the afternoon before, the ordinary sound of the building coming on.

He went and got his coffee from the thermos on the shelf in the furnace room, the same shelf where Lillian packed it every morning and where it had been every morning for eighteen years.

His rounds were done.
