# What Language

"I'm looking for whoever manages the school's rowing dock," she said.

He was coming out of his classroom. He stopped when he saw her and took her in: the notebook, the working clothes, the look of someone who had come from the harbor.

"Mrs. Bowman," he said.

She had come at half past three on a Tuesday. The school was letting out—she'd had to step aside twice on the east stairs, students going down in a rush. Up here the hallway was quiet now. A door at the far end stood open; she could hear someone erasing a blackboard, the long soft strokes of the eraser going back and forth.

"The rowing dock," she said. "The mooring anchor registration is expired. Two years at least. I need to speak with whoever is responsible for the facility."

"I don't manage the dock," he said. He thought for a moment. "I believe it falls to athletics. Mr. Folger." He reached back and switched off his classroom light. "But I know where the dock is. I can walk you to it, if that is useful."

It was useful. She said so.

She had been to the school three times in eight years. Once for a spring fair when Owen was still alive, when that was still the kind of event she attended. Once for the fuel allocation matter in '43 that had sent the wrong delivery order to the school's account and required a correction in person. Once when Hannah Pfeiffer had been sent home early in November with a fever and there was no one else to walk her the three miles to the farm. She had come to this building and now she had come again, and the fact that she had the dock question—an actual dock question, a real permit matter—made the trip a trip she could enter in no ledger but the one she kept for herself.

They went down the east stairs and out through the side door.

---

The school's east side faced a gravel lot and a row of birch saplings planted too close together, their trunks beginning to crowd. Past the birches the ground dropped toward the Reach. She could see the water between the trees—flat and gray-green today, the tide close to full, the late May light lying on it without any shadow.

"The athletics director," she said. "Folger. He'll need to come to my office before June. Vessel description and two dollars. There's a compliance matter as well—I'll document that separately."

"I will tell him," Marcus said.

They went down through the birches. The May ground was soft underfoot still, giving a little with each step, and the smell coming up the slope was mud and brine and the cut-grass smell of the bank. She had grown up on that smell. It was the smell of the harbor's edge everywhere along the Reach, the particular mix of what the tide brought in and what the land gave back.

The dock was at the foot of the slope: a twenty-foot timber platform set close to the waterline. Old construction—she could see it in the framing before she was down the bank. The stringers were mortised rather than bolted, the joints pegged with wood. Before 1937, probably. Before the new tide-study figures had gone into the compliance requirements for floating structures on the Reach. She made a note of it.

Two rowing shells were tied on the outside—cedar strip, matched pair, the school's name in black stencil on each bow. She checked the dock lines first. No rot at the hitches. Proper leads on the cleats, the bitter ends coiled and tucked. She checked the cleats: older hardware, the heads worn smooth, but the bolts were set well and there was no corrosion at the wood line. She stepped out onto the dock. The planks were sound—no give, no flex at the joints, no sound of water getting into the grain. A dock that had been looked after, whatever else it might be missing.

She walked the length of it and knelt at the landward end.

The mooring anchor was a forty-pound block, chain run through a fairlead and down to an eyebolt in the sill. She pulled the chain. No play at the eyebolt—that was correct, and she wrote it down. She ran her thumb along three feet of chain: corroded on the surface, the surface links gone orange, but the metal was solid underneath. She had seen worse. She had passed worse. This would do for another season if Folger got the registration filed.

The mooring tag was looped through the ring at the top of the chain. A hardware-store tag, the kind the office issued with each permit, the registration year stamped in red.

Nineteen forty-one.

She wrote it down. She wrote the chain scope and the platform height above the mean waterline and the dock's approximate position on the Reach. She would mark it on the chart when she got back. She would write the note about the platform height—four inches below the new compliance standard, a matter of record, not urgent—and Folger could come in and they would deal with it in order.

She stood up.

Marcus Klein was standing at the shore end of the dock, his hands in his coat pockets, looking at the water. He had not moved or spoken while she worked. He was the kind of man who did not fill a silence—she had noticed this the first time at the harbor in December, the way he had stood at the foot of the wharf and waited until she was ready to speak, not finding words to put in the space. She had regarded it then with something close to approval. It was not a common quality in Coldwater Reach, where silence made most people nervous.

A lobster smack was crossing the middle water—she could see its shape, too far out to hear. The tide was as full as it was going to get. In an hour it would be running out.

She closed the notebook.

---

"There's something else I want to ask you," she said. "Not about the dock."

He turned.

She kept her eyes on the Reach.

She had not said this to anyone. She said it the way she said things that required care: directly, without preamble.

"Last October," she said. "The night before the body came in. I was doing a late check of the commercial moorings. Past eleven." A pause. "There was a man on the dock—the commercial dock, not this one. He said something. Two or three words, quietly. Not to me. I was thirty feet away, maybe more."

The anchor chain shifted once against the fairlead, the metal sound small and clear.

"It wasn't English," she said. "I've been trying to determine what language it was. I understand you speak several."

He was quiet for a moment. He was watching her face.

"Say it for me," he said.

---

She had been holding the sounds for seven months. They had worn down in that time—she knew that. Memory of sound was not like memory of a date or a measurement. She had done what she could to keep it: not calling it up too often, the way you kept anything fragile by not handling it. She had said it to herself a few times, in the early morning on the commercial dock, the harbor empty and the tide going out, standing where he had been standing. Trying to hear it again by saying it in the same place.

She said it: "'Prish-teh.' Something like that. And before it—a consonant cluster I didn't know. A zh sound with something harder behind it."

He was listening. The stillness of a man listening carefully, not waiting for his turn to speak.

"Say it again," he said.

She did. She could hear, saying it a second time, how imprecise it was. She had not known, when she first heard it, that she was committing it to memory. By the time she understood that she was, the man had already gone still and the moment was already going and what she was left with was this: two syllables, the stress, the consonant she couldn't reproduce properly. She had worked with worse instruments.

"Can you give me more?" he said. "Anything else you remember."

She thought. "The stress was on the first syllable," she said. "Hard on the first—harder than English. Harder than German. I know some German from trade, over the years. The stress in German follows the word. This didn't. It was fixed on the first syllable, and the rest was lower."

She stopped. That was all she had.

He was quiet. Not long.

"I think it was Czech," he said.

She looked at him.

His expression was precise. He was giving her what he knew, and he was being careful about the boundary between what he knew and what he was inferring.

"I cannot be certain," he said. "From that fragment, certainty is not possible. But the consonant cluster you are describing—the sound behind the zh—and the stress pattern: first syllable, invariable, hard. That is Czech. It is also consistent with Slovak. Czech is more likely."

"Czech," she said.

"Yes."

She looked at the Reach. The smack had gone behind the point.

Czech. He had been speaking Czech on the commercial dock in October, in the dark, past eleven at night.

She had spent seven months not knowing what she had heard, and now she knew. The knowledge was smaller than the not-knowing. It was always smaller. It did not close anything. It fit.

---

"The Coast Guard sent a letter in April," she said. "They identified the body. The name was Jan Václav Horak. Czech national. Last known location Halifax. October 1942."

She was watching his face when she said the name.

He looked at the Reach. One long beat. Then he nodded.

"Yes," he said. "That would be consistent."

She waited.

"Consistent with what?" she said.

He was still for a moment. She understood he was not avoiding the question—he was selecting. There was a difference, and she had been in enough conversations that required precision to know which one she was looking at.

"With a certain kind of person," he said. "A man moving through unofficial arrangements, in wartime. There were people who needed to reach places and had no official channel. There were networks for this—not organized in any central way, not documented in any record. Arranged, person to person, contact to contact. A man who needed to move from Halifax to Maine and had no other means." He paused. "I know the general shape of it. I don't know more than that."

The water moved small and steady against the pilings below.

She nodded once.

---

"Did you know him?" she said.

"No." A clean beat. "I knew the kind of person he might have been."

She looked at the Reach. She thought about what she was going to say. She had had it, she realized, since the letter came in April and she had read the name and the nationality and the last known location and understood what they added up to. She had not known she had it until now.

"So did I," she said. "After a fashion."

Neither of them spoke.

The May afternoon held the dock in its warmth. From somewhere in the school above them, a window came down—the sound of the sash, brief and ordinary, and then quiet. From where she was standing, she could see over the birch tops the edge of the commercial wharf. A quarter mile south and east. The place where she had been standing in October.

She was aware that both of them were telling the truth. He had said: I knew the kind of person. She had said: so did I. Neither of them was saying more than that. Neither of them was required to.

He did not ask her what she meant by it. She did not ask him what he meant. They were standing at a school rowing dock in late May and the tide was turning and both of them had said, in precise terms, exactly what they had to say.

"Thank you," she said.

"Of course."

---

She stepped off the dock and went up the slope. The May grass gave softly under her boots, the ground still carrying the winter's water. She went through the birch saplings—their branches beginning to reach across the path, a few more years and the gap would close—and around the east side of the building and through the front lot to the main road.

The harbor was ten minutes down the hill.

The tide was turning when she got there. She could see it in how the boats had swung at their moorings—all of them around now, noses pointed toward the harbor mouth. The working day was almost done. The smacks were in. A man was coiling line at the end of the commercial wharf and did not look up when she passed.

She unlocked the office. Set the notebook on the chart table. The end-of-month register was still open on the desk from the morning, the last entry in her own handwriting: fuel delivery confirmed, Pelletier account, May 19.

She would need to add the rowing dock: anchor registration lapsed, platform noncompliant by four inches, Folger to come in before June. The fee. Two dollars.

Czech. Jan Václav Horak. Last known location Halifax, October 1942.

She picked up the pen.

# D-Day

The field telephone rang at two minutes past three.

She was awake — had been since midnight, sitting at the chart table with the logbook open and the kerosene stove turned to its lowest heat. This happened sometimes, in the high seasons or the weeks after a difficult tide event, when the body refused the ordinary schedule and there was nothing useful to do about it but go to the office. She had the prior week's entries in front of her. She was not reading them.

She picked up the receiver.

"Eira." Lawrence Cary's voice, Rockland, who had been on the Portland relay since at least midnight. She heard the quality of it before the words arrived. "It's on. The landing."

She held the receiver. Outside the harbor made its ordinary sounds: a hull settling against the dock, water at the breakwater base.

"When," she said.

"Hours ago. By now they're ashore."

"Thank you, Lawrence."

"I thought you'd want to know."

"I did."

She replaced the receiver. The kerosene stove ticked. Through the window the harbor was dark and still — the boats at their moorings, the breakwater a low shape against the sky that was not quite sky yet, the channel running south beyond it in the dark.

She opened the logbook to June sixth and wrote the notation. Time, source, content. *At 03:02, L. Cary, Rockland, relays: landing at Normandy underway, troops reported ashore.* She kept it to the facts. The log required facts.

She read the notation back. She closed the book.

She sat.

Three hours yet before the boats would move. She had the five o'clock tide reading, the mooring check, the loose cleat on dock 3 she had been carrying the wrench for since April without stopping to use it. These things were not going anywhere. She sat at the chart table for a while with the stove ticking and the harbor outside, and she let the hour be what it was.

---

Dawn came at four forty-three. She had the tide reading by five: six-foot ebb, running clean past the breakwater on schedule. She entered the figure in the column beside the prior days — June fourth, June fifth, June sixth, the same eleven-foot range the harbor had been running since the tidal surveys of the 1890s, the channel doing on this particular morning exactly what it had done on the morning before it. She wrote the numbers in the column. They were correct. She shelved the book.

The boats began going out before the light was fully up. The morning was the finest of the early summer so far — clear sky high and pale, no cloud anywhere, the air holding the particular stillness of a calm June morning before the southwest wind found the channel. She stood in the doorway and watched the *Fair Weather* clear the breakwater at five thirty-nine, the *Edna May* following at five forty-two. The diesels carrying south on the flat water. A fine morning for it. She did not finish the thought.

She went out to the dock at six for the mooring check. South row first, then north. Fourteen boats in harbor this morning — she counted them by name and knew each berth, each owner, each boat's usual schedule. The count was down from the twenty-two she had managed before the fuel allocations reduced the working fleet to what it could sustain. Fourteen. She walked the south row and made her notes.

Dock 3. She stopped at the second post. The cleat was iron, surface-rusted, the near bolt working loose since the ice-out, and she had been carrying the wrench in her coat pocket for six weeks at least and had noted the cleat each time and kept walking. Not this morning. She pulled the wrench out and put it to the bolt and tightened. The cleat held. She checked the second bolt — still sound. She stood up and put the wrench back.

---

Galen Fuller was twenty-two. She had watched him on this dock since he was twelve years old, carrying his father's bait boxes and getting his hands wrong on the lines and learning the dock the way you learned it. Before the Army took him in the spring of 1943 he had crewed the *Helena* for a season and a half after his father's back gave out, and she had signed off on his vessel certification herself. She knew his hands from the bowline. She knew his father's boat, registered to Calvin Fuller, laid up since the back gave out entirely.

Robert Cates was twenty-four. Third generation on this dock. His grandfather had fished the Reach before the harbormaster's records existed in ledger form. His father had the *Bethia*, dock 7, which was at dock 7 this morning with Robert Cates not aboard it. The family had not received a telegram since the spring. This was, for now, how they had to read their information.

She did not know which beach. She did not know if either of them had made it off it. She did not know if either of them was alive.

She entered the morning departures. Time, vessel name, estimated return. Weather notation: *clear, no wind, sea state 1.*

---

At Beal's the radio had been on since early morning. She could hear WLBZ through the screen door before she pushed it open. The signal was clear today — the weather giving it a clean run down from Bangor, the BBC relay coming through with only the background static that never entirely went away.

Small crowd for noon. Bertrand Hatch off his lunch break, standing near the wall with his coat on — she looked at him once. Two women from the canning cooperative, a fisherman she didn't place, possibly from Spruce Harbor. Agnes Vane in her winter coat, collar up despite the June warmth. A boy of twelve or so on the counter, told to wait and waiting. Dumont behind the register with his hands flat on the counter, listening.

The broadcast filled the room. The voice on the other end of the wire was flat and formal, the cadence of a text prepared in advance for reading, not speaking — the quality of something composed for the record rather than the room. She stood near the door and listened.

*...this great crusade, toward which we have striven these many months. The eyes of the world are upon you. The hopes and prayers of liberty-loving people everywhere march with you...*

The static ran under the words. The words ran over the static. She listened to the whole thing — the voice going on with its large sentences, its nouns assembled for history. She noticed the distance between the voice and this room, the compression of the wire and the signal that was the only reason the voice was here at all. She thought about the two men. She let the voice finish.

She bought her ration items: two points of tinned goods, the sugar allotment, a spool of wicking for the stove. She brought them to the counter. Dumont totaled the points without speaking.

Agnes Vane, near the radio, said: "God willing they'll come home by Christmas."

Nobody answered. The static continued. The broadcast continued. Eira counted back her change and put it in her coat pocket.

---

At two o'clock a boat came in with a bent prop shaft.

She could see the trouble from the dock. The vibration in the stern as it came through the harbor mouth — a particular shudder she knew, the kind that meant the shaft had found something solid and the boat had made the run back running rough, the blade bent off true and the whole aft section shaking with it. She went out.

The captain was already over the transom looking at the shaft when she reached the dock. A forty-footer from up the coast, out of somewhere north — Castine, maybe, or Sedgwick. She had seen him once at a Knox County meeting and not since.

"What did you hit," she said.

"A ledge, I think. Past the Thornton island marker. Not on my chart."

"It won't be on your chart." She looked at the shaft. Blade bent thirty degrees off true, maybe thirty-five. "You've been running like that since the marker."

"Almost two miles. I didn't know if she'd hold together."

"She held." She went to the office and called the repair yard at Searsport. She gave them the damage description — bent shaft, probable twenty-two inches, unclear if the strut bearing had taken secondary damage. They had a slip on Thursday. She came back out to the dock and gave the captain the day and told him what he needed for the documentation.

"There's also a shoal notification to file," she said. "Your encounter goes to the chart service. What's your best position on the ledge?"

He told her. She wrote it down. When he went off to see about an interim berth she returned to the office and wrote up the shoal report: the coordinates, the depth estimate, the vessel name, the date of encounter. She filled in the date — June 6, 1944 — and looked at it and looked at the rest of the form and finished the form.

The afternoon was the afternoon. The shoal notification. The vessel registration. A call from the Coast Guard station about a dragged buoy needing reset on Tuesday. She logged it for Tuesday's schedule. She answered the calls and wrote the entries and did the work, which was here regardless of what was in France, which was here because it was always here, which required what it had always required.

At four-thirty she opened the logbook again. *At 03:02, L. Cary, Rockland, relays: landing at Normandy underway, troops reported ashore.* She read the notation through once. She turned the page and checked the prop shaft documentation. The figures were correct.

---

At five she walked out to the end of the breakwater.

Not a habit. Not something she did every evening or even most evenings. Something she did when the day had given her enough that the going-out seemed like the right motion for the close of it. She walked the granite blocks out to the harbor mouth and stood at the end in the June evening light, which was very good light — the long kind that lingered past the end of the work day, high and pale, the kind of light that had no intention of going down on schedule.

The fishing boats were coming in on the evening tide. She counted them: the *Edna May* first, clearing the gap at a few minutes past five, Amos Frye at the wheel. The *Fair Weather* behind it, then the *Persephone* with Gus Hollis running the deck loaded, throttling down as he made the turn. She knew the sound of each engine by now in the same way she knew the voices in the post office or the shape of the handwriting in the dock registers. Eight boats in tonight, the full count of those that had gone out.

The *Bethia* was in the count. She watched it come through the gap — Robert Cates's father, running it alone, bringing it around to dock 7 with the practiced ease of a man who had been putting a boat in this berth for thirty years and would put it there without thinking as long as his body let him. She watched the *Bethia* make the turn.

Behind each boat was a family's calculation. Not a safe one — she had learned what happened when the safety failed, had learned it in the harbor before dawn, eight and a half years back, standing on the dock with a coil of line she had no use for anymore. Not safe. Reasonable. The calculation that a working life on the water was worth the terms it came on. She had been watching this calculation from this breakwater since before the post was hers.

The *Helena* was not in the count. Hadn't been since the autumn of 1942, the berth taken over by Winslow's *Penelope Ann* on a monthly arrangement. She did not look at the *Helena*'s berth particularly. She looked at the boats that were there.

Galen Fuller might be dead. He might have been dead since before the harbor woke, since the dark hours when she was sitting at the chart table with Lawrence Cary's voice in the receiver. He might be in France tonight, alive, eating whatever they had given him, writing or not writing a letter home. She did not know. She would not know for some time. Robert Cates the same.

The last boat through the gap was the *Margaret Jean*, running behind as it sometimes did. She listened to the engine at idle — a vibration she didn't like, a loose fitting somewhere in the cooling system. She would mention it to Hollis Vane in the morning or she would not, depending on whether he came to the office before she went to the dock.

The harbor quieted, boat by boat. The diesels going down. The water at the breakwater base doing what it did at this hour — a low sound, not the harbor sound of noon or the harbor sound of the winter gales, but the specific sound of the harbor at the end of a June evening when the tide was turning and the boats were in and the light had not gone yet but was thinking about it.

She turned and walked back along the granite toward the shore.

# The Unfinished Letter

The school had released him for the summer at the end of June, and by the second week of July Marcus had not yet found the right orientation to days without schedule.

Not that the days were empty. He had a list — *Virgil to page ninety; the third decade of Livy; irregular verb forms for the fall section's second year; composition notes he had promised himself he would work through before September*. He had been at the desk at eight in the morning for three days running, and the list was present on the desk, and by ten he was at the window, having done none of it.

Henry left for the school each morning at his usual time. The summer maintenance schedule was apparently as various and demanding as the school-year one — more so, Henry said, since in summer you could finally get into the boiler room without the fire burning and do what needed doing. He left at a quarter to seven with his thermos and his key ring, and Marcus heard the door and came down for his own breakfast and was back upstairs before the kitchen had fully settled, and then the day was his.

Lillian was mostly in the garden. The tomatoes were coming in.

The window faced the street. Elm Street in July was not the same street as in October — the trees were full, the light moved differently through them, a filtered green-gold that arrived at the desk at an angle that changed across the morning. Two boys went past on bicycles at nine o'clock, arguing over something neither of them was conceding. A woman with a market basket turned the corner at nine-thirty. The harbor smell was there, as it always was — three blocks, the south wind — but summer muted it; the cold months concentrated it to something penetrant and specific, but July gave it back as simple salt.

He had the composition paper out by nine.

---

The difficulty was not beginning the letter. He knew who Professor Stern was — had known him since the autumn of 1940, when the Emergency Committee was still accommodating itself to the scale of what it would be asked to do, and Stern had been one of the men on the routing committee who moved names from the waiting list to the housing list to the placement list. Specifically, he had been the one who placed Marcus's name in front of the Coldwater High School hiring notice in the spring of 1942, when the previous Latin instructor's enlistment left the board with a classroom and no one for it. They exchanged letters occasionally. The last one had come in November — a brief report that the displaced scholars network was still processing applications, that two men from Prague had been placed at small colleges in Ohio, that the backlog in Halifax remained substantial. It was the kind of letter that said, between its lines, that the work continued, that the people moving through the channels were still moving or still trying to, that Stern himself was still at his desk in Cambridge six mornings a week doing what he could with what he had.

Marcus had begun a reply in December and not finished it. Then the school board review in February had taken whatever attention he might have given to correspondence, and then there had been the spring term, and then there had been May.

What he sat down to write this morning was not the December letter.

He drew the date at the upper right — July 10, 1944. He wrote the salutation. Then he considered, for what was probably longer than it needed, what the first sentence of the letter should be and what claim it would be making.

The first paragraph was not difficult. It was the official paragraph: Jan Václav Horak, Czechoslovak national, displaced person, last known location Halifax, October 1942. Found on the breakwater of Coldwater Reach, Maine, October 27, 1943. Official ruling amended April 1944: accidental drowning consistent with storm exposure, identification supplied. This was the public record, and to set it down was not to commit himself to any interpretation of it.

He wrote it. Five lines. He reread it, changed one phrase from *having arrived in Coldwater Reach* to *having apparently reached the Coldwater Reach area*, which was more precise and also more honest about what the record knew and did not know. Then he moved to the second paragraph.

The second paragraph was where he had to be careful — which was the first sign that *careful* might be the wrong principle for it.

What he wanted to write — what the letter needed, if it was to be a letter that could produce a useful reply from a man of Stern's knowledge — was an account of how he understood the probable route that had brought Horak to a breakwater in coastal Maine. Not what he could prove. What he understood, from his own understanding of how such movements worked: the way a name was passed from one contact to the next along a chain that no single person held entire, the way a farm in the right county of the right state could be a stopping point that appeared in no official record, the way a route that began with a legitimate transit document ended, sometimes, in an arrangement that was not quite anything the paperwork anticipated. He understood this the way you understood something you had been inside. He had been inside it — Paris to London in 1938 along a line of contacts whose names he had been given in the form of short descriptions only; London to a boat in 1939 that was not advertising its itinerary, a crossing that had ended in Sherbrooke, which had been the wrong end, the locked end, the one he had not anticipated and that had cost him two years.

He wrote the second paragraph. He wrote what he understood about the probable shape of such a route without naming specific people, specific farms, specific vessels. He wrote as a man of some structural knowledge who wished to provide context. He was accurate. The paragraph was precise. And when he reread it, what he found was that a reader of Stern's experience — which was to say, a reader who had spent four years moving people through exactly the kind of channel Marcus was describing — would read the paragraph and understand at once that Marcus was not an observer of these arrangements but a man who had traveled inside them himself.

He sat with this for a moment.

He was not afraid of Stern knowing. Stern almost certainly already knew — the Emergency Committee's files on Marcus's own case were not thin, and a man who read files as part of his daily work would have assembled the shape of the transit from the paperwork before he ever wrote about the Coldwater position in 1942. What Stern would read between the lines of the second paragraph was not new information. It was confirmation. He set this consideration aside.

The third paragraph was the actual question: was Jan Václav Horak known to any of the networks moving displaced persons through the Halifax-to-New England corridor in 1942 or 1943? Had anyone expected him at a particular point along that route? Was there a family that had not received word?

He wrote it. Four sentences, asking for only what could reasonably be shared.

He read the third paragraph again, and what he saw was this: if he sent the letter, and if Stern made inquiries, those inquiries would begin with the Halifax end — the last known location — and work toward the point of terminus, which was Coldwater Reach. Which meant they would work toward whoever had been the contact node in Coldwater Reach. He did not know with certainty who that had been. He had assembled a probable picture in May, walking home along Elm Street in the late-afternoon light, and the picture's most likely answer was the Pfeiffer farm, three miles inland on Route 9 — a German-American family, naturalized citizens, with four German prisoners on their property and a wife who had retreated from the world in ways that predated the war and would outlast it. A family already living at the margin of a social position that had grown considerably more precarious since December 1941.

If Stern inquired, and if the inquiry reached Albrecht Pfeiffer, what light it would bring would not be the kind Albrecht could manage without difficulty. He was a careful man who had held things carefully for a long time, and the light that came with official inquiry — even the unofficial inquiry of a well-meaning professor — was not careful. It spread. It did not stop where you asked it to stop.

Marcus set the pen down. He looked at the street.

There was also Eira Bowman. She had been at the commercial dock the night of October 26, 1943, and she had told him this in May at the school rowing dock — given it to him across a distance that was not quite close enough to be overheard and not quite far enough to require raising her voice. She had given him the language fragment she could not place, and he had placed it for her. Czech, probably Czech. She had received this without adding anything to what she had already said, which was the professional compression of a woman who had decided what she knew and what she was not going to say beyond the deciding. She had trusted him with something by saying it. He did not know what a letter to Cambridge would do to her position if an inquiry found its way back to this harbor, to this dock, to the night of October 26. He did not know that it would. He also did not know that it would not.

The fourth paragraph was simpler: he had written in a private capacity; he understood the sensitivity of the question; he asked only for what could be responsibly shared. He was reachable at the Elm Street address through September, and at the school from September forward.

He read all four paragraphs through.

The letter filled one and a half pages of composition paper, his handwriting smaller than usual because the questions required a certain density to sit on the page without spilling. It said what it needed to say. It asked a question that deserved asking — about a man who had died in October, whose name had arrived nine months later, whose family, if there was family, had not been told. The letter was correct. As an act of correspondence, it was what it should be.

He considered whether the precision of the second paragraph could be removed without losing the letter's usefulness, and took up the pen and tried — a fifth paragraph, a revision, working around the network knowledge with more circumspect language, gesturing at the probable route rather than indicating it. He wrote seven sentences, read them, crossed out three, rewrote them. What he had was a paragraph that a man in Stern's position would read as the work of a well-meaning outsider offering his vague impressions, which was not what Stern needed and was not what Jan Václav Horak deserved. The precision was what made the letter worth sending. Removing it removed that.

He crossed out the fifth paragraph.

He put the letter — four paragraphs, the fifth crossed out, one and a half pages of composition paper — in the right-hand drawer of the desk and closed the drawer.

---

He walked at two o'clock. The July town moved at its July pace — slower than April, but a different kind of slow; summer's was deliberate where winter's had been reluctant. He went north on Elm Street and then turned along the harbor road, the long way, which had better shade. Two lobster boats were in at dock and two still out. He saw Abel Holt working his stern post from a distance and raised a hand; Holt raised one back without looking up.

The harbor smell was the summer version of itself: the diesel still present but the cold brine softened to something almost mild, the kind of smell that in October would sharpen back to something that got into your coat. He walked the length of the commercial wharf. At the near end he could see the breakwater running two hundred feet out, the granite gray in the flat afternoon light, the algae line at the waterline dark and consistent. He did not walk out to the seaward end. He continued along the wharf road and turned back at the fish house.

The question the letter raised was still present. He did not try to close it.

What Jan Václav Horak had been, and what he had been trying to reach, and whether he had reached it in the fourteen hours or so between when Eira saw him at the bollard and when the lobsterman found him on the ocean face of the breakwater — these were things Marcus had assembled to the point where his assembly ran out. Past that point, nothing. The letter would not have resolved the nothing; it would have moved the nothing into the hands of a man in Cambridge who was busy moving other people through the same impossible channels, who would do what he could with what he had, which might be very little or might be something — and who would, in the process of finding out, illuminate a set of lives that had balanced themselves carefully in the dark for several years and had not asked to be lit.

He crossed Elm Street and went up the walk.

---

Lillian had made a cold supper, as she had been doing on warm evenings since the middle of June: tomatoes from the garden, sliced, with salt; bread; a wedge of cheese; water poured and waiting at his place. The tomatoes had come in that afternoon, and they were still warm from the field, the skin tight, and she said that they were ahead of schedule — usually she wasn't cutting them until the second week of August, but the warm June had pushed everything forward. He said they were excellent. He meant it.

Henry came in at six-thirty with his work bag and the day's Bangor Daily News. He set the paper on the corner of the table and read the front page standing up, the way he had done for as long as Marcus had lived in the house, then folded it and said something about weather building in the northwest, which usually meant a change in the next two days. They sat. Lillian poured from the water pitcher. Henry took the bread, and they ate in the comfortable quiet of an evening in the third year of a household arrangement that had found its settled shape some time ago.

Marcus did not mention the letter. He ate his tomatoes and his bread and his cheese, and the kitchen was the kitchen on an early July evening — the window open to the garden, the south wind carrying what it carried, the Bangor Daily News folded on its corner with whatever the day had sent down the coast. The light went slow and golden through the west window the way it went in July, and in July only, and Henry and Lillian were at the table, and supper was supper, and the harbor was three blocks south in the dark that had not quite arrived yet.

He went upstairs after. He read four pages of the Aeneid — the second half of Book Four, which he had been working through at no particular pace since June — and then closed the book and lay in the narrow bed with the window open to the street.

The drawer was closed. The question inside it was the same question it had been at nine in the morning, unaltered by the afternoon — still present in the way that some questions were present not because they awaited an answer but because they marked a position: *this is what you know; this is what you cannot do with it; this is what remains*. He had understood, writing the fifth paragraph and crossing it out, that the not-sending was not nothing. It was the same kind of answer the letter would have been, only it pointed inward rather than to Cambridge. There were people he had come to have some small obligation toward — not heroically, not in the language of obligation, but in the ordinary way that came from inhabiting the same rooms, the same winter, the same harbor road for two and a half years. He did not want to be the thing that lit them up. He had chosen, when it was a choice, not to be.

Somewhere down toward the harbor a door closed. The July insects had begun to thin, and what filled the dark outside the window was closer to silence than it had been a month ago. He turned on his side.

He slept.

# August

The harbor in August looked like money, and in a working harbor that was exactly what it was. Two dozen boats' worth of fuel and catch and dock fees, the sardine shed processing three hundred cases a day against its peacetime two hundred, the mooring fields at capacity for the first time since the summer of 1941. The breakwater algae line sat dried and pale at the low-water mark. The gulls were loud. The smell from the processing shed — brine and the sharper, organic smell of the sardines themselves, the whole compound of a building working at capacity — rode the afternoon wind south and settled over the commercial wharf and didn't move.

She noted it the way she noted the fuel figures. Not with pleasure, exactly. With accuracy.

---

The *Halcyon* needed to move, and the *Eda L.* with her, to free up room for the two seasonal boats that had come up the coast on the sardine run: the *Nancy Marie* out of Spruce Head, a seiner with a shallow draft and a captain who had opinions about his inside-approach requirements, and a double-ended lobster boat called the *Ida May* whose owner, Kell, had worked north from Penobscot Bay and seemed content enough with whatever berth he was given so long as he had access to the fuel line.

Getting the four boats into a configuration that worked had taken two mornings and three conversations with captains who did not want the conversations.

By Thursday morning she had them settled. She walked the inside wharf with a measuring line to confirm the clearance, which was what she had calculated it to be, and wrote the new positions in the mooring log and moved on.

The rest of Thursday was the fuel log and the accounts. The allocation she had argued for in December — in Portland, in a room with seven other harbormasters, the one from Searsport doing most of the talking while she sat with her figures and waited — had held through the season. Three hundred gallons above forecast with six weeks left in the summer schedule. If September ran long she had room for it. If January ran cold she had room for that too. She entered the week's consumption and set the log on the shelf and went outside.

Fourteen working boats. All of them running consistent schedules, logging catches above the July average, the whole fleet moving in and out of the channel like a mechanism that had been correctly adjusted and left to run. She had the departure and return log for July and the first weeks of August in front of her when she came back inside, forty-odd pages of entries in the standard format, and what those pages showed was a harbor operating within its own patterns. Nothing short. Nothing disrupted.

She noted this. The way you noted a boat's trim when it was running right — not because you were surprised, but because you kept checking. The checking was part of it.

The fleet operational. The accounts balanced. The tide log accurate and complete.

She put the ledger on the shelf and went back out to count the morning departures.

---

The news about Galen Fuller came on a Tuesday, mid-morning.

She was at the office with the provisioning log when Henry Cates came in. Robert's father — she placed him by vessel before face, the way she placed everyone: the *Bethia*, dock 7, a steady man who had worked that boat for over twenty years without presenting her with anything she could not solve in a conversation. He stood in the doorway without speaking, and she understood from this that he had not come about the boat.

She waited.

"Bertrand was on Bay Street this morning," he said. "The Fuller house."

She set her pencil down.

He told her the rest of it in the flat, factual manner in which such things were delivered. Galen Fuller. June seventeenth. Normandy — the telegram said Normandy, it did not say where in Normandy, and she did not ask. Two months and a few days between that date and this Tuesday morning in August.

She held the numbers. June seventeenth was eleven days after the landing. Sixty-six days between the seventeenth and this Tuesday morning in August. Both figures presented themselves and she let them sit without deciding what to do with them, the way she sat with a weather forecast that was only probably right.

She had known, since June sixth, that both of those young men could be dead and their families might not know yet. The notification system was not indifferent, only slow — no pattern she had been able to establish in the lag between the fact and the word of it, no correlation with branch of service or theater of operation or any other variable she had tried. Some telegrams came in two weeks. Some took months. She had set this knowledge aside the way you set aside what you cannot act on, and she had watched June go into July and July into August, and she had kept the log and managed the fleet.

Now one of them had resolved.

The confirmation had a different quality than the anticipation had. She couldn't have said exactly how.

"The family all right," she said.

"As well as you'd expect." He said it carefully, the words measured, the way Bertrand measured his own words on Bay Street. "Ruth's sister came up from Tenant's Harbor last week. She's still there. Bertrand stayed until nine."

Calvin Fuller had been working the *Helena* alone since the spring of 1943, sixteen months now, since the Army took Galen and Calvin's back gave out the same season. She saw him in the departure log most Tuesdays: *Helena*, dock 3 row, one operator, going out and coming back in without notation beyond the required times. The log had no column for the rest of it.

Robert Cates had been on the same beach. She looked at Henry Cates standing in her doorway and understood that the only thing she could offer him was the absence of bad news, which was not the same as good news, but was what she had. You did not say: *your son has not been killed yet.* You did not say it because the sentence was true and incomplete in equal measure, and because a man standing in your doorway with another family's telegram fresh in his mind did not need to be told what he already knew.

"Thank you," she said.

He nodded and went.

She sat with the provisioning log for a moment without working through it. The morning's entries were a sardine supplier's count and two mooring payments. She looked at the figures.

June seventeenth. She did not know what the front's position had been on that date — whether the worst of the landing's chaos had passed by then or was still present, whether eleven days was enough time for anything she might call a consolidation. It did not change the date. She picked up her pencil and returned to the provisioning log.

---

She saw Ruth Fuller two days later, at the harbor store.

Beal's ran a counter at the harbor end — not the full general store up the hill on Main Street, but the harbor account, closer to the dock: flour, salt, kerosene wicks, tobacco, a few canned goods. She went Thursday mornings. She had not expected to find Ruth Fuller there, and she supposed Ruth had not expected to find her.

Ruth was at the counter when Eira came in, a provisioning slip in her hand, waiting for Myra Beal to come out from the back. The store was not large. The counter was the counter. Eira set her own list down.

She had known Ruth for nine years in the way you knew everyone in a town of eight hundred: by context rather than occasion, by sight at the general store and the Legion hall and the dock, by the accumulated familiarity of years of shared weather and errand. She knew that Ruth ran her dragger herself, on the days the fuel allocation allowed, and had been running it since Galen went to the Army in 1943. She knew that Ruth Fuller was not a woman who came apart in front of the harbor store when she could avoid it.

She was aware, standing two feet from Ruth, of the inventory of things she might say. She ran through it quickly. Something about how sorry she was. Something about what Galen had been part of — about the campaign, its progress, its meaning, the several framings that arranged a man's death in the vocabulary of something large enough to hold it. She knew these framings. She had received versions of all of them after Owen, and she had accepted each one with something that had felt, at the time, like gratitude, and none of them had reached the actual thing, which was that Owen was gone and the harbor was not and she had the work to do. You could not receive a framing and be changed by it. You could only receive it.

What she could offer Ruth Fuller was what she knew from the inside of the harbor work. Not the other kind.

She looked up.

She said: "He was a good man with a boat."

Ruth Fuller looked at her. Not grateful, not surprised. She looked at the sentence the way you looked at a measurement that came out right — as if confirming something she had already known, and was glad to have confirmed by someone with standing to say it.

"He was," she said.

Myra came through from the back with Ruth's order. They moved aside. Eira paid for her flour and her wicks and walked back down to the harbor.

She did not spend time considering whether she had said the right thing. She had known before she said it that it was right, not because it was the formal condolence — it wasn't that — but because it was specific and true and complete and asked nothing of Ruth Fuller that Ruth was not already holding. You said what you knew, from the work you both understood. He had been a good man with a boat. She had watched it from the dock log and from the mooring rotation and from the fifteen years of entries in the departure record. That was her authority. She had used it.

The rest of the afternoon was the ordinary work: the mooring rotation check, the fuel certificate for the *Eda L.* that had been sitting in the district mail tray since the week before, a note to the sardine shed foreman about the truck-pickup window she had moved in July. She dealt with each of them in turn and entered the results in their columns and set the logbooks on their shelves.

---

She did the breakwater walk at four o'clock, as she did each week in the season.

The summer tides ran lower than the spring or winter tides, which pulled back the harbor enough to expose the lower granite courses — the places where winter storm damage showed as cracking or displacement that the high water covered the rest of the year. She went block by block, running the seams with her eye, checking the mortar courses for new fracture, noting the algae line at the waterline and its position against the August low-water prediction. The algae line in August had a different quality than in November: dried pale and brittle on the upper face, the smell less sharp in the heat, the whole surface texture of it different from the slick November version that cost you your footing if you weren't careful.

Nothing to flag. The two blocks on the north-facing run she had marked in May were unchanged — the crack in the lower seam had not progressed. She would note them stable and carry them on the winter watch list.

She walked to the seaward end and stood.

The harbor was behind her. The afternoon light came from the southwest at this hour — flat on the water, turning the surface pewter-gray where it ran in shadow and a thin, particular silver where it caught the sun direct. The chop was easy, the kind that came off the channel in a moderate southwest. A lobster smack on the north approach, hull-down still, making its run in. She watched it until she had the hull line and the approach angle: the *Bethia*, coming in on the north track that Henry Cates always used for dock 7. Expected in the count. She had expected him.

She had been standing at this end of this breakwater for eight years.

The first time had been in November of 1935, a week and a half after Owen's funeral, with the December cold already working its way in from the north and the fleet uncertain who it was taking direction from. She had not stood at the seaward end very long that first time. There was too much to do, and she had been in the part of learning the harbor that was also the part of learning to be someone the harbor would take seriously, and she had not yet learned to trust that simply doing the work was the answer to every question the situation was asking. She had walked the breakwater for the inspection and she had done the inspection and she had walked back.

At some point in the years since, the harbor had stopped being a thing she held at a slight remove, the way you held something that had belonged to another person. She could not locate when. It was not an event she could find in the log.

Galen Fuller was dead in France, his telegram sixty-six days in transit. His wife was going to run the dragger herself and the departure log would show it beginning this fall and probably through the next several years, and Eira was going to enter those departures without annotation because they required none. The harbor made room for competence. She had been demonstrating this.

The body that came in on the ocean face of this breakwater last October — she was standing at the approximate end where Hector Brann had found him in the lower course on the morning of the twenty-eighth — had been a man named Jan Václav Horak, Czech national, displaced person, last address Halifax in 1942. He had gotten this far. He had not gotten the rest of the way to wherever he had been going. The record had his name now, and the official ruling, and the date. What the record did not have was what it did not have, and she had understood this clearly since last October and understood it the same way standing here now.

She was still here. The harbor was still here.

The *Bethia* made the turn at the harbor mouth and came down the line to dock 7, clean and even, the way a man worked a boat he had worked for twenty years and would work until his body stopped letting him.

She turned and walked back to the office.

---

The tide was at three-foot-eight on the ebb, on schedule. She entered the reading in the log and set her pencil on the book.

Through the window: the commercial wharf settling into its evening quiet, the last of the day's work done, the two new boats in their adjusted positions on the inside. The light going long and gold over the water the way it went in August and only in August, too good to last, already tilting toward the ordinary dark.

She sorted the week's mooring fee receipts in order, the *Halcyon* and the *Eda L.* and the *Nancy Marie* and the *Ida May* in their new positions, everything accounted for. The harbor smell came through the bottom crack of the window — brine, diesel, the last of the processing shed's day.

She had the receipts sorted and the desk cleared by five-thirty.

She closed the ledger. She turned off the lamp. She went out, and the harbor was behind her, and the hill road was ahead, and the August evening was doing what August evenings did in Coldwater Reach — holding its light past the end of the work day, the sky going pale and clear in the west before it finally, gradually, let the dark come in.

# Harvest

The corn came in the last week of September. Twenty-two rows of it, the stalks dried to their final paleness and the ears heavy on the stem, and the work of it the same work it always was: pull the ear, snap the stem, walk the row. The prisoners worked two rows at a time, Karl and Fischer on the near side and Brunner and Krebs on the far. Lonzo sat at the field's edge with his rifle across his knees and the Bangor Daily News folded open in his lap, turned to whatever page he was on.

By the end of the second day she had the figure in her mind without meaning to count it: Karl was moving faster than the other three.

She had noticed it the way she noticed a slow cow before she could have named which one — without counting, and then with counting, and then the count confirming what she already knew. The other three moved with the efficient, conserving pace of men in their thirties and forties who had enough experience of physical work to husband it. Karl moved differently. He pulled the ears and walked the rows in a rhythm that was not rushing but was not conserving either. It was the rhythm of a man going at the work because the work was all he had to go at, and this was, in a way she could not quite close the door on, a thing she recognized.

She watched Lonzo once while she was watching Karl. His eyes had gone past the paper to the far row where Karl was working, and he was wearing the expression she had come to know over fourteen months as the expression he wore when he was looking at a thing he had already thought about and filed. Not suspicion. Not concern. An older man recognizing something in a young man that required no action and no comment and was, on the list of things that happened on this farm, simply one of the things that happened.

She went back to her own work.

The corn took two and a half days. The late hay after that, two days of baling in the September warmth, the kind of work where everything smells of cut grass and diesel and you move from the field to the baler to the barn without stopping. Then the kitchen garden — the squash that had been ready since August and needed the last pulling before the first hard frost, the potatoes still in the ground, the few remaining tomatoes off the vines. Magda did most of the garden in her measured way, moving from the kitchen to the rows and back without hurry. Hannah did the heavy pulling. Her father moved between the garden and the barn and the field in the route he had worked for thirty years.

The icehouse light was on past nine o'clock those nights. She had noticed this before harvest, but in harvest it was more visible because the days were long and physical and should have put everyone to bed early. Karl, she thought, with Lonzo's newspapers. She had seen him through the small window some evenings — the paper spread across his knees, angled toward the lamp, lips moving slightly in the careful way of someone who was reading in a language he had built one word at a time. She had known about the newspapers since winter. She had not thought about what to do with knowing until spring.

---

The fence meetings had been going since June — or since before June, if she was honest, which she mostly was not.

Not every day. Only when the work put her at the south fence section and Karl at the corresponding part of his field, which happened twice a week, sometimes three times, sometimes once. She had stopped tracking it as an event. She had also not told anyone about it, which was its own kind of tracking.

They talked about the farm, mostly. The soil in the south section, which drained toward the lower field in wet years and could sit waterlogged into May if the winter was bad. The squash, which needed a particular pulling so the vine didn't rip. What cover crop was worth putting in after the corn stubble turned under — she favored winter rye, and so did he, though he had reasons that were different from her father's reasons and she had found this interesting. He knew farming; he knew a continental kind that had rules overlapping with the Pfeiffer farm's rules without being identical, and the differences were worth discussing with someone who understood the question from the inside.

He was getting better at English. Not in the way a student got better at a conjugation, but in the way of someone who had learned the grammar before the fluency and was adding fluency to an already correct frame. He made errors — verb placement mostly, the position of *not* in a question — and the errors were consistent, which meant he was still working from rules rather than ear. But the sentences were longer. By August he had sentences with two parts: a main clause and something attached to it that complicated or qualified the main clause, which she had come to understand as Karl's natural way of thinking.

In German he was fully himself. The Franconian vowels she had been hearing from her father since before she could name them were the vowels Karl spoke, and in German there was less labor on either side. She could not follow everything — there were idioms and agricultural terms that she would have needed more years of Albrecht's country to have. But she could follow the shape, and she could make herself understood, and there were conversations in German that she came back from feeling as though she had been somewhere. Not somewhere with Karl specifically. Somewhere where the language was working the way it was built to work.

She carried the carved bird in her coat pocket most days. She had recognized this as a habit — a thing she was doing without deciding to do it — sometime in July, when she'd reached for her penknife and closed her hand around the bird instead. It was small and smooth, worn at the edges in the way of a thing that had been handled often; she had been handling it without noticing. She had not given it back. The opportunity had not arisen, she told herself. She understood this was not everything that was true, and she let the rest of it lie.

What she told herself the fence meetings were: two agricultural people, a fence between them, comparing notes on what they both knew. This was accurate. It left things out.

---

The conversation with her father happened on a Tuesday evening in early October, the harvest nearly done, the kitchen garden pulled, the whole farm in its post-harvest settling. She was at the sink with the supper dishes when she heard him come in.

She knew his sounds as well as she knew any sound in the house — the particular pull of the chair from the table, the way his left boot came down differently from his right on the kitchen boards. She kept her hands in the water.

He sat for a moment without speaking. The kitchen had the smell of the end of a harvest day: soil, woodsmoke, the warmth from supper still in the room. The October light through the window was already at its early evening quality, pale and going.

"*Du solltest vorsichtig sein*," he said.

She kept her hands in the water. She knew, when the phrase arrived, that she had been waiting for it or something like it; she had known without letting herself know in the way she'd become practiced at.

"*Womit?*" she said.

"*Am Zaun.*"

She turned and looked at him. He was looking at the table — at the grain of it, or at a water ring two summers old that she had been meaning to work out with oil. His hands were flat on the wood. The right little finger with its old bend. She could see from the set of his shoulders that this was not something he was working up to. He had already worked up to it. This was the speaking of it.

"*Ich bin nicht wütend*," he said. "*Ich sage dir, vorsichtig zu sein.*"

She looked at his hands for a moment.

"*Hast du etwas zu Lonzo gesagt?*" she asked.

"*Nein.*" A breath, quiet. "*Und ich habe nicht vor, es zu tun.*" He looked up then — not at her, at the wall past her left shoulder, and then briefly at her. "*Aber Lonzo ist nicht der Einzige, der an diesem Hof vorbeiläuft.*"

She turned back to the dishes.

He got up after another moment and went to his chair in the other room. She heard the German paper unfold — it came Thursdays, had come Thursdays for as long as she could remember. The sound of it was the sound of a thing that went on unchanged.

She finished the dishes and dried her hands. She did not go into the other room. She went upstairs, and through the floor she could hear him turning the pages, and she lay on the bed looking at the ceiling and did not think about what she was going to do, because she did not know yet, and the not-knowing was its own country that she was not yet ready to leave.

---

In the morning she watched Lonzo more carefully than she had since the early months.

He arrived at seven the way he always arrived: truck on Route 9, the gravel, the stool and the rifle and the paper under his arm. Twelve months of mornings in this same configuration. She had never seen him deviate from it.

She was in the near field with the corn stubble, running the disk harrow behind the mule, breaking the stalks into the turned earth. The work required enough attention that she did not have to be obvious about where she was looking.

He opened the paper to the Pacific section first. She knew this habit; she had watched it since February, when he'd mentioned his son was on a ship she'd never heard of. Pacific first, then the front page, then the agriculture column he read without fail and sometimes showed her if he found something relevant. He was reading now and not looking at anything besides the page.

She ran two passes.

He looked up in the middle of the second — she was at the far end of the field, eighty feet of turned earth between them, and when his eyes came up from the paper she was looking at him.

He nodded.

She nodded.

He went back to the paper.

She turned the mule at the row end and came back.

She could not read the nod. She could not tell, from twelve months of observation, whether she was in his report or not in his report — whether what he filed at the end of each day at the Coastal Patrol office said *four prisoners, seven hours, no incidents*, the way it always said, or whether it said something else in some column she could not see from here. She did not know what it would mean to be in the report. She did not know what it meant not to be.

What she knew — not because she had been told, but because she was not stupid and she had been watching for a long time — was that Lonzo had looked at the south fence section and made a decision about it. Some kind of decision, its terms unknown to her. She was inside the decision. She did not know what she had been decided about.

Lonzo had a son in the Pacific who didn't write often enough. He read that section of the paper first. In December his left hand gave him trouble. He had been sitting on this stool since October of 1943 and he had not, as far as she knew, said anything to anyone.

That was what she knew. She ran the last pass.

---

The following afternoon she was at the south fence with the compost cart, spreading the last load before the freeze came and made the ground too hard to work it in. Fork work — heavy and rhythmic, the kind that didn't require thought and so let her mind go to wherever it went on its own.

Karl came to that section from the far end of his row.

He had been working the stubble turnover, the same work she had done on her side in the morning, and he moved toward the fence the way he moved through everything — steadily, without hurrying. She kept her fork moving. When she looked up he was there.

He did not speak. She did not speak.

The distance was the fence, which was not very far.

The first hard cold front had come through the night before, and the October air had the quality she recognized as the turning: clear and with an edge to it, the shadows long at this hour, the field reading differently than it had for four months. The whole quality of the light changed at some point in September — she had never been able to say exactly when — and now the south fence looked like October instead of August, the same fence with a different face.

She drove the fork into the compost pile and let it rest.

He was looking at the turned earth on his side. She was looking at the turned earth on hers.

She did not know what she was going to do. This was, for the moment, the only thing she was sure was true.

The whole quality of the light changed at some point in September — she had never been able to say exactly when — and now the south fence looked like October instead of August, the same fence with a different face.

She drove the fork into the compost pile and let it rest.

He was looking at the turned earth on his side. She was looking at the turned earth on hers.

She did not know what she was going to do. This was, for the moment, the only thing she was sure was true.
