# The Harbor Log

The last of the seasonal boats were gone. The Nancy Marie had cleared for Spruce Head the final week of September; the Ida May had followed on the third of October, Kell running her out on the morning tide in a light northwest wind. The harbor was back to its winter numbers — twelve working moorings, the lobster fleet centered again, the summer berths empty and their cleats washed clean by the equinox blow. The sardine shed had closed its processing run the week prior. This was what October looked like, and it had looked this way for nine years under her management and for a good many years before that.

She was at the chart table by seven. Tide log open, the morning reading copied in at 0715. She set it aside and pulled the annual binder from the lower cabinet.

Log review. Every first full working week of October: twelve months of entries confirmed and closed, mooring registrations checked against the current register, incident notations followed to their official resolution, fuel allocation log balanced against the Portland figures. The accountancy of a year's harbor work — not audit, exactly, more the verification that the record said what had actually happened, entry by entry, so that when the district office asked she could answer for any month. She had done it every October for nine years. The previous harbormaster had done it before her, and she had learned the practice from his version of it and kept the structure without revision.

This year's review covered October 1943 through the present.

She had known, since January, what month it would eventually reach.

She opened to January and started.

---

January: equipment inventory, logged on the third. Chain counts, grapple hooks, the spare bollard hardware ordered in November and received on the 29th. Maintenance checks done. No incidents. She had done the January counts the same morning she found Owen's 1934 ledger in the back of the lower cabinet while tallying the chain. The old ledger was not part of the annual review; she had set it aside. She had come back to it later in the morning. The January log entry was complete.

February: a Coast Guard district letter on the ninth, standard quarterly operations acknowledgment, no action required. Nothing further on the October matter. She had not expected anything. Routine harbor operations. No incidents.

March: the spring opening. The Bethia on the fourth, Henry Cates bringing her down from the Camden haul-out on the morning tide. Mooring assigned to dock seven, as it had been for as long as Eira had been keeping this log and for some years before. Fleet registrations coming in. She checked each against the register. All current.

April: the main registration push. Six boats in, three renewals, two new mooring assignments from boats relocating out of Jonesport. She had processed the paperwork in a single afternoon at the chart table. The Portland fuel allocation confirmed on the 18th. All matched.

May: maintenance week. A corroded ring bolt on dock four's approach fitting, which she had replaced on the 14th with Declan Walsh's help. Materials and hours logged. No incidents. She checked the entry against the maintenance log. It matched.

June sixth: the D-Day notation. She had logged the radio call at 0302 — *Allied landings, Normandy coast; per radio, WLBZ 0300. Harbor routine* — and below it, same date, the dock-three cleat replacement she had done that morning in the window between the call and the fleet departure at 0530. She had also noted Eisenhower's address on WLBZ at 1820 — not harbor business, but she had put it in as context, as she had been in the habit of noting major radio events when the harbor was immediately involved. Fleet out on schedule. No incidents.

She held the June entry for a moment.

Then she turned the page.

July: the Nancy Marie arrived on the twelfth, temporary berth at dock eight, mooring fee paid in advance. The Ida May arrived the nineteenth at dock nine, Kell's double-ended hull needing the longer slip. Both registrations current. Sardine processing shed at capacity through July; harbor boat count and fuel draw elevated accordingly. She confirmed the allocation against the Portland records. They matched.

August: fuel margin held at three hundred gallons above forecast, confirmed on the 15th when the Portland figures came in. Ruth Fuller's dragger registered at dock six with Ruth as sole operator — she had updated the entry in July, Ruth having been running the boat herself on fuel-allocation days since the spring. Three mooring adjustments in August for the high-summer sandbar drift on the north channel approach. All corrected and logged.

September: no incidents. The sardine shed winding toward close. The Nancy Marie's departure logged September 29th, cleared for Spruce Head as anticipated. The Ida May logged October 3rd, Kell out on the morning tide.

She confirmed the departure entries against the register. They matched.

October 1944: current entries. Two and a half weeks of routine operations, tide readings, mooring notations, the weekly fuel draws. An approach-marker adjustment at dock seven on the 9th when Henry Cates came in on the strong northwest chop with the Bethia riding heavy. She had moved the marker eighteen inches north and logged it. The entry was current.

She confirmed the present entries against the register.

Everything matched.

She closed the front section of the binder.

She turned to October 1943.

---

The entries were present.

October 11th, 1943: barometric drop, storm advisory from the Coast Guard district office. Fleet pulled back from the outer moorings per standard protocol. She had confirmed the outer mooring lines herself on the afternoon of the 12th, walking the full dock in the blow. Entry complete.

October 14th, 1943: body found on the seaward face of the breakwater by Hector Brann, crew of the Alicia B., at approximately 0700. She had logged the notification at 0750, the Coast Guard arrival at 0820, the removal of the body from harbor jurisdiction at 0930. Unknown male individual, civilian appearance, no papers found on the person. Entry complete.

The entries following through the month: Lt. Parsons's visit on the 17th, her formal statement, the official ruling received in November. Accidental drowning, unknown individual, case closed to harbor records. Notation dated and signed. Entry complete.

She turned back one day.

October 13th, 1943.

Her entry for the thirteenth: *Mooring check completed, commercial dock, 2300. Fleet secure. No incidents. Tide reading 11.2 ft.*

She read it twice.

The entry was accurate in what it contained. The mooring check had been completed. The fleet had been secure. The tide had read 11.2 feet at 2300 hours. Nothing on the dock that night had required notification to the Coast Guard, or action of any official kind she had been empowered to take.

She had not entered what she had seen at the far bollard.

---

Owen's J.T. entry: January 8th, 1934, with the later addition below the original notation in his handwriting, the slope different from the dated entries above it. *This not entered at time of incident; entering here as complete account.* Then the account. His initials at the bottom.

He had been in Portland when the incident with J.T. happened. His deputy had logged the surface facts. Owen had read the entry when he returned and had made it complete.

She had been thinking about this since January. The difference between Owen's practice and hers. He had deferred completeness and returned to it; there was a word for what he had done. What she had done was different. She had written the tide reading and the mooring check and the words *no incidents* and turned off the lamp and gone home and done it again the next morning and the morning after that, for twelve months.

He had come back to it.

She set her pencil down on the chart table.

---

At 2300 hours on October 13th, 1943, she had completed the mooring check and was walking back along the commercial dock toward the office. The storm had been clearing for the previous two hours, the harbor settling, the boats riding more easily at their lines as the blow moved northeast. She had made the outward pass down the full length of the commercial dock checking each bollard and cleat, and on the return she had seen the man at the far end.

Civilian coat, not oilskins or harbor work wear. Standing at the far bollard with his weight shifted forward, not at his sides in the way of someone working a line. The posture of a person waiting at a specific location rather than passing through. She had not recognized him. Not a registered vessel operator, not a face from the fleet or the dock work or anywhere she could place him.

He had been facing the water when she went past. He had not turned.

She had caught the second figure at the edge of the dock light — a shape in motion, already turning away, already in the first steps of departure. She had heard something: two or three words, spoken low, an exchange between the two of them. Not English. A sound she could not place at the time, consonants she had no frame for. The second figure walked inland before she reached the far bollard end. An ordinary pace, not running.

She had stood at the bollard end for a moment, long enough to see that the first man was still there, that his coat was wet at the shoulders and that he had not turned toward her. She had looked at him for the length of three or four seconds.

She had not approached. She had not called out. She had turned and gone back to the office and logged what the log said now: mooring check complete, fleet secure, no incidents, tide 11.2 feet.

When she turned off the lamp she had told herself there was nothing to enter: a man on a public dock after hours, a second person who had already departed, a few words in a language she did not recognize. No law broken that fell within harbor jurisdiction.

She had known, as she locked the office door behind her, that this was not everything that was true.

---

She knew things now that she had not known that October night.

Jan Václav Horak: Czech national, displaced person, last known address Halifax, Nova Scotia, 1942. Thirty-eight years old or thereabouts. No papers. The Coast Guard district office had sent her the name in a form letter five months after they closed the case, in April 1944. She had read it twice, noted it in her own log margin, and filed the letter.

She knew the language. In the spring she had gone to Marcus Klein — she had brought him what she could reconstruct of the sounds, the consonants she had been carrying for seven months — and he had given her the answer with the careful precision he gave to answers: Czech. Not German. Czech.

A Czech displaced person, last known Halifax, moving south along the coast through the channels that a man without papers moved through in 1943. Making for Coldwater Reach, for whatever he had been making for here. The second figure at the dock had walked inland. She had not identified that person. She had assembled what she could, from what she had seen and what Marcus Klein had been willing to tell her, and it stopped there.

None of this fell within harbor jurisdiction. None of it changed the official ruling.

What it had changed, slowly, across twelve months: the quality of the blank in the October 13th entry. She had known the blank was different from an ordinary omission since the morning Hector Brann found the body. She had carried that knowledge through the official inquiry, through the case closing, through the winter, through reading Owen's J.T. entry in January, through the spring and summer and this October. She had watched the blank and she had known what it was.

She picked up the pen.

---

She wrote below the original entry, in the space remaining on the dated page. The late notation format was the same regardless of what it corrected; she had used it twice before in nine years, both times for routine administrative matters. She wrote steadily, in the same hand she used for all harbor log entries:

*Late entry, dated October 1944: 2300 hours, 13 October 1943: completed mooring check, commercial dock. One unidentified individual present at the far bollard, civilian appearance, not a known registered vessel operator. Observed in the company of a second party who departed walking inland before I could make identification. No approach made. Not entered at original time. Entering now in accordance with complete record.*

Below that:

*— E. Bowman, Harbormaster, October 1944.*

She set the pen down.

---

She read it.

The entry said what had happened. An unidentified individual at the far bollard. A second party, direction inland, departed before identification. No approach made. Not entered at original time.

It did not say that she had known the next morning, looking at the body in the gray light on the breakwater face, that the man at the bollard and the body were the same. It did not say that she had spent twelve months aware that the Coast Guard's official record rested on the incomplete version — not falsely, not through anything she had told them that was untrue, but through the omission, the tide reading and the words *no incidents* and everything that those words did not say. The entry said what she had seen, at the distance and in the light she had seen it, on the night of October 13th, 1943. It said that she had not entered it at the time and was entering it now.

The entry did not name Horak. She had not known the man's name on October 13th, 1943. The entry was the night's evidence, and the night's evidence was an unidentified individual. That was accurate. She had not identified him then and could not identify him in this entry now.

The second party was also unidentified. She had not been able to identify them that night and had not been able to identify them since. The entry said exactly that.

She read it a second time.

The record was complete.

---

She closed the binder. The stove was ticking on its steady burn, the morning cold fully pushed back from the desk. Outside the office window the harbor was at its October work: the lobster smacks at their moorings, the northwest chop making the small easy motion the boats were rigged for at this time of year, the channel mouth open and grey under the overcast. The Bethia in dock seven. Ruth Fuller's dragger in dock six, tied up for the morning. The two empty berths where the Nancy Marie and the Ida May had been.

She sat at the chart table for a few minutes with her hands flat on the closed binder.

Horak was still dead. The second person on the dock was still unknown. The Coast Guard had its ruling and had not reopened it. The case had been closed for twelve months and would not reopen; no one had reason to reopen it and no evidence had emerged that would compel them to. The body had been recovered and interred somewhere in the official processes that handled bodies without families to claim them.

The entry she had written was in a log that the Coast Guard district office read only in the event of an inquiry. There would be no inquiry.

What the entry changed was not any of this. What it changed was the record. By her hand, in her handwriting, in the log she had kept for nine years. This log, not Owen's — hers. The record now said what had been on the dock on October 13th, 1943. An unidentified individual and a second party and no approach made and not entered at the time. This was the truth of what she had seen, and it was in the log. She had done what Owen had done, what a harbormaster did when they were doing it honestly. She had come back to the omission and she had made it complete.

Whatever she had assembled or suspected or held without saying in the months between then and now — that was not the log's business. The log's business was what she had seen. She had entered what she had seen.

She opened the current log.

She wrote the noon tide reading. Eleven feet, four inches. Clear. Wind north-northwest, seven to ten. Fleet at moorings.

She closed the log.

She took her coat from the hook by the door and went down the dock to walk the breakwater.

The October tides exposed the lower granite courses on the seaward face; she checked them as she went, working from the shore end out. The seam between the first and second course on the north face had been taking some water since spring; she crouched and ran a hand along the joint. Dry today. The iron pin on the third section was holding, which she had been watching since August. She went all the way out to the end, which was the habit, and stood at the seaward edge looking back at the harbor.

The office at the foot of the wharf. The cedar shingles. The fleet at the inside moorings. The empty summer berths. The harbor at its winter numbers, which were its honest numbers, what it was when the seasonal work cleared off and left the actual work.

She stood there for a moment. Not long.

Then she turned and walked back. There were mooring receipts to sort. There was the fuel report from the Portland office she had not yet opened, which would need to be answered by Thursday. The review was done.

She went inside and latched the door.

# The Names on the Board

Henry was at the table when Marcus came downstairs, the coffee already made and the bread on its board. He set his cup down when Marcus came in.

"Two men from Coldwater," he said. "In the German counteroffensive. I heard it this morning — a parent came to the building before seven." He paused. "The other name is Calvin Wilkes."

Marcus stood at the stove and poured his coffee. He did not say anything yet.

"He was in your Latin class," Henry said. "First year you were here."

"Yes," Marcus said. "I remember him."

He sat down. The kitchen was the same as it was every morning: the lamp over the table, the stove working, the window on the south side fogged where the warmth inside met the cold outside. Henry's cup made a small sound against the wood when he set it down. Neither of them spoke.

The boy's face came without effort. Calvin Wilkes — not a strong student in the grammatical sense, which was to say that his ablative constructions had been uncertain throughout the fall of 1942 and had never quite settled in the spring. But he had had a real facility for the rhythm of the sentences, which was not something Marcus could teach and not something he had expected from a student whose case endings required the kind of repeated correction that tended, in his experience, to indicate that the language was simply not going to come. Most students learned the structure and kept it at a distance, handling it as a formal object rather than working through it from the inside. Calvin had been different. He could recite the Virgil passages with a quality of feeling that Marcus had noticed and not remarked upon — remarking tended to kill it. He had kept marking the ablative errors down all year and had kept hoping the recitation would eventually close the gap.

It had not.

"The other man," Henry said. "Ned Harker's boy. He was on Galen Fuller's dragger before he enlisted. His mother's on Mast Street."

"I do not think I knew him," Marcus said.

Henry stood and took his cup to the stove.

---

The servicemen's board was in the hallway to the right of the main entrance — a framed corkboard, the white cards in rows going back to the spring of 1942. Marcus had walked past it every school day for two years and ten months. He could account for the position of each name.

Calvin Wilkes's card was in the third row. It had gone up in June of 1943, when he enlisted at seventeen. It had been a white card like the others since June of 1943.

It was not white like the others now. There was a black border around it — a thin frame, not theatrical, the standard thing that Bertrand Hatch placed on the card when the telegram arrived. Marcus stopped in the hallway and looked at it.

Fall of 1942, spring of 1943. One complete school year: the ablative absolute in November, the passive periphrastic in February, the Virgil in April. Calvin Wilkes in the second row, right side, the seat he had claimed by the second week of September and held for the year. The way he had set his pen down when Marcus called for the recitation, which was not something most of them did.

Marcus went to his classroom.

---

Third period was his third-year section — eleven students working through Caesar's *De Bello Gallico*, the standard text for the year and the text that came next in order. He wrote the construction on the board: *quo cum consilio convenerant*, explained the relative clause of purpose, and worked through the passage: translate, identify the case, identify the construction, explain the choice.

The passage was not the wrong text only because it was about war. Caesar's *De Bello Gallico* was always about war; that was its nature and its curriculum reason for being there. It was the wrong text because it was about a Roman army moving through a country with the calm procedural vocabulary of completed action — a vocabulary that assumed the events were finished and could now be held at the distance from which patterns became legible. He had taught it for two years in this school and had never entirely resolved what it meant to do so: students with brothers in the Pacific, fathers at the six o'clock radio. He had decided, sometime in the spring of 1943, that the resolution was not his to make. What he could offer was the grammar, and the attention, and the occasional passage that a student might hold for reasons Marcus would not always know.

He did not mention the Ardennes. He did not mention Calvin Wilkes. He taught the lesson, assigned the written exercise for the following morning, and dismissed the class at the bell.

After the last period — the first-year fundamentals section, which was where Calvin Wilkes had been in the fall of 1942, the same room, the same window light in the same mid-afternoon position — he stayed. He had papers to grade and he graded them. The school emptied around him, the hallway voices going, the main door at the far end of the corridor closing and closing again, and then the building going quiet in the way it went quiet at the end of a school day in winter, with the furnace working inside the silence and nothing else.

He graded the papers. He did not hurry.

Calvin Wilkes had sat in the third seat from the window. He had written his exercises in a slightly cramped hand that had improved through the year. By April he had been writing the ablatives correctly most of the time.

By April he had also been able to recite the opening lines of Book Two of the *Aeneid* with a quality of feeling Marcus had not anticipated — in part because Calvin Wilkes was not, technically, supposed to have encountered the passage at all; Marcus had used it as an example of a syntactic construction in February, and Calvin had held it. *Conticuere omnes, intentique ora tenebant.* All fell silent and held their faces intent. The sentence that opens Aeneas's own account of the fall of Troy. Calvin had not known what it was the opening of; they had not gotten there. But something in his reading of it had been right, in the way that some students arrived at a language before they could explain how, and Marcus had marked the ablative down and said nothing about the rest.

He finished the papers. He put on his coat and hat and went out.

---

The walk home was three blocks. He had made it in every weather since March of 1942 and knew it the way he had come to know a small number of things in this town — the exact position of the January ice on the school's side-yard steps, the way the harbor road received the wind off the inlet, the particular sound the Elm Street corner made at night when the cold had been extended for some days. He had not intended to know it so well. He had not intended most of what came from having been in one place for nearly three years, which was longer than he had been anywhere since Vienna.

January in Coldwater Reach was a particular kind of dark — the sun not fully up until after eight, gone before five, the sky between those hours a flat pewter that gave no warmth but gave light enough to work by, which was all the light a working town required. He had learned to find this adequate.

He was thinking about accumulation.

He had his brother in Vienna, from whom he had had no word since the autumn of 1940. That was more than four years of silence, which had become its own kind of knowledge: not the absence of information but a form of information, indicating that the channels through which word might have come had closed, or that his brother had reasons of his own for not reaching them, or both. He had worked through it from many angles in the early years and had eventually stopped working through it from angles and simply carried it.

He had his colleague from Paris — Kessler, a classicist who had been at the Sorbonne since 1933 and whom Marcus had known for three years of occasional conversation before leaving Paris in 1938. In September of 1942 a second-hand source with the Emergency Committee in Cambridge had sent word that Kessler had been arrested in August. He had received nothing since. That was what *status unknown* meant in January 1945.

He had the men from Sherbrooke: a handful he had remained in contact with for the first year after his own release, and had then stopped, not because they had ceased to matter but because the contact had become indistinguishable from the carrying, and he had enough to carry.

He had Horak — the dead man who had come to rest on a Coldwater Reach breakwater in October of 1943, whose name and probable history Marcus had assembled and placed in the drawer where he kept the things he held without further examination.

And now he had Calvin Wilkes, who had been alive eight months ago in this town and who was dead now in eastern Belgium in what the radio called a counteroffensive. He had known this boy. He had graded his papers. He had listened to him recite *Conticuere omnes* in February of 1943 with a quality of feeling that had warranted more than the ablative correction Marcus had put in the margin. He had taught him for a year in the classroom at the end of this three-block walk, and Calvin Wilkes was dead in Belgium, and Marcus was walking home in the January dark past the same houses he passed every evening.

This was not the same as the other losses.

He considered this again. What he meant: this was the first loss that belonged to this life, this town, this specific classroom. The other losses had followed him here; this one had been waiting for him when he arrived.

He was not certain the distinction held.

He turned the corner onto Elm Street. The Crow house with its kitchen light on — the lamp over the table visible through the window, the yellow square of it in the dark. He had been looking for it when he turned the corner for longer than he had recognized. He had become aware of the looking at some point in the fall and had not done anything about the awareness.

---

Henry was there when Marcus came in, and Lillian was at the stove. She had made soup — the bean soup she made through the winter months, with bread and what remained of the week's butter. They sat down and ate. Henry had the fuller account from Beal's: the two names confirmed, the approximate circumstances, the Battle of the Bulge establishing itself now as the phrase replacing German counteroffensive in the way that phrases settled as an event accumulated its name. Lillian had heard some of it from the church women's group. They covered it between them and then moved on, the way the kitchen moved on: the woodpile question, the Congregational women's event Saturday, whether the coffee at Beal's had improved or whether the November blend was now simply what coffee was going to be.

The kitchen was warm. The stove had been going since afternoon.

After supper Lillian went to her sister's on Birch Street, as she did most Wednesdays. Henry cleared the table and began the dishes. Marcus sat.

"Did you know the Harker boy?" Henry said. He was at the sink, back to the table, running the water.

"Not from the school," Marcus said. "He would have finished before I arrived, or nearly."

Henry washed a bowl and set it in the rack. "He was good with boats. That's what Fuller always said." He paused. "Ned's going to take it hard."

Marcus said: "You knew Calvin Wilkes."

"Since he started at the school. He was a talker in the halls — always had something to say about something. I used to let him keep going while I was doing the floors in the morning." Henry set another bowl in the rack. "That's what you remember. Not the quiet ones."

"He could recite Virgil," Marcus said.

Henry turned slightly from the sink. "Is that something they do in the first year?"

"I used passages as examples — syntactic constructions. He held one. More than most students do." Marcus paused. "He could not explain the grammar behind it. He could do the thing itself."

Henry turned back to the sink.

After a moment Marcus said: "I find I think about my students long after."

"I suppose that's what teaching is," Henry said. He said it not as consolation but as a fact that had simply been true for a long time and had not changed its character.

He finished the dishes and dried his hands and put the plates away, the bowls, the cups, each thing where it went. Then he sat down across from Marcus with what remained in his cup.

---

Outside, the cold was at the clapboard — the small sounds a house makes in January when the temperature drops after dark, the contraction of the sills, the occasional shudder in the window glass when the wind came at it. The lamp over the table. Henry with his cup and his own particular quiet; he had his losses too, twenty years' worth of them in this town, and Marcus knew some of them and not others, and they did not, as a practice, place their losses alongside each other's. They were not the same kind of loss. Both of them knew this well enough not to say so.

Marcus had his hands on the table and nothing in them.

He was thinking about the board in the hallway — not Calvin Wilkes's card specifically but the whole of it: the rows of white cards going back to 1942, the names he had walked past every school day for two years and ten months. He knew those names. He knew which ones had come from the fishing families and which from the inland farms, which had brothers still here, which had been in his classroom and which had not. He had been here long enough to know them.

Nearly three years. The arithmetic of his displacements had recently stopped adding up in the way it once had: Vienna, Paris, London, Sherbrooke, Cambridge, and now here for nearly three years — longer than Paris and London and Cambridge combined. He had arrived in March of 1942 with his document file and his tea and his understanding that this was provisional, and the provisional had extended long enough that he was no longer certain what it was provisionally in the way of.

He could not say exactly when the arithmetic had changed.

He had this kitchen. He had this table, this man across it with his cup, the lamp over them both making the window a dark mirror. He had a classroom at the end of a three-block walk and a board in the hallway with names he had come to know. One of those names had a black border around it now, and he had graded that boy's papers for a year, and the boy was dead in Belgium, and Marcus was sitting at this table in January of 1945 and he had not moved.

He could not yet say what this was.

He was sitting in it.

# The Spring Opening

April, and the harbor moving.

The ice had been out of the main channel since the third week of March — long gray pans of it riding the ebb tide south past the breakwater mouth, dissolving in the chop before they reached open water. She had watched from the office window without going out. There was nothing useful to do about ice going out; it went when it went, same as it always had.

The first week of April she had walked all the mooring lines. Three on the east row had ice-chafe bad enough to need ricing; she found one on the main float that had chafed through to the splice entirely, which meant it had been weakening since before the freeze and she had missed it in the fall inspection. She replaced the whole length. She had riced the east row lines herself, kneeling on the dock planking in the early cold with the caulking iron, and entered both repairs in the mooring log. Standard notation. The usual spring assessment of what winter had taken.

Now it was the standard spring inventory, and she worked through it the way she always did: depth soundings off the north pier at low tide, the mooring condition check, the fleet registration review. Ten years of spring openings, and the sequence was her own by now — not Owen's sequence handed down but the order she had settled on in her second year, when she understood what the harbor needed first. Depth soundings before slip assignments; mooring check before registration. It fit her the way any well-worn procedure fit: not noticed, just the shape of the work.

Depth soundings: two days running, the tide gauge and the weighted line, working along the north pier face from the bollard to the end. The year before's sounding log had two shallow readings at the channel's edge, same location both times, which meant winter silting from the January storm surge. She marked the position on the sounding chart and flagged it for the summer dredge schedule; the channel was still inside clearance for the second float's boats, but narrowly. She would watch it through the month.

Fleet registration review: nine boats on the main float, three on the east pier, one at the commercial wharf. She pulled the registration files and went through them against the winter registry.

The fleet was smaller than it had been in 1940. She had taken twenty-three boats through the spring opening of that year; this spring it was thirteen. The difference was in the ledger if you wanted to count it — boats sold, men gone, the war and the fuel allocation together. She did not count it this morning. She went through the files against the registry and noted what had changed.

Two new registrations. The first was a lobster dragger that had come down from Owls Head when the operation there folded — the owner, a man named Severance, had done the Portland transfer and come to her for the slip assignment. She had assigned him the outside berth on the east pier, right for the dragger's draft, and entered him in the Coldwater fleet ledger: vessel name, tonnage, operator's certification, assigned slip. Standard form. The second was Danny Jessup's first boat, a twenty-two-foot trap boat he had worked two seasons to buy. The engine was sound; she had checked the documentation and the certifications and assigned him berth seven on the main float, the small-boat row. She entered both and noted the dates.

Two boats out since last fall.

Haskell's sloop, sold in November to a Rockland man. She had sent the release notice to Knox County in November and heard nothing since, which was how Knox County handled these things; the transfer was complete in the record.

Galen Fuller's dragger. Ruth Fuller had renamed it and reregistered it in her own name, coming in on a Monday morning in February with the completed forms and a check for the registration fee. She had sat across the chart table from Eira and signed where the form required. She said she was thinking about running the lobster route herself come May, if she could find a mate who knew the ground. Eira had said there were a few men who knew it; they had talked through who was available and what the pound was paying. Then Ruth Fuller had stood and shaken Eira's hand and gone out. Eira had entered the registration in the fleet ledger under the new name, Ruth Fuller as registered operator, and filed the original in the back cabinet. Fifteen minutes, start to finish. She had not stopped over it; the paperwork was the same paperwork, which was what it was supposed to be.

She had processed Robert Cates's spring mooring renewal the day before. Berth 14 — his grandfather's berth and his father's berth before him, the third-generation berth that had sat empty for fourteen months. He had come home from France in February, thirty pounds lighter. She had heard this from his father in March, running into him outside the post office: the old man red-eyed and saying Robert was standing, that he was home. By April, Cates had been out in his boat three times — twice coming in with a decent haul, once with nothing. A normal spring. She wrote the mooring renewal in the ledger: berth 14, April 18, 1945, confirmed and paid.

Cates's renewal was the first berth reassignment moving back into the fleet, rather than out of it, since the previous spring opening. She noted it the same way she noted everything else.

By mid-morning she had the registration review done and the depth soundings entered. She checked the mooring assignments against the harbor chart. Everything in its place. She set the chart on the drying rack and went to make coffee.

---

At noon she walked to Beal's for flour and two kerosene wicks.

The radio was on. It was always on at Beal's now, had been since November — the Ardennes and then the push east and then the Rhine crossings, Manny Beal keeping WLBZ on the shelf behind the counter where he could reach the dial without putting down what he was doing. She had grown used to the sound of it coming through the store door as she came up the steps.

Today the voice was different. Not the tone; the tone was always measured. What the voice was saying.

Three men at the counter: Harris Vane, Elliot Pease, old Cullen from the lobster pound. Manny had his coffee cup set down and both hands on the counter's edge.

She went to the flour bin and measured what she needed.

Germany. Berlin. The German state radio and then the Allied command's confirmation: April 30th. She listened and tied off the flour bag.

At the counter she waited while Manny tallied her items. Harris Vane and Elliot Pease were talking, low — not the kind of talking that calculated what the news meant for the next push, the next month, the winter holding or breaking. This was the other kind. Old Cullen said nothing and looked at the counter.

Manny made change. She thanked him.

Six blocks to the office. The harbor was opening. The war in Europe was ending. She walked the six blocks in the April air, the breakwater visible at the channel's edge, the water flat and gray-green in the midday light.

---

In the afternoon she went to the breakwater.

Not for any reason the log would record. She went the way she went sometimes — down the wharf, left at the bollard, out along the granite face. Two hundred feet. The blocks cut and laid in the 1890s, rough-faced and gray where they were above the waterline, dark and algae-striped below it, the stripe marking the tidal range exactly: eleven feet, the same it had always been.

Harbor on one side. Open water on the other. The April chop, a foot and a half, the surface running gray-green where the channel went deep. She stood at the end.

She had been standing at this breakwater since 1935. October of that year she had worn Owen's work gloves because her own were still packed and the post was a month old; the gloves were too large for her hands and the tools were Owen's tools, and she had been learning what they were for by using them. She had stood here in January 1944 when the ice came in early and locked the east pier's second float, working through the dredge sequence and what would have to wait. She had stood here on the morning of June 7th, 1944, the harbor quiet before the boats came in, not yet knowing whether Robert Cates or Galen Fuller had been on a Normandy beach the morning before.

Nine winters. The breakwater kept no account of any of it. Granite and seawater and the tidal stripe.

She thought about Horak.

Jan Václav Horak — Czech, displaced, last known Halifax in October 1942. The name had come in a letter from the Coast Guard regional office in Portland in April 1944, six months after the body came in off the blow. It was in the cabinet with the 1944 binders. She had seen him on the commercial dock on the night of October 26th, 1943, moving south from the herring shed toward the lobster landing. She had heard the language Marcus Klein had placed for her from what she'd carried across seven months: Czech, the consonant cluster, the first-syllable stress. She had written it all into the late entry in October 1944 — the standard format, her own hand, the record of what she had seen and had not logged at the time. The record was complete. That was what a late entry was for.

The second person on the dock. The one who had been there when she came around the corner of the lobster landing and had walked away before she reached them — not running, just walking, back toward the head of the wharf and out of the dock light. She had not found a name for it. Nineteen months since the night of the blow and she had nothing more than she'd had that first morning, when she opened the tide log and read the gap her silence had left.

She didn't know if she needed to.

The harbor log was not a record of everything. It was a record of what a harbormaster could enter in good faith. Owen had known this. His 1934 entry about J.T. — she had found it in January the year before, the deferred notation eventually made whole: what he had seen, in the standard format, when he had what he needed to put it down. He had not entered what he couldn't confirm. Neither had she. The record stood on what could be entered with certainty; what fell outside that was the record's limit, which was what it had always been.

She stood at the breakwater's end another minute. The spray at the south corner where the chop hit the face. The lobster pound at the far side of the harbor, Cullen's truck already back in the lot. The open water south, gray under the April overcast, the horizon gone into the sky.

She turned and walked back.

The wharf, the cedar-shingled office at the foot of it, the window with the tide board visible from ten feet: May figures, her handwriting. She had put the new month's tables up on Monday. The numbers the numbers regardless of what the radio at Beal's was saying.

---

Owen's ledger was in the cabinet. She had not opened it since October's log review, and she would not open it today.

She sat at the chart table.

Her log was open to Wednesday, May 2nd. The day's entry was started but not finished — the six-forty-five tide, the weather notation, the morning fleet status. The spaces below were blank.

She picked up her pen.

The noon notation: wind shift from northwest to west-northwest, gusting ten to twelve. Fleet status unchanged. The Jessup boy had gone out at ten-thirty and come back in at noon; she had noted it in the transit log and she transferred the notation now: departure time, return, no significant events.

The two-o'clock mooring check. All lines good. East pier, second slip — slight fraying at the nip, the same she had noted Tuesday. She entered it formally: slip number, location, description, assessment. *Monitor. No action yet.* Next week she would pull the line and measure what was there.

Hanson brothers: due Thursday to open their season. Three slips reserved on the main float, the same positions every year. She wrote the pending reservation, the dates, the standard mooring-fee condition. It was what you wrote down.

Robert Cates's renewal confirmation. She had entered it yesterday but she added the season notation now in the space reserved for it — *Spring 1945* — and underlined the year the way she always underlined the first confirmed renewal of a new season. The underline meant the season was open.

Outside the window the harbor held what it held. The boats on the main float riding the small chop of the afternoon, the light on the water thin and flat in the overcast. A gull on the bollard at the dock's end. The breakwater at the channel's edge, gray in the afternoon, the algae line invisible at this hour of tide but there — she knew where it was.

She turned to the next page.

*May 1945.* She wrote the heading in the top right corner the way she always did, the month and year and nothing else. Below it, the entry for Wednesday was still unfinished — the afternoon's remaining notations waiting, the six o'clock tide still to come, the evening fleet check, whatever else the harbor brought before the day was done.

She kept writing.

# The Dock, and After

The three-day blow had backed around to the northwest and gone quiet by Tuesday afternoon, but the harbor was still running rough when Eira Bowman left the office at quarter past eleven. She pulled the door shut behind her — the latch was stiff in cold weather; you had to lift the handle as you turned it, a small piece of knowledge the carpenter could have fixed in an afternoon but that she'd left as it was — and stood a moment on the planking outside to let her eyes adjust. The lantern was already lit. No moon. Cloud cover from the Reach to wherever the sky ended. She could hear the fleet working against their lines in the chop and feel the planking underfoot where it moved: that particular rhythm of float and strain that wasn't distress but wasn't settled either.

Standard late check. After every major blow she walked the dock once at night: confirm the Osgood brothers' trap boat, which had dragged on Monday and which she'd reset herself; then the far end, where Bertrand Foss kept three smacks she hadn't liked the look of going into the storm. Three boats. Twenty minutes out, back to the office, then home. She'd been doing this check, or something like it, for eight years — since November of '35, when she'd taken Owen's post because she'd been the one who knew the harbor and the selectmen had run out of other options.

She walked out onto the commercial wharf.

---

The harbor smelled of low tide and diesel and wet rope. The channel was still rough — whitecaps at the mouth, spray coming up off the breakwater blocks and catching in the lantern light before it fell — but inside the water was a heavy chop, nothing that threatened. She walked the planking at a working pace, holding the lantern to her right where it would show her the deck and lines of each vessel she passed.

She checked what she passed: a smack with the new mooring line she'd authorized in September — holding; good — the trap boat that belonged to the Gavel boy, who'd gone to the merchant marine in '42 and left his father paying the slip fee, and two gillnetters in for the season that she noted and passed on. Eight years of this harbor and she'd built the catalog Owen had started and added to it herself: which owners checked their rigging and which left it to luck, where the tide ran strange in a northerly and what happened when it did, which lines were aging out and which owners would argue about it when she told them. Owen had left gaps in the log where his head-knowledge had covered the ground. She'd found most of the gaps in the first two winters and had filled them in, in her own handwriting, in the same columns.

The Osgood trap boat was fine. She held the lantern down, checked the chain at the waterline, and found it right. Good.

She went on toward the far end of the dock.

---

The dock turned at a right angle near the breakwater foot, and she came around this angle — past the last set of cleats, past the empty slip where the MacPherson boat had been before it went for scrap in August — and she saw the two people.

One had their back to her: a figure standing close to the man at the bollard, turned inland, already in motion when she saw them. They went quickly and without noise and were into the dark beyond the streetlight on the wharf road in two seconds. She'd registered: a back, a movement, gone.

The man at the bollard didn't move.

She slowed. She kept walking — stopping at a distance wasn't procedure, and she was going to do this correctly — until she was thirty feet from him, and then she stopped.

He was sitting, or nearly sitting, against the bollard at the dock's end, facing the harbor mouth. She could not see his face from here — he wasn't looking at her; he was watching the water where the mouth opened into the outer harbor — but she could see his coat clearly enough in the lantern light.

His coat was wrong. She registered this before anything else: before the absence of any vessel he might have come from, before the question of the person who had walked inland. The coat was not oilskin. Not the heavy canvas or the wool watch coat she saw on every man who worked this dock in October. The cut of it was European — she could see that in the silhouette, in the fall of the shoulders, in the line of the collar. A traveling coat, a city coat, and it was wet through at the shoulders and back, and it had not been made for a harbor.

He had his hands in his pockets and he was watching the harbor mouth and he had not turned at the lantern.

Unauthorized persons on the commercial dock. Harbor Commission regulation — she'd handled it twice since Pearl Harbor, when the war had given the regulations teeth they'd lacked before. She was the harbormaster. Authorized and obligated to challenge.

She stood there for the length of time it takes to know you've already decided.

A cold reached her that wasn't the wind off the harbor mouth. It was in her hands, which had nothing wrong with them.

She turned back.

She went to the far smacks and checked Bertrand Foss's first mooring line and found it tight, then the second and third. The chafing gear on the last boat's bow line was rubbing against the dock cleat in a way she'd been watching since September. She pressed it back against the line and held it a moment before releasing it. Then she stood at the seaward edge and looked at the harbor mouth, at the spray still coming white off the breakwater granite even now, this long after the blow had eased, and then she walked back along the dock.

She did not look at the far bollard as she passed.

In the office she put the lantern on the chart table and opened the tide log. She wrote the 11 p.m. gauge reading — she'd taken it before she'd gone out — and wrote the mooring notation: *Osgood trap, all fast. Foss smacks, all fast.* She read what she'd written. She did not write anything else.

The stove had died down while she was out. She considered relighting it and did not. She put on her coat and walked home.

---

The 6 a.m. tide was 4.3 feet above mean low, running out. She'd been at the office before five, lighting the stove, running the gauge, making the first notation of the day. Clear morning after the blow, north breeze, cold. The harbor was going quiet in the way it always did after three days of rough weather — the swell flattening toward a long, low pull, the chop settling. The lobster boats had gone out before first light and she could see their running lights from the office window, already small against the pale.

She wrote a wicking requisition in the requisition book — the stove had been burning crookedly; the wick needed replacing before the end of the month. Owen's handwriting for the first thirty-seven pages of the book, then hers. The changeover was visible if you looked. She had not needed to look since the first year.

She processed the fuel-allocation chart. She made two calls on the field telephone: the sardine cannery about their September billing, the harbor office in Rockland about a slip-fee dispute that had been sitting unanswered since August. The Rockland man was apologetic and slow, and she was writing up the notation for that call when Hector Brann came to the door at half past ten.

He had his hat in his hands.

Hector Brann did not take his hat off. He'd kept it on at the ration board, at the Legion hall, in the general store through the whole of last winter. She'd seen him hold it over his chest during a prayer and put it back on after. She looked up from the chart.

"Morning, Hector."

"Morning, Eira." He was looking past her left shoulder. "Something on the breakwater end. You'll want to see."

She looked at him.

"What kind of something."

"A man," Hector said. "Dead. He's in the seam, ocean side. I think the tide brought him around."

She got her coat from the hook by the door.

---

The breakwater ran two hundred feet from the north shore out to the harbor mouth — granite blocks from the 1890s, green-black below the waterline, gray-brown above, algae-striped at the tidal bands. The ocean side took the full run of weather. In a blow the spray came over the blocks clean. Even now, the storm over, the swell was still running heavy enough at the harbor mouth to break white at the granite's foot.

The man had come in on the tide and settled in the joint between two blocks, in the seam, face up. His coat was spread around him in the way moving water arranges things. He had not arranged himself.

Eira picked her way out over the granite.

She put her hand to his throat because that was procedure. No pulse. He was cold in a way that was past accounting for with weather and exposure time — a finished cold. His face had gone the color she'd seen twice before and had no interest in seeing again: the blue-white at the lips and jaw, the flatness of the closed eyes.

Somewhere between thirty-five and fifty. Medium build. Several days of beard.

His coat was the coat from the dock.

She looked at his hands.

The calluses were wrong. She knew what a fisherman's hands looked like, and a farmer's, and a cannery worker's — the base of the fingers, the inner edge of the palm, where rope or shovel or the packing table worked across years. These calluses were in the centers of the palms. She didn't know what work put them there. It wasn't any work she recognized from the harbor, from any harbor she'd been in.

No papers visible. She didn't search the coat — that was for the Coast Guard — but she looked at what was accessible: nothing in the outer pocket, no wallet bulge at the breast.

She went back across the breakwater to the office and called the Coast Guard station on the field telephone.

---

While she waited she went back out and stood at the foot of the breakwater and looked at him from there. He was visible clearly enough: the coat bright against the gray granite, the harbor mouth behind him with its running swell. A pair of terns worked the inside water, and the sound of them came and went on the wind. The harbor was the harbor — the chop, the diesel smell, the sardine cannery boat at the far dock. He was small at this distance. Everything was the size it was supposed to be.

She'd known it was him when Hector said *a man*. Before that, even — if she were being precise about it, though she was not required to be precise about it to anyone.

She went back inside and stood at the chart table and did not open the log.

---

The lieutenant's name was Parsons — Arthur Parsons, his Coast Guard uniform correctly pressed despite the drive down from the station, a man of forty or so with the manner of someone who had done this before and intended to do it properly. He had a clipboard. He asked to see the harbor log from the previous night.

She gave it to him.

He read it without hurrying. The 11 p.m. gauge reading. The mooring notation. The columns ruled through where there was nothing to enter.

"Anything unusual last night?" he said. "Any vessels in the harbor you didn't recognize? Anyone on the docks who shouldn't have been?"

"The fleet's in," Eira said. "Storm's been over. Nothing I need to note."

She heard those words come out of her. They were accurate and they were not complete.

Parsons nodded and wrote on his clipboard. He asked about the body — position, whether anything had been moved. She gave him the exact description: the seam between the blocks, the face-up orientation, the coat, the hands. He walked out to the breakwater with one of his men and she watched through the window as he looked at the coat, then at the hands, and noted both without comment.

He came back.

"Drowning appears to be the cause," he said. "Storm exposure, possibly — we'll know more after the examination." He looked at her. "Do you know the man?"

"No."

"Seen him before? On the dock, at the fuel float?"

"No."

"Papers on the body?"

"None visible. I didn't search."

"That's right, you wouldn't." He made a note. He paused. "Anyone you know of who might have been on the water last night, or in the past few nights? Unauthorized vessel traffic?"

"No," Eira said.

Parsons held her gaze a moment, then wrote it down. "We'll be in touch." He turned toward the door and back. "The man who found him?"

"Hector Brann. He lobsters out of here. The *Irene M.*, green hull, third slip."

Parsons wrote the name and thanked her. He directed his men to the stretcher and she watched them carry it across the breakwater granite and the wharf planking and load it into their vehicle. The engine turned over. She listened to it go up the wharf road and onto the main road, and then the sound diminished and was gone.

The breakwater was empty.

She went back inside.

---

The tide log was open to Tuesday. Her own handwriting: the 23:00 gauge reading, the 00:10 check, the mooring notations for the Osgood boat and Foss's smacks. The columns ruled through where there was nothing to record. Complete, legible, accurate in what it contained.

Nothing about the far dock. Nothing about a figure walking inland with their back turned before she'd had time to see their face. Nothing about a coat that was wrong for the harbor, or thirty feet of planking between her lantern and a man watching the harbor mouth, or the length of time she'd stood there, or what she'd decided in that time.

She had the pen in her hand without remembering picking it up.

The tide log lay open on Owen's chart table, in the office that had been his office and was hers — the stove going properly now, the room warming in the way it did when it had been burning long enough — and she was reading what she had written and what she had not written.

Outside, the harbor went on.

# The Icehouse

The barn door was stiff with October damp. She pushed it open with her shoulder, the way she always did now, and stood a moment in the opening before she went inside — her father had taught her this without teaching it, by doing it every morning alongside her until she did it herself: hold still, let the animals hear you first. The dark inside was warmer than the yard. She could feel it on her face. Behind her the east field ran black to the tree line, Route 9 invisible through the maples beyond.

She went in.

The smell came at her the way it always did: the warm hide smell of twenty-two animals in an enclosed space, the manure smell she'd stopped noticing by September, and over everything the sweet rot of silage from the silo on the north end. She'd grown up smelling this. She didn't know what her room smelled like to someone who didn't live there. She went to the peg, hung her coat, rolled her sleeves.

Her father was already in the third bay, his lantern on the hook above the grain box. His back was to her, his shoulders moving in the slow careful rhythm of the early work. He kept a low murmur going with the animals — not words she could make out, just the rhythm of a voice — and the nearest Holstein turned toward it. He didn't look up when she came in.

She waited a moment.

*Fang an*, he said, without turning.

She started.

Twenty-two of them, and she knew them by now the way you knew anything you spent two hours with every morning in the dark: not by thinking but by the accumulated weight of attention that had stopped being attention and become something else — the kind of knowledge that was in the hands and not the head. She moved stall to stall. Her father worked from the other end, not speaking, and the lantern hung between them and swung slightly when the nearest animal shifted. The barn had its own sound at this hour, the sound that was not any single thing but the sum of all of it: breath, movement, the rhythmic work, the chains.

Through the window above the third stall she could see the icehouse.

She hadn't meant to look. She had looked. There was a lamp burning inside — the light leaked out around the covered window in a narrow seam along the bottom of the curtain — and they were already awake in there, or some of them were. She didn't know at what hour they woke, or what the whitewashed partitioned room was like at five in the morning, whether the two cots and two pallets the Houlton men had installed were adequate or whether the four of them lay awake long before the work started. She had wondered about this in the first week, had constructed and discarded several versions of what it was like to be inside that room, and had eventually let the wondering go.

Three weeks since they'd come. The farm had arranged itself around their presence the way it arranged itself around any new constraint — not happily or unhappily, just as a fact of the season. They worked the east field in the mornings and the north end of the corn in the afternoons. They ate their meals in the icehouse. In the evenings they went back to the icehouse and the door closed and the light showed at the curtain's edge until it didn't.

She'd watched their arrival from this same window: the Coastal Patrol truck pulling up on the road, the four of them climbing down with their packs, the men from Camp Houlton doing the handover on the gravel while her father stood in the yard and didn't speak. Her mother in the doorway behind the screen. Hannah here, at this window, uncertain what she'd expected but watching.

She went back to work.

---

Lonzo came at seven the way he always came — the truck on the road, the cab door, his boots on the gravel — and settled onto his stool at the barn door. He was sixty-three or close to it, with a face that had been weathered into something that communicated very little. He pulled the Bangor Daily from his coat pocket and opened it. He had a son in the Pacific who didn't write often enough, Hannah had heard her father say to her mother once; she didn't know if this was why he sat the way he sat, with the patience of a man who had decided a long time ago what he was going to do with an afternoon and was going to do it regardless. He laid the Springfield across his knees.

He looked up when she looked at him.

She nodded. He nodded.

That was all.

At quarter past seven the icehouse door opened and all four of them came out into the gray cold and walked in a loose cluster toward the near field where the last rows of winter corn waited. She watched from the barn doorway — the way she watched most mornings now, a habit that had started without her deciding to start it and that she hadn't been able to stop. Three of them she knew well enough by now to have put shapes to, though not names: the heavyset one whose step she could hear from inside the barn, who walked with his shoulders rolling, always first; the thin one who carried a slight lean to the left, a habit of the body she recognized from men who had done hard work on one side for too long; the older one with the bald patch, who moved deliberately, as if he had been told where to go so many times that he'd stopped having opinions about the direction. The fourth walked quickly at the back of the group, keeping pace with the others by moving faster, the way you moved when you were the shortest.

She'd heard Lonzo call his name three days after they arrived — *Reinmar*, sharp, pointing at the east fence — and had not forgotten it.

Karl Reinmar. The youngest of the four.

---

She was carrying feed buckets to the far end of the barn when she heard the clatter. Small sound, something dropped. She set the buckets down and looked: a short-handled cultivating tool — the kind her father used for the kitchen garden bed — had fallen into the gap at the base of the east fence post. The fence ran close to the barn wall on that side, close enough that something dropped from the near field could slip into the gap without being reachable from outside without going all the way around to the gate.

She picked it up.

He was on the other side of the fence.

She hadn't heard him come to the fence. He was two feet away through the boards and wire, closer than she had been to any of them, and there was nothing to do about it — no time to decide how to hold her face or what to think about first. She'd had some half-formed expectation of something, she realized now, standing here with the tool in her hand: some quality to the face that would explain what he was or what it meant that he was here. There was no such quality. He was young, that was the first thing — younger than she'd thought from the distance of the barn window, which had reduced all four of them to shapes. His face was wind-chapped, the skin across his cheekbones roughened by weeks of October cold. His hair had been cut short and not carefully. He had a tired quality that was not the tiredness of a single bad night but the kind that accumulated over time until it stopped showing as tiredness and showed only as the particular stillness of a face that had stopped expecting things to change. His eyes were gray-blue, the color of the harbor on a cold morning when the sky was low.

He was looking at the tool, not at her.

*Danke*, he said.

She pushed the tool through the gap at the bottom of the fence and he took it and stepped back and went back to work.

From his stool at the barn door, Lonzo turned a page in the Bangor Daily. The paper made its flat, dry sound. She had picked up a tool that had fallen and passed it through a fence and a person had said thank you.

She picked up the feed buckets. Her hands did not feel like they had done anything remarkable. She carried the feed to the far stall and finished the work.

---

She walked the three miles the long way, under the maples along the edge of the Hallet property, where the leaves were still coming down in the cold morning. She counted things when she didn't want to think — fence posts, the crows on the wire above the Osborn field — and got to twenty-three fence posts before she stopped counting and let herself think instead.

*Danke.* She had known what that meant since she was four years old, since before she'd known what anything in English meant. Her father's voice in the kitchen before it had been her father's house, before the rules had settled: *Danke, Liebling.* He hadn't called her that in a long time. The word was such a small one that using it barely counted as language, barely counted as deciding to speak.

She thought: Karl Reinmar is nineteen. He has been in Tunisia and in Houlton and now he is on a farm in Maine in October. He said *Danke* for a cultivating tool through a fence. She had handed the tool through because there was nothing else to do with it.

She thought: he is a person. She arranged the facts in a row — the tool, the fence, the word, the gray-blue eyes not looking at her — and they were still just facts. She walked the rest of the three miles and arrived at school before the first bell.

---

The lesson was on indirect discourse. *Oratio obliqua*, Mr. Klein said — the grammar of reported speech, how a statement became secondary when it was embedded in another clause, the verb shifted, the meaning changed depending on what tense the main clause had been given. She wrote the examples in her notebook and worked through the practice sentences twice. She got three wrong the first time and corrected them. She thought about the fence and told herself to stop thinking about the fence.

At lunch Ada Wheeler sat across from her with her tray.

"Raymond Foss says his father says the Coast Guard thinks it was a German agent," Ada said. "The body on the breakwater. That he came off a submarine. A spy."

Hannah ate a bite of her sandwich. The body on the breakwater had been town news for a week. She'd heard three versions: the spy, a merchant sailor from a vessel wrecked on the outer ledges in the blow, and something involving a man from Ellsworth and a debt she hadn't quite followed. Raymond Foss's father worked at the cannery and was known to have opinions on many things.

"Maybe," Hannah said.

"Doesn't it worry you? Right here in Coldwater?"

She thought about saying: Raymond Foss's father doesn't know anything about submarines. She thought about saying: the body is in Rockland now with the Coast Guard. She thought about saying: a lot of things wash up after a blow. She didn't say any of these.

"I didn't know him," she said.

Ada looked at her as if this had missed the point. Two other girls sat down and the conversation moved on and Hannah ate the rest of her sandwich and thought about indirect discourse and the way a verb changed depending on what it was embedded in.

---

The evening milking was done by six and the dark had come in solid before she got back to the house. She stood a moment in the yard and looked at the kitchen window — the lamp lit inside, the yellow square of it in the dark, her mother's shape moving past — and then went in.

Her father was at the far end of the table with the German-language Bangor Daily, the edition he received by post on Thursdays. He read it folded open to the inside pages, elbows on the table, in the way he'd always read. Her mother was at the stove, her back to the room, stirring something that smelled of potato.

Hannah sat down with her Latin book.

The kitchen had its own kind of silence in the evenings, a silence she'd grown up inside, which meant she knew its textures the way she knew the animals' sounds: what it weighed when nothing was about to happen and what it weighed when something was. The clock above the door ran a minute fast. The stove made its sounds. Her mother's spoon made its sounds. Her father's newspaper turned once every several minutes. Outside the window the dark was complete.

She worked through the indirect discourse drill and corrected the errors she found. Her father reached the end of the page and let the paper fall slightly in his hands and read the next page without turning it, the way he did when he'd found something he was going to stay on for a while.

He said something under his breath. A single word, low, not directed at her or at anyone. The sound a person made when reading something that had confirmed what they'd known it was going to say. She glanced up. His expression was unchanged, his eyes on the page.

She went back to the drill.

Then her mother said: *Wir hätten früher gehen sollen.*

She said it to the stove, or to the window above the stove, her voice flat and without inflection — not quiet, exactly, not a whisper.

Her father looked up.

They looked at each other across the kitchen — he at his end with the newspaper still folded in his hands, she at the stove with the spoon held out to one side where it wouldn't drip. The clock made its sound. The stove made its sound. Something passed between them that Hannah could not have named, and she did not try. Four seconds. Five.

Her father looked back at the paper.

Her mother looked back at the pot.

Hannah looked at the indirect discourse drill. In the margin beside the third set of sentences she had written, before she had decided to write anything: *Wir hätten früher gehen sollen.* She read it. She pressed the pen down and crossed it out, once and again and again, until the paper was dark there and nothing showed through.

---

She took the lamp upstairs after supper and finished the last of the homework and then sat on the edge of her bed and didn't move for a while. From the window, when she lifted the curtain, she could see the shape of the icehouse against the sky — just the roofline, the dark mass of it — and below the roofline the narrow strip of light at the curtain's edge, still burning. Whatever they did in the evenings in there she didn't know. Whether they talked or read or sat with their own language, with their own thinking, in the whitewashed room where the cold must come up through the boards. Whether they thought about the places they'd come from or had decided that direction didn't help.

The strip of light at the icehouse window went out.

She sat with that a moment — the dark where the light had been, the shape of the roof still present, the sky above it that was slightly lighter than the roofline. Then she blew out her own lamp and lay down in the dark and listened.

The barn sounds came through the wall: an animal shifting in its stall, the knock of a board, the wind at the eaves. The silage smell moved through on the air and then didn't and then did again, the way smells moved at night when the temperature dropped and the air settled.

*Wir hätten früher gehen sollen.*

She knew what the words meant. What they were about — what her mother had meant by *earlier*, what *leaving* was and what had been left and what had been meant to be left behind — she didn't know yet. She thought she might not know for a long time. She thought she was probably going to have to find out.
