# What He Left

The mud came up through March the way it always did — not melting exactly but surrendering, the frozen ground releasing one layer at a time, first along the south wall of the barn where the sun hit it earliest, then the path between the house and the milk house, then by the second week the full yard. The Holsteins came in from the morning pasture with it halfway up their legs. Hannah scraped the stalls twice a day now and still the mud came back. It was the season's particular tax.

Her father told her at supper. In German; it was still German at the supper table.

"Lonzo came by this afternoon," he said. He set his bread down and looked at his hands for a moment. "The men are being sent back to the camp. Thursday."

"All four of them?"

"All four." He picked up his bread again. "From Houlton they will go back eventually. To Germany, when the arrangements are made. It takes time, with the war not finished."

She ate the rest of her soup. She heard something in how he said *all four* — a flatness that was not nothing. But she did not ask about it.

After supper she went out to do the late check — water lines, the heat lamp over the new calf, a walk through the stalls with the lantern. The icehouse window was lit at the far edge of the yard. She stopped in the barn doorway and stood looking at it the way she had stood looking at it all winter, from November to now — watching the low amber square of it, the shape of Karl reading at his small table by lamplight.

Four days.

She went inside.

---

She spent those four days in the rhythm of the farm. The 5 a.m. milking, school, the afternoon chores, the 6 p.m. milking, the late check. The prisoners were on their winter schedule: Brunner and Krebs on the wood lot, Fischer running repairs on the east fence, Karl working the strip below the lower field where the dead growth from winter had come down. She could see them from the kitchen window in the mornings and from the barn doorway in the evenings. She kept her distance the way she had been keeping it since October, the choice made once and then remade every day, which was how she knew it was a choice.

She told herself she would not go to the south fence. On the second day she didn't. On the third day she went out with the post bar and the tamping rod, because the south fence needed work — the same corner post on the south section that had heaved in November of 1943 had shifted again over the winter, and she had been putting off the repair since February when the ground was still frozen. The frost heave was real. She had not invented it.

She carried the tools around the barn and set her footing in the mud.

---

He was working the strip between the fence and the lower wood lot, clearing the winter deadfall. When she first came around the corner of the barn, he had his back to her.

She put the bar in and worked the post. Drive, pull, reset — the mud closing back in around the bar each time she pulled out, the cold still in the ground below the first thawed layer. She was thinking about the heel of the post and whether she needed gravel beneath it when she heard him stop.

She looked up. He was at the fence on his side, his hands in his coat pockets, looking at her.

She straightened.

She said: "Guten Morgen."

He said: "Good morning."

She put the bar down.

She had not been this close to him since October. He looked the same and did not look the same — the sun-chapped skin still there, the gray-blue eyes, but something in his bearing that was different. The first year's watchfulness was gone; so was the second year's settled tiredness. He looked like a man who had been somewhere long enough to know it and was now preparing to leave.

She reached into her coat pocket and took out the carved bird. Three inches of birch, the wings folded against the body, the head angled slightly down. The corrected ridge on the breast where the blade had slipped. She had been carrying it for more than a year.

She held it out over the fence toward him.

"You should take this back," she said. In English, because that was what felt right.

He looked at the bird. He looked at her hand. He said: "No."

Just that word.

She kept her hand out a moment longer, then let it drop. She did not put the bird away.

"Will you have somewhere to go," she said. "When you get back. After the war."

He thought about this. She could see him working through it — not performing the thinking but actually moving through it, word to word, the way he had all last summer at the fence.

"Back is not a place," he said. He placed each word carefully. "Not anymore."

The fence between them. Three feet of air, the top wire, the mud on both sides the same mud. Behind him the lower wood lot, spruce going dark where the sun had not yet reached. Behind her the barn.

"What will you do," she said.

"I don't know." He shifted his weight slightly. "Start." A pause. "The same thing as everyone."

She looked at the bird in her hand. She turned it once. The grain of the birch, the corrected ridge on the breast, the tail cut to a clean notch.

She had been carrying it for more than a year. In October when staying at a distance was its own kind of heaviness. In December when she stood in the barn doorway watching his lamp. This morning when she loaded the tools and came around the corner.

"I don't know what to do with this," she said.

"Keep it."

She put the bird back in her coat pocket.

Then she became aware of her father at the barn door. He had the pitchfork at his side — he had come out of something in the middle of it, or he had taken up the pitchfork to have something to hold. He was not coming toward them. He was watching. He had warned her to be careful, not stop; he had made his judgment about what was happening at this fence, and the judgment was held in whatever place he kept such things, and he was watching the end of it now without a word.

She had been at the fence perhaps five minutes.

"Good luck," she said.

Karl nodded once. He put his hands back in his coat pockets and turned back to his work.

She picked up the post bar and the tamping rod and walked back across the yard. Her father said nothing when she passed him at the barn door. She went inside and finished what needed to be done.

---

Thursday came in with rain, the fine kind that was mostly mist.

She woke at five and did the morning milking and came back to the house for breakfast. Her father was at the table with his coffee made. Magda was at the stove. Nobody said anything about the truck.

It came at eight. She was in the kitchen and she did not go out.

She watched from the window over the sink.

The four of them came out of the icehouse in order: Brunner first, then Krebs, then Fischer. Karl last. Each carried what he had. Brunner had a bag over his shoulder; the others had bundles or coat pockets that were full. Karl's hands were empty.

The Coastal Patrol truck had a canvas back. The driver stayed in the cab. Lonzo was at the tailgate with the Springfield over his shoulder.

Brunner climbed in first, then Krebs, then Fischer. Lonzo said something to the driver. Karl stood in the mud of the yard for a moment.

He did not look at the house.

He looked at the barn — the long, even look of a man registering what he is leaving. Then he put one foot on the tailgate and climbed up.

Lonzo folded his carrying sling around the Springfield and put it behind the seat in the truck cab. Seventeen months on this farm with that rifle, and now he was putting it away. He turned to where Albrecht had come out of the barn and was standing at the yard's edge.

They had been on this farm together for seventeen months. In that time they had exchanged the morning's schedule and whether the ground was passable and whether the rain was likely to hold, and nothing that needed more than that. Lonzo nodded to him. Albrecht nodded back. Neither said anything.

The truck turned out of the yard and went down Route 9.

She watched it until it passed the willow at the bend and was gone. The willow's branches had gone yellow at the tips, the early yellow that came before the leaves.

---

Her father padlocked the icehouse door himself, not long after. She watched through the window: he crossed the yard without hurrying, fitted the shackle through the hasp, pressed it closed. He stood with his hand on the lock for a moment, not doing anything with it. Then he went back to the barn.

She did the morning work. There was always work to do in a dairy barn in late March — the stalls, the milk lines, the new calf that needed checking twice before noon. The farm had its own schedule and did not care what else had happened in the yard.

Around midday her father came in from the barn, knocked the mud from his boots at the door, and hung his coat. Magda had made the white bean soup — Monday's soup, and this was a Thursday, but the soup was there regardless, on the stove where it always was. The bread was on its board. The lamp was on over the table.

Hannah came in and hung her coat on the hook by the door. She could feel the weight of the bird in the pocket — three inches of birch, lighter than she always expected when she closed her hand around it.

She sat down. Magda set a bowl in front of her and went back to the stove.

Outside, Route 9 ran east toward town and west toward the rest of Maine, and the truck was somewhere on it now, or had long since turned north toward Houlton. The icehouse sat at the edge of the yard with its door locked. Through the window the willow at the bend was yellow-tipped, the tips a little more yellow than they had been in the morning.

The bird was in her coat pocket and she would feel it there in the morning when she went out, and it would still be hers.

Her father reached for his bread.

Magda sat.

The farm went on.

# The Spring Opening

April, and the harbor moving.

The ice had been out of the main channel since the third week of March — long gray pans of it riding the ebb tide south past the breakwater mouth, dissolving in the chop before they reached open water. She had watched from the office window without going out. There was nothing useful to do about ice going out; it went when it went, same as it always had.

The first week of April she had walked all the mooring lines. Three on the east row had ice-chafe bad enough to need ricing; she found one on the main float that had chafed through to the splice entirely, which meant it had been weakening since before the freeze and she had missed it in the fall inspection. She replaced the whole length. She had riced the east row lines herself, kneeling on the dock planking in the early cold with the caulking iron, and entered both repairs in the mooring log. Standard notation. The usual spring assessment of what winter had taken.

Now it was the standard spring inventory, and she worked through it the way she always did: depth soundings off the north pier at low tide, the mooring condition check, the fleet registration review. Ten years of spring openings, and the sequence was her own by now — not Owen's sequence handed down but the order she had settled on in her second year, when she understood what the harbor needed first. Depth soundings before slip assignments; mooring check before registration.

Depth soundings: two days running, the tide gauge and the weighted line, working along the north pier face from the bollard to the end. The year before's sounding log had two shallow readings at the channel's edge, same location both times, which meant winter silting from the January storm surge. She marked the position on the sounding chart and flagged it for the summer dredge schedule; the channel was still inside clearance for the second float's boats, but narrowly. She would watch it through the month.

Fleet registration review: nine boats on the main float, three on the east pier, one at the commercial wharf. She pulled the registration files and went through them against the winter registry.

The fleet was smaller than it had been in 1940. She had taken twenty-three boats through the spring opening of that year; this spring it was thirteen. The difference was in the ledger if you wanted to count it — boats sold, men gone, the war and the fuel allocation together. She did not count it this morning. She went through the files against the registry and noted what had changed.

Two new registrations. The first was a lobster dragger that had come down from Owls Head when the operation there folded — the owner, a man named Severance, had done the Portland transfer and come to her for the slip assignment. She had assigned him the outside berth on the east pier, right for the dragger's draft, and entered him in the Coldwater fleet ledger: vessel name, tonnage, operator's certification, assigned slip. Standard form. The second was Danny Jessup's first boat, a twenty-two-foot trap boat he had worked two seasons to buy. The engine was sound; she had checked the documentation and the certifications and assigned him berth seven on the main float, the small-boat row. She entered both and noted the dates.

Two boats out since last fall.

Haskell's sloop, sold in November to a Rockland man. She had sent the release notice to Knox County in November and heard nothing since, which was how Knox County handled these things; the transfer was complete in the record.

Galen Fuller's dragger. Ruth Fuller had renamed it and reregistered it in her own name, coming in on a Monday morning in February with the completed forms and a check for the registration fee. She had sat across the chart table from Eira and signed where the form required. She said she was thinking about running the lobster route herself come May, if she could find a mate who knew the ground. Eira had said there were a few men who knew it; they had talked through who was available and what the pound was paying. Then Ruth Fuller had stood and shaken Eira's hand and gone out. Eira had entered the registration in the fleet ledger under the new name, Ruth Fuller as registered operator, and filed the original in the back cabinet. Fifteen minutes, start to finish. She had not stopped over it; the paperwork was the same paperwork.

She had processed Robert Cates's spring mooring renewal the day before. Berth 14 — his grandfather's berth and his father's berth before him, the third-generation berth that had sat empty for fourteen months. He had come home from France in February, thirty pounds lighter. She had heard this from his father in March, running into him outside the post office: the old man red-eyed and saying Robert was standing, that he was home. By April, Cates had been out in his boat three times — twice coming in with a decent haul, once with nothing. A normal spring. She wrote the mooring renewal in the ledger: berth 14, April 18, 1945, confirmed and paid.

By mid-morning she had the registration review done and the depth soundings entered. She checked the mooring assignments against the harbor chart. Everything in its place. She set the chart on the drying rack and went to make coffee.

---

At noon she walked to Beal's for flour and two kerosene wicks.

The radio was on. It was always on at Beal's now, had been since November — the Ardennes and then the push east and then the Rhine crossings, Manny Beal keeping WLBZ on the shelf behind the counter where he could reach the dial without putting down what he was doing. She had grown used to the sound of it coming through the store door as she came up the steps.

Today the voice was different. Not the tone; the tone was always measured. What the voice was saying.

Three men at the counter: Harris Vane, Elliot Pease, old Cullen from the lobster pound. Manny had his coffee cup set down and both hands on the counter's edge.

She went to the flour bin and measured what she needed.

Germany. Berlin. The German state radio and then the Allied command's confirmation: April 30th. She listened and tied off the flour bag.

At the counter she waited while Manny tallied her items. Harris Vane and Elliot Pease were talking, low — not the kind of talking that calculated what the news meant for the next push, the next month, the winter holding or breaking. This was the other kind. Old Cullen said nothing and looked at the counter.

Manny made change. She thanked him.

Six blocks to the office. The harbor was opening. The war in Europe was ending. She walked the six blocks in the April air, the breakwater visible at the channel's edge, the water flat and gray-green in the midday light.

---

In the afternoon she went to the breakwater.

Not for any reason the log would record. She went the way she went sometimes — down the wharf, left at the bollard, out along the granite face. Two hundred feet. The blocks cut and laid in the 1890s, rough-faced and gray where they were above the waterline, dark and algae-striped below it, the stripe marking the tidal range exactly: eleven feet, the same it had always been.

Harbor on one side. Open water on the other. The April chop, a foot and a half, the surface running gray-green where the channel went deep. She stood at the end.

She had been standing at this breakwater since 1935. October of that year she had worn Owen's work gloves because her own were still packed and the post was a month old; the gloves were too large for her hands and the tools were Owen's tools, and she had been learning what they were for by using them. She had stood here in January 1944 when the ice came in early and locked the east pier's second float, working through the dredge sequence and what would have to wait. She had stood here on the morning of June 7th, 1944, the harbor quiet before the boats came in, not yet knowing whether Robert Cates or Galen Fuller had been on a Normandy beach the morning before.

Nine winters. The breakwater kept no account of any of it. Granite and seawater and the tidal stripe.

She thought about Horak.

Jan Václav Horak — Czech, displaced, last known Halifax in October 1942. The name had come in a letter from the Coast Guard regional office in Portland in April 1944, six months after the body came in off the blow. It was in the cabinet with the 1944 binders. She had seen him on the commercial dock on the night of October 26th, 1943, moving south from the herring shed toward the lobster landing. She had heard the language Marcus Klein had placed for her from what she'd carried across seven months: Czech, the consonant cluster, the first-syllable stress. She had written it all into the late entry in October 1944 — the standard format, her own hand, the record of what she had seen and had not logged at the time. The record was complete.

The second person on the dock. The one who had been there when she came around the corner of the lobster landing and had walked away before she reached them — not running, just walking, back toward the head of the wharf and out of the dock light. Nineteen months since the night of the blow and she had nothing more than she'd had that first morning, when she opened the tide log and read the gap her silence had left.

She didn't know if she needed to.

The harbor log was not a record of everything. It was a record of what a harbormaster could enter in good faith. Owen had known this. His 1934 entry about J.T. — she had found it in January the year before, the deferred notation eventually made whole: what he had seen, in the standard format, when he had what he needed to put it down. He had not entered what he couldn't confirm. Neither had she.

She stood at the breakwater's end another minute. The spray at the south corner where the chop hit the face. The lobster pound at the far side of the harbor, Cullen's truck already back in the lot. The open water south, gray under the April overcast, the horizon gone into the sky.

She turned and walked back.

The wharf, the cedar-shingled office at the foot of it, the window with the tide board visible from ten feet: May figures, her handwriting. The numbers the numbers regardless of what the radio at Beal's was saying.

---

Owen's ledger was in the cabinet. She had not opened it since October's log review, and she would not open it today.

She sat at the chart table.

Her log was open to Wednesday, May 2nd. The day's entry was started but not finished — the six-forty-five tide, the weather notation, the morning fleet status. The spaces below were blank.

She picked up her pen.

The noon notation: wind shift from northwest to west-northwest, gusting ten to twelve. Fleet status unchanged. The Jessup boy had gone out at ten-thirty and come back in at noon; she had noted it in the transit log and she transferred the notation now: departure time, return, no significant events.

The two-o'clock mooring check. All lines good. East pier, second slip — slight fraying at the nip, the same she had noted Tuesday. She entered it formally: slip number, location, description, assessment. *Monitor. No action yet.* Next week she would pull the line and measure what was there.

Hanson brothers: due Thursday to open their season. Three slips reserved on the main float, the same positions every year. She wrote the pending reservation, the dates, the standard mooring-fee condition.

Robert Cates's renewal confirmation. She had entered it yesterday but she added the season notation now in the space reserved for it — *Spring 1945* — and underlined the year the way she always underlined the first confirmed renewal of a new season.

Outside the window the harbor held what it held. The boats on the main float riding the small chop of the afternoon, the light on the water thin and flat in the overcast. A gull on the bollard at the dock's end. The breakwater at the channel's edge, gray in the afternoon, the algae line invisible at this hour of tide but there — she knew where it was.

She turned to the next page.

*May 1945.* She wrote the heading in the top right corner the way she always did, the month and year and nothing else. Below it, the entry for Wednesday was still unfinished — the afternoon's remaining notations waiting, the six o'clock tide still to come, the evening fleet check, whatever else the harbor brought before the day was done.

She kept writing.

## Macro arc assessment

### Overall arc shape

*Coldwater Reach* is a 30-chapter, four-phase novel (Setup 1–10, Middle 11–20, Turn 21–27, Close 28–30) braiding three POVs around a central mystery that the structure promises will stay partially in shadow. The arc design is sound: the Setup is disciplined, the Close is appropriately lean for the novel's aesthetic, and the Turn has genuine escalation energy. The main structural risks are concentrated in a specific pocket of the Middle and in two places where the same emotional beat plays twice.

---

### Midbook sag: chapters 11–13 (Jan–March 1944)

This is the novel's most vulnerable stretch. From chapter 10 to chapter 14 — a four-chapter run — **Thread 1 (the Horak spine) is dormant**. Chapter 11 (Owen's Ledger) is introspective and single-threaded. Chapter 12 (The School Board) is strong as an institutional set-piece but resolves cleanly and advances no forward pressure on the central mystery. Chapter 13 (The Gift) advances only Thread 4 (Hannah and Karl) and is described as a single-thread chapter even in the thread design notes.

Three quiet chapters in a row — each individually warranted, none individually fat — compose a stillness that, cumulatively, reads as a sag. The school board hearing is the Middle's most dramatic action beat, but it resolves (ch12 ends in resolved-beat), and the two chapters framing it are atmospheric retreats. A reader arriving at chapter 14 (Horak named) after this stretch will have gone roughly 7,500–9,000 words without spine advancement. This is where midbook sag typically takes root: not in any single underperforming chapter, but in a sequence of individually defensible quiet chapters that compound into lost momentum.

**Recommended check at the per-chapter pass:** Verify that chapters 11 and 13 are pulling their maximum narrative weight. In ch11, ask whether Owen's ledger precedent is doing enough dramatic work or whether it is primarily setup for ch26's payoff (making it feel thin in place). In ch13, the carved bird is a load-bearing object, but the chapter is 2,500–3,200 words — if the scene is dwelling in atmosphere at the expense of pressure, the sag is structural, not stylistic.

---

### Doubled beat: Marcus's drawer (chapters 19 and 22)

Chapter 19 (*After Eira*) ends with Marcus holding the assembled picture and deciding to put it away — specifically located in "the drawer." Chapter 22 (*The Unfinished Letter*) ends with Marcus drafting a letter he cannot send and putting *it* in the drawer. Both end on the identical image: a man choosing not to act, the thing going in a drawer. Both end in deliberately non-urgent modes (coda, elliptical). The emotional note — Marcus arriving at the edge of action and retreating — is played twice in a three-chapter span (with only ch20 D-Day between them).

The draft intends these as different choices (the first is about protecting the Pfeiffers; the second is about protecting Eira and the Pfeiffers from official exposure). But from a pacing perspective, both chapters deliver **Marcus in stasis after assembly**. The reader who has watched him assemble the picture carefully across five chapters (6, 9, 15, 18, 19) and then watches him not-act at ch19 has already understood his choice. Chapter 22 then repeats the not-action with a different object, and the drawer reappears. This risks making Marcus feel passive across the Turn's opening rather than making a meaningful second decision.

**Recommended check:** If the per-chapter pass confirms ch22 largely restates ch19's emotional position, consider whether the chapter earns its length or whether its function (the letter as evidence that Marcus has things to protect) could be accomplished with significantly fewer words.

---

### Hannah's ending-mode uniformity

Seven of Hannah's nine chapters end in literary-fade (2, 5, 8, 13, 16, 27, 29). The chapter map's non-consecutive rule is respected, but because Hannah's chapters are not consecutive, the cumulative pattern still creates a register imprint: her chapters collectively feel like they recede. The two departures — ch21 (resolved-beat, Karl's English sentence) and ch24 (mid-action, harvest/Albrecht warning) — are the chapters where something changes in Hannah's arc. The literary-fade dominance in her other chapters is consistent with her porous, immersive register, but it means her chapters as a type create less forward pull than Eira's or Marcus's. Per-chapter passes should flag any Hannah chapter where the atmospheric close is substituting for a forward hook rather than genuinely completing the chapter's emotional beat.

---

### Close section balance (chapters 28–30)

Three chapters for the resolution of all three character arcs, the Albrecht non-reveal, and the thematic landing is compact. This leanness is almost certainly correct given the aesthetic — this is a novel that trusts restraint, and an over-extended coda would betray it. But the compactness means any one of these three chapters that underperforms cannot be rescued by the others. The per-chapter pass should verify that ch28 (Marcus's loss and the kitchen) is doing full emotional work for Thread 3's resolution and not merely gesturing at it; that ch29 (Hannah's farewell) is complete as written and not relying on the reader's assumed investment; and that ch30 (Eira at the breakwater) carries enough specific physical and narrative detail to function as the book's final resting place rather than a summary of what has already been established.

---

### D-Day placement (chapter 20): a defensible risk

D-Day arrives at the end of the Middle as a single-thread chapter advancing only Eira's arc through professional procedure. The restraint is tonally correct and thematically honest — this is a home-front novel. But this is the novel's historically largest moment and it is filtered through the most procedurally spare POV in the book. The risk is that the novel has been careful to avoid the war-as-backdrop problem everywhere except here, where the war's biggest event *becomes* the backdrop by design. The per-chapter pass should confirm that ch20 has sufficient specific weight — concrete details particular enough to make the D-Day chapter feel like the novel's D-Day chapter, not just a competent execution of its concept.

---

### Summary of priority concerns

1. **High — midbook sag at ch11–13**: spine dormant for four chapters; compound quietness without compound pressure.
2. **High — doubled drawer beat at ch19/ch22**: same emotional position played twice; risks making Marcus feel passive rather than deliberate.
3. **Medium — Hannah's literary-fade uniformity**: seven of nine chapters recede; check that no individual chapter's fade is unearned.
4. **Medium — Close section thinness**: three chapters for three arc resolutions; each must land cleanly without rescue from its neighbors.
5. **Low — D-Day as procedural chapter**: the novel's largest historical moment handled in the most spare register; verify the chapter has enough specific gravity.

# The Icehouse

The barn door was stiff with October damp. She pushed it open with her shoulder, the way she always did now, and stood a moment in the opening before she went inside — her father had taught her this without teaching it, by doing it every morning alongside her until she did it herself: hold still, let the animals hear you first. The dark inside was warmer than the yard. She could feel it on her face. Behind her the east field ran black to the tree line, Route 9 invisible through the maples beyond.

She went in.

The smell came at her the way it always did: the warm hide smell of twenty-two animals in an enclosed space, the manure smell she'd stopped noticing by September, and over everything the sweet rot of silage from the silo on the north end. She'd grown up smelling this. She didn't know what her room smelled like to someone who didn't live there. She went to the peg, hung her coat, rolled her sleeves.

Her father was already in the third bay, his lantern on the hook above the grain box. His back was to her, his shoulders moving in the slow careful rhythm of the early work. He kept a low murmur going with the animals — not words she could make out, just the rhythm of a voice — and the nearest Holstein turned toward it. He didn't look up when she came in.

She waited a moment.

*Fang an*, he said, without turning.

She started.

Twenty-two of them, and she knew them by now the way you knew anything you spent two hours with every morning in the dark: not by thinking but by the accumulated weight of attention that had stopped being attention and become something else — the kind of knowledge that was in the hands and not the head. She moved stall to stall. Her father worked from the other end, not speaking, and the lantern hung between them and swung slightly when the nearest animal shifted. The barn had its own sound at this hour, the sound that was not any single thing but the sum of all of it: breath, movement, the rhythmic work, the chains.

Through the window above the third stall she could see the icehouse.

She hadn't meant to look. She had looked. There was a lamp burning inside — the light leaked out around the covered window in a narrow seam along the bottom of the curtain — and they were already awake in there, or some of them were. She didn't know at what hour they woke, or what the whitewashed partitioned room was like at five in the morning, whether the two cots and two pallets the Houlton men had installed were adequate or whether the four of them lay awake long before the work started. She had wondered about this in the first week, had constructed and discarded several versions of what it was like to be inside that room, and had eventually let the wondering go.

Three weeks since they'd come. The farm had arranged itself around their presence the way it arranged itself around any new constraint — not happily or unhappily, just as a fact of the season. They worked the east field in the mornings and the north end of the corn in the afternoons. They ate their meals in the icehouse. In the evenings they went back to the icehouse and the door closed and the light showed at the curtain's edge until it didn't.

She'd watched their arrival from this same window: the Coastal Patrol truck pulling up on the road, the four of them climbing down with their packs, the men from Camp Houlton doing the handover on the gravel while her father stood in the yard and didn't speak. Her mother in the doorway behind the screen. Hannah here, at this window, uncertain what she'd expected but watching.

She went back to work.

---

Lonzo came at seven the way he always came — the truck on the road, the cab door, his boots on the gravel — and settled onto his stool at the barn door. He was sixty-three or close to it, with a face that had been weathered into something that communicated very little. He pulled the Bangor Daily from his coat pocket and opened it. He had a son in the Pacific who didn't write often enough, Hannah had heard her father say to her mother once; she didn't know if this was why he sat the way he sat, with the patience of a man who had decided a long time ago what he was going to do with an afternoon and was going to do it regardless. He laid the Springfield across his knees.

He looked up when she looked at him.

She nodded. He nodded.

That was all.

At quarter past seven the icehouse door opened and all four of them came out into the gray cold and walked in a loose cluster toward the near field where the last rows of winter corn waited. She watched from the barn doorway — the way she watched most mornings now, a habit that had started without her deciding to start it and that she hadn't been able to stop. Three of them she knew well enough by now to have put shapes to, though not names: the heavyset one whose step she could hear from inside the barn, who walked with his shoulders rolling, always first; the thin one who carried a slight lean to the left, a habit of the body she recognized from men who had done hard work on one side for too long; the older one with the bald patch, who moved deliberately, as if he had been told where to go so many times that he'd stopped having opinions about the direction. The fourth walked quickly at the back of the group, keeping pace with the others by moving faster, the way you moved when you were the shortest.

She'd heard Lonzo call his name three days after they arrived — *Reinmar*, sharp, pointing at the east fence — and had not forgotten it.

Karl Reinmar. The youngest of the four.

---

She was carrying feed buckets to the far end of the barn when she heard the clatter. Small sound, something dropped. She set the buckets down and looked: a short-handled cultivating tool — the kind her father used for the kitchen garden bed — had fallen into the gap at the base of the east fence post. The fence ran close to the barn wall on that side, close enough that something dropped from the near field could slip into the gap without being reachable from outside without going all the way around to the gate.

She picked it up.

He was on the other side of the fence.

She hadn't heard him come to the fence. He was two feet away through the boards and wire, closer than she had been to any of them, and there was nothing to do about it — no time to decide how to hold her face or what to think about first. She'd had some half-formed expectation of something, she realized now, standing here with the tool in her hand: some quality to the face that would explain what he was or what it meant that he was here. There was no such quality. He was young, that was the first thing — younger than she'd thought from the distance of the barn window, which had reduced all four of them to shapes. His face was wind-chapped, the skin across his cheekbones roughened by weeks of October cold. His hair had been cut short and not carefully. He had a tired quality that was not the tiredness of a single bad night but the kind that accumulated over time until it stopped showing as tiredness and showed only as the particular stillness of a face that had stopped expecting things to change. His eyes were gray-blue, the color of the harbor on a cold morning when the sky was low.

He was looking at the tool, not at her.

*Danke*, he said.

She pushed the tool through the gap at the bottom of the fence and he took it and stepped back and went back to work.

From his stool at the barn door, Lonzo turned a page in the Bangor Daily. The paper made its flat, dry sound. She had picked up a tool that had fallen and passed it through a fence and a person had said thank you.

She picked up the feed buckets. Her hands did not feel like they had done anything remarkable. She carried the feed to the far stall and finished the work.

---

She walked the three miles the long way, under the maples along the edge of the Hallet property, where the leaves were still coming down in the cold morning. She counted things when she didn't want to think — fence posts, the crows on the wire above the Osborn field — and got to twenty-three fence posts before she stopped counting and let herself think instead.

*Danke.* She had known what that meant since she was four years old, since before she'd known what anything in English meant. Her father's voice in the kitchen before it had been her father's house, before the rules had settled: *Danke, Liebling.* He hadn't called her that in a long time. The word was such a small one that using it barely counted as language, barely counted as deciding to speak.

She thought: Karl Reinmar is nineteen. He has been in Tunisia and in Houlton and now he is on a farm in Maine in October. He said *Danke* for a cultivating tool through a fence. She had handed the tool through because there was nothing else to do with it.

She thought: he is a person. She arranged the facts in a row — the tool, the fence, the word, the gray-blue eyes not looking at her — and they were still just facts. She walked the rest of the three miles and arrived at school before the first bell.

---

The lesson was on indirect discourse. *Oratio obliqua*, Mr. Klein said — the grammar of reported speech, how a statement became secondary when it was embedded in another clause, the verb shifted, the meaning changed depending on what tense the main clause had been given. She wrote the examples in her notebook and worked through the practice sentences twice. She got three wrong the first time and corrected them. She thought about the fence and told herself to stop thinking about the fence.

At lunch Ada Wheeler sat across from her with her tray.

"Raymond Foss says his father says the Coast Guard thinks it was a German agent," Ada said. "The body on the breakwater. That he came off a submarine. A spy."

Hannah ate a bite of her sandwich. The body on the breakwater had been town news for a week. She'd heard three versions: the spy, a merchant sailor from a vessel wrecked on the outer ledges in the blow, and something involving a man from Ellsworth and a debt she hadn't quite followed. Raymond Foss's father worked at the cannery and was known to have opinions on many things.

"Maybe," Hannah said.

"Doesn't it worry you? Right here in Coldwater?"

She thought about saying: Raymond Foss's father doesn't know anything about submarines. She thought about saying: the body is in Rockland now with the Coast Guard. She thought about saying: a lot of things wash up after a blow. She didn't say any of these.

"I didn't know him," she said.

Ada looked at her as if this had missed the point. Two other girls sat down and the conversation moved on and Hannah ate the rest of her sandwich.

---

The evening milking was done by six and the dark had come in solid before she got back to the house. She stood a moment in the yard and looked at the kitchen window — the lamp lit inside, the yellow square of it in the dark, her mother's shape moving past — and then went in.

Her father was at the far end of the table with the German-language Bangor Daily, the edition he received by post on Thursdays. He read it folded open to the inside pages, elbows on the table, in the way he'd always read. Her mother was at the stove, her back to the room, stirring something that smelled of potato.

Hannah sat down with her Latin book.

The kitchen had its own kind of silence in the evenings, a silence she'd grown up inside, which meant she knew its textures the way she knew the animals' sounds: what it weighed when nothing was about to happen and what it weighed when something was. The clock above the door ran a minute fast. The stove made its sounds. Her mother's spoon made its sounds. Her father's newspaper turned once every several minutes. Outside the window the dark was complete.

She worked through the indirect discourse drill and corrected the errors she found. Her father reached the end of the page and let the paper fall slightly in his hands and read the next page without turning it, the way he did when he'd found something he was going to stay on for a while.

He said something under his breath. A single word, low, not directed at her or at anyone. The sound a person made when reading something that had confirmed what they'd known it was going to say. She glanced up. His expression was unchanged, his eyes on the page.

She went back to the drill.

Then her mother said: *Wir hätten früher gehen sollen.*

She said it to the stove, or to the window above the stove, her voice flat and without inflection — not quiet, exactly, not a whisper.

Her father looked up.

They looked at each other across the kitchen — he at his end with the newspaper still folded in his hands, she at the stove with the spoon held out to one side where it wouldn't drip. The clock made its sound. The stove made its sound. Something passed between them that Hannah could not have named, and she did not try. Four seconds. Five.

Her father looked back at the paper.

Her mother looked back at the pot.

Hannah looked at the indirect discourse drill. In the margin beside the third set of sentences she had written, before she had decided to write anything: *Wir hätten früher gehen sollen.* She read it. She pressed the pen down and crossed it out, once and again and again, until the paper was dark there and nothing showed through.

---

She took the lamp upstairs after supper and finished the last of the homework and then sat on the edge of her bed and didn't move for a while. From the window, when she lifted the curtain, she could see the shape of the icehouse against the sky — just the roofline, the dark mass of it — and below the roofline the narrow strip of light at the curtain's edge, still burning. Whatever they did in the evenings in there she didn't know. Whether they talked or read or sat with their own language, with their own thinking, in the whitewashed room where the cold must come up through the boards. Whether they thought about the places they'd come from or had decided that direction didn't help.

The strip of light at the icehouse window went out.

She sat with that a moment — the dark where the light had been, the shape of the roof still present, the sky above it that was slightly lighter than the roofline. Then she blew out her own lamp and lay down in the dark and listened.

The barn sounds came through the wall: an animal shifting in its stall, the knock of a board, the wind at the eaves. The silage smell moved through on the air and then didn't and then did again, the way smells moved at night when the temperature dropped and the air settled.

*Wir hätten früher gehen sollen.*

She knew what the words meant. What they were about — what her mother had meant by *earlier*, what *leaving* was and what had been left and what had been meant to be left behind — she didn't know yet. She thought she might not know for a long time. She thought she was probably going to have to find out.

# The Second Bedroom

Clara Walsh had been looking at the board long enough that Marcus had started to wonder whether she was still working on the grammar or had already made it through to something on the other side of it.

He had explained the ablative absolute twice — once in its architecture and once in what the architecture was meant to convey. The grammatical explanation had been correct, and the class had received it in the way that students received correct explanations of things they could not yet feel: as information to be held until the feeling arrived, if it arrived. The second explanation had been an attempt at the feeling itself: *his rebus gestis*, he had written on the board, translated it, then tried to show what it was doing — how it took an action, its agent and its verb, and pushed the whole of it into the background, completed, settled into the past before the main clause began. Caesar built his bridge, and the grammar had already performed the accomplishment, had arranged the earlier action as the prior condition of everything that followed.

Clara Walsh looked up from the board.

"So it is like circumstances," she said.

"Yes," Marcus said. "Exactly like circumstances." He waited a moment. "The subordinate action is finished before the main clause begins. It becomes the background against which the main action is possible at all."

She wrote something in the margin of her notebook with the focused economy of a student who had understood and was now recording it for herself, not for Marcus. The class around her was working through it more slowly, which was what classes did with new constructions, and Marcus had the patience for it: he had explained the ablative absolute for the first time approximately twenty-five times and had watched students arrive at the same understanding by different routes and at different intervals. The patience was not indifference. It was its own form of attention.

He moved them through the Livy passage he had assigned for the following week — the Macedonian campaigns, which he had chosen in part because the ablative absolutes came at close intervals and the students would encounter the construction in context before they were asked to produce it themselves. Then the declension review.

Raymond Foss, in the back left seat, committed the same error in the third declension dative plural that he had been committing since the end of September: put the accusative ending where the dative belonged. Marcus corrected him. Raymond Foss corrected himself and committed it again. Marcus corrected him again and had him read the ending aloud before writing it, the body's memory being on occasion more reliable than the pencil's. Raymond Foss read it aloud and wrote it down and had it wrong a third time.

Marcus corrected it a third time, with the patience that came from knowing the ending would one day feel inevitable — that a point existed in Raymond Foss's future at which this confusion would be as incomprehensible to him as the grammar was natural now, and that reaching that point required only the correction given and given and given again until it accumulated into knowledge. He believed this about grammar because the evidence consistently supported it.

He assigned the Livy passage and dismissed the class.

---

The teachers' room had a coffee tin and a teapot on the radiator shelf, a table with two chairs against the window, and a view of the north side of the building where the maples had finished dropping their leaves the previous week. He made his tea — he brought his own, in a paper bag in his coat pocket, the situation at Beal's having been irregular since early 1942 — and sat at the end of the table.

Edna Price and Ralph Garland were at the other end. Marcus had been there perhaps two minutes when he understood that they were talking about the body on the breakwater, which had been the town's conversation for the better part of a week and had arrived at this table in what he recognized as its hardened form: the original cluster of possibilities had collapsed into a single confident explanation.

"A U-boat agent," Garland said. "It is the only explanation that makes any sense. A man washes up here with no papers, in foreign civilian clothing — of course he came off a submarine. Of course."

"Mildred Foster's husband says the Coast Guard is calling it a regular drowning," Edna Price said.

"Well. They would say that."

Marcus drank his tea. He looked at the window. The maples were bare, their branches precise against the gray sky.

He was aware of several explanations that were not the U-boat theory. He was aware of them because he had lived through the period of European history that produced them. A man in civilian clothes, no papers, washed up on a foreign coast: the correct first hypothesis was displacement, not espionage. A man moved through the unofficial channels that wartime Europe had developed for people who could not move through official ones — through the arrangements of borrowed boats and borrowed names and borrowed trust that he knew, from his own passage through something like them, to be more extensive and less organized than the people outside them supposed. Such a man could arrive on a coastline and not survive the arriving. This required no submarine. It required only the war, and a coast, and bad luck.

He also knew that this was not an explanation he could introduce into a conversation in the teachers' room at Coldwater High School.

He drank his tea.

He was thinking about the calluses he had heard about — not at the base of the fingers, not the callus pattern of a fishing hand or a farm hand or a cannery hand, but in the centers of the palms. He had heard this detail the way that details from a death moved through a small town: passed between people, softened by transit, arriving with less precision than it had started with. He filed it. The calluses were specific. The specificity was useful.

Garland was describing the U-boat in some detail, with a confidence that bore no evident relation to any knowledge of submarines. Marcus thought of the third time he had corrected Raymond Foss's declension — the patience that had been required, the giving of the right ending until it accumulated — and then he thought that there was a version of patience like that, in situations like this one, that was not patience at all. It was only silence. Because the correction would cost more than the correction would ever be worth.

He rinsed his cup and went to the next class.

---

He left the building at half past three. The cold had arrived in its late-October depth in the past week — not the fresh cold of early October but the cold that had weight and intention to it, that was beginning to mean November. He turned up his collar and walked.

Three blocks to Elm Street. He had walked this route every school day since the middle of March, 1942, and knew it now with the thorough knowledge of daily repetition: which boards in the Maple Street sidewalk were soft, that the elm at the corner of Birch had a root that had forced a ridge in the pavement, that the Garson house had a broken gutter that dripped onto the path in a particular way. He passed the harbor road without turning onto it, as he did every afternoon. The smell of brine and diesel reached him briefly from the south and then was gone.

He was thinking about the Livy passage. He had been thinking about it since the class — this was what happened sometimes when a grammatical construction moved into the foreground of his attention, it stayed there for a day or two, reorganizing the way he saw things, until it receded. *Dum haec geruntur* — while these things were being done. Not technically the ablative absolute, but in the same territory: the action happening in the background while the main clause went forward in the foreground. One event held in suspension while another was accomplished. The thing that was also happening.

He turned onto Elm Street.

---

The smell reached him when he was still on the front step: fish chowder, which meant Lillian had found what she had been looking for all week. He hung his coat and hat on the peg inside the door and went to the kitchen.

She was at the stove, her back to him. The pot was on the back burner, the lid trembling slightly with the heat.

"Fish chowder," she said, without turning. "Real milk. Not the powder."

He sat at the kitchen table. "Where did you find it?"

She set the wooden spoon on its rest and turned around. "Pfeiffer farm sends milk on Tuesdays. Twice a week if the week is good." She said it with the satisfaction of a practical problem solved — the quieter kind, belonging to a person who had paid attention and been proved right. "It was a good week."

He knew the Pfeiffer farm because he knew the Pfeiffer daughter, who was in his Latin class and worked harder than the work required of her. He did not say this. He said: "It smells very good."

"It is very good," she said, and turned back to the pot.

She asked about Vienna while she worked — she asked about Vienna most evenings, at intervals close enough that he had come to understand it as genuine curiosity rather than courtesy, which were different kinds of asking. He had learned to answer a piece of it each time, which was the only honest way to handle something that large: a piece that could be given without requiring everything that came after it.

Tonight he told her about the Prater in October. The park, the chestnut trees along the main avenue, which had shed their nuts in September and dropped their leaves by mid-October, leaving the avenue yellow-brown and the ground beneath it scattered with split casings. The smell of roasted chestnuts from the cart near the eastern entrance. The Sunday-morning habit he had maintained for several years — the walk before noon, the light in the leaves at this time of year. He described it. He gave her the years before the years he did not give her.

He did not get to 1938. He had learned at this table that stopping before 1938 was the right stopping place — not because of what came after so much as because the before was what answered what she was actually asking, which was: what was the place, before everything that happened to the place. He could answer that honestly. He had found it was better to have something he could answer honestly than to preface every answer with where it could not go.

Henry came in at ten past six.

He brought the smell of coal on his jacket — not the faint background smell Marcus had associated with him for a year but the immediate working version. He pulled the jacket off and hung it on the peg by the kitchen door.

"East furnace flue needed clearing," he said. He sat down. He looked at the bowl Lillian had set at his place and then at his wife. "Real milk," he said.

"Pfeiffer farm," she said.

He picked up his spoon.

They ate. The kitchen was warm in the way the kitchen was always warm in the evenings, which was a warmth Marcus had come to understand, over a year, as belonging specifically to this room and these people. Outside, the dark had settled fully, the October dark arriving earlier each week on its way to becoming the winter dark. He ate his chowder. He tasted the milk in it, which Lillian had been right about. He drank his tea.

Henry had brought home the copy from the teachers' room. He set it on the table and folded it in half and read the front page. Then he said, without looking up: "Someone in town was asking about you. Earlier in the week."

Marcus looked at him.

"The German teacher," Henry said.

A moment. Marcus thought of Ralph Garland and the U-boat and the particular logic by which a week of speculation hardened into a theory that required a local figure to be suspicious of.

"What did you tell them?" Marcus said.

Henry turned the page. "That you teach Latin too. Figured that was the useful part."

Marcus said: "That is accurate."

Lillian came to the table with the bread she had been keeping at the oven's edge and they ate, and Henry read the rest of the paper, and Lillian did the dishes. Marcus thanked her for the chowder. She said it was nothing. He had known for a year at least that it was not.

---

He went upstairs at half past eight.

The second bedroom was at the end of the hall, window facing the street. The room was tidy with the tidiness he had maintained long enough that it required no maintenance — the desk clear, the books on the shelf ordered by subject and then by size, the narrow bed made tightly in the European habit of order as a form of dignity. He took his coat off and hung it. He stood a moment in the center of the room. The kitchen sounds came up through the floor: water in the pipes, Lillian's voice briefly, Henry's reply.

He went to the shelf and took down a book.

He had had it since Vienna: *Einführung in die deutsche Grammatik*, published in Leipzig in 1929, which he had carried through several countries and arrived with in Maine with a water-damaged cover and a spine repaired with tape that had since yellowed and dried. He did not use it for teaching; he had better materials for teaching. He used it sometimes at the end of days for reasons he had not felt the need to articulate.

He sat at the desk and opened the book to the middle, where it fell open naturally from having been opened there enough times. The pages in front of him carried his own marginal notes in pencil — a paragraph on the genitive of possession, several observations on adjectival constructions, some marginal dialogue with the text. His handwriting from 1937, which he could identify by the particular formation of the *d*, the angle of the lettering, the specific way the lowercase *g* closed: the handwriting of a man in Paris, in a room on the Rue des Ecoles, writing notes in a book he had brought from Vienna in preparation for a teaching life that had not yet arrived, in a year that had not yet become what followed it.

He read one paragraph. The observation his 1937 self had set down was still accurate.

He closed the book.

He sat at the desk for a while without moving. The window faced Elm Street and through it he could hear the elm moving in the wind, its bare branches audible now that the leaves were gone. A car on the main road a block over. The house made its sounds around him — the furnace, the pipes, the small adjustments of a wooden building against the cold.

The room was cold. He was not, not entirely, not yet: the kitchen's warmth was still in him in the way that warmth stayed in the chest for a while after a person left a warm room, diminishing slowly.

He put the book back on the shelf.

# Official Report

She was finishing the seven o'clock entry when she heard a vehicle on the harbor road.

The tide gauge reading, the fleet status: three smacks out since before light — the *Ruth Ann*, the *Mabel*, the *Cornelia Best* — and the *Dorothy Mead* still on her mooring with the engine trouble Alderman had promised to see to by Wednesday. Today was Thursday. She blotted the entry and set the pen in the groove of Owen's chart table.

The Coast Guard vehicle parked at the foot of the wharf at three minutes past nine. Dark green, the Sector designation stenciled on its door. She recognized it from October.

Parsons came up the dock with his clipboard under his arm and his cap on against the cold. He came through the door — the latch caught on the first try — and looked at the office with the brief professional scan of a man checking a space against his memory of it: chart table, tide log, field telephone, kerosene stove. He looked at the window and the harbor, and back at her. She gestured to the chair across the table. He sat and uncapped his pen.

"Harbormaster."

"Lieutenant."

He was in his late thirties — the right age for the Coast Guard in 1943: too young for the last war, a few years past the eligible window of this one. She had seen the type before, not that he minded being it. He had the manner of a man for whom these interviews had become genuinely his through practice — professional, careful, not warm and not unkind.

"We'll go through the morning of the twenty-eighth," he said.

"Ready when you are," she said.

---

He started with the timeline. She gave it to him the way she kept the log: in order, each item complete before moving to the next. Time of notification: seven-fourteen, Hector Brann at the harbor road telephone. Response time: she had been in the office when the call came in and reached the breakwater by seven thirty-five. He asked if she could have moved faster. She said she had stopped for the tide gauge reading she would need for the official account; the data was there when he asked for it. He wrote that down.

The body: male, face up, arms at his sides, in the granite seam on the ocean side of the breakwater approximately forty feet from the harbor-side opening of the seam. Eastern face. No sign of prior injury. She had confirmed the absence of a pulse and sent Hector Brann for the constable's telephone and stayed until the Coast Guard arrived.

"You have the tide data," he said.

She brought out the charts — the gauge readings she had taken during the blow, the fleet status records, the weather notations for the preceding forty-eight hours, each logged in the standard format. She had organized them before he arrived: chronological order, the relevant entries tabbed at their edges. He did not remark on this. He went through them with the focus of a man reading instruments he understood.

He asked about the seam — whether it would hold something deposited by water, or whether the tide would carry material back out. She explained: the blocks had settled unevenly since the 1890s, leaving a joint where the ebb current dropped what the flood had brought. The angle of the eastern face. The specific dynamic at that location. He listened without interrupting and wrote.

"Your estimate for when the body arrived," he said.

"Twelve to two a.m. on the twenty-eighth," she said. "Given the seam and the position. That's the window I'd put it in."

"Based on."

"The tidal data, the deposit pattern, the orientation of the body. All consistent." A pause. "I've thought about it."

He wrote.

He asked about the clothing: what she had observed on scene, what was in the log. The heavy civilian coat, unfamiliar in its cut, double-breasted, buttons she had not recognized. He asked if she had searched the pockets. She had not — once she called it in, the body was under Coast Guard authority and she had not touched it. Correct procedure, he said.

She answered each question in the scope it was asked. He had a good method.

---

"The preceding night," he said. He turned to a new page on his clipboard. "The blow was at its worst the preceding forty-eight hours?"

"Mostly. It had eased some by Tuesday evening."

"Did anything unusual occur in the harbor area during the blow? Any unauthorized vessels in the inner anchorage? Anyone on the dock who shouldn't have been there?"

The stove ticked once. Outside the north window the harbor lay in its November gray: flat water, flat light, the smell of brine that came through the window frame even when the glass was shut. The smacks were out or in. The season was what the season was. Everything visible from this window was where it was supposed to be.

"The blow kept most activity down," she said. "The fleet was in." One pause, one breath. "I did a late mooring check at approximately twenty-three hundred hours."

He looked up from the clipboard.

"I didn't enter anything unusual."

He held the pen for a moment — not suspicion; only the habitual check of a careful man making sure the answer was complete before he committed it to paper. Then he wrote.

"Any vessels you can't account for? Unregistered moorings, traffic you couldn't identify?"

"Nothing in the log," she said.

He looked at the tide log open on the table beside the charts. The October entries were visible in her handwriting — the standard format, the black ink, entry after entry. He did not ask to see Tuesday night's page specifically. If he had asked she would have shown him: the entry was there, it had been there since she wrote it. *2300: mooring check completed, fleet secure.* He did not ask.

He wrote, turned the page on his clipboard, and moved on.

---

He asked to walk where the body had been found.

November on the breakwater was the cold that came off open water — not the dry cold of the interior but the cold with moisture in it, the kind that worked through wool over time. The algae on the lower courses were slick. She wore her heavy coat and her work hat and went first; she knew every place on that granite where a foot would hold and where it would not. She had walked this breakwater since 1935 in every weather and every hour. She knew its two hundred feet the way she knew the distance from the chart table to the tide log shelf.

She brought him to the seam. The joint between two blocks on the eastern face, forty feet from the harbor-side opening.

Parsons looked at it with the same methodical eye he had given the charts. The approach angles from the open water side. The tidal marks on the lower granite, the algae growing in horizontal bands that marked the tidal range. The distance from the harbor mouth. He looked long enough that she understood he was done looking and was now confirming what he had already concluded.

"Two previous bodies on this breakwater," he said. The note she had given him in the office.

"Neither in this seam," she said.

He made a note. They turned back.

---

On the return along the granite, the harbor road ahead and the diesel smell from the smacks in the inner anchorage reaching them on the wind, he told her what the investigation had found.

Cause of death: hypothermia and drowning consistent with storm exposure. No injury prior to exposure. The body's condition was consistent with twelve to thirty-six hours in the water before discovery — a broad window, unavoidable given the storm and the water temperature. No military markings of any kind. No insignia, no service items.

The clothing: civilian, European in manufacture. The cut of the coat, the style of the buttons, the weight and weave of the lining fabric — all consistent with continental production. Not British. Not American. Wartime manufacture, based on the fabric quality and the composition of the buttons. The working estimate was 1941 to 1942.

No papers. No wallet, no letters, no documents of any kind. The pockets had been empty.

She asked: "Any theory on how he got there?"

"Storm exposure is the most probable account," Parsons said. "A man overboard from a vessel that didn't report it — that happens in a blow on a small boat. Or he was already in the water when the storm reached this coast." The wind was at their backs, off the Atlantic. "There's been talk in town. The U-boat line. We've looked at it. We're not pursuing it. The acute period on this coast was last year — the tactical situation has changed considerably. A man in civilian clothes, European manufacture, no papers — there are other explanations for how a man ends up in the water."

She said she understood.

They went the rest of the way in without talking.

---

At the office door he gave her the formal close. The case would be classified as accidental drowning, unidentified. Her statement would be on file at the District office in Portland. He'd keep her number in case an identification came in — a missing-persons report from another jurisdiction, something that matched the description. He said this without particular expectation.

She said she would be here.

He shook her hand — dry, brief — and went to his vehicle. She stood in the doorway and watched him back off the dock and turn up the harbor road, the vehicle rounding the curve toward town and out of sight. When the sound of his engine was gone there was only the harbor — the line of the water, the cold, the smell of it.

She pulled the door closed. The latch required a slight lift on the handle as she turned it; she gave it the lift and the latch seated. The trick Owen had shown her. The carpenter had offered to fix it twice and she had told him twice it didn't need fixing.

---

The stove had been going since seven and the room was warm. The cold she had brought in from the breakwater eased.

She stood at Owen's chart table without sitting. The November light came through both windows and made nothing particular of anything — everything the same flat distance. Through the north window the breakwater ran out to the harbor mouth, two hundred feet, empty and salt-whitened, the water behind it going gray to the horizon. She had looked at that breakwater from this window every morning for eight years. It looked the way it looked.

She sat.

The tide log was open to this morning — the seven o'clock entry she had written before Parsons arrived, two lines: gauge reading, fleet status, Alderman's engine not yet resolved. Her handwriting, black ink, in the format she had used for eight years. Owen's format, because it was correct.

She turned the pages back through October.

Her handwriting through all of it: tides, fleet conditions, mooring inspections, fuel inquiries, the cannery pier. The record of the harbor continuing — it had to continue; it did continue — in the format that made the record useful and the harbor manageable. She had kept it this way since the first morning she had taken the post and understood what she had been given.

She found the week of the twenty-eighth.

The Thursday entry — the morning Hector Brann had called — was written more carefully than the entries around it. Not dramatically. She would not have noticed it without looking. But she was looking, and she could see it: the letter formation tighter, the spacing a little wider than her habit.

She turned back one more day.

Tuesday.

Date, tides, fleet conditions. The weather notation for the blow, logged at each of her checks. Alderman's engine noted. The mooring check times for the early morning and the noon watch and the evening. At the bottom of the right column, added when she returned from the dock at half past eleven:

*2300: mooring check completed, fleet secure.*

She read it.

She read it a second time.

She knew everything that was in that line and she knew everything that was not in it. Both were facts, as durable as the paper and the ink and the cabinet on the far wall where the decade's records sat in chronological order. The record said what it said. Everything in it was accurate.

She closed the log.

The cabinet held Owen's volumes in the lower shelves, their spines worn pale with handling. The 1934 volume was on the third shelf from the bottom. She had taken it down once, in the first November she had the post, to understand what keeping the record meant and what it looked like to keep it honestly. She had put it back. She did not take it down now.

She set her hand flat on the closed log for a moment.

Then she opened it to this morning, looked at the office clock, and wrote the nine o'clock entry: tides, fleet status, the harbor doing what the harbor did.

Nothing unusual to note.
