# Fifty Kilometers

The fence posts on the south side of the near field had heaved over the summer and needed straightening before the ground froze solid and made the work impossible until March. Albrecht had said so at breakfast in the tone that meant today, not this week. Hannah put on his old coat and met him at the south gate at half past eight.

The work had its rhythm: she gripped the post at the base with both hands and leaned her weight against it while he raised the driver and swung it down. The driver was a section of heavy iron pipe with capped ends, two feet long, and she felt every impact travel through the post and into her palms and up her arms, even when the swing went well. Her job was to hold the post true and her father's job was the swing, and they had done this enough times that she knew how to shift her weight for the angle and he knew how hard to swing for the resistance. They didn't talk. The work didn't need it.

Lonzo Reed had arrived at seven with the four prisoners and put them to work in the near field: the three older ones at the drainage ditch along the far boundary, and Karl Reinmar on the rock section — the near quarter of the field that gave up stones every year, heaved up by frost and thaw, needing to be cleared before spring tilling. He was working with his back mostly toward them, thirty feet away. She could see the effort of it when he lifted a larger stone — the set of his back, the shift of weight, the pause to gauge where it would sit on the wall — and then the rock placed and his hands going back to find the next one.

She was watching the fence. Then the line of posts toward the stone wall at the south boundary. Then the grey stubble of the corn rows stretching back toward the barn. The stalks had gone brittle after the first frosts and stood pale and discarded-looking, the way they did every year and the way she had not entirely stopped noticing. She breathed out and the cold made her breath visible and she breathed in and held the post steady for her father's next swing.

There was a sound from the field.

Not a word, exactly. More the sounds a person makes before words arrive — the consonants that come with lifting something heavier than expected, the involuntary noise that the effort produces before the person decides to say anything. An oath, maybe, or a complaint muttered at the ground. It came from Karl's direction, and it was in German, and she would have registered it and moved past it the way she moved past the German her father spoke at her back all morning, except that the German was shaped differently.

She could not have said how she knew this. Her German was the kitchen, the barn, her father's reading voice, the careful German Marcus Klein put on the board like a specimen pinned in place. What she heard from the field was none of those. The vowels sat lower in the mouth and had a particular rounded quality, the consonants softened in places she was unused to softening them. Like her father's voice when he was tired enough to stop attending to himself. Like something that had been shaped in one place and had traveled a long way without losing the shape.

Albrecht's arm stopped at the top of the arc.

The driver hung in the air. She felt the stillness of it as a change in the pressure she'd been bracing against — the downswing she'd been ready for, not arriving. One second. Two. She counted in the part of her that counted without being asked.

Then the driver came down. The impact traveled through her palms, the usual way.

He pulled the driver off the post and walked to the next one. He didn't speak and he didn't look toward the field. Hannah moved with him and took hold of the next post.

Karl set the stone down and went to find another.

---

At eleven they stopped. She felt the cold more in her hands now than she had at the start; the post-holding had held it off earlier, but standing still she noticed it. They walked back to the barn and she ran the pump at the corner of the barn wall and rinsed her hands in the cold water and stepped aside for her father.

She said: "Vater. Where exactly were you born? In Bavaria — which town?"

He looked at her. Not a suspicious look. More the look of a man who has been given something unexpected and is considering what to do with it.

"Feuchtwangen," he said.

She turned the name over: *Feuchtwangen*. She didn't know it. "Is it near Ansbach?" She had seen Ansbach on the map in the geography classroom — a city label somewhere in the right general region, the part marked Bayern.

Her father dried his hands on the side of his trousers. He thought for a moment. "Forty kilometers or so. South."

He went into the barn. She stood at the pump for another second with the cold still in her hands and then followed.

He did not ask why she wanted to know.

---

She walked to school in just over an hour. The road was frozen in its ruts from the last week's mud and the sky was low and white, the kind of November sky that committed to nothing. She thought about the fence and then about the pump and then about neither, or she thought about them without exactly thinking — the way a stone turns in water without going anywhere, just moving with the current.

*Feuchtwangen.* Forty kilometers south of Ansbach. She had a fact. She didn't yet know what it was a fact about.

The afternoon session was Latin. Marcus Klein was going over the gerundive of obligation — *legendus, legenda, legendum*, must be read, needing to be read, the construction that made a thing's necessity part of its name. She wrote down what he put on the board and the parsing that went with it, but the lesson was sitting on the surface of her attention without going in. Across the row, Ada Wheeler was taking notes with the absorbed efficiency of someone who intended to do well on the end-of-term examination. Hannah looked at her own notes. *Legendum est.* It is necessary to read. It must be read. She wrote it and turned the page.

The geography classroom was across the hall and empty in the afternoons except for study hall. She went there during free period.

The European map was on the center wall — the large one with the colored zones that had been updated twice since she'd started paying attention to it. She had looked at this map before, everyone had, everyone had stood in front of it since December 1941 looking for the names the radio announced. Tunisia. Sicily. The long boot of Italy with the colored lines marking where the armies currently were. She moved past those now and found Germany.

Ansbach was there, labeled in the southern half of Germany, in the region the legend marked *Bayern*. She put her thumb on it. Forty kilometers south. She moved her finger down, measuring against the map's scale by eye. Feuchtwangen was not labeled — it was not a large enough town for a map that fit the continent on a single sheet — but she could find the rough zone of it. A territory about the size of her palm, south of Ansbach, in the country that was her father's first country.

She thought about fifty kilometers. She didn't know Karl's town. She hadn't been told and she couldn't determine it from a sound heard once across a field. But she could see the region on this map. What looked like a broad area was small in the way that mattered — the kind of distance where a phrase, a particular way of shaping a vowel low in the mouth, would carry from one town to the next and still arrive recognizable a generation later. Less than a morning's drive, if there were such a thing as driving for pleasure, which there wasn't, not anymore.

Her thumb was still on Ansbach. She moved it slowly south and then stopped.

There was a shape to it — the pause, the name, the fifty kilometers she was approximating here with her eye — but she couldn't yet say what the shape was the outline of. She had the geography. She didn't have the rest.

She heard the door.

Ruth Stanhope came in carrying her lunch bag and stopped when she saw Hannah at the map. "Bavaria? Are you doing a report?"

"No," Hannah said.

Ruth sat down and opened her bag. Hannah looked at the map for a moment longer, then went to sit across from her.

---

The cows were already in from the pasture when she got home. She could hear them through the barn wall — the shifting weight, the low sounds they made when nothing was wrong. She changed her clothes and went out.

The evening milking took until six. She did the far half of the stalls and her father did the near half and they worked toward each other in the usual way, the sound of the milk in the bucket changing pitch as the bucket filled. Her father spoke to the cows in German, the occasional word, *ruhig, ruhig*, nothing that required an answer. She spoke to hers too, in whatever came, English mostly. The cows didn't distinguish.

She was at the barn door when the prisoners came in from the field at half past four, before she'd started. Lonzo Reed had them moving back along the fence line toward the icehouse: the heavyset one first, then the thin one who walked with his weight shifted left, then the older one, then Karl. Lonzo walked behind. They moved in the way they moved at the end of the day — finished, the work behind them instead of ahead.

Karl passed within ten feet of where she was standing.

He didn't look at her. His eyes were on the ground in front of him or on the icehouse door. But when he came level with Lonzo's stool he turned his head and nodded — just that, a brief drop and lift of his chin, nothing elaborate. And Lonzo, folding his newspaper to tuck it under his arm, looked up and nodded back. The same register. Neither of them spoke.

Karl went into the icehouse. Lonzo set his back against the outer wall.

She went into the barn.

---

Supper was the white bean soup Magda made on Mondays. By Wednesday it had developed further in the pot, richer, the beans softer. Hannah ate it without thinking about it and then noticed she had eaten most of the bowl.

Her father said grace in German. His hands were flat on the table and his voice was quiet in the way it was only for the grace — unhurried, without performance. The same words she had heard every evening of her life. They had become a texture she moved through rather than words she followed, and she felt the usual faint guilt about this.

The radio in the corner was on and turned low. The six o'clock news, or possibly already past it. She couldn't have said which front the announcer was reporting on tonight; the voice arrived in the kitchen as a murmur rather than language, general meaning without specific fact. Her father did not turn it up. He had stopped turning it up some weeks ago.

Magda was at the table. She had set it, as she always did, and she was eating now in the same efficient, present way she did everything in the kitchen. She was not absent. She was precisely here. She looked at her bowl and occasionally at nothing in particular.

Hannah looked at her father's hands around his soup bowl. Wide across the knuckle. The skin at the back darkened in the deep creases the way farm skin got.

*Feuchtwangen.* The word came up and she held it quietly, without pushing at it. Two seconds of stillness at the top of a post-driver's arc.

She had what she had tonight. Tomorrow she would have whatever tomorrow gave her.

The kitchen smelled of the soup and the wood smoke and underneath both, through the west wall, faintly but reliably, the silage from the barn. The smell that was always there.

Her father's hands around his bowl.

The lamp on the table.

The radio, low, saying something about somewhere far away.

# The Half-Question

The conjugation *fero, ferre, tuli, latum* was on the board in his handwriting, which was smaller than the board required and which he had been compensating for, with limited success, since his first day at the school in March of the previous year. Third-period Latin, third-year students, eleven-thirty in the morning. The furnaces were working at full effort and losing to the cold that had flattened itself against the building sometime overnight. The panes fogged from the inside — not ice, not yet — but the thick condensation of two temperatures meeting each other at the glass. Through the clear portion at the upper edges of the nearest window, the schoolyard was grey and approximate, the far spruce a dark shape against a sky that had committed to nothing.

He went through the conjugation with the class. *Fero, ferre* — the shift from the root *fer-* to *tul-* in the perfect that required what he had come to think of, privately, as an act of trust: the language had been that particular way for long enough that arguing with it was beside the point. The passive forms were further difficulty. Michael Bates, third row from the left, had been having trouble with *fertur* since the Tuesday of the previous week — the same slight adjustment before the word arrived, as if it were sitting half a degree off-center in his mouth and needed correcting before it could be produced. Marcus had not mentioned this yet. He had been watching the gap narrow on its own.

"Bates," he said. "Once more."

"*Fertur*." A half-second. "Is carried."

"Again."

Bates said it without the gap this time. Marcus noted this without comment and moved on.

The exercises occupied the rest of the period. He moved between the rows as the class worked, pausing to confirm a form here or redirect an error there. Clara Walsh had finished early and was reviewing her answers with the composed efficiency of someone who was not checking her conclusions so much as reacquainting herself with them. In the back half of the room, the work was slower, more visible — the pencils pausing, the pages turned back. *Arma ferenda sunt.* Weapons must be carried. He looked at it on Donna Packard's paper and thought, not for the first time, that the textbook's choice of example sentences had a certain bluntness to it that the writers probably had not considered before 1941.

The bell. The chairs.

---

He was collecting the exercise papers from the desks when Hannah Pfeiffer came up.

She stayed after class with some regularity — not every week but with a consistency that established it as a pattern rather than an exception. Latin questions most often; German questions occasionally; sometimes both, when she was working through a construction that her two languages were resolving in conflicting ways. She had been in his courses since September of last year, and he had formed the opinion early and not revised it: she approached language as a system of logic rather than a series of items to be memorized, which was the quality that made the work interesting. He had noted this about her and considered the noting sufficient.

She set her notebook on the nearest desk and did not open it. Not a Latin question.

He waited.

"What does *Landsman* mean?" she said. "I think I have the German approximately right — *Landsmann*. Or is it —"

"*Landsmann*," he said. "The plural would be *Landsmänner*, yes." He looked up from the folder. "Where did you hear it?"

She considered for a moment. "One of the men at our farm. I think he said it to himself."

He placed the remaining exercise papers in the folder and closed it. He did this without hurrying.

"The word," he said, "is a term of affiliation. Literally: a person from the same land, the same region. It is not a synonym for *Landsleute* — for countrymen in the national sense — though it can be used loosely that way. Used precisely, it implies a shared *Gegend*." He paused. "Do you know the word?"

"Home district," she said. "Home ground."

"Near enough. It names a specific common origin — not *I am German and you are German*, which is nationality, but *we come from the same part of the world*, which is something more particular. A man from Munich would not naturally call a man from Hamburg his *Landsmann*, or not with any content to it. The word belongs to a smaller geography than the nation."

She was listening with the posture he had identified as her taking-in posture — not yet assembling, simply receiving. He waited to see what she would do with it.

"I see," she said.

"Said it to himself," he said. "Or to someone?"

"I don't — I'm not sure." A small motion of her hand on the notebook cover. "Maybe to someone. I wasn't close."

"Which farm?"

"Pfeiffer." He knew the Pfeiffer farm the way he knew most things about Coldwater Reach — indirectly, through accumulation, through the town's habit of circulating information about itself through every available channel. The German family on Route 9. The dairy farm, the milk that Lillian picked up Tuesday mornings when the week permitted. The prisoners placed there in October, under the Houlton program — he had heard this at Beal's, at the school, without seeking it.

"It is an interesting word to use in that context," Marcus said.

He did not elaborate. There was more to elaborate on — rather a lot more, in fact — and he set all of it aside, on the other side of the sentence, where it would wait. The word was doing its work without his assistance. Hannah Pfeiffer was seventeen years old and one of his better students and she had asked what was, for her, a vocabulary question, and he had answered it accurately, and that was the scope of what had happened here.

She looked at him for a moment. Waiting for further, calculating whether it was coming.

"He's from Franconia," she said.

"I see," Marcus said.

He did.

She gathered her notebook and her coat from the back chair. "Thank you, Mr. Klein."

"Fräulein Pfeiffer."

She went out.

---

He stood by the window.

The schoolyard was grey and still. A line of dead leaves at the east fence. The spruce boughs bending under nothing in particular — the cold air held enough moisture to make the light heavy. Two boys on the stone wall at the far end of the yard, small from this distance, doing something that did not require motion. He looked at the spruce, the boys, the fence, the flat grey sky above the roof of the woodshop, and registered none of it with any precision, which he recognized as a sign that he was looking at something else instead.

He had been not thinking about something for three weeks.

The body had been found in the last days of October — the storm, the breakwater, Hector Brann's boat coming in with the discovery. The town had settled quickly on its preferred account. U-boat, or something connected to submarines, or the relevant period of submarine activity along this coast and what it might have left behind — the exact theory had softened with each retelling until what circulated was a general agreement that this was a wartime thing and the proper people had addressed it. Parsons had come and gone. The record was presumably closed.

Marcus had not offered his version of events. He had been careful, in fact, not to develop his version to the point at which it would require offering, which was a more precise operation than simply keeping quiet.

The detail about the calluses had reached him through Edna Price and then through one of the fishermen at the counter at Beal's — centers of the palms, she had said, though by the time it had moved through two or three people the precision had softened somewhat. He had filed the softened version alongside the version he held, which was somewhat more specific and which had arrived in his mind fully formed and unwanted approximately three days after the body was found: a man in European civilian clothes with palm-center calluses and no papers was not a military operative. Military operatives had documentation, or the specific absence of documentation that constituted its own kind of record. What this man had was no papers — which was a different category entirely, not the no papers of a spy but the no papers of a person who had been traveling by means that did not generate documentation, which was to say by means available to people for whom the documented means were not available.

He had known this since October. He had spent November not following the thought further.

The reason had to do with what following it required.

He knew the logic of wartime displacement from the inside — not from study, not from the reports and lectures that circulated through refugee-aid organizations and emergency committees, but from the specific, physical experience of having been a person who moved through it. His passage from London to Sherbrooke in the summer of 1939 had involved, among other things, arrangements of the unofficial kind: a contact in a city he did not name, a boat that did not advertise its route, a farm somewhere in maritime Canada where he had spent two days in a room he was not registered as occupying. The people who had made these arrangements had not made them for personal advantage. They had made them because the official channels had stopped working for people in his category, and they understood this, and they had built something that worked in the spaces the official channels left empty. He had been grateful. He was still grateful. He had not discussed any of it since, partly from caution and partly because the people who had helped him had helped him in order to get him somewhere, not in order to become part of a story he told at dinner tables in coastal Maine.

He had spent two years in this town working at the project of being a different kind of person: one who taught Latin and German irregular verbs and walked the same three blocks to Elm Street every school day and told Lillian Crow about the Prater in October, a piece at a time, and ate fish chowder at a kitchen table that was warm enough to stay in for as long as the evening allowed. This was not a performance or a disguise. It was where he had arrived after everything that came before it. He valued it, and he had been, since the end of October, protecting it from the question that was waiting for him at the window.

A German prisoner from Franconia.

On the Maine coast. On a farm owned by a family from Feuchtwangen, Bavaria, which was Franconia — the same region, the same regional dialect, the specific vowels that would make a man use the word *Landsmann* and mean it precisely, in the sense of the same ground, the same particular piece of the world, down to a day's walk.

And a body on the breakwater in European civilian clothes with palm-center calluses and no papers, deposited by a three-day blow.

He was not forming an argument. He wanted to be careful with himself about this: what he had was a probable shape, assembled from inadequate evidence, which was not the same as a conclusion, and he was aware of the distinction. The shape suggested — not a spy operation, not the machinery of military intelligence, nothing of that genre — a different logic. The logic of a long chain of people trying to reach people, across distances that were not primarily geographical. A Czech man in transit — he held *Czech* as inference, not fact; the clothing, the route, the kind of person who was still in irregular motion across the Atlantic in the autumn of 1943 — who had known someone, and that someone had known of a farm on the Maine coast where a Bavarian family had come from the right general region of Europe, a family that might have been known to someone somewhere along the chain, or known of, or simply represented a recognizable kind of contact: the immigrant family with the old country still in them, in the right place at the right time, with a farm and a fence and the cold New England distance from official scrutiny.

Not spies. Refugees. The long effort of people who were trying not to be lost.

He did not know this. What he had was the probable shape of it, and the fact that a seventeen-year-old girl asking about a vocabulary word had made the shape visible to him in a way that three weeks of deliberate not-looking had not. He had no obligation to pursue it. He had no means to pursue it and no standing to pursue it and the official record was, by all accounts, closed. He was a man who taught Latin and German at a school in a coastal Maine town and who had been, for two years, the person this particular version of himself required him to be.

He turned away from the window.

The exercise papers were in the folder. Bates's *fertur* was in there, finally said without the gap. He had the afternoon.

---

Ralph Garland was at the table in the teachers' room with the Bangor Daily opened to the sports section. Edna Price was marking tests, red pencil, the focused efficiency she brought to everything she put the pencil to. The gas ring had been on since before seven o'clock that morning and the coffee in the pot had arrived at the particular density of late-session conviction.

Marcus rinsed his cup at the small sink, dried it once on the dish towel, filled it at the pot. He stood by the counter.

Ralph said, without looking up: "Cold today."

"Yes," Marcus said.

He stood by the counter and drank the coffee and thought about the gerundive of obligation, which was the afternoon's subject. *Legendum est.* It must be read. Needing to be read. The construction in which a thing's necessity was built into its grammatical form, inseparable from the name of the thing itself. He thought about how to present this. The passive periphrastic, which was the technical name for the construction, was not a phrase he would open with; he would arrive at the name after the students had the feel of the form, which was the order that worked best. He had the afternoon's preparation in the folder with the exercise papers. He would look at it before the period began.

Edna made a mark on her test and turned to the next one. Ralph turned a page. The gas ring made its small continuous sound.

Marcus finished the coffee and rinsed the cup. He retrieved the folder from the shelf, opened it to the afternoon's notes. *Legendum, legenda, legendum.* The thing that must be done. He read through what he had written on the walk in this morning and made one small change in the margin, a different example sentence, something with less bluntness to it.

The question at the window was still there. He was aware of this in the way you are aware of the contents of a drawer you have just opened and then closed again — it did not require anything of him yet, and there was work to do.

He put on his coat. The afternoon was waiting.

# Mutter

At five in the morning the barn was warmer than the house, which Hannah had stopped thinking about as fortunate and had started thinking about as simply the way December worked.

She moved through the left row first — Marta, Brunhilde, Sophie, Clara, and then the eight she'd given her own count-names when her mother stopped naming them and her father declined to take up the practice. Her hands knew the sequence without her deciding to follow it. Pull, strip, pull. The particular resistance at the start, the rhythm finding itself after the first thirty seconds. The steam off the cows' backs going up into the dark of the rafters where the lamp couldn't reach. She had hung the lamp on the second hook from the far end because the first hook swung it into her eyes when the drafts came in through the door seam, and she'd learned this in October and moved it and hadn't thought about it since.

She had heard her father's truck at four-thirty. Not the starting of it — she'd slept through that — but the sound of it going out of the yard and turning onto Route 9, the engine going quieter by degrees until she couldn't hear it anymore. By the time she came downstairs the kitchen lamp was low on the table, still burning, and the coffee was warm in the pot and the overnight case was not in the mud room. Twice a year, Rockland. The feed cooperative ran in June and December.

She tied her coat, pulled on her father's old barn coat over it, and went out.

The ice at the base of the east wall was still the same inch it had been since Tuesday. She checked it in passing — not because there was anything to do about it but because she had started checking it and now she checked it; the habit was its own reason. The wind outside was clean and cold and smelled of nothing. December wind sometimes lost its smell when the snowpack hardened enough that there was nothing left to carry. She went back to the cows.

Forty-three minutes for the full row. She dumped the milk pails and cleaned up without rushing and came back through the dark to the house.

---

Upstairs: the hallway smelled of cold wood and the cedar sachet her mother kept in the linen press. Hannah stood in the doorway of her parents' room.

Magda was on her side of the bed, eyes open, looking at the ceiling.

Not asleep. Not distressed in the way that meant the doctor. Hannah had been in this doorway enough times now to know there were three kinds, and this was the third kind — the one that required nothing from anyone but time and company at the edges. Magda's chest rose and fell steadily. Her hands lay flat on the coverlet.

Hannah went to the nightstand and set a cup of water there.

"Ich bin gleich wieder da," she said.

Her mother's eyes did not move. Her chest continued to rise and fall.

Hannah straightened the edge of the coverlet where it had bunched at the pillow and went downstairs to put on her school coat.

---

She sat through English and through history without being called on in either. Had Magda moved. Had she drunk any of the water. Had she gotten up to use the bathroom or to find something to eat.

She had no way to answer any of these questions until four o'clock.

In Latin, toward the end of the period, Marcus wrote a sentence on the board and set the chalk down and waited with his back still turned. He did this — this particular pause, chalk still, back to the class — and Hannah had figured out by October that it was for Michael Bates, who always needed the extra two seconds and knew that he needed them and knew that Marcus knew and that Marcus wasn't going to say so. The pause cost Marcus nothing and cost Michael Bates nothing and nobody had to speak about it. She found this precise in a way she didn't have a better word for.

Marcus turned, said Bates's name in the tone that was directive without being reproachful, and Bates read the form from the board and it was right.

At lunch she sat with Ruth and unwrapped her sandwich and ate half of it and then the inventory in her head came back louder than the sandwich and she folded the other half back into the wax paper.

"Saving it?"

"I'll eat it later."

She let it go. Hannah put the sandwich in her coat pocket and walked through the afternoon.

---

The prisoners were in the icehouse by the time she came up the farm lane — she could see the lamplight through the door seam and hear the low murmur of German from inside, not words, just the rhythm of the language settling in for the evening. Lonzo had already gone. He did that in December when the short days cut the work hours short enough that his signing-out made sense; he'd be back at seven in the morning, the route to the door and the stool and the Springfield rifle as familiar to him as the route to his own kitchen.

She went to the barn.

The afternoon milking was slower. The cows more settled, more inclined to take their time, Hilde in particular requiring three minutes of patience before she'd cooperate.

She came out of the barn and the light was already gone. Not fading — gone. The sky in the west a dark blue above the spruces, no color left in it. She stood a moment in the yard.

The icehouse lamp was still going. She turned and went inside.

---

Upstairs, Magda had not moved. Or nearly not — there was a difference in how her hands lay on the coverlet, one over the other where before they'd been flat, which meant she had shifted at some point in the eight hours Hannah had been gone. The cup of water was untouched.

Hannah went back down and heated the broth — Sunday's broth, the last of the chicken carcass she'd been stretching for a week, careful with the fat because they were down to the last two months of their fat allotment and it was only December. She brought it up on the tray with a folded cloth underneath and sat on the edge of the bed and held the bowl.

Magda did not reach for it. But after a minute she turned her head.

Not toward the window. Toward Hannah.

Hannah kept still. She had learned that the stillness was what mattered — not talking, not asking, just the presence in the room and the bowl of broth and the lamp going on the nightstand. Her mother's face in the lamplight was calm and far and also present, the way someone is present at the edge of sleep: there and registering, somewhere behind the eyes.

She put the bowl on the tray and reached for her history textbook, which she'd left at the foot of the bed when she'd come up that morning to check the curtains.

She began to read aloud.

*In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve of the thirteen states gathered in Philadelphia to revise the Articles of Confederation. The convention met in secret; the windows of the State House were kept shut against the July heat despite the conditions, to prevent speeches from carrying to the street below.*

She read without performing it. Marcus had said, once, that Latin should be read for its sense, not its sound — the meaning moving through the voice, not the voice moving over the meaning. She wasn't sure that was quite the right distinction but she understood what he was getting at. She read about James Madison and his notes. She read about the Great Compromise. She read two full pages and did not look up.

Magda's eyes were not closed.

Then, without planning it and without a pause, she went back to the top of the page and started again in German. Or in the German she had, which was not her father's German — it had the seams of its assembly showing, the words she reached for and the words she substituted when the first ones didn't come.

"Im Sommer des Jahres siebzehnhundert—" she had to count through the compound number carefully, and the counting broke the sentence, but she said it and continued — "versammelten sich die Abgeordneten von zwölf der dreizehn Staaten in Philadelphia." She got stuck on *revise* and said *ändern* and wasn't certain it was right. The Articles of Confederation she left in English because she had no German for it and her mother had been in Maine for twenty-one years and would know the English phrase. "Das Treffen war geheim gehalten. Die Fenster"—she checked the page—"blieben geschlossen, trotz der Hitze."

The German in her mouth had the shape of something she'd carried without knowing she was carrying it. Not her father's formal compounds, not the Sunday church German, not the German of the kitchen after supper when her father talked to himself over the accounts. Something more ordinary. Something that had gotten into her by living alongside it for seventeen years.

Magda's eyes were moving slightly. Tracking the sound.

Hannah read to the bottom of the second page and stopped. The room was quiet. The broth on the tray had cooled. Her mother had not taken it and was not going to take it tonight, which Hannah had known before she came upstairs and which was all right — the being there was its own thing, separate from the eating.

She collected the tray. "Ich mache das Abendessen," she said, and went down.

---

She was at the stove, the white bean soup coming up to a simmer — dried beans from the pantry shelf, onion, the bit of salt pork she'd been saving since last week — when the phrase came to her.

It arrived the way phrases sometimes did: completely, without preliminary, the way a smell arrives when you open a drawer you haven't opened in a long time. She was stirring and heard herself say it under her breath:

*Wenn das Wasser steigt, verlässt man das Dorf.*

She stopped stirring.

It was not her father's German. His sayings were about the worth of things, about the weather, about what a day's work required — practical and specific and never poetic, the German of a man who used language to move information from one place to another. It had the density of something old. Not literature-old, but grandmother-old, the particular weight of a sentence that had been in use in someone's mouth for a long time before it reached her.

She thought it might be Inge. Magda's mother — a woman in the hall photograph, small, upright, grey braid pinned, looking at the camera the way people looked at cameras then, as if the image were a thing to be done correctly. Hannah had met her once, at five or six, and remembered nothing of it except a table edge at eye height and the smell of something baking. Inge had died in 1937 and Hannah had heard it from her mother in two sentences and not again. She might have said the phrase. Or it might have been Magda, before.

Before was a word with no firm edges in Hannah's understanding of her mother. Before the quiet. Before the worst of the quiet. Before whatever it was that had drawn the line between the Magda who had named the cows in German and the Magda who lay in the room upstairs and tracked the sound of language without responding to it.

She said the phrase again, quietly. *Wenn das Wasser steigt, verlässt man das Dorf.*

It was about water and about a village and about leaving. Not about whether to leave. Not about whether it was the right thing or the wrong thing. When the water rises — this is what happens. You leave the village. The sentence had already decided. It was reporting a fact about behavior, the way weather reports the temperature: not a question, not a negotiation.

Her parents had left. They had left Bavaria in 1922 and come to Maine and she had been born here and the stone walls and the barn and the icehouse and the dairy operation were what you built after a leaving. She was seventeen and had grown up inside that construction and had never been told much about the water. Whether it had already been rising when they left. Whether leaving was before the worst of it or during it or after it had gotten as bad as it could get. Whether Magda's grandmother had been right and the leaving was the correct response to the water, or whether the water had followed them somehow.

The soup was ready.

She turned the burner low and set the table for three.

---

Her father's headlights came across the kitchen wall at nine-fifteen. She heard the truck, the kitchen door, his boots on the mat — the particular sound of a man returning from somewhere, a stiffness in the coat that was not their own cold.

He went upstairs without speaking. She heard his voice from the bedroom — brief, in German, two or three sentences she couldn't make out through the floor — and then silence, and then his footsteps on the stairs.

She set his plate in front of him and he sat and ate with the focused attention of someone who had been driving for four hours and had not yet come all the way back. She sat across from him and did not fill the silence.

After a few minutes he set down his fork.

"Sie hatte diese Zustände schon, bevor wir hierher kamen," he said.

Nothing else. He picked up his fork and finished eating.

She did not ask.

She cleared his plate when he was done and ran the hot water. The radio was on the counter, its dial at WLBZ, its face dark. She washed and dried and set the plates back on the shelf. Behind her she could hear her father packing his pipe, the tin of tobacco opening, the small wooden sound of the bowl being knocked clean against his palm.

She could hear the Holsteins from the barn.

Not a distressed sound. The settled sound of animals in winter, the shift of weight, the occasional low of a cow adjusting her position. The farm going on in the dark the way it did, the way it did when she was asleep and when she was awake, the continuous sound of it.

She dried her hands and hung the dish towel on the hook.

The lamp on the table threw its light across the pine. Her father's hands, rough at the knuckle, cupped around the pipe. The windows were blue-black with the clear December night.

She said good night.

The phrase was still in her head at the bottom of the stairs, and at the top, and in the hallway where the cedar smell came off the linen press and the door to her parents' room was dark underneath. She did not yet know where it had come from. She did not know yet what it meant that she couldn't put it down.

# Private Reed

The truck needed a minute. Lonzo sat in the cab while the light came up — barely gray at six-fifty, the spruce line solidifying first, then the barn roof, then the near fence posts finding their shapes against the pale sky. The icehouse light showed through the barn gap: already on. He wouldn't need to knock anyone up.

He got the Springfield from behind the seat. Bolt, magazine, safety — the check was the same as every morning. He had not fired it since an April exercise on the range, unrelated to this posting, and was not going to fire it today. But you checked it and so you checked it.

The ground was iron-hard under his boots. The cold had a dry character today, the kind that carried sound; he could hear the Holsteins shifting in the barn before he reached the barn door. He hung his lantern on the door nail, set his stool beside the entrance, positioned his thermos on the wooden crate. Six fifty-four.

At seven the icehouse door came open.

Fischer first, the way Fischer was always first — the heavyset one, deliberate in his walk, the man who set the pace for the others whether he intended to or not. Brunner behind him, leaning left the way he always leaned, a habit of the shoulder that twelve weeks of watching hadn't explained. Then Krebs — the oldest of the four, bald on the crown, missing the upper third of his right ear from something that had happened before Tunisia. Then the young one, Reinmar.

Four. Lonzo said "guten Morgen" the way he said it every morning, which was the only German he'd managed to retain, and Fischer nodded, and the others went to the field.

He poured half a cup from his thermos and settled in.

He knew this field now. Twelve weeks of watching gave you that — the patterns of the work, the patterns of the men in it. Fischer organized whatever needed organizing; the other three read from him without being told. Brunner and Krebs worked the heavy things together, reliably, which left Reinmar to the far end and whatever tasks didn't require a second man. Lonzo had wondered at first whether the young one was being pushed to the margins or whether he chose them. He'd watched long enough to decide it was neither: Reinmar simply found the work that was waiting at the far end and went at it, and at the far end there was always work waiting. Character or nineteen years old. Couldn't always tell those apart.

The December field was maintenance — hauling the last equipment to the barn, attending to what the season had broken. Pale light coming in flat from the south; by ten it would be as good as it got. Albrecht Pfeiffer came out at nine and gestured toward the stone-wall line, and the four of them went. Pfeiffer did not speak to them and they did not speak to him.

—

At ten, Pfeiffer went to the south fence.

Lonzo had seen this before. The posts along that line had heaved over the wet autumn, and Hannah and her father had been working them in November before the ground went hard. One post in particular was still wrong somehow; Pfeiffer stopped there on his way through most mornings. He walked the line now with his hand on the top wire, testing tension, bending to check each post in turn.

Reinmar's work had moved him to the same fence by then — the south edge of the near field, loading out the last of the broken corn stalks into the cart. He was within talking distance of Pfeiffer when he said something. Low — Lonzo couldn't hear it at forty yards — but he could see the shape of it, the mouth moving, something said under the breath while the young man was working a heavy load and not quite landing it the way he wanted.

Pfeiffer stopped.

Not dramatically. Not the stop of a man startled. The stop of a man who has heard something that requires a moment to sit.

Two seconds. Three. Pfeiffer's hand was still on the wire.

Then he moved his hand and kept walking the fence line. Reinmar got the cart loaded and wheeled it toward the barn.

Lonzo made a note. In his head, not on the clipboard.

The young prisoner had some way of running his words — vowels that sat in a particular place, a shape to the sounds that Pfeiffer had recognized from a long way back and a long way away. Lonzo had grown up on lobster boats on the bay and could tell a Jonesport hull from a Friendship sloop by the width of the stern; he figured a man from Bavaria could hear where another man was from by how his vowels moved.

Not an incident. He would not write it.

He finished his cup and refilled it.

—

He ate at noon. Bread, cheese, mustard, wax paper going soft against the crate. He ate without tasting it and read the Bangor Daily News he'd folded into his coat pocket that morning before five-thirty.

Front page for the general situation, then he turned to the Pacific.

He always read the Pacific first, then went back to the front. This habit had organized itself around Jimmy in February when the orders came through. Jimmy was on a Buckley-class destroyer escort — that was what Lonzo knew, plus the theater, and from there he was reduced to inference. The censors had taken the specifics out of every letter, which meant he tried to locate his son by reasoning about what the newspapers reported and where a Buckley-class was likely not to be, and the zone that remained was several thousand miles of open water with Jimmy somewhere in it.

The Pacific news today covered the operations in the Gilberts, the mopping-up after Tarawa. He read every line. He had no way to know if the Gilberts was where Jimmy was. He read it anyway.

Jimmy wrote every six weeks or so when things were going well. He had written seven weeks ago. The letter was in Lonzo's jacket pocket, where it had been sitting for two weeks now. He had been meaning to answer it. The letter said the ship was a good one and the men on it were good, said the food was adequate, said don't worry, Dad in the second paragraph. Lonzo had put that last phrase in the category of things he was not going to look at too carefully.

—

The afternoon light was going by three o'clock. The field was nearly done. Fischer directed the last of the winterizing from the barn entrance and the other three moved around him in the established pattern, and Lonzo watched it all from his stool the way he'd been watching it for twelve weeks.

Hannah Pfeiffer came out of the barn at close to three-twenty. She was carrying something small — hardware or a tool, he couldn't tell from his position. She went to the near fence where Reinmar was working. He turned toward her. She passed something to him, or he handed something back — the low afternoon light made it hard to read direction. They said something. A few exchanges. Maybe two or three minutes.

Lonzo watched without moving.

The particular quality of attention that didn't come from anything you could put in a report.

He knew what dangerous looked like. This wasn't it.

He'd watch.

At three-forty the prisoners came in from the field.

—

He walked them to the icehouse. Fischer, Brunner, Krebs, Reinmar — counted them through the door and locked it behind them. Checked the lock.

He filled out the Coastal Patrol report form at the tailgate of the truck. The form had the usual blanks: date, prisoner count, hours worked, incidents, violations. His handwriting was large and slightly unsteady in the cold; he had lost sensation in the first two joints of his left hand after a winch accident in 1931, and it showed in December. He wrote carefully anyway.

December 9, 1943. Prisoner count: four. Hours worked: seven.

He got to incidents and wrote: None.

He got to violations and wrote: None.

He read it back.

It was accurate.

He signed it.

—

The road went through three miles of spruce before the harbor lights showed. Full dark by ten past four. He drove with the heater running and his left arm against the door.

He went over the day the way he always did on the drive home — ran through it, filed it, let it go. Pfeiffer at the south fence. Hannah at the near fence. Reinmar at the far end of the field all morning, working ahead of the work.

Then he stopped thinking about the farm.

He was thinking about Reinmar being nineteen years old and what the war from his direction had probably looked like before they took him in Tunisia. He was thinking about Jimmy.

He had learned this line of thinking didn't go anywhere useful. He let it go.

The road came over the last rise and the harbor was below and to his left — the wharf lights, the shapes of the lobster smacks at the inside dock, the long dark of the breakwater reaching out into the black water. He downshifted and followed the road down.

Jimmy's last letter was in his jacket pocket. He was going to write back tonight. He would tell Jimmy the weather had been cold and clear. He would ask about the ship. He would write that he was well.

The truck leveled out at the harbor road and Lonzo drove the last quarter-mile home, the harbor sitting quiet off his left window.

# Owen's Ledger

The inventory form had twelve columns and ran to four pages when she did it thoroughly, which she did every year in the first week of January. Eira set it on the chart table on the morning of January seventh and began at the left.

Dock hardware, itemized by category, quantity, condition. The hardware section always took longer than it should. Items had accumulated across years — some from Owen's inventory, some from hers, the category names drifting so that she couldn't always determine whether a "dock bollard, standard" and a "mooring bollard, harbor-grade" were two things or one thing entered twice by two different hands. She had been standardizing the categories since 1941 and was not yet done. She worked through the list: cleats by type and quantity, shackles, dock line coiled in the dock locker, winch components, the spare hardware in the deep bin under the north-facing shelf. The south mooring shackle showed rust at both joints — she had seen it in November, and it was worse now. She noted it and recommended replacement before the summer season.

The kerosene stove had been burning since seven and the office was as warm as it was going to get. With the coat on, that was warm enough. Outside the window the harbor showed its January shape. Five lobster boats at the inside moorings — Brann's Irene M., Hollis's boat, three others she recognized by the silhouettes of their cabins in the flat southern light. The commercial wharf was empty. The fleet came down to the lobstermen in January, and even they ran shorter days; they were out before light and back by early afternoon, and between their comings and goings the harbor was as quiet as it got.

Ice in the shallows. The tidal range in this harbor was eleven feet, which meant the shallows froze every night and thawed with each flood and froze again with each ebb. She had watched this for eight winters. The ice never broke apart quite the same way twice — sometimes a continuous plate from the north shore down to the mooring field, sometimes panels, sometimes absent entirely for two or three days before the overnight cold reasserted itself. Right now the flood was running, the panels separating, dark water widening between them. By four o'clock the water would recede and the process would reverse.

She worked through the hardware columns, column by column. This was reliable work. It had the quality of work that could be done in any weather, in any frame of mind, because it required only accuracy and time. She had learned the inventory in her first year from Owen's prior-year form, the same twelve columns, and had been using it since. The form knew what it needed. All she had to do was tell it true.

She finished hardware and moved to the mooring chain assessment.

The north mooring blocks had been on her list since October. She had noted wear on the anchor pins before the blow — written it in the September notes as something to watch, then again in October as something to address. She needed the block replacement date to know how much runway remained.

Nineteen thirty-two, she thought. But Owen's records would say.

The cabinet on the far wall held the annual logs going back thirty years — Owen's years, and before Owen a man named Ames whose record-keeping had been approximate enough that she'd checked several of his entries against the District office copies before she would trust them. Owen had taken the post in the late twenties. His logs ran through 1935. Then hers: 1936 in her own handwriting on page thirty-eight of the requisition book, where his stopped at page thirty-seven.

She had been using his logs as a format guide from her first week. Not deliberately, not as a studied practice — she had simply opened the volumes to see how the job had been done, and his handwriting was there, and she'd read it, and taken from it what the recording of the harbor required. What he documented. How he handled the line between a note and a notation.

She went to the cabinet and found 1932 on the lower shelves. The mooring block entry was in August: north blocks replaced, August 18, work completed by Alderman and crew, new anchor hardware, both sets. She noted it on the inventory form. Then she checked 1933 for any repair — nothing on the north blocks. Then she pulled 1934, for the inspection record.

Owen's handwriting in the 1934 log was the same as it was in all the volumes she had read over the years. She knew it by now the way you came to know any script you had read long and often enough — not letter by letter but as a whole, a characteristic rhythm of the line. It was a neat hand. Careful in its letterforms, smaller than she would have expected if she hadn't known Owen. His hands had been large, thick through the knuckle, the hands of a man who had handled lines since he was old enough to haul. The writing was another thing entirely — small and precise, as deliberate as a surveyor's marks.

She found the 1934 maintenance records. The north blocks had been inspected in June: condition satisfactory, no action needed. She noted it: last inspection June 1934, satisfactory. That put the blocks at twelve years since replacement. She filled in the form: present condition serviceable; wear on anchor pins within operational tolerance; recommend replacement within two to three years.

She was closing the 1934 volume when the October section opened under her hands.

It was the binding. Some years fell open at their most-used section — the spine working loose at the point of most handling. This one had been used in October, or had been consulted and reconsulted until the October pages separated from the rest. She hadn't used this volume enough to have worn it open herself. She steadied it on the chart table.

The entry was dated October 14, 1934.

*Body of male individual, identified as Elias Foss, fisherman, Vinalhaven. Reported missing from vessel 9/29/34. Recovered at end of commercial dock by night crew, E. Hollis, at approximately 0600 hrs October 14. Medical examiner J.H. Pell notified 0700; examination completed 0900; death attributed to drowning, circumstances consistent with extended exposure; estimated time of death 10/6 or 10/7. Body in water eleven to twelve days. Coast Guard District Portland notified, formal report filed. Family contacted per standard procedure. Body released to family October 16.*

The official documentation. Notification chain, examination, classification, resolution. It was complete — the structure she had learned from reading Owen's logs and had built her own entries on. A man missing twelve days, found at the end of the dock. Owen had written it fully and in the correct order.

Below the entry, set off by a line break and in a slightly smaller hand — the same hand, but the letters compressed, the pen moving faster or at a different hour:

*J.T. came in on the 12th. I met him at the dock. He was in a bad way and needed some time before he was in any state for the official record. This not entered at time; entering here as complete account.*

She read it again.

She read it a third time.

The stove ticked. Outside the window the harbor was gray and still. Brann's boat showed its green hull through the frost on the glass.

She stood at the chart table.

J.T. — not further identified. Someone who had come to the dock in the middle of the search, or after the finding, in a state Owen had judged unsuitable for the official record in that hour. Owen had met him there. He had waited, or stayed nearby, for whatever time the man needed. And then he had not written it when it happened. He had written it afterward, with the small notation that explained the gap: *not entered at time; entering here as complete account.*

The record was complete. The 1934 log had an entry that accounted for what had happened, and the entry was dated to the correct year, and anyone reading the 1934 log would find what had occurred. Owen had decided when to write it. But he had written it.

She looked at the window for a while. The flood tide was still running. The ice panels were wider apart than they'd been at seven, the dark water between them the color of the overcast above.

She thought about when Owen might have gone back to write the J.T. note — whether it had been a week later or a month. Whether J.T. was someone he'd known from before or someone he'd only met that morning at the dock. Whether writing it had felt like completing the record or like something else. The log didn't say, and he hadn't annotated the annotation.

She set the 1934 volume on the chart table and went to the shelf where the current logs were kept.

*Tuesday, October 26, 1943. Wind SSW at 14, backing. Barometric pressure 29.61, falling. Swell 4 feet at harbor mouth, increasing.*

*2100: fuel allocation check, Hollis and three lobster smacks. 2300: mooring check completed, fleet secure.*

She read it straight through. The 2300 entry was accurate in everything it contained. She had done the mooring check. The fleet had been secure. The barometric reading was correct for that night.

She stood with both volumes open on the chart table — Owen's 1934, her 1943 — the October pages of each showing side by side.

Owen's entry had a gap and said so. *Not entered at time; entering here as complete account.* The record was complete.

Hers had no such notation.

She closed the 1943 log.

She put the 1943 book back on the shelf and returned the 1934 volume to the cabinet. As she did she noticed the 1935 volume — thin, half the width of the others. Owen had started it in January and his entries ran through October. The last entry: a weather note, a routine mooring check, the approach of the November storm. She knew what it said.

She pushed the 1935 volume back into alignment with its neighbors and closed the cabinet.

Back at the chart table she picked up the inventory form and checked it through. Hardware: complete. Mooring chains: assessed and documented. Three staging planks at the far end needing replacement — she'd been watching them since September, and there was no point deferring the notation further. The dock ladder's second-from-bottom rung: stress cracking at the left joint, the same as it had been in September and unchanged in three months. She would need to write up the spring budget request in the next week — south mooring shackle, staging planks, dock ladder rung. These were the priorities.

The north mooring blocks she wrote on the final line: last replaced August 1932, twelve years, present condition serviceable, wear on anchor pins within tolerance, recommend replacement within two to three years.

She set the form aside and made tea from the tin on the stove shelf. The water had been keeping warm on the back of the stove since she'd boiled it that morning; it was still hot enough. She poured a cup and stood at the window.

The flood tide had done what she'd expected. The ice panels were well-separated now, open water showing the full width between them, the near shallows mostly clear. The light was the flat undifferentiated gray of a January midday — it would stay like this until it began to fail at three, the darkness coming in from the east without any transition from the gray.

She finished the tea and put the cup in the rack.

She dated the bottom of the inventory form, signed it, and put it in the current file.

The office was quiet. The stove ticked and settled.

She put on her coat.

The south mooring shackle needed a closer look before the tide turned. She had noted the rust in November and again today on the form, but she wanted to see what it looked like up close before she put a specific dollar figure on the replacement request. Surface rust at the joint was one thing; rust into the threads was another; the form she sent to Portland needed to know the difference.

She lifted the door handle while she turned it — the way you had to in cold weather, the way she had learned from Owen, the latch she had never had the carpenter fix — and went out onto the dock.

# The School Board

Henry had told him on a Monday, at supper. Someone had filed a question with the selectmen — *question* was the word Henry used, and Marcus registered both the accuracy and the careful choice — about the German-language instructor at the school, and the selectmen had passed it to the school board. The board would address it at the February meeting. Three members would be present, not the full board: Dwight Hatch, Agnes Vane, Gordon Sears. Marcus knew Hatch by sight and Vane by name. He had not encountered Sears.

Henry said: "Your credentials are on file."

Marcus said: "Yes."

He had gone upstairs after supper and opened the bottom drawer of the chest. The file had been with him since Cambridge — since before Cambridge, since London, some of it dated from the years between Vienna and Paris when there had still been institutions willing to put letterheads on things. He laid the papers on the desk and went through them. Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars, dated November 1940, signed by Harrington, Whitmore's predecessor. His Vienna university credentials: the teaching certification, the faculty appointment letter. These were dated 1934. The letterhead was the university's, as it had existed before the annexation — the institution itself, its seal, its address, the name of the rector who had signed. He was aware that the letterhead cut two ways. The same date that documented his legitimate academic standing also marked it as belonging to an institution that no longer functioned as it had, in a country no longer sovereign. A board member predisposed to suspicion could read the letterhead as easily as one predisposed to fairness.

He included the documents anyway. A man who withheld his best evidence because the evidence had a complicated history was not a man who would be persuasive. The Cambridge letter. His Maine teaching certificate, issued in the spring of 1942 after the state board had reviewed his credentials and satisfied itself that a man with his qualifications could instruct the children of Maine in the German language. He thought briefly about the draftsmanship of that particular irony and put it aside.

He arranged the papers in order of probable utility. Emergency Committee letter first — it was the document most legible to an American institutional mind, because it was American, and because it named what he was: a scholar displaced by circumstances the Committee had determined to be genuine. His credentials after that. The outcomes list at the end, because the outcomes list was the argument that would land with a school board, and it should arrive last.

He spent the next day as he spent most Tuesday afternoons: teaching the Latin third-year through the gerundive, then the German second-year through the passive voice, then correcting the third-year examination papers in the empty classroom while the building went quiet around him. He had considered the probable objections while walking the three blocks home. Agnes Vane would raise something articulate; she had the reputation of a woman who chose her concerns precisely. Gordon Sears would raise something direct. Hatch, who organized such meetings, would say the least and carry the most weight.

He thought about what Vane might mean by *articulate but not specific*, which was the phrase Henry had used. He had encountered this category before. It was more resistant than outright hostility, because outright hostility could be countered with evidence, and this other thing — the concern that takes care to avoid stating itself as prejudice while remaining, at its foundation, exactly that — could not be countered by the same instruments. It required a different approach. Not engagement on its terms, but refusal to engage on its terms while appearing to engage. He had made an art of this, over the years, in several languages.

Henry had said: "I'll be there." And Marcus had said he didn't need a witness; Henry had said he knew; and without either of them elaborating further Marcus had understood that Henry would come anyway.

---

The Legion hall on February evenings had the quality of a room borrowed from its proper use. The rationing board used it from nine to four on weekdays; the folding tables were still arranged in that configuration — two parallel rows facing the front — and the school board had simply relocated the chairs and positioned a single additional chair, unambiguously solitary, before the table. The American Legion banner ran the width of the back wall, its gold fringe losing color at the folds. The electric light was two bulbs in ceiling fixtures and was adequate and no more. The windows on the north side showed the street: black, empty, the temperature below ten and still dropping. It was seven twenty-two.

Marcus was early. He had learned this from experience in rooms not unlike this one — preferred the physical fact before the people arrived, preferred to know where the door was, where his chair sat in relation to theirs, how the light fell across the table, whether there was anything in the room that would require management. He had done it in Vienna before the meeting where they had informed him that his faculty position would need to be reviewed in light of recent developments. In Paris before two consular appointments. In London at the Home Office. In Sherbrooke — not preparation, there, because in Sherbrooke one arrived as instructed rather than early, but in the waiting rooms at Sherbrooke he had learned what the same instinct looked like when it had no purchase on the room. In Cambridge, twice. In Coldwater Reach, in March 1942, before the school board had offered him the appointment.

He straightened his documents once and did not touch them again.

Henry came in at twenty past. He crossed directly to the chair along the right wall — not at the table, not at Marcus's chair — settled into it, and opened the Bangor Daily News he had folded under his arm. He did not look at Marcus; he gave his attention to the newspaper with the ease of a man who had arranged himself exactly where he meant to be and saw no reason to comment on it.

The positioning was correct. Henry knew it was correct, and Marcus knew it, and there was nothing to say about it. The one wrong thing would have been to acknowledge it. He kept his eyes on the table.

Hatch came in at twenty-eight minutes past, followed by Vane and then Sears. They were carrying their coats — they had not been here long enough to have hung them anywhere — and they settled into their chairs with the efficiency of people who had occupied positions at this table before and had no need to establish the configuration. Hatch had a yellow legal pad and a pen. Vane had a folder.

Sears had nothing. He folded his hands on the table and looked at Marcus with the directness of a man who found the whole proceeding tiresome in ways he was not at leisure to say.

---

"We've had some concerns raised," Hatch began, with the tone of a man measuring how much weight to give the word. "From parents. About the, ah — the current situation. Whether it's appropriate to have a German-language instructor at the school, given the national circumstances."

"The national circumstances," Marcus said.

"The country of the instructor's birth being currently at war with this country."

"I was born in Austria," Marcus said. "Which was annexed by Germany in March 1938, against the will of its government, and which I departed in 1936 — two years before that annexation — for reasons that I can detail for the board if it wishes." He moved the Emergency Committee letter across the table. "I have been on the rolls of the Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars since November 1940. I was hired by Coldwater High School in March 1942. I have been teaching here for twenty-three months."

He laid the outcomes list on the table. Examination results, progression rates, the comparative data from the three years prior to his hire when the German course enrollment had been running at a different level. The numbers were legible. He had prepared them to be legible to a school board, which was different from preparing them to be legible to a faculty committee — less subordinate structure, more column alignment — and he had done it without particular satisfaction but with the same care he brought to anything that was worth doing correctly.

Hatch read the Emergency Committee letter. Vane opened her folder and produced a copy of something — Marcus could see from across the table it was his teaching certificate, already on file as Henry had said. She compared it to the document in front of her, set both on the table, and looked at him.

Agnes Vane was a composed woman. She had the specific composure of someone who had been in rooms where things were decided, who had learned that the most effective way to carry weight was not to display it. She said: "We understand your history, Mr. Klein. The concern that was brought forward has to do, specifically, with —" She paused. She was, he thought, genuinely searching for a formulation. "The language itself. At this particular time."

Marcus waited.

She let the sentence end where it was.

"I teach German," Marcus said, "to American students who may need to speak it. In a military capacity, in an administrative capacity — in whatever capacity the period following this war creates a need for Americans who can speak German to German-speaking people. The utility of that instruction does not diminish because the language is currently spoken by an enemy government. It increases, if we are thinking about the war's conclusion and what follows it."

"That's a long view," Vane said.

"The instruction of languages generally requires a long view," Marcus said. "One does not teach a child the subjunctive for immediate tactical deployment."

Something crossed Vane's face that was not quite a reaction and was not quite suppressed. She looked down at her folder.

"The thing I don't see," Sears said — he had been watching Marcus throughout with the patient expression of a man waiting for the moment when the real question became available — "is why we need it at all. German. I don't see that the school was worse off before we had a German-language course."

"The school had a German-language course before I arrived," Marcus said. "I replaced the previous instructor when he enlisted."

Sears considered this. "Well, I know that." He appeared to feel this was a beside-the-point correction. "What I mean is, why should we have one now. Given everything."

"Because the language does not belong to the government using it," Marcus said. "And because the students in my classroom will live through whatever comes after this war, and they will find the capacity to speak German more useful then than it has been in the last two years."

Sears looked at him for a long moment. His expression was the expression of a man who understood perfectly well that the person in front of him had the better argument and who had not yet decided whether the better argument was sufficient.

"You understand our position," Sears said.

"I understand it perfectly," Marcus said.

There was a pause in which the room was very quiet. Outside one of the north windows a car passed on the street — the only vehicle Marcus had heard in the twenty minutes since he arrived. Then it was quiet again.

Hatch cleared his throat. "I think we have what we need here." He looked at Vane, who nodded. He looked at Sears, who held Marcus's gaze for another half-second before he looked down at the table and nodded as well. "The board votes to continue Mr. Klein's appointment. Unanimous." He made a notation on his yellow legal pad. "We'll note in the record that a formal review was conducted and the appointment confirmed."

Marcus gathered his documents. The Emergency Committee letter, the credentials, the outcomes list, back into the file in the order he had removed them. He was aware, as he did this, of the quality of the action — the same action he had performed at the end of several other meetings of this kind, the returning of papers to the file that had accompanied him through too many such rooms, and the specific texture of collecting those papers from a table where they had been sufficient for the purpose.

The meeting had lasted thirty-eight minutes.

---

Outside, the night was clear and cold in the particular way of a February in coastal Maine — the cold not heavy or wet, as it was in a storm, but dry and still and absolute, the kind that entered the collar and the cuffs and made the walk home a matter of economy: the fewest unnecessary motions, the steadiest pace, the breath that went out and came back cold and went out again.

The street was empty. Coldwater Reach cleared itself by seven on nights like this; the residents who were inside were inside and the ones who had gone out had already returned. The door of the Legion hall closed behind them, and the sound of it carried in the cold air farther than the same door would have carried in any other season.

They walked without speaking. Down to the corner of Bridge Street, left toward the harbor road. This was not the most direct route and Marcus was aware that he had not chosen it, had simply found himself beside Henry on this bearing without registering the decision. The harbor in February showed itself as it did in January — the dark water, the moored boats, the lights on the commercial wharf, the breakwater running out from the north shore, the algae line black at the waterline. The cold sat on the surface of the water without disturbing it. Very still.

They turned onto Birch Street. They turned onto Elm.

Three blocks from the Legion hall Henry said: "You were very calm."

"I have had some practice," Marcus said.

"I know," Henry said.

They walked.

The footsteps on the cold pavement were the only sound between the buildings. Marcus watched the light in the kitchen window of the house ahead — it was their house, theirs — and did not look away from it.

"I have too," Henry said.

Marcus did not answer.

They walked the rest of the way home in silence.

---

The house on Elm Street had a light in the kitchen window and the quality of the light was warm — the particular quality that distinguished a lit window from a lit-and-heated window, something in the color of it, in the depth, that Marcus had learned to read from the outside as he learned to read the inside of the house itself. Lillian had left the stove going. She was not in the kitchen — he could see through the glass that the kitchen was empty — but the pot was on the back element and the room was warm.

Henry hung his coat on the hook inside the door and went to the sink to fill the kettle without discussing it.

Marcus sat down at the kitchen table. He set his file folder on the chair beside him. The table was pine, the surface marked with years of use — the rings from cups and glasses, a long pale scratch across one corner from something Lillian used the table for that he had never identified, the general worn smoothness that accumulated in things that were used and attended to and neither replaced nor preserved. He put his hands flat on it.

The stove ticked. Henry filled the kettle.

Outside, February continued: the cold still, the street empty, the harbor somewhere below the last rise with its winter shape in the dark. He had his documents in the file. He had his classroom tomorrow, the Latin third-year in the first period, the German second-year in the third.

The kettle began to warm.
