# The Unfinished Letter

The school had released him for the summer at the end of June, and by the second week of July Marcus had not yet found the right orientation to days without schedule.

Not that the days were empty. He had a list — *Virgil to page ninety; the third decade of Livy; irregular verb forms for the fall section's second year; composition notes he had promised himself he would work through before September*. He had been at the desk at eight in the morning for three days running, and the list was present on the desk, and by ten he was at the window, having done none of it.

Henry left for the school each morning at his usual time. The summer maintenance schedule was apparently as various and demanding as the school-year one — more so, Henry said, since in summer you could finally get into the boiler room without the fire burning and do what needed doing. He left at a quarter to seven with his thermos and his key ring, and Marcus heard the door and came down for his own breakfast and was back upstairs before the kitchen had fully settled, and then the day was his.

Lillian was mostly in the garden. The tomatoes were coming in.

The window faced the street. Elm Street in July was not the same street as in October — the trees were full, the light moved differently through them, a filtered green-gold that arrived at the desk at an angle that changed across the morning. Two boys went past on bicycles at nine o'clock, arguing over something neither of them was conceding. A woman with a market basket turned the corner at nine-thirty. The harbor smell was there, as it always was — three blocks, the south wind — but summer muted it; the cold months concentrated it to something penetrant and specific, but July gave it back as simple salt.

He had the composition paper out by nine.

---

The difficulty was not beginning the letter. He knew who Professor Stern was — had known him since the autumn of 1940, when the Emergency Committee was still accommodating itself to the scale of what it would be asked to do, and Stern had been one of the men on the routing committee who moved names from the waiting list to the housing list to the placement list. Specifically, he had been the one who placed Marcus's name in front of the Coldwater High School hiring notice in the spring of 1942, when the previous Latin instructor's enlistment left the board with a classroom and no one for it. They exchanged letters occasionally. The last one had come in November — a brief report that the displaced scholars network was still processing applications, that two men from Prague had been placed at small colleges in Ohio, that the backlog in Halifax remained substantial. It was the kind of letter that said, between its lines, that the work continued, that the people moving through the channels were still moving or still trying to, that Stern himself was still at his desk in Cambridge six mornings a week doing what he could with what he had.

Marcus had begun a reply in December and not finished it. Then the school board review in February had taken whatever attention he might have given to correspondence, and then there had been the spring term, and then there had been May.

What he sat down to write this morning was not the December letter.

He drew the date at the upper right — July 10, 1944. He wrote the salutation. Then he considered, for what was probably longer than it needed, what the first sentence of the letter should be and what claim it would be making.

The first paragraph was not difficult. It was the official paragraph: Jan Václav Horak, Czechoslovak national, displaced person, last known location Halifax, October 1942. Found on the breakwater of Coldwater Reach, Maine, October 27, 1943. Official ruling amended April 1944: accidental drowning consistent with storm exposure, identification supplied. This was the public record, and to set it down was not to commit himself to any interpretation of it.

He wrote it. Five lines. He reread it, changed one phrase from *having arrived in Coldwater Reach* to *having apparently reached the Coldwater Reach area*, which was more precise and also more honest about what the record knew and did not know. Then he moved to the second paragraph.

The second paragraph was where he had to be careful — which was the first sign that *careful* might be the wrong principle for it.

What he wanted to write — what the letter needed, if it was to be a letter that could produce a useful reply from a man of Stern's knowledge — was an account of how he understood the probable route that had brought Horak to a breakwater in coastal Maine. Not what he could prove. What he understood, from his own understanding of how such movements worked: the way a name was passed from one contact to the next along a chain that no single person held entire, the way a farm in the right county of the right state could be a stopping point that appeared in no official record, the way a route that began with a legitimate transit document ended, sometimes, in an arrangement that was not quite anything the paperwork anticipated. He had been inside it — Paris to London in 1938 along a line of contacts whose names he had been given in the form of short descriptions only; London to a boat in 1939 that was not advertising its itinerary, a crossing that had ended in Sherbrooke, which had been the wrong end, the locked end, the one he had not anticipated and that had cost him two years.

He wrote the second paragraph. He wrote what he understood about the probable shape of such a route without naming specific people, specific farms, specific vessels. He wrote as a man of some structural knowledge who wished to provide context. He was accurate. The paragraph was precise. And when he reread it, what he found was that a reader of Stern's experience — which was to say, a reader who had spent four years moving people through exactly the kind of channel Marcus was describing — would read the paragraph and understand at once that Marcus was not an observer of these arrangements but a man who had traveled inside them himself.

He sat with this for a moment.

He was not afraid of Stern knowing. Stern almost certainly already knew — the Emergency Committee's files on Marcus's own case were not thin, and a man who read files as part of his daily work would have assembled the shape of the transit from the paperwork before he ever wrote about the Coldwater position in 1942. What Stern would read between the lines of the second paragraph was not new information. It was confirmation.

The third paragraph was the actual question: was Jan Václav Horak known to any of the networks moving displaced persons through the Halifax-to-New England corridor in 1942 or 1943? Had anyone expected him at a particular point along that route? Was there a family that had not received word?

He wrote it. Four sentences, asking for only what could reasonably be shared.

He read the third paragraph again, and what he saw was this: if he sent the letter, and if Stern made inquiries, those inquiries would begin with the Halifax end — the last known location — and work toward the point of terminus, which was Coldwater Reach. Which meant they would work toward whoever had been the contact node in Coldwater Reach. He did not know with certainty who that had been. He had assembled a probable picture in May, walking home along Elm Street in the late-afternoon light, and the picture's most likely answer was the Pfeiffer farm, three miles inland on Route 9 — a German-American family, naturalized citizens, with four German prisoners on their property and a wife who had retreated from the world in ways that predated the war and would outlast it. A family already living at the margin of a social position that had grown considerably more precarious since December 1941.

If Stern inquired, and if the inquiry reached Albrecht Pfeiffer, what light it would bring would not be the kind Albrecht could manage without difficulty. He was a careful man who had held things carefully for a long time, and the light that came with official inquiry — even the unofficial inquiry of a well-meaning professor — was not careful. It spread. It did not stop where you asked it to stop.

Marcus set the pen down. He looked at the street.

There was also Eira Bowman. She had been at the commercial dock the night of October 26, 1943, and she had told him this in May at the school rowing dock — given it to him across a distance that was not quite close enough to be overheard and not quite far enough to require raising her voice. She had given him the language fragment she could not place, and he had placed it for her. Czech, probably Czech. She had received this without adding anything to what she had already said. She had trusted him with something by saying it. He did not know what a letter to Cambridge would do to her position if an inquiry found its way back to this harbor, to this dock, to the night of October 26. He did not know that it would. He also did not know that it would not.

The fourth paragraph was simpler: he had written in a private capacity; he understood the sensitivity of the question; he asked only for what could be responsibly shared. He was reachable at the Elm Street address through September, and at the school from September forward.

He read all four paragraphs through.

The letter filled one and a half pages of composition paper, his handwriting smaller than usual because the questions required a certain density to sit on the page without spilling. It said what it needed to say. It asked a question that deserved asking — about a man who had died in October, whose name had arrived nine months later, whose family, if there was family, had not been told. The letter was correct.

He considered whether the precision of the second paragraph could be removed without losing the letter's usefulness, and took up the pen and tried — a fifth paragraph, a revision, working around the network knowledge with more circumspect language, gesturing at the probable route rather than indicating it. He wrote seven sentences, read them, crossed out three, rewrote them. What he had was a paragraph that a man in Stern's position would read as the work of a well-meaning outsider offering his vague impressions, which was not what Stern needed and was not what Jan Václav Horak deserved. The precision was what made the letter worth sending. Removing it removed that.

He crossed out the fifth paragraph.

He put the letter — four paragraphs, the fifth crossed out, one and a half pages of composition paper — in the right-hand drawer of the desk and closed the drawer.

---

He walked at two o'clock. The July town moved at its July pace — slower than April, but a different kind of slow; summer's was deliberate where winter's had been reluctant. He went north on Elm Street and then turned along the harbor road, the long way, which had better shade. Two lobster boats were in at dock and two still out. He saw Abel Holt working his stern post from a distance and raised a hand; Holt raised one back without looking up.

The harbor smell was the summer version of itself: the diesel still present but the cold brine softened to something almost mild, the kind of smell that in October would sharpen back to something that got into your coat. He walked the length of the commercial wharf. At the near end he could see the breakwater running two hundred feet out, the granite gray in the flat afternoon light, the algae line at the waterline dark and consistent. He did not walk out to the seaward end. He continued along the wharf road and turned back at the fish house.

He crossed Elm Street and went up the walk.

---

Lillian had made a cold supper, as she had been doing on warm evenings since the middle of June: tomatoes from the garden, sliced, with salt; bread; a wedge of cheese; water poured and waiting at his place. The tomatoes had come in that afternoon, and they were still warm from the field, the skin tight, and she said that they were ahead of schedule — usually she wasn't cutting them until the second week of August, but the warm June had pushed everything forward. He said they were excellent. He meant it.

Henry came in at six-thirty with his work bag and the day's Bangor Daily News. He set the paper on the corner of the table and read the front page standing up, the way he had done for as long as Marcus had lived in the house, then folded it and said something about weather building in the northwest, which usually meant a change in the next two days. They sat. Lillian poured from the water pitcher. Henry took the bread, and they ate in the comfortable quiet of an evening in the third year of a household arrangement that had found its settled shape some time ago.

Marcus did not mention the letter. He ate his tomatoes and his bread and his cheese, and the kitchen was the kitchen on an early July evening — the window open to the garden, the south wind carrying what it carried, the Bangor Daily News folded on its corner with whatever the day had sent down the coast. The light went slow and golden through the west window the way it went in July, and in July only, and Henry and Lillian were at the table, and supper was supper, and the harbor was three blocks south in the dark that had not quite arrived yet.

He went upstairs after. He read four pages of the Aeneid — the second half of Book Four, which he had been working through at no particular pace since June — and then closed the book and lay in the narrow bed with the window open to the street.

The drawer was closed. The question inside it was the same question it had been at nine in the morning, unaltered by the afternoon — still present in the way that some questions were present not because they awaited an answer but because they marked a position: *this is what you know; this is what you cannot do with it; this is what remains*. There were people he had come to have some small obligation toward — not heroically, not in the language of obligation, but in the ordinary way that came from inhabiting the same rooms, the same winter, the same harbor road for two and a half years. He did not want to be the thing that lit them up. He had chosen, when it was a choice, not to be.

Somewhere down toward the harbor a door closed. The July insects had begun to thin, and what filled the dark outside the window was closer to silence than it had been a month ago. He turned on his side.

He slept.

# August

The harbor in August looked like money, and in a working harbor that was exactly what it was. Two dozen boats' worth of fuel and catch and dock fees, the sardine shed processing three hundred cases a day against its peacetime two hundred, the mooring fields at capacity for the first time since the summer of 1941. The breakwater algae line sat dried and pale at the low-water mark. The gulls were loud. The smell from the processing shed — brine and the sharper, organic smell of the sardines themselves, the whole compound of a building working at capacity — rode the afternoon wind south and settled over the commercial wharf and didn't move.

She noted it the way she noted the fuel figures. Not with pleasure, exactly. With accuracy.

---

The *Halcyon* and the *Eda L.* needed to move to free up room for the two seasonal boats that had come up the coast on the sardine run: the *Nancy Marie* out of Spruce Head and a double-ended lobster boat called the *Ida May*, working north from Penobscot Bay. Getting the four boats into a configuration that worked had taken two mornings and three conversations with captains who did not want the conversations. By Thursday morning she had them settled. She walked the inside wharf with a measuring line to confirm the clearance, which was what she had calculated it to be, and wrote the new positions in the mooring log and moved on.

The rest of Thursday was the fuel log and the accounts. The allocation she had argued for in December — in Portland, in a room with seven other harbormasters, the one from Searsport doing most of the talking while she sat with her figures and waited — had held through the season. She entered the week's consumption and set the log on the shelf and went outside.

Fourteen working boats. All of them running consistent schedules, logging catches above the July average, the whole fleet moving in and out of the channel like a mechanism that had been correctly adjusted and left to run. She had the departure and return log for July and the first weeks of August in front of her when she came back inside, forty-odd pages of entries in the standard format, and what those pages showed was a harbor operating within its own patterns. Nothing short. Nothing disrupted.

She noted this. The way you noted a boat's trim when it was running right — not because you were surprised, but because you kept checking.

The fleet operational. The accounts balanced. The tide log accurate and complete.

She put the ledger on the shelf and went back out to count the morning departures.

---

The news about Galen Fuller came on a Tuesday, mid-morning.

She was at the office with the provisioning log when Henry Cates came in. Robert's father — she placed him by vessel before face, the way she placed everyone: the *Bethia*, dock 7, a steady man who had worked that boat for over twenty years without presenting her with anything she could not solve in a conversation. He stood in the doorway without speaking, and she understood from this that he had not come about the boat.

She waited.

"Bertrand was on Bay Street this morning," he said. "The Fuller house."

She set her pencil down.

He told her the rest of it in the flat, factual manner in which such things were delivered. Galen Fuller. June seventeenth. Normandy — the telegram said Normandy, it did not say where in Normandy, and she did not ask. Two months and a few days between that date and this Tuesday morning in August.

She held the numbers. June seventeenth was eleven days after the landing. Sixty-six days between the seventeenth and this Tuesday morning in August. Both figures presented themselves and she let them sit without deciding what to do with them, the way she sat with a weather forecast that was only probably right.

She had known, since June sixth, that both of those young men could be dead and their families might not know yet. The notification system was not indifferent, only slow — no pattern she had been able to establish in the lag between the fact and the word of it, no correlation with branch of service or theater of operation or any other variable she had tried. Some telegrams came in two weeks. Some took months. She had set this knowledge aside the way you set aside what you cannot act on, and she had watched June go into July and July into August, and she had kept the log and managed the fleet.

Now one of them had resolved.

"The family all right," she said.

"As well as you'd expect." He said it carefully, the words measured, the way Bertrand measured his own words on Bay Street. "Ruth's sister came up from Tenant's Harbor last week. She's still there. Bertrand stayed until nine."

Calvin Fuller had been working the *Helena* alone since the spring of 1943, sixteen months now, since the Army took Galen and Calvin's back gave out the same season. She saw him in the departure log most Tuesdays: *Helena*, dock 3 row, one operator, going out and coming back in without notation beyond the required times.

Robert Cates had been on the same beach. She looked at Henry Cates standing in her doorway and understood that the only thing she could offer him was the absence of bad news, which was not the same as good news, but was what she had. You did not say: *your son has not been killed yet.* You did not say it because the sentence was true and incomplete in equal measure.

"Thank you," she said.

He nodded and went.

She sat with the provisioning log for a moment without working through it. The morning's entries were a sardine supplier's count and two mooring payments.

June seventeenth. She did not know what the front's position had been on that date — whether the worst of the landing's chaos had passed by then or was still present, whether eleven days was enough time for anything she might call a consolidation. It did not change the date. She picked up her pencil and returned to the provisioning log.

---

She saw Ruth Fuller two days later, at the harbor store.

Beal's ran a counter at the harbor end — not the full general store up the hill on Main Street, but the harbor account, closer to the dock: flour, salt, kerosene wicks, tobacco, a few canned goods. She went Thursday mornings. She had not expected to find Ruth Fuller there, and she supposed Ruth had not expected to find her.

Ruth was at the counter when Eira came in, a provisioning slip in her hand, waiting for Myra Beal to come out from the back. The store was not large. The counter was the counter. Eira set her own list down.

She had known Ruth for nine years in the way you knew everyone in a town of eight hundred: by context rather than occasion, by sight at the general store and the Legion hall and the dock, by the accumulated familiarity of years of shared weather and errand. She knew that Ruth ran her dragger herself, on the days the fuel allocation allowed, and had been running it since Galen went to the Army in 1943. She knew that Ruth Fuller was not a woman who came apart in front of the harbor store when she could avoid it.

She was aware, standing two feet from Ruth, of the inventory of things she might say. She ran through it quickly. Something about how sorry she was. Something about what Galen had been part of — about the campaign, its progress, its meaning, the several framings that arranged a man's death in the vocabulary of something large enough to hold it. She knew these framings. She had received versions of all of them after Owen, and she had accepted each one with something that had felt, at the time, like gratitude, and none of them had reached the actual thing, which was that Owen was gone and the harbor was not and she had the work to do.

What she could offer Ruth Fuller was what she knew from the inside of the harbor work. Not the other kind.

She looked up.

She said: "He was a good man with a boat."

Ruth Fuller looked at her. Not grateful, not surprised. She looked at the sentence the way you looked at a measurement that came out right — as if confirming something she had already known, and was glad to have confirmed by someone with standing to say it.

"He was," she said.

Myra came through from the back with Ruth's order. They moved aside. Eira paid for her flour and her wicks and walked back down to the harbor.

He had been a good man with a boat. She had watched it from the dock log and from the mooring rotation and from the fifteen years of entries in the departure record. That was her authority.

The rest of the afternoon was the ordinary work: the mooring rotation check, the fuel certificate for the *Eda L.* that had been sitting in the district mail tray since the week before, a note to the sardine shed foreman about the truck-pickup window she had moved in July. She dealt with each of them in turn and entered the results in their columns and set the logbooks on their shelves.

---

She did the breakwater walk at four o'clock, as she did each week in the season.

The summer tides ran lower than the spring or winter tides, which pulled back the harbor enough to expose the lower granite courses — the places where winter storm damage showed as cracking or displacement that the high water covered the rest of the year. She went block by block, running the seams with her eye, checking the mortar courses for new fracture, noting the algae line at the waterline and its position against the August low-water prediction. The algae line in August had a different quality than in November: dried pale and brittle on the upper face, the smell less sharp in the heat, the whole surface texture of it different from the slick November version that cost you your footing if you weren't careful.

Nothing to flag. The two blocks on the north-facing run she had marked in May were unchanged — the crack in the lower seam had not progressed. She would note them stable and carry them on the winter watch list.

She walked to the seaward end and stood.

The harbor was behind her. The afternoon light came from the southwest at this hour — flat on the water, turning the surface pewter-gray where it ran in shadow and a thin, particular silver where it caught the sun direct. The chop was easy, the kind that came off the channel in a moderate southwest. A lobster smack on the north approach, hull-down still, making its run in. She watched it until she had the hull line and the approach angle: the *Bethia*, coming in on the north track that Henry Cates always used for dock 7. Expected in the count. She had expected him.

She had been standing at this end of this breakwater for eight years.

The first time had been in November of 1935, a week and a half after Owen's funeral, with the December cold already working its way in from the north and the fleet uncertain who it was taking direction from. She had not stood at the seaward end very long that first time. There was too much to do, and she had been in the part of learning the harbor that was also the part of learning to be someone the harbor would take seriously. She had walked the breakwater for the inspection and she had done the inspection and she had walked back.

At some point in the years since, the harbor had stopped being a thing she held at a slight remove, the way you held something that had belonged to another person. It was not an event she could find in the log.

Galen Fuller was dead in France, his telegram sixty-six days in transit. His wife was going to run the dragger herself and the departure log would show it beginning this fall and probably through the next several years, and Eira was going to enter those departures without annotation because they required none.

The body that came in on the ocean face of this breakwater last October — she was standing at the approximate end where Hector Brann had found him in the lower course on the morning of the twenty-eighth — had been a man named Jan Václav Horak, Czech national, displaced person, last address Halifax in 1942. He had gotten this far. He had not gotten the rest of the way to wherever he had been going. The record had his name now, and the official ruling, and the date.

She was still here. The harbor was still here.

The *Bethia* made the turn at the harbor mouth and came down the line to dock 7, clean and even, the way a man worked a boat he had worked for twenty years and would work until his body stopped letting him.

She turned and walked back to the office.

---

The tide was at three-foot-eight on the ebb, on schedule. She entered the reading in the log and set her pencil on the book.

Through the window: the commercial wharf settling into its evening quiet, the last of the day's work done, the two new boats in their adjusted positions on the inside. The light going long and gold over the water the way it went in August and only in August, too good to last, already tilting toward the ordinary dark.

She sorted the week's mooring fee receipts in order, the *Halcyon* and the *Eda L.* and the *Nancy Marie* and the *Ida May* in their new positions, everything accounted for. The harbor smell came through the bottom crack of the window — brine, diesel, the last of the processing shed's day.

She had the receipts sorted and the desk cleared by five-thirty.

She closed the ledger. She turned off the lamp. She went out, and the harbor was behind her, and the hill road was ahead, and the August evening was doing what August evenings did in Coldwater Reach — holding its light past the end of the work day, the sky going pale and clear in the west before it finally, gradually, let the dark come in.

# Harvest

The corn came in the last week of September. Twenty-two rows of it, the stalks dried to their final paleness and the ears heavy on the stem, and the work of it the same work it always was: pull the ear, snap the stem, walk the row. The prisoners worked two rows at a time, Karl and Fischer on the near side and Brunner and Krebs on the far. Lonzo sat at the field's edge with his rifle across his knees and the Bangor Daily News folded open in his lap, turned to whatever page he was on.

By the end of the second day she had the figure in her mind without meaning to count it: Karl was moving faster than the other three.

She had noticed it the way she noticed a slow cow before she could have named which one — without counting, and then with counting, and then the count confirming what she already knew. The other three moved with the efficient, conserving pace of men in their thirties and forties who had enough experience of physical work to husband it. Karl moved differently. He pulled the ears and walked the rows in a rhythm that was not rushing but was not conserving either. It was the rhythm of a man going at the work because the work was all he had to go at, and this was, in a way she could not quite close the door on, a thing she recognized.

She watched Lonzo once while she was watching Karl. His eyes had gone past the paper to the far row where Karl was working, and he was wearing the expression she had come to know over twelve months as the expression he wore when he was looking at a thing he had already thought about and filed. Not suspicion. Not concern.

She went back to her own work.

The corn took two and a half days. The late hay after that, two days of baling in the September warmth, the kind of work where everything smells of cut grass and diesel and you move from the field to the baler to the barn without stopping. Then the kitchen garden — the squash that had been ready since August and needed the last pulling before the first hard frost, the potatoes still in the ground, the few remaining tomatoes off the vines. Magda did most of the garden in her measured way, moving from the kitchen to the rows and back without hurry. Hannah did the heavy pulling. Her father moved between the garden and the barn and the field in the route he had worked for thirty years.

The icehouse light was on past nine o'clock those nights. She had noticed this before harvest, but in harvest it was more visible because the days were long and physical and should have put everyone to bed early. Karl, she thought, with Lonzo's newspapers. She had seen him through the small window some evenings — the paper spread across his knees, angled toward the lamp, lips moving slightly in the careful way of someone who was reading in a language he had built one word at a time. She had known about the newspapers since winter. She had not thought about what to do with knowing until spring.

---

The fence meetings had been going since June — or since before June, if she was honest, which she mostly was not.

Not every day. Only when the work put her at the south fence section and Karl at the corresponding part of his field, which happened twice a week, sometimes three times, sometimes once. She had stopped tracking it as an event. She had also not told anyone about it, which was its own kind of tracking.

They talked about the farm, mostly. The soil in the south section, which drained toward the lower field in wet years and could sit waterlogged into May if the winter was bad. The squash, which needed a particular pulling so the vine didn't rip. What cover crop was worth putting in after the corn stubble turned under — she favored winter rye, and so did he, though he had reasons that were different from her father's reasons and she had found this interesting. He knew farming; he knew a continental kind that had rules overlapping with the Pfeiffer farm's rules without being identical, and the differences were worth discussing with someone who understood the question from the inside.

In German he was fully himself. The Franconian vowels she had been hearing from her father since before she could name them were the vowels Karl spoke, and in German there was less labor on either side. She could not follow everything — there were idioms and agricultural terms that she would have needed more years of Albrecht's country to have. But she could follow the shape, and she could make herself understood, and there were conversations in German that she came back from feeling as though she had been somewhere. Not somewhere with Karl specifically. Somewhere where the language was working the way it was built to work.

She carried the carved bird in her coat pocket most days. She had recognized this as a habit — a thing she was doing without deciding to do it — sometime in July, when she'd reached for her penknife and closed her hand around the bird instead. It was small and smooth, worn at the edges in the way of a thing that had been handled often; she had been handling it without noticing. She had not given it back. The opportunity had not arisen, she told herself. She understood this was not everything that was true, and she let the rest of it lie.

What she told herself the fence meetings were: two agricultural people, a fence between them, comparing notes on what they both knew. This was accurate. It left things out.

---

The conversation with her father happened on a Tuesday evening in early October, the harvest nearly done, the kitchen garden pulled, the whole farm in its post-harvest settling. She was at the sink with the supper dishes when she heard him come in.

She knew his sounds as well as she knew any sound in the house — the particular pull of the chair from the table, the way his left boot came down differently from his right on the kitchen boards. She kept her hands in the water.

He sat for a moment without speaking. The kitchen had the smell of the end of a harvest day: soil, woodsmoke, the warmth from supper still in the room. The October light through the window was already at its early evening quality, pale and going.

"*Du solltest vorsichtig sein*," he said.

She kept her hands in the water. She knew, when the phrase arrived, that she had been waiting for it or something like it; she had known without letting herself know in the way she'd become practiced at.

"*Womit?*" she said.

"*Am Zaun.*"

She turned and looked at him. He was looking at the table — at the grain of it, or at a water ring two summers old that she had been meaning to work out with oil. His hands were flat on the wood. The right little finger with its old bend. She could see from the set of his shoulders that this was not something he was working up to. This was the speaking of it.

"*Ich bin nicht wütend*," he said. "*Ich sage dir, vorsichtig zu sein.*"

She looked at his hands for a moment.

"*Hast du etwas zu Lonzo gesagt?*" she asked.

"*Nein.*" A breath, quiet. "*Und ich habe nicht vor, es zu tun.*" He looked up then — not at her, at the wall past her left shoulder, and then briefly at her. "*Aber Lonzo ist nicht der Einzige, der an diesem Hof vorbeiläuft.*"

She turned back to the dishes.

He got up after another moment and went to his chair in the other room. She heard the German paper unfold — it came Thursdays, had come Thursdays for as long as she could remember.

She finished the dishes and dried her hands. She did not go into the other room. She went upstairs, and through the floor she could hear him turning the pages, and she lay on the bed looking at the ceiling and did not think about what she was going to do, because she did not know yet, and the not-knowing was its own country that she was not yet ready to leave.

---

In the morning she watched Lonzo more carefully than she had since the early months.

He arrived at seven the way he always arrived: truck on Route 9, the gravel, the stool and the rifle and the paper under his arm. Twelve months of mornings in this same configuration.

She was in the near field with the corn stubble, running the disk harrow behind the mule, breaking the stalks into the turned earth. The work required enough attention that she did not have to be obvious about where she was looking.

He opened the paper to the Pacific section first. She knew this habit; she had watched it since February, when he'd mentioned his son was on a ship she'd never heard of. Pacific first, then the front page, then the agriculture column he read without fail and sometimes showed her if he found something relevant. He was reading now and not looking at anything besides the page.

She ran two passes.

He looked up in the middle of the second — she was at the far end of the field, eighty feet of turned earth between them, and when his eyes came up from the paper she was looking at him.

He nodded.

She nodded.

He went back to the paper.

She turned the mule at the row end and came back.

She could not read the nod. She could not tell, from twelve months of observation, whether she was in his report or not in his report — whether what he filed at the end of each day at the Coastal Patrol office said *four prisoners, seven hours, no incidents*, the way it always said, or whether it said something else in some column she could not see from here. She did not know what it would mean to be in the report. She did not know what it meant not to be.

What she knew — not because she had been told, but because she was not stupid and she had been watching for a long time — was that Lonzo had looked at the south fence section and made a decision about it. Some kind of decision, its terms unknown to her. She was inside the decision. She did not know what she had been decided about.

Lonzo had a son in the Pacific who didn't write often enough. He read that section of the paper first. In December his left hand gave him trouble. He had been sitting on this stool since October of 1943 and he had not, as far as she knew, said anything to anyone.

That was what she knew. She ran the last pass.

---

The following afternoon she was at the south fence with the compost cart, spreading the last load before the freeze came and made the ground too hard to work it in. Fork work — heavy and rhythmic, the kind that didn't require thought and so let her mind go to wherever it went on its own.

Karl came to that section from the far end of his row.

He had been working the stubble turnover, the same work she had done on her side in the morning, and he moved toward the fence the way he moved through everything — steadily, without hurrying. She kept her fork moving. When she looked up he was there.

He did not speak. She did not speak.

The distance was the fence, which was not very far.

The first hard cold front had come through the night before, and the October air had the quality she recognized as the turning: clear and with an edge to it, the shadows long at this hour, the field reading differently than it had for four months. The whole quality of the light changed at some point in September — she had never been able to say exactly when — and now the south fence looked like October instead of August, the same fence with a different face.

She drove the fork into the compost pile and let it rest.

He was looking at the turned earth on his side. She was looking at the turned earth on hers.

She did not know what she was going to do. This was, for the moment, the only thing she was sure was true.

# The Harbor Log

The last of the seasonal boats were gone. The Nancy Marie had cleared for Spruce Head the final week of September; the Ida May had followed on the third of October, Kell running her out on the morning tide in a light northwest wind. The harbor was back to its winter numbers — twelve working moorings, the lobster fleet centered again, the summer berths empty and their cleats washed clean by the equinox blow. The sardine shed had closed its processing run the week prior. This was what October looked like, and it had looked this way for nine years under her management and for a good many years before that.

She was at the chart table by seven. Tide log open, the morning reading copied in at 0715. She set it aside and pulled the annual binder from the lower cabinet.

Log review. Every first full working week of October: twelve months of entries confirmed and closed, mooring registrations checked against the current register, incident notations followed to their official resolution, fuel allocation log balanced against the Portland figures. The accountancy of a year's harbor work — not audit, exactly, more the verification that the record said what had actually happened, entry by entry, so that when the district office asked she could answer for any month. She had done it every October for nine years. The previous harbormaster had done it before her, and she had learned the practice from his version of it and kept the structure without revision.

This year's review covered October 1943 through the present.

She had known, since January, what month it would eventually reach.

She opened to January and started.

---

January: equipment inventory, logged on the third. Chain counts, grapple hooks, the spare bollard hardware ordered in November and received on the 29th. Maintenance checks done. No incidents. She had done the January counts the same morning she found Owen's 1934 ledger in the back of the lower cabinet while tallying the chain. The old ledger was not part of the annual review; she had set it aside. She had come back to it later in the morning. The January log entry was complete.

February: a Coast Guard district letter on the ninth, standard quarterly operations acknowledgment, no action required. Nothing further on the October matter. She had not expected anything. Routine harbor operations. No incidents.

March: the spring opening. The Bethia on the fourth, Henry Cates bringing her down from the Camden haul-out on the morning tide. Mooring assigned to dock seven, as it had been for as long as Eira had been keeping this log and for some years before. Fleet registrations coming in. She checked each against the register. All current.

April: the main registration push. Six boats in, three renewals, two new mooring assignments from boats relocating out of Jonesport. She had processed the paperwork in a single afternoon at the chart table. The Portland fuel allocation confirmed on the 18th. All matched.

May: maintenance week. A corroded ring bolt on dock four's approach fitting, which she had replaced on the 14th with Declan Walsh's help. Materials and hours logged. No incidents. She checked the entry against the maintenance log. It matched.

June sixth: the D-Day notation. She had logged the radio call at 0302 — *Allied landings, Normandy coast; per radio, WLBZ 0300. Harbor routine* — and below it, same date, the dock-three cleat replacement she had done that morning in the window between the call and the fleet departure at 0530. She had also noted Eisenhower's address on WLBZ at 1820 — not harbor business, but she had put it in as context, as she had been in the habit of noting major radio events when the harbor was immediately involved. Fleet out on schedule. No incidents.

She held the June entry for a moment.

Then she turned the page.

July: the Nancy Marie arrived on the twelfth, temporary berth at dock eight, mooring fee paid in advance. The Ida May arrived the nineteenth at dock nine, Kell's double-ended hull needing the longer slip. Both registrations current. Sardine processing shed at capacity through July; harbor boat count and fuel draw elevated accordingly. She confirmed the allocation against the Portland records. They matched.

August: fuel margin held at three hundred gallons above forecast, confirmed on the 15th when the Portland figures came in. Ruth Fuller's dragger registered at dock six with Ruth as sole operator — she had updated the entry in July, Ruth having been running the boat herself on fuel-allocation days since the spring. Three mooring adjustments in August for the high-summer sandbar drift on the north channel approach. All corrected and logged.

September: no incidents. The sardine shed winding toward close. The Nancy Marie's departure logged September 29th, cleared for Spruce Head as anticipated. The Ida May logged October 3rd, Kell out on the morning tide.

She confirmed the departure entries against the register. They matched.

October 1944: current entries. Two and a half weeks of routine operations, tide readings, mooring notations, the weekly fuel draws. An approach-marker adjustment at dock seven on the 9th when Henry Cates came in on the strong northwest chop with the Bethia riding heavy. She had moved the marker eighteen inches north and logged it. The entry was current.

She confirmed the present entries against the register.

Everything matched.

She closed the front section of the binder.

She turned to October 1943.

---

The entries were present.

October 11th, 1943: barometric drop, storm advisory from the Coast Guard district office. Fleet pulled back from the outer moorings per standard protocol. She had confirmed the outer mooring lines herself on the afternoon of the 12th, walking the full dock in the blow. Entry complete.

October 14th, 1943: body found on the seaward face of the breakwater by Hector Brann, crew of the Alicia B., at approximately 0700. She had logged the notification at 0750, the Coast Guard arrival at 0820, the removal of the body from harbor jurisdiction at 0930. Unknown male individual, civilian appearance, no papers found on the person. Entry complete.

The entries following through the month: Lt. Parsons's visit on the 17th, her formal statement, the official ruling received in November. Accidental drowning, unknown individual, case closed to harbor records. Notation dated and signed. Entry complete.

She turned back one day.

October 13th, 1943.

Her entry for the thirteenth: *Mooring check completed, commercial dock, 2300. Fleet secure. No incidents. Tide reading 11.2 ft.*

She read it twice.

The entry was accurate in what it contained. The mooring check had been completed. The fleet had been secure. The tide had read 11.2 feet at 2300 hours. Nothing on the dock that night had required notification to the Coast Guard, or action of any official kind she had been empowered to take.

She had not entered what she had seen at the far bollard.

---

Owen's J.T. entry: January 8th, 1934, with the later addition below the original notation in his handwriting, the slope different from the dated entries above it. *This not entered at time of incident; entering here as complete account.* Then the account. His initials at the bottom.

He had been in Portland when the incident with J.T. happened. His deputy had logged the surface facts. Owen had read the entry when he returned and had made it complete.

She had been thinking about this since January. He had deferred completeness and returned to it; there was a word for what he had done. She had written the tide reading and the mooring check and the words *no incidents* and turned off the lamp and gone home and done it again the next morning and the morning after that, for twelve months.

He had come back to it.

She set her pencil down on the chart table.

---

At 2300 hours on October 13th, 1943, she had completed the mooring check and was walking back along the commercial dock toward the office. The storm had been clearing for the previous two hours, the harbor settling, the boats riding more easily at their lines as the blow moved northeast. She had made the outward pass down the full length of the commercial dock checking each bollard and cleat, and on the return she had seen the man at the far end.

Civilian coat, not oilskins or harbor work wear. Standing at the far bollard with his weight shifted forward, not at his sides in the way of someone working a line. The posture of a person waiting at a specific location rather than passing through. She had not recognized him. Not a registered vessel operator, not a face from the fleet or the dock work or anywhere she could place him.

He had been facing the water when she went past. He had not turned.

She had caught the second figure at the edge of the dock light — a shape in motion, already turning away, already in the first steps of departure. She had heard something: two or three words, spoken low, an exchange between the two of them. Not English. A sound she could not place at the time, consonants she had no frame for. The second figure walked inland before she reached the far bollard end. An ordinary pace, not running.

She had stood at the bollard end for a moment, long enough to see that the first man was still there, that his coat was wet at the shoulders and that he had not turned toward her. She had looked at him for the length of three or four seconds.

She had not approached. She had not called out. She had turned and gone back to the office and logged what the log said now: mooring check complete, fleet secure, no incidents, tide 11.2 feet.

When she turned off the lamp she had told herself there was nothing to enter: a man on a public dock after hours, a second person who had already departed, a few words in a language she did not recognize. No law broken that fell within harbor jurisdiction.

She had known, as she locked the office door behind her, that this was not everything that was true.

---

She knew things now that she had not known that October night.

Jan Václav Horak: Czech national, displaced person, last known address Halifax, Nova Scotia, 1942. Thirty-eight years old or thereabouts. No papers. The Coast Guard district office had sent her the name in a form letter five months after they closed the case, in April 1944. She had read it twice, noted it in her own log margin, and filed the letter.

She knew the language. In the spring she had gone to Marcus Klein — she had brought him what she could reconstruct of the sounds, the consonants she had been carrying for seven months — and he had given her the answer with the careful precision he gave to answers: Czech. Not German. Czech.

A Czech displaced person, last known Halifax, moving south along the coast through the channels that a man without papers moved through in 1943. Making for Coldwater Reach, for whatever he had been making for here. The second figure at the dock had walked inland. She had not identified that person. She had assembled what she could, from what she had seen and what Marcus Klein had been willing to tell her, and it stopped there.

None of this fell within harbor jurisdiction. None of it changed the official ruling.

What it had changed, slowly, across twelve months: the quality of the blank in the October 13th entry. She had known the blank was different from an ordinary omission since the morning Hector Brann found the body. She had carried that knowledge through the official inquiry, through the case closing, through the winter, through reading Owen's J.T. entry in January, through the spring and summer and this October. She had watched the blank and she had known what it was.

She picked up the pen.

---

She wrote below the original entry, in the space remaining on the dated page. The late notation format was the same regardless of what it corrected; she had used it twice before in nine years, both times for routine administrative matters. She wrote steadily, in the same hand she used for all harbor log entries:

*Late entry, dated October 1944: 2300 hours, 13 October 1943: completed mooring check, commercial dock. One unidentified individual present at the far bollard, civilian appearance, not a known registered vessel operator. Observed in the company of a second party who departed walking inland before I could make identification. No approach made. Not entered at original time. Entering now in accordance with complete record.*

Below that:

*— E. Bowman, Harbormaster, October 1944.*

She set the pen down.

---

She read it.

The entry said what had happened. An unidentified individual at the far bollard. A second party, direction inland, departed before identification. No approach made. Not entered at original time.

It did not say that she had known the next morning, looking at the body in the gray light on the breakwater face, that the man at the bollard and the body were the same. It did not say that she had spent twelve months aware that the Coast Guard's official record rested on the incomplete version. The entry said what she had seen, at the distance and in the light she had seen it, on the night of October 13th, 1943.

The entry did not name Horak. She had not known the man's name on October 13th, 1943. The entry was the night's evidence, and the night's evidence was an unidentified individual. She had not identified him then and could not identify him in this entry now.

The second party was also unidentified. She had not been able to identify them that night and had not been able to identify them since.

She read it a second time.

The record was complete.

---

She closed the binder. The stove was ticking on its steady burn, the morning cold fully pushed back from the desk. Outside the office window the harbor was at its October work: the lobster smacks at their moorings, the northwest chop making the small easy motion the boats were rigged for at this time of year, the channel mouth open and grey under the overcast. The Bethia in dock seven. Ruth Fuller's dragger in dock six, tied up for the morning. The two empty berths where the Nancy Marie and the Ida May had been.

She sat at the chart table for a few minutes with her hands flat on the closed binder.

The entry she had written was in a log that the Coast Guard district office read only in the event of an inquiry. There would be no inquiry.

What the entry changed was not any of this. What it changed was the record. By her hand, in her handwriting, in the log she had kept for nine years. This log, not Owen's — hers. The record now said what had been on the dock on October 13th, 1943. An unidentified individual and a second party and no approach made and not entered at the time.

Whatever she had assembled or suspected or held without saying in the months between then and now — that was not the log's business. The log's business was what she had seen.

---

She opened the current log.

She wrote the noon tide reading. Eleven feet, four inches. Clear. Wind north-northwest, seven to ten. Fleet at moorings.

She closed the log.

She took her coat from the hook by the door and went down the dock to walk the breakwater.

The October tides exposed the lower granite courses on the seaward face; she checked them as she went, working from the shore end out. The seam between the first and second course on the north face had been taking some water since spring; she crouched and ran a hand along the joint. Dry today. The iron pin on the third section was holding, which she had been watching since August. She went all the way out to the end, which was the habit, and stood at the seaward edge looking back at the harbor.

The office at the foot of the wharf. The cedar shingles. The fleet at the inside moorings. The empty summer berths. The harbor at its winter numbers, which were its honest numbers, what it was when the seasonal work cleared off and left the actual work.

She stood there for a moment. Not long.

Then she turned and walked back. There were mooring receipts to sort. There was the fuel report from the Portland office she had not yet opened, which would need to be answered by Thursday. The review was done.

She went inside and latched the door.

# November Weather

The animals were inside by the first week of November, a week earlier than usual, which meant more silage than Hannah had planned for and a barn that never quite emptied of its warmth once the doors were closed. Her father had brought them in on the night the temperature dropped without warning—the 31st of October, the fourth cow already stiff-legged when he found her at supper—and after that it was clear the season was done. The fields the prisoners had spent October picking over for the last of the corn and the last of the squash were bare now under the sky, which had gone the flat white of early winter. The first real snow came the second week of November and stayed.

She did the morning milking at five and the evening milking at six and the late check at nine, which she had taken on in October and not set down. Three times a day into the barn, and between those: the school run, the Latin exercises at the kitchen table, the cooking on the evenings her mother did not come to make it herself.

The prisoners were doing maintenance. The four of them patched the north-facing boards of the barn wall in the mornings, working in pairs with oakum and pitch from the supply shed, their breath making small clouds in the cold air. By afternoon they were in the side yard splitting firewood, and she could hear it from inside the barn: the swing of the maul, the pause, the sound of wood giving. Lonzo sat at his stool near the yard gate with his rifle across his knees and his newspaper, his coat buttoned to the top.

Her father cut the work hours shorter as November went on. By the second week Lonzo was walking the four men into the icehouse by three in the afternoon, and the yard went quiet. The firewood stack grew against the south wall of the icehouse, and the barn wall held its new pitch, and the farm contracted the way it did every year: the fields empty, the animals inside, everything that had been spread out through the working season pulled back into a smaller perimeter.

---

Several evenings, when the late check took her to the barn's far end and she came back up the aisle toward the door, she stopped.

From the barn door she could see the icehouse window.

Karl's lamp was on most nights by that hour—a low warm square in the dark, steady. She could not see him clearly at this distance and did not try; she could see the light and the shadow of the table, and sometimes, if the lamp's angle was right, the small movement of a page turning. She had started noticing this in the first week of November. She had not gone closer.

She had not spoken to him since the first week of October.

The decision had been easy enough to make in Mr. Klein's classroom, with the four categories laid out and repatriation as the word that made the timeframe comprehensible. She had walked home from school that afternoon with it settled, and it had not wavered. Not going to the south fence felt, each time the work took her near it, like something she was doing rather than not doing. She was making a choice in October and she was still making it in November, every time the late check brought her to the barn door and the icehouse window was lit.

He looked different in November than he had in June. Not physically—not thinner or marked by the work in any way she could name. In June he had held himself with a particular watchfulness, the readiness of a person who does not yet know what a place will ask of him. She had seen it in the way he stood at the fence, the careful attention he brought to everything, the alertness of someone for whom being wrong about the landscape had once had consequences. By November that was gone. He knew the farm. He knew what it asked. He was reading the newspaper in the icehouse by lamplight with his head bent to the page, and his hands, when the angle of the lamp showed them, were still.

She knew what he was reading. The front page of the Bangor Daily had been running the word counterattack since the middle of December—the German advance in eastern Belgium, the Ardennes, the Allied lines pushed back. She could read the American reports; he could read them too, and could subtract from them what the American papers did not know how to say. What he did with that, when he bent his head to the comics page instead, she could not see from where she stood.

The cold came through the open doorway.

She went back to the Holsteins.

---

Her father turned the radio up in December.

He had been turning it down for two years, since the fall of 1942, when the news began going the direction it went. She had grown used to the low volume—the announcer's voice in the kitchen, available but not quite filling the space. In December he turned it up.

She was at the table doing her Latin exercises when the six o'clock broadcast began, and he turned the volume up before the announcer had finished the date. He sat in his chair—the straight-backed chair he had pulled to the radio in October of last year and kept there—and he did not speak.

The announcer was naming Belgian towns.

She heard them and held them inside her head for the geography book she would look at later, after her father went to the barn. The Ardennes, which the announcer said with a flat American vowel. The German counterattack—that was the phrase the radio used, the phrase the Bangor Daily used, the phrase her father listened to with his hands on his thighs and his face toward the speaker.

He held very still.

The lamp made his shadow long on the kitchen wall. He was not looking at her; he was not looking at anything in the room. She had watched him listen to these broadcasts across the fall, and she had thought at first that it was his way of paying attention, and later she had thought it was grief, and now she thought it was neither of those exactly. He was somewhere else. He was here and also in the country he had left, in the hills and the winter forest that the announcer was describing in flat American syllables. She had not understood this before the last year—not what it meant, not why the radio made the kitchen a room he was only partly in.

The broadcast ended. He turned the volume down. He stood, took his coat, and went out for the last barn check. She put the geography book away without consulting it.

---

Magda's spell came the second week of November.

Four days. The bedroom door closed when Hannah came to the kitchen at five-thirty; breakfast carried to the hall table and left, the coffee half-drunk, the bread gone. Her father went through his work without comment—the barn, the morning feeding, the maintenance work alongside the prisoners—as if this were the farm's normal pattern, which in one sense it was. He had been carrying these days for as long as Hannah could remember. She had seen him do it before the war, when she was twelve and fourteen. He did not speak about it. She had learned not to ask.

She did the cooking. She kept the kitchen warm. She went to school and came home and started supper, and her father came in from the barn and they ate. Three days, four days. The farm ran on fewer conversations and did not stop.

On the fifth morning she came in from the six-thirty milking and her mother was at the stove.

The lamp was on. The smell of coffee already—Magda must have been up a while. She was standing at the stove in her dress and apron, hair down and unbrushed, making the coffee with the care she brought to it: the measuring, the cold tap water, each step in the order it went.

She said: "Es ist heute kalt."

Hannah took off her coat and hung it on the hook. She sat down at the kitchen table.

"Ja, Mutter," she said.

That was all. The most ordinary sentence in the world—not apology, not announcement, not I'm back, just the temperature, the simple fact of November. It was cold today. Magda turned to get the cups, and Hannah set the table, and the kitchen moved through the ordinary morning.

She had stopped expecting this to be the last time. Not this winter—some time before this winter, without being able to say exactly when. She had also stopped believing the returns were fragile, had stopped watching her mother with that particular care as if looking directly at her would send her back. Whatever Magda moved between—whatever the distance was that she traveled when the door stayed closed—it was older than the war and would not end with it. What she could do was be in the kitchen when her mother came back to it.

The coffee came. They sat. Magda drank hers without speaking again and then moved to the icebox for breakfast, and Hannah set out the bread and the plates, and the morning went.

---

On a Tuesday morning in early December she was cutting across the south yard from the barn, going back to the kitchen for the seven o'clock breakfast, and she saw it on the outside sill of the icehouse window: a Bangor Daily, folded open, its corners wind-curled from being outside.

Not inside the window. On the outside ledge, where the cold had been at it overnight.

She stopped when she saw the fold. Even from where she stood she could read the page it was open to: not the front page, not the war news. The comics—the small square panels with their outlined figures and their speech bubbles, the idiom gathered in short lines that sounded nothing like the articles. She knew whose paper this was.

She picked it up. The date in the corner put it two Tuesdays back, not this week's edition. The paper was slightly swollen from the cold, the fold stiffened. She turned it over: the other side was the crossword, worked through in pencil—English words in German-shaped handwriting, the across clues and some of the downs.

She carried it inside and set it on the kitchen table.

She did not mention it. Her father came in at seven-thirty and she had coffee and bread ready, and the newspaper sat where she had put it. Later, when she came home from school, it had been moved to the side of the table where he kept his papers. She did not ask him about it.

---

The nine o'clock check, the last round of the night.

She went stall by stall with the lamp, checking the water and the feed, watching how the animals stood. Number four was eating steadily—good; she had been watching the fourth cow since October. Number twelve was against the back rail, and Hannah stopped and put her hand on the cow's neck until the animal shifted and settled. The barn was the warmest place on the farm at this hour, the twenty-two Holsteins in their stalls generating a warmth that had nothing to do with the stove.

She came back up the aisle and stopped at the barn door.

The icehouse window was lit.

She stood there—the cold on her face from the open doorway and her own lamp in her hand and her breath making small clouds—and looked at the amber square in the dark. No movement she could see, just the steady lamp and the dark around it and the snow between here and there, unmarked except for the boot-print path going to and from the icehouse door.

Behind her the Holsteins shifted in their stalls, the slow sounds of animals settling.

She stood until the cold had come through her coat.

Then she pulled the barn door closed and went back to the house.
