# What Language

"I'm looking for whoever manages the school's rowing dock," she said.

He was coming out of his classroom. He stopped when he saw her and took her in: the notebook, the working clothes, the look of someone who had come from the harbor.

"Mrs. Bowman," he said.

She had come at half past three on a Tuesday. The school was letting out—she'd had to step aside twice on the east stairs, students going down in a rush. Up here the hallway was quiet now. A door at the far end stood open; she could hear someone erasing a blackboard, the long soft strokes of the eraser going back and forth.

"The rowing dock," she said. "The mooring anchor registration is expired. Two years at least. I need to speak with whoever is responsible for the facility."

"I don't manage the dock," he said. He thought for a moment. "I believe it falls to athletics. Mr. Folger." He reached back and switched off his classroom light. "But I know where the dock is. I can walk you to it, if that is useful."

It was useful. She said so.

She had been to the school three times in eight years. Once for a spring fair when Owen was still alive, when that was still the kind of event she attended. Once for the fuel allocation matter in '43 that had sent the wrong delivery order to the school's account and required a correction in person. Once when Hannah Pfeiffer had been sent home early in November with a fever and there was no one else to walk her the three miles to the farm. She had come to this building and now she had come again, and the fact that she had the dock question—an actual dock question, a real permit matter—made the trip a trip she could enter in no ledger but the one she kept for herself.

They went down the east stairs and out through the side door.

---

The school's east side faced a gravel lot and a row of birch saplings planted too close together, their trunks beginning to crowd. Past the birches the ground dropped toward the Reach. She could see the water between the trees—flat and gray-green today, the tide close to full, the late May light lying on it without any shadow.

"The athletics director," she said. "Folger. He'll need to come to my office before June. Vessel description and two dollars. There's a compliance matter as well—I'll document that separately."

"I will tell him," Marcus said.

They went down through the birches. The May ground was soft underfoot still, giving a little with each step, and the smell coming up the slope was mud and brine and the cut-grass smell of the bank. She had grown up on that smell.

The dock was at the foot of the slope: a twenty-foot timber platform set close to the waterline. Old construction—she could see it in the framing before she was down the bank. The stringers were mortised rather than bolted, the joints pegged with wood. Before 1937, probably. Before the new tide-study figures had gone into the compliance requirements for floating structures on the Reach. She made a note of it.

Two rowing shells were tied on the outside—cedar strip, matched pair, the school's name in black stencil on each bow. She checked the dock lines first. No rot at the hitches. Proper leads on the cleats, the bitter ends coiled and tucked. She checked the cleats: older hardware, the heads worn smooth, but the bolts were set well and there was no corrosion at the wood line. She stepped out onto the dock. The planks were sound—no give, no flex at the joints, no sound of water getting into the grain. A dock that had been looked after, whatever else it might be missing.

She walked the length of it and knelt at the landward end.

The mooring anchor was a forty-pound block, chain run through a fairlead and down to an eyebolt in the sill. She pulled the chain. No play at the eyebolt—that was correct, and she wrote it down. She ran her thumb along three feet of chain: corroded on the surface, the surface links gone orange, but the metal was solid underneath. She had seen worse. She had passed worse. This would do for another season if Folger got the registration filed.

The mooring tag was looped through the ring at the top of the chain. A hardware-store tag, the kind the office issued with each permit, the registration year stamped in red.

Nineteen forty-one.

She wrote it down. She wrote the chain scope and the platform height above the mean waterline and the dock's approximate position on the Reach. She would mark it on the chart when she got back. She would write the note about the platform height—four inches below the new compliance standard, a matter of record, not urgent—and Folger could come in and they would deal with it in order.

She stood up.

Marcus Klein was standing at the shore end of the dock, his hands in his coat pockets, looking at the water. He had not moved or spoken while she worked. He was the kind of man who did not fill a silence—she had noticed this the first time at the harbor in December, the way he had stood at the foot of the wharf and waited until she was ready to speak, not finding words to put in the space.

A lobster smack was crossing the middle water—she could see its shape, too far out to hear. The tide was as full as it was going to get. In an hour it would be running out.

She closed the notebook.

---

"There's something else I want to ask you," she said. "Not about the dock."

He turned.

She kept her eyes on the Reach.

She had not said this to anyone. She said it the way she said things that required care: directly, without preamble.

"Last October," she said. "The night before the body came in. I was doing a late check of the commercial moorings. Past eleven." A pause. "There was a man on the dock—the commercial dock, not this one. He said something. Two or three words, quietly. Not to me. I was thirty feet away, maybe more."

The anchor chain shifted once against the fairlead, the metal sound small and clear.

"It wasn't English," she said. "I've been trying to determine what language it was. I understand you speak several."

He was quiet for a moment. He was watching her face.

"Say it for me," he said.

---

She had been holding the sounds for seven months. They had worn down in that time—she knew that. Memory of sound was not like memory of a date or a measurement. She had done what she could to keep it: not calling it up too often, the way you kept anything fragile by not handling it. She had said it to herself a few times, in the early morning on the commercial dock, the harbor empty and the tide going out, standing where he had been standing. Trying to hear it again by saying it in the same place.

She said it: "'Prish-teh.' Something like that. And before it—a consonant cluster I didn't know. A zh sound with something harder behind it."

He was listening. The stillness of a man listening carefully, not waiting for his turn to speak.

"Say it again," he said.

She did. She could hear, saying it a second time, how imprecise it was. She had not known, when she first heard it, that she was committing it to memory. By the time she understood that she was, the man had already gone still and the moment was already going and what she was left with was this: two syllables, the stress, the consonant she couldn't reproduce properly. She had worked with worse instruments.

"Can you give me more?" he said. "Anything else you remember."

She thought. "The stress was on the first syllable," she said. "Hard on the first—harder than English. Harder than German. I know some German from trade, over the years. The stress in German follows the word. This didn't. It was fixed on the first syllable, and the rest was lower."

She stopped. That was all she had.

He was quiet. Not long.

"I think it was Czech," he said.

She looked at him.

His expression was precise. He was giving her what he knew, and careful not to go past it.

"I cannot be certain," he said. "From that fragment, certainty is not possible. But the consonant cluster you are describing—the sound behind the zh—and the stress pattern: first syllable, invariable, hard. That is Czech. It is also consistent with Slovak. Czech is more likely."

"Czech," she said.

"Yes."

She looked at the Reach. The smack had gone behind the point.

Czech. He had been speaking Czech on the commercial dock in October, in the dark, past eleven at night.

She had spent seven months not knowing what she had heard, and now she knew. The knowledge was smaller than the not-knowing. It did not close anything. It fit.

---

"The Coast Guard sent a letter in April," she said. "They identified the body. The name was Jan Václav Horak. Czech national. Last known location Halifax. October 1942."

She was watching his face when she said the name.

He looked at the Reach. One long beat. Then he nodded.

"Yes," he said. "That would be consistent."

She waited.

"Consistent with what?" she said.

He was still for a moment. She understood he was not avoiding the question—he was selecting.

"With a certain kind of person," he said. "A man moving through unofficial arrangements, in wartime. There were people who needed to reach places and had no official channel. There were networks for this—not organized in any central way, not documented in any record. Arranged, person to person, contact to contact. A man who needed to move from Halifax to Maine and had no other means." He paused. "I know the general shape of it. I don't know more than that."

The water moved small and steady against the pilings below.

She nodded once.

---

"Did you know him?" she said.

"No." A clean beat. "I knew the kind of person he might have been."

She looked at the Reach. She thought about what she was going to say. She had had it, she realized, since the letter came in April and she had read the name and the nationality and the last known location and understood what they added up to. She had not known she had it until now.

"So did I," she said. "After a fashion."

Neither of them spoke.

The May afternoon held the dock in its warmth. From somewhere in the school above them, a window came down—the sound of the sash, brief and ordinary, and then quiet. From where she was standing, she could see over the birch tops the edge of the commercial wharf. A quarter mile south and east. The place where she had been standing in October.

"Thank you," she said.

"Of course."

---

She stepped off the dock and went up the slope. The May grass gave softly under her boots, the ground still carrying the winter's water. She went through the birch saplings—their branches beginning to reach across the path, a few more years and the gap would close—and around the east side of the building and through the front lot to the main road.

The harbor was ten minutes down the hill.

The tide was turning when she got there. She could see it in how the boats had swung at their moorings—all of them around now, noses pointed toward the harbor mouth. The working day was almost done. The smacks were in. A man was coiling line at the end of the commercial wharf and did not look up when she passed.

She unlocked the office. Set the notebook on the chart table. The end-of-month register was still open on the desk from the morning, the last entry in her own handwriting: fuel delivery confirmed, Pelletier account, May 19.

She would need to add the rowing dock: anchor registration lapsed, platform noncompliant by four inches, Folger to come in before June. The fee. Two dollars.

Czech. Jan Václav Horak. Last known location Halifax, October 1942.

She picked up the pen.

# After Eira

He was past the school road corner before he became aware of his own pace.

Slow — not the brisk deliberate pace he made in the mornings, when there was weather to account for and a furnace to arrive before Henry had to bank it up. The unhurried kind, the kind that had nothing to do with time remaining or legs that were tired. Three of his afternoon students were ahead of him on the road and moving fast, the way students moved at three-thirty — a purposeful erasure of the school day behind them — and he watched them recede and then did not watch them, his eyes dropping to the road surface, the late May afternoon doing whatever it liked above him. On the south wind the harbor was present: brine and low-tide mud, the flat particular note the channel made at half-ebb, the smell that was this town's smell and that he had been breathing for two years and two months and had not yet stopped noticing, which he considered, on balance, a small mercy.

He had three blocks. The students had gone around a corner. The road was empty in front of him.

---

The name had been with him since the rowing dock.

Jan Václav Horak — she had said it the way she said things, directly, without ornament, and he had heard the name and the nationality and the last known location and understood at once what they added up to, which was not quite knowledge but was the shape that knowledge would take if it arrived. He had been working toward this shape for several weeks before she gave him the name. The name itself had come to him first through the ordinary channels of a small town: the post office counter, the Beal's store noon hour, the way information moved in a place where everyone picked up their own mail. He had heard "Czech national" and "Halifax" in April, in the same week, from two separate sources neither of which connected them to anything, and he had noted the conjunction and set it aside and then found it not staying aside.

The Pfeiffer farm.

He had not gone looking for the connection. It was the kind of thing that arrived if you had enough pieces in a certain order and the patience — or the training — not to reach for an explanation before the pieces were actually pointing to one. Albrecht Pfeiffer: Feuchtwangen, eastern Franconia, the emigration of 1922. A farming family from the part of Franconia that sat closest to the old Bohemian border — fifty, sixty kilometers of hilly country between the German-speaking towns and the Czech, with generations of agricultural contact across it, the kind of contact that produced not a common language but a willingness to meet in one. If a displaced Czech national had come south from Halifax in the autumn of 1943, seeking a connection in the German-émigré community scattered thinly along the Maine coast, the geography would have pointed to the Pfeiffer farm. Not certainly. Not by any proof that could be brought before anyone. But the direction of probability was not ambiguous, and he had learned, over a long time, to regard the direction of probability as a thing worth knowing.

And Karl Reinmar.

Karl was from the same border country. Marcus had heard it before Hannah confirmed it — in the flat vowels and the particular way the final consonants were handled, the specific regional texture that distinguished eastern Franconian from the Bavarian spoken further south. The dialect that shaded toward Czech in its rhythms, the vowel sounds that had been rubbing against Czech for centuries across that border. He had taught enough German in enough rooms to know the difference between a speaker from Munich and a speaker from fifty kilometers from the old Bohemia line.

He walked past the lilac hedge at the Whitmore property — bloomed out by now, the flowers going brown at their edges, the branch-ends heavy and nodding — and crossed to the far side of the road where the afternoon shadow ran cooler.

What he had: a Czech national, last known Halifax, October 1942, found dead on a breakwater twelve months later. A figure on the dock in the dark, speaking Czech, walking inland after. A probable network of the kind that had moved people south through Nova Scotia and into Maine during the worst of the Atlantic years — not documented, not organized in any formal sense, arranged person to person along chains of people who knew people, the links often having nothing in common but geography and a willingness to be a link. And a farm, three miles inland, run by a man from eastern Franconia who had been in this country for twenty-one years and who stopped in the middle of a field when a prisoner with the same vowels spoke to him in a language they both, by the routes of their separate lives, had come to carry.

What he did not have: any certainty that Albrecht Pfeiffer and Jan Václav Horak had ever met. Any knowledge of whether Albrecht was the connection Horak had sought, or whether the figure on the dock — the person who had been there in the dark and had walked inland before Eira reached the water — was Albrecht, or someone else, or someone Marcus had no access to. Any understanding of why Horak was dead.

He held this for a moment, on the road, in the ordinary light. The probable shape, honest about its own edges.

Someone had been on the dock with Horak. She had heard one voice — his. She had not mentioned a second, which did not mean there had not been one, only that the second had kept quiet, or that she had not been close enough. The second figure had walked inland. Whether they walked because they saw her coming, or because the exchange was complete, or because something had gone wrong and walking was the only available response — he could not determine, and he had trained himself, over a long period of being in situations that required it, not to fill the space between what was probable and what was known with anything more substantial than the acknowledgment of the space.

---

He had, over his years of movement, developed what he considered a working ethic about this kind of knowledge.

It was not dangerous — not to anyone living, not in this particular summer of the war. The coast was quiet; the patrols had relaxed by degrees since 1942; whoever had moved Jan Václav Horak south from Halifax had no reason to fear anything from Marcus Klein's private assembly of a probable picture. It was a burden in the other sense: it involved people who had not invited him into their lives and who were already carrying enough.

Albrecht Pfeiffer was a naturalized citizen with a dairy operation and a wife who had not been well. Whatever he had done or not done, he had done it for reasons that belonged to a life Marcus did not have access to — a life that had started in Bavaria and crossed an ocean and arrived at a red barn in Maine and had remained, for twenty years, in a kind of half-exile that Marcus recognized in its quality without claiming equivalence. Albrecht Pfeiffer did not need Marcus to take a probable picture and walk it up the road to anyone's office.

Karl Reinmar was nineteen years old. He had been a soldier since he was seventeen. He had been a prisoner for more than a year. He had done nothing in Coldwater Reach except work a field and speak his regional German to an old man from the same border country, which was not nothing — it was, in fact, something Marcus understood precisely and would not have had undone — but which was the furthest possible thing from anything that required attention from Marcus Klein.

And Eira Bowman had made her own choices. He recognized them as judgment rather than negligence: the judgment of someone who understood what the harbor log required and what it did not, and who had answered for what she had seen in the way she considered honest. She had not asked for his opinion about this, and she would not. She did not need him to carry her portion of this further than she had chosen to carry it herself.

He crossed the next street. One block left.

---

There was something else. He had not examined it directly in some months and he was not going to examine it directly on the public road, not today, possibly not anywhere; there were things that could be held in a particular internal drawer, accessed only when the drawer was essential, and this was one of them. He was aware of it — the awareness itself was sufficient.

The picture he had assembled was a picture he had been inside.

He had been the person moving through an unofficial channel. He had been the one who needed to reach a city where he knew no one and who arrived at an address given by a contact who had a contact, who was handed a room for two nights and a name for the next city and a time of departure and then not handed anything more, because the person who handed it over did not know anything more. Paris to London, 1938. London to a boat that was not advertising its route, 1939. He had been the person who relied on the chain's holding and had not examined the chain's individual links too closely, because examination was one of the things that made chains break.

The chain had held. He was here — walking three blocks home in late May, in a town that had not yet fully decided how it felt about him, carrying someone else's probable picture.

Horak's had not held.

He came to Elm Street and turned toward the house.

---

Lillian was at the kitchen stove when he came in. The smell reached him before he was all the way through the door: real coffee, not the ersatz barley mixture that had been the household's standard since the early part of the spring. He stopped in the doorway.

"Where did you find this," he said.

She turned from the stove. She was smiling. "Ellis. Off the supply boat. He found two bags at the back of the locker and said he couldn't account for how they'd gotten there — said we might as well have them."

"Ellis," Marcus said, "is a man of considerable virtue."

"He is." She lifted the pot. "Sit down."

He hung his coat and hat on the hook and came to the table. Henry was there with the evening edition — the Bangor paper, which came to Elm Street two days behind schedule most weeks and three days behind on weeks when the delivery arrangement found something to object to. He had folded it to the inside pages. Marcus pulled out his chair.

"Later than usual," Henry said. This was not a complaint; Henry did not complain about the household's schedule.

"I had a few things to finish at the school," Marcus said. He considered for a moment. "The harbormaster came by as well. There was a matter with the rowing dock."

Lillian set a cup in front of him — the china one she brought out for occasions she had decided deserved it. The smell of the coffee was more particular than anything else in the house — a specific dark insistence, the real thing distinguishing itself from its substitutes without any effort at all.

"The school has a rowing club?" she said.

"It does," Marcus said. "Or it did, apparently, at some point." He picked up the cup. "The mooring registration has been expired since 1941. Two shells at the dock and no one using them."

Henry lowered the paper. "Three of the rowers enlisted," he said, with the measured evenness he used for facts he had already considered from several angles. "Hennessey's boy. The two Vance brothers."

They were quiet for a moment — the three of them, the expired tag, the two shells, the year and a half.

"The athletics director will need to come to the office before June," Marcus said. "There is also a compliance matter — four inches, a height question. Mrs. Bowman mentioned it." He drank. "I will tell Folger."

Henry returned to the paper.

---

After a little while Henry turned to the back pages — the tide tables, which Marcus had observed him reading every evening for two years without quite understanding what pleasure it gave him, though he suspected the pleasure had something to do with the certainty of them, the way they told you what the water was going to do before it did it — and said, without looking up: "The news is better from the Mediterranean. The Anzio situation."

He turned the paper to show the headline.

Marcus read it. The Anzio beachhead had been static since January, the winter dispatches full of grid coordinates and tactical stalemates that had stopped meaning much to anyone reading them in a Maine kitchen. The line was moving now. "They will be in Rome before June," Marcus said.

"That's what the paper is saying."

"In this case I believe they may be right."

Lillian sat down with her own cup. They talked about the Mediterranean for a few minutes — what it implied for the invasion everyone knew was coming but that had not yet come, whether the push north out of Anzio meant the German defensive line in Italy was genuinely broken or only interrupted. It was the conversation of people who had been listening to the same broadcast each evening, assembling from dispatches what they could, which was never quite enough and was always more than nothing.

---

After a while Henry went back to the tide tables and Lillian got up to see to the stove. Marcus held his cup. The coffee was almost gone.

"I had an interesting thing today," he said. He had not planned to say it — it arrived the way small true things arrived when you were sitting in a kitchen with decent coffee and people who were not requiring anything of you.

Lillian turned from the stove. Henry lowered the paper two inches.

"A student," Marcus said. "In the afternoon section. The passage they were working on concerned soldiers far from home — a standard enough passage, and not a difficult one, but it required a specific word. The Latin word for the longing a person feels for someone absent. Not sadness generally. Not grief in the broad sense. The particular ache that belongs to absence itself — to the missing of a specific person from a specific place."

Henry set the paper down.

"Most students reach for 'tristitia,'" Marcus said, "which means sadness, or 'dolor,' which means pain — grief, suffering, the word that covers a great deal of ground. Either is usable. Neither is the right word." He turned the cup slightly in both hands. "This student wrote 'desiderium.'"

Lillian said: "Which is the one that means the other thing."

"Yes. Exactly the other thing. The precise word for the precise feeling." He was quiet a moment. "I had not expected it. I found it —" He considered. "Genuinely pleasing."

She said: "That's the best part of teaching, I think. When they find the right one."

He thought about it. The afternoon classroom, the pencil moving across the page, the student looking up to see if it was correct.

"Yes," he said. "I think it is."

---

Henry refolded the paper. Lillian got up for the pot. The kitchen held its warmth — the day's heat collected under the low ceiling, the west window still carrying the evening light, the slow generous light of late May that went on longer than was useful, longer than the workday had any claim on.

Marcus sat with his hands around the empty cup.

Outside, somewhere down toward the harbor, a screen door banged once in the wind off the water. Then it was quiet.

# D-Day

The field telephone rang at two minutes past three.

She was awake — had been since midnight, sitting at the chart table with the logbook open and the kerosene stove turned to its lowest heat. She had the prior week's entries in front of her. She was not reading them.

She picked up the receiver.

"Eira." Lawrence Cary's voice, Rockland, who had been on the Portland relay since at least midnight. She heard the quality of it before the words arrived. "It's on. The landing."

She held the receiver. Outside the harbor made its ordinary sounds: a hull settling against the dock, water at the breakwater base.

"When," she said.

"Hours ago. By now they're ashore."

"Thank you, Lawrence."

"I thought you'd want to know."

"I did."

She replaced the receiver. The kerosene stove ticked. Through the window the harbor was dark and still — the boats at their moorings, the breakwater a low shape against the sky that was not quite sky yet, the channel running south beyond it in the dark.

She opened the logbook to June sixth and wrote the notation. Time, source, content. *At 03:02, L. Cary, Rockland, relays: landing at Normandy underway, troops reported ashore.* She kept it to the facts.

She read the notation back. She closed the book.

She sat.

Three hours yet before the boats would move. She had the five o'clock tide reading, the mooring check, the loose cleat on dock 3 she had been carrying the wrench for since April without stopping to use it. These things were not going anywhere. She sat at the chart table for a while with the stove ticking and the harbor outside, and she let the hour be what it was.

---

Dawn came at four forty-three. She had the tide reading by five: six-foot ebb, running clean past the breakwater on schedule. She entered the figure in the column beside the prior days — June fourth, June fifth, June sixth, the same eleven-foot range the harbor had been running since the tidal surveys of the 1890s. She wrote the numbers in the column. They were correct. She shelved the book.

The boats began going out before the light was fully up. The morning was the finest of the early summer so far — clear sky high and pale, no cloud anywhere, the air holding the particular stillness of a calm June morning before the southwest wind found the channel. She stood in the doorway and watched the *Fair Weather* clear the breakwater at five thirty-nine, the *Edna May* following at five forty-two. The diesels carrying south on the flat water. A fine morning for it.

She went out to the dock at six for the mooring check. South row first, then north. Fourteen boats in harbor this morning — she counted them by name and knew each berth, each owner, each boat's usual schedule. The count was down from the twenty-two she had managed before the fuel allocations reduced the working fleet to what it could sustain. Fourteen. She walked the south row and made her notes.

Dock 3. She stopped at the second post. The cleat was iron, surface-rusted, the near bolt working loose since the ice-out, and she had been carrying the wrench in her coat pocket for six weeks at least and had noted the cleat each time and kept walking. Not this morning. She pulled the wrench out and put it to the bolt and tightened. The cleat held. She checked the second bolt — still sound. She stood up and put the wrench back.

---

Galen Fuller was twenty-two. She had watched him on this dock since he was twelve years old, carrying his father's bait boxes and getting his hands wrong on the lines and learning the dock the way you learned it. Before the Army took him in the spring of 1943 he had crewed the *Helena* for a season and a half after his father's back gave out, and she had signed off on his vessel certification herself. She knew his hands from the bowline. She knew his father's boat, registered to Calvin Fuller, laid up since the back gave out entirely.

Robert Cates was twenty-four. Third generation on this dock. His grandfather had fished the Reach before the harbormaster's records existed in ledger form. His father had the *Bethia*, dock 7, which was at dock 7 this morning with Robert Cates not aboard it. The family had not received a telegram since the spring. This was, for now, what they had to go on.

She did not know which beach. She did not know if either of them had made it off it. She did not know if either of them was alive.

She entered the morning departures. Time, vessel name, estimated return. Weather notation: *clear, no wind, sea state 1.*

---

At Beal's the radio had been on since early morning. She could hear WLBZ through the screen door before she pushed it open. The signal was clear today — the weather giving it a clean run down from Bangor, the BBC relay coming through with only the background static that never entirely went away.

Small crowd for noon. Bertrand Hatch off his lunch break, standing near the wall with his coat on — she looked at him once. Two women from the canning cooperative, a fisherman she didn't place, possibly from Spruce Harbor. Agnes Vane in her winter coat, collar up despite the June warmth. A boy of twelve or so on the counter, told to wait and waiting. Dumont behind the register with his hands flat on the counter, listening.

The broadcast filled the room. The voice on the other end of the wire was flat and formal, the cadence of a text prepared in advance for reading, not speaking. She stood near the door and listened.

*...this great crusade, toward which we have striven these many months. The eyes of the world are upon you. The hopes and prayers of liberty-loving people everywhere march with you...*

The static ran under the words. The words ran over the static. She listened to the whole thing — the voice going on with its large sentences, its nouns assembled for history. She noticed the distance between the voice and this room, the compression of the wire and the signal that was the only reason the voice was here at all. She thought about the two men. She let the voice finish.

She bought her ration items: two points of tinned goods, the sugar allotment, a spool of wicking for the stove. She brought them to the counter. Dumont totaled the points without speaking.

Agnes Vane, near the radio, said: "God willing they'll come home by Christmas."

Nobody answered. The static continued. The broadcast continued. Eira counted back her change and put it in her coat pocket.

---

At two o'clock a boat came in with a bent prop shaft.

She could see the trouble from the dock. The vibration in the stern as it came through the harbor mouth — a particular shudder she knew, the kind that meant the shaft had found something solid and the boat had made the run back running rough, the blade bent off true and the whole aft section shaking with it. She went out.

The captain was already over the transom looking at the shaft when she reached the dock. A forty-footer from up the coast, out of somewhere north — Castine, maybe, or Sedgwick. She had seen him once at a Knox County meeting and not since.

"What did you hit," she said.

"A ledge, I think. Past the Thornton island marker. Not on my chart."

"It won't be on your chart." She looked at the shaft. Blade bent thirty degrees off true, maybe thirty-five. "You've been running like that since the marker."

"Almost two miles. I didn't know if she'd hold together."

"She held." She went to the office and called the repair yard at Searsport. She gave them the damage description — bent shaft, probable twenty-two inches, unclear if the strut bearing had taken secondary damage. They had a slip on Thursday. She came back out to the dock and gave the captain the day and told him what he needed for the documentation.

"There's also a shoal notification to file," she said. "Your encounter goes to the chart service. What's your best position on the ledge?"

He told her. She wrote it down. When he went off to see about an interim berth she returned to the office and wrote up the shoal report: the coordinates, the depth estimate, the vessel name, the date of encounter. She filled in the date — June 6, 1944 — and looked at it and looked at the rest of the form and finished the form.

The afternoon was the afternoon. The shoal notification. The vessel registration. A call from the Coast Guard station about a dragged buoy needing reset on Tuesday. She logged it for Tuesday's schedule. She answered the calls and wrote the entries and did the work, which was here regardless of what was in France, which required what it had always required.

At four-thirty she opened the logbook again. *At 03:02, L. Cary, Rockland, relays: landing at Normandy underway, troops reported ashore.* She read the notation through once. She turned the page and checked the prop shaft documentation. The figures were correct.

---

At five she walked out to the end of the breakwater.

Not a habit. She walked the granite blocks out to the harbor mouth and stood at the end in the June evening light — the long kind that lingered past the end of the work day, high and pale, the kind of light that would not go down on schedule.

The fishing boats were coming in on the evening tide. She counted them: the *Edna May* first, clearing the gap at a few minutes past five, Amos Frye at the wheel. The *Fair Weather* behind it, then the *Persephone* with Gus Hollis running the deck loaded, throttling down as he made the turn. She knew the sound of each engine by now in the same way she knew the voices in the post office or the shape of the handwriting in the dock registers. Eight boats in tonight, the full count of those that had gone out.

The *Bethia* was in the count. She watched it come through the gap — Robert Cates's father, running it alone, bringing it around to dock 7 with the practiced ease of a man who had been putting a boat in this berth for thirty years and would put it there without thinking as long as his body let him. She watched the *Bethia* make the turn.

Behind each boat was a family's calculation. Not a safe one — she had learned what happened when the safety failed, had learned it in the harbor before dawn, eight and a half years back, standing on the dock with a coil of line she had no use for anymore. Not safe. Reasonable. The calculation that a working life on the water was worth the terms it came on. She had been watching this calculation from this breakwater since before the post was hers.

The *Helena* was not in the count. Hadn't been since the autumn of 1942, the berth taken over by Winslow's *Penelope Ann* on a monthly arrangement. She did not look at the *Helena*'s berth. She looked at the boats that were there.

Galen Fuller might be dead. He might have been dead since before the harbor woke, since the dark hours when she was sitting at the chart table with Lawrence Cary's voice in the receiver. He might be in France tonight, alive, eating whatever they had given him, writing or not writing a letter home. She did not know. She would not know for some time. Robert Cates the same.

The last boat through the gap was the *Margaret Jean*, running behind as it sometimes did. She listened to the engine at idle — a vibration she didn't like, a loose fitting somewhere in the cooling system.

The harbor quieted, boat by boat. The diesels going down. The water at the breakwater base doing what it did at this hour — a low sound, not the harbor sound of noon or the harbor sound of the winter gales, but the specific sound of the harbor at the end of a June evening when the tide was turning and the boats were in and the light had not gone yet but was going.

She turned and walked back along the granite toward the shore.

# Karl Speaks

The radio had gone on until past eleven the night before. She had heard it through the floorboards — her father's voice first, calling her mother, *Magda, komm* — and then the radio sound rising a little above its usual murmur, the evening news expanded to something that required more time than evenings usually gave it. She had lain in the dark at the top of the stairs and listened to the voice of it without the words, and when the voice she could not make out stopped she heard her father say something low and then say nothing more, and the radio went off, and the house was the house in the June dark with the insects going and the cows settled for the night in the barn.

In the morning he said nothing.

Not in German, not in English. He drank his coffee with both hands around the mug and she ate her bread and Magda was at the stove and the kitchen was the kitchen at six in the morning in June with the flies already starting where the cream pitcher had sat overnight. When she looked at him he was looking at the glass in the window, or at something on the other side of the glass that was not the yard.

*Er weiß es schon*, she thought. Whatever they said on the radio last night, her father was holding it now in the way he held things since the war started — somewhere interior, somewhere she could see the outside of but not the inside.

The bread needed finishing. The cows needed doing.

June cows were restless. The flies were back — the black biting kind that made the Holsteins shuffle and switch their tails and ran the milking time up to close to an hour instead of the forty minutes of March. She worked the far half while her father worked the near, and they went through it in the silence that was the usual silence of morning milking, except that this morning the silence had something in it. The quality of held air, a room where something had just been said or was about to be said, and neither had happened. By six-thirty the cans were set and the light was fully up and she went to the north field.

The bean stakes she and Karl had started setting two days ago needed the second check — three had gone in crooked and she could see it from the end of the row, and June meant the plants were already reaching for the first stakes, already committed to whatever structure she gave them. She walked the rows with the mallet and reset the crooked ones, tamping each level before she moved on. The field smelled the way it smelled in the good part of June: damp-warm, the particular richness of soil that had taken last week's rain and was working with it now. The beans were up, curled at their tips, pale green, tender and already sure of themselves.

Lonzo came at seven. She heard the truck on Route 9 before it turned onto the drive and then saw the dust and then heard him park and come around with his stool and his rifle and the Bangor Daily News folded under his arm. He set up at the barn door in his usual configuration — stool angled to see the icehouse and the near field at once, rifle across his knees, newspaper folded in his lap. The ordinary shape the day took when it began.

The prisoners came out from the icehouse at ten past seven. Fischer first, pulling on his work gloves as he walked. Brunner and Krebs behind him. Then Karl, a half-step after the others, blinking once in the morning light the way he always did — she had noticed this about him in October and it had not changed, his eyes adjusting from the dimness of the icehouse more slowly than the rest, like a man who had spent a good deal of time recently with his eyes half-closed.

They came across the yard. Lonzo watched them come.

He opened the paper. He had been reading the Pacific section first since at least February — she knew this from something he'd mentioned in passing back in the winter — but today he opened it straight to the front and looked at it for a moment and then looked up at the four men.

"ALLIED ARMIES LAND IN FRANCE," he said. The voice he used when he needed to give information to the whole yard without making an occasion of it: level, factual, no performance in it. "Yesterday, June sixth. Normandy. Multiple Allied divisions. Troops reported ashore."

He folded the newspaper back along its crease.

Fischer and Brunner had stopped walking. They looked at each other — the quick sideways exchange she had spent eight months learning to read and still could not read all the way through. Brunner made a sound that was not quite a word, low in his chest, and she could not tell from the sound whether it was the end of something or the beginning of something; it might have been both. Fischer looked at the field for a long moment. Then he picked up his tools and went to work.

Krebs said nothing. He had been the quiet one all along.

Karl was already at the north fence. She had watched him change course for the north field as soon as he came through the yard — his mind already at the next task, the way it usually was. When Lonzo read the headline Karl had a stake in one hand and the string line in the other and he did not look up. He checked the string line. He went to the next stake.

He heard every word, she thought. And set the stake anyway.

Her father came out of the barn at eight with a milk can he had missed in the first pass. He carried it to the stand and set it and stood there with his hands open at his sides looking out at the field in the direction of the north fence without quite looking at it. He stood there for the length of time it took her to walk from the east end of the row to the third stake in. Then he went back into the barn.

He had heard the news last night. The landing had been in the house since six o'clock the evening before and he had said nothing at breakfast in any language — not the usual *Guten Morgen*, not *Noch Kaffee*, not even the silence that was companionable rather than the other kind. He had held it all morning alone, whatever he held with it, the calculation she could not quite see him making. She thought of the fence in May: his hands leaving the fence rail, going into his coat pockets, the ten seconds of stillness before the work resumed.

She went back to her stakes.

---

The afternoon came in flat and held there. By two o'clock the heat was at the part of itself where it stayed for three hours and the north field was full of the June smell of plants working — bean leaves, the soil drying on top while it stayed wet three inches down, the occasional warm smell of the cow barn when the south wind came through.

She was back at the north fence with the second-row stakes. Karl was on the other side. He had been working his own second row from the west end, east, and she had been working from the east end, west, and they had been moving toward the same section of fence all afternoon. She had been aware of this for the last hour and had not mentioned it to herself.

When they reached the middle section — six feet of fence between them and the same three stakes needing setting on either side — she said: "Did you hear the news?"

More words at once than she had said to him since February, maybe since before the bird.

He looked up. The gray-blue eyes, the wind-chapped skin that the warm months had eased somewhat but not entirely, the settled quality she had first read as tiredness in October and had come to understand as something more considered than tiredness. He looked at her and nodded.

She waited. She tamped her stake and straightened and let the silence sit there.

He said: "I did not think I would live to see it."

The English was deliberate. Each word placed before the next one came, the way he set stakes — level first, then tamp, no shortcuts. He had spent the winter reading Lonzo's newspapers in the icehouse by lamplight; she had seen him through the window sometimes in January, the paper held at an angle toward the lamp, his lips moving in the slight way of someone reading carefully in a second language. It sounded like something he had composed first and then read aloud, and the reading was true to the composition.

She sat with the sentence for a moment. She did not try to open it further.

"Are you glad?" she said.

He didn't answer right away. His hands were still on the stake. He looked toward the far end of the field — Brunner and Fischer and Krebs at the south trelliswork, Lonzo visible beyond them at the barn with his paper, the sky above the field the even blue of a June afternoon with nothing happening in it. He looked back at her.

"I think I am tired," he said.

She said: "Yes."

Nothing else. He went to his next stake. She went to hers. Lonzo sat at his end with the paper on his knee and the rifle propped at its angle beside him, not aimed at anything and not forgotten. The afternoon continued to be what it was: warm, green-smelling, the farm doing what June farms did.

---

She carried the two sentences through the rest of the day. She just had them, the way she had the weight of the mallet, the smell of the soil, the specific tired that arrived at four o'clock in the afternoon of a full farm day.

*I did not think I would live to see it.*

*I think I am tired.*

She had expected something else — she hadn't known this until he spoke and the something else didn't arrive. What she had instead was Karl in his second language, carefully, saying what was actually true.

He was nineteen. He had been a soldier since he was seventeen, two years of war as the whole of his adult life. What he had at the end of it — when the news came that the end was beginning — was being tired.

He would be repatriated when the war ended. Back to Franconia, to somewhere fifty kilometers from where her father had been born, in a place she had never seen and could not picture except as a word her father had made German-shaped by the way he never quite said it. She would stay here. The arrangement was the same whether she was glad about it or not.

The evening milking ran to six. She and her father worked the cows in the usual silence, which by now was just the silence of two people who knew the work well enough to do it without talking about it. Magda had the bean soup on when Hannah came through the kitchen door — white beans, Thursday's soup, right on its day. Magda turned once when Hannah came in, a small nod, and turned back to the stove.

Her father said grace the way he always said it, in German, the words she had known since before she understood them: *Herr, segne diese Gaben, die wir von Deiner Güte empfangen.* Lord bless these gifts which we receive from Your goodness. His voice was even. Magda sat and folded her hands and unfolded them and picked up her spoon. Hannah ate her bread and the soup and the last of the spring radishes from the cold cellar, and no one said anything in any language, and the kitchen was the kitchen on a Thursday evening in June with the long light going in the west window.

Her father's hand on the bread plate. The farmer's hand — the calluses on the palms and on the first fingers, the right little finger slightly bent from the break that had healed wrong when she was five, the hands she had been knowing since before she had hands of her own. Whatever he held with it was still in him, held in the old way, the way a man held things for twenty years and knew by now not to put them down in a room where other people might trip on them.

*Sei nicht so neugierig*, Magda would have said, in the time before she stopped saying things. She was still curious.

She helped with the dishes. Her father turned the radio to WLBZ for the nine o'clock broadcast and then went out to the barn for the last check, and she could hear the announcer's voice under the sound of the water, the same voice that had been running through every kitchen in the country all day. France. The landing. What was known. What was not.

She went upstairs at eight.

---

Through the open window came the farm sounds: the cows settling, a loose board against the icehouse wall where the warm afternoons expanded the wood and the cool evenings brought it back, the June insects constant in the yard. The radio voice came up through the floor until her father came in from the barn and switched it off and the house went quiet.

She had heard him speak in English, carefully, and what he said was true.

She thought: *das ist es*.

She turned over and closed her eyes.

# The Unfinished Letter

The school had released him for the summer at the end of June, and by the second week of July Marcus had not yet found the right orientation to days without schedule.

Not that the days were empty. He had a list — *Virgil to page ninety; the third decade of Livy; irregular verb forms for the fall section's second year; composition notes he had promised himself he would work through before September*. He had been at the desk at eight in the morning for three days running, and the list was present on the desk, and by ten he was at the window, having done none of it.

Henry left for the school each morning at his usual time. The summer maintenance schedule was apparently as various and demanding as the school-year one — more so, Henry said, since in summer you could finally get into the boiler room without the fire burning and do what needed doing. He left at a quarter to seven with his thermos and his key ring, and Marcus heard the door and came down for his own breakfast and was back upstairs before the kitchen had fully settled, and then the day was his.

Lillian was mostly in the garden. The tomatoes were coming in.

The window faced the street. Elm Street in July was not the same street as in October — the trees were full, the light moved differently through them, a filtered green-gold that arrived at the desk at an angle that changed across the morning. Two boys went past on bicycles at nine o'clock, arguing over something neither of them was conceding. A woman with a market basket turned the corner at nine-thirty. The harbor smell was there, as it always was — three blocks, the south wind — but summer muted it; the cold months concentrated it to something penetrant and specific, but July gave it back as simple salt.

He had the composition paper out by nine.

---

The difficulty was not beginning the letter. He knew who Professor Stern was — had known him since the autumn of 1940, when the Emergency Committee was still accommodating itself to the scale of what it would be asked to do, and Stern had been one of the men on the routing committee who moved names from the waiting list to the housing list to the placement list. Specifically, he had been the one who placed Marcus's name in front of the Coldwater High School hiring notice in the spring of 1942, when the previous Latin instructor's enlistment left the board with a classroom and no one for it. They exchanged letters occasionally. The last one had come in November — a brief report that the displaced scholars network was still processing applications, that two men from Prague had been placed at small colleges in Ohio, that the backlog in Halifax remained substantial. It was the kind of letter that said, between its lines, that the work continued, that the people moving through the channels were still moving or still trying to, that Stern himself was still at his desk in Cambridge six mornings a week doing what he could with what he had.

Marcus had begun a reply in December and not finished it. Then the school board review in February had taken whatever attention he might have given to correspondence, and then there had been the spring term, and then there had been May.

What he sat down to write this morning was not the December letter.

He drew the date at the upper right — July 10, 1944. He wrote the salutation. Then he considered, for what was probably longer than it needed, what the first sentence of the letter should be and what claim it would be making.

The first paragraph was not difficult. It was the official paragraph: Jan Václav Horak, Czechoslovak national, displaced person, last known location Halifax, October 1942. Found on the breakwater of Coldwater Reach, Maine, October 27, 1943. Official ruling amended April 1944: accidental drowning consistent with storm exposure, identification supplied. This was the public record, and to set it down was not to commit himself to any interpretation of it.

He wrote it. Five lines. He reread it, changed one phrase from *having arrived in Coldwater Reach* to *having apparently reached the Coldwater Reach area*, which was more precise and also more honest about what the record knew and did not know. Then he moved to the second paragraph.

The second paragraph was where he had to be careful — which was the first sign that *careful* might be the wrong principle for it.

What he wanted to write — what the letter needed, if it was to be a letter that could produce a useful reply from a man of Stern's knowledge — was an account of how he understood the probable route that had brought Horak to a breakwater in coastal Maine. Not what he could prove. What he understood, from his own understanding of how such movements worked: the way a name was passed from one contact to the next along a chain that no single person held entire, the way a farm in the right county of the right state could be a stopping point that appeared in no official record, the way a route that began with a legitimate transit document ended, sometimes, in an arrangement that was not quite anything the paperwork anticipated. He had been inside it — Paris to London in 1938 along a line of contacts whose names he had been given in the form of short descriptions only; London to a boat in 1939 that was not advertising its itinerary, a crossing that had ended in Sherbrooke, which had been the wrong end, the locked end, the one he had not anticipated and that had cost him two years.

He wrote the second paragraph. He wrote what he understood about the probable shape of such a route without naming specific people, specific farms, specific vessels. He wrote as a man of some structural knowledge who wished to provide context. He was accurate. The paragraph was precise. And when he reread it, what he found was that a reader of Stern's experience — which was to say, a reader who had spent four years moving people through exactly the kind of channel Marcus was describing — would read the paragraph and understand at once that Marcus was not an observer of these arrangements but a man who had traveled inside them himself.

He sat with this for a moment.

He was not afraid of Stern knowing. Stern almost certainly already knew — the Emergency Committee's files on Marcus's own case were not thin, and a man who read files as part of his daily work would have assembled the shape of the transit from the paperwork before he ever wrote about the Coldwater position in 1942. What Stern would read between the lines of the second paragraph was not new information. It was confirmation.

The third paragraph was the actual question: was Jan Václav Horak known to any of the networks moving displaced persons through the Halifax-to-New England corridor in 1942 or 1943? Had anyone expected him at a particular point along that route? Was there a family that had not received word?

He wrote it. Four sentences, asking for only what could reasonably be shared.

He read the third paragraph again, and what he saw was this: if he sent the letter, and if Stern made inquiries, those inquiries would begin with the Halifax end — the last known location — and work toward the point of terminus, which was Coldwater Reach. Which meant they would work toward whoever had been the contact node in Coldwater Reach. He did not know with certainty who that had been. He had assembled a probable picture in May, walking home along Elm Street in the late-afternoon light, and the picture's most likely answer was the Pfeiffer farm, three miles inland on Route 9 — a German-American family, naturalized citizens, with four German prisoners on their property and a wife who had retreated from the world in ways that predated the war and would outlast it. A family already living at the margin of a social position that had grown considerably more precarious since December 1941.

If Stern inquired, and if the inquiry reached Albrecht Pfeiffer, what light it would bring would not be the kind Albrecht could manage without difficulty. He was a careful man who had held things carefully for a long time, and the light that came with official inquiry — even the unofficial inquiry of a well-meaning professor — was not careful. It spread. It did not stop where one asked it to stop.

Marcus set the pen down. He looked at the street.

There was also Eira Bowman. She had been at the commercial dock the night of October 26, 1943, and she had told him this in May at the school rowing dock — given it to him across a distance that was not quite close enough to be overheard and not quite far enough to require raising her voice. She had given him the language fragment she could not place, and he had placed it for her. Czech, probably Czech. She had received this without adding anything to what she had already said. She had trusted him with something by saying it. He did not know what a letter to Cambridge would do to her position if an inquiry found its way back to this harbor, to this dock, to the night of October 26. He did not know that it would. He also did not know that it would not.

The fourth paragraph was simpler: he had written in a private capacity; he understood the sensitivity of the question; he asked only for what could be responsibly shared. He was reachable at the Elm Street address through September, and at the school from September forward.

He read all four paragraphs through.

The letter filled one and a half pages of composition paper, his handwriting smaller than usual because the questions required a certain density to sit on the page without spilling. It said what it needed to say. It asked a question that deserved asking — about a man who had died in October, whose name had arrived nine months later, whose family, if there was family, had not been told. The letter was correct.

He considered whether the precision of the second paragraph could be removed without losing the letter's usefulness, and took up the pen and tried — a fifth paragraph, a revision, working around the network knowledge with more circumspect language, gesturing at the probable route rather than indicating it. He wrote seven sentences, read them, crossed out three, rewrote them. What he had was a paragraph that a man in Stern's position would read as the work of a well-meaning outsider offering his vague impressions, which was not what Stern needed and was not what Jan Václav Horak deserved. The precision was what made the letter worth sending. Removing it removed that.

He crossed out the fifth paragraph.

He put the letter — four paragraphs, the fifth crossed out, one and a half pages of composition paper — in the right-hand drawer of the desk and closed the drawer.

---

He walked at two o'clock. The July town moved at its July pace — slower than April, but a different kind of slow; summer's was deliberate where winter's had been reluctant. He went north on Elm Street and then turned along the harbor road, the long way, which had better shade. Two lobster boats were in at dock and two still out. He saw Abel Holt working his stern post from a distance and raised a hand; Holt raised one back without looking up.

The harbor smell was the summer version of itself: the diesel still present but the cold brine softened to something almost mild, the kind of smell that in October would sharpen back to something that got into one's coat. He walked the length of the commercial wharf. At the near end he could see the breakwater running two hundred feet out, the granite gray in the flat afternoon light, the algae line at the waterline dark and consistent. He did not walk out to the seaward end. He continued along the wharf road and turned back at the fish house.

He crossed Elm Street and went up the walk.

---

Lillian had made a cold supper, as she had been doing on warm evenings since the middle of June: tomatoes from the garden, sliced, with salt; bread; a wedge of cheese; water poured and waiting at his place. The tomatoes had come in that afternoon, and they were still warm from the field, the skin tight, and she said that they were ahead of schedule — usually she wasn't cutting them until the second week of August, but the warm June had pushed everything forward. He said they were excellent. He meant it.

Henry came in at six-thirty with his work bag and the day's Bangor Daily News. He set the paper on the corner of the table and read the front page standing up, the way he had done for as long as Marcus had lived in the house, then folded it and said something about weather building in the northwest, which usually meant a change in the next two days. They sat. Lillian poured from the water pitcher. Henry took the bread, and they ate in the comfortable quiet of an evening in the third year of a household arrangement that had found its settled shape some time ago.

Marcus did not mention the letter. He ate his tomatoes and his bread and his cheese, and the kitchen was the kitchen on an early July evening — the window open to the garden, the south wind carrying what it carried, the Bangor Daily News folded on its corner with whatever the day had sent down the coast. The light went slow and golden through the west window the way it went in July, and in July only, and Henry and Lillian were at the table, and supper was supper, and the harbor was three blocks south in the dark that had not quite arrived yet.

He went upstairs after. He read four pages of the Aeneid — the second half of Book Four, which he had been working through at no particular pace since June — and then closed the book and lay in the narrow bed with the window open to the street.

The drawer was closed. The question inside it was the same question it had been at nine in the morning, unaltered by the afternoon — still present in the way that some questions were present not because they awaited an answer but because they marked a position: *this is what you know; this is what you cannot do with it; this is what remains*. There were people he had come to have some small obligation toward — not heroically, not in the language of obligation, but in the ordinary way that came from inhabiting the same rooms, the same winter, the same harbor road for two and a half years. He did not want to be the thing that lit them up. He had chosen, when it was a choice, not to be.

Somewhere down toward the harbor a door closed. The July insects had begun to thin, and what filled the dark outside the window was closer to silence than it had been a month ago. He turned on his side.

He slept.

# August

The harbor in August looked like money, and in a working harbor that was exactly what it was. Two dozen boats' worth of fuel and catch and dock fees, the sardine shed processing three hundred cases a day against its peacetime two hundred, the mooring fields at capacity for the first time since the summer of 1941. The breakwater algae line sat dried and pale at the low-water mark. The gulls were loud. The smell from the processing shed — brine and the sharper, organic smell of the sardines themselves, the whole compound of a building working at capacity — rode the afternoon wind south and settled over the commercial wharf and didn't move.

She noted it the way she noted the fuel figures. Not with pleasure, exactly. With accuracy.

---

The *Halcyon* and the *Eda L.* needed to move to free up room for the two seasonal boats that had come up the coast on the sardine run: the *Nancy Marie* out of Spruce Head and a double-ended lobster boat called the *Ida May*, working north from Penobscot Bay. Getting the four boats into a configuration that worked had taken two mornings and three conversations with captains who did not want the conversations. By Thursday morning she had them settled. She walked the inside wharf with a measuring line to confirm the clearance, which was what she had calculated it to be, and wrote the new positions in the mooring log and moved on.

The rest of Thursday was the fuel log and the accounts. The allocation she had argued for in December — in Portland, in a room with seven other harbormasters, the one from Searsport doing most of the talking while she sat with her figures and waited — had held through the season. She entered the week's consumption and set the log on the shelf and went outside.

Fourteen working boats. All of them running consistent schedules, logging catches above the July average, the whole fleet moving in and out of the channel like a mechanism that had been correctly adjusted and left to run. She had the departure and return log for July and the first weeks of August in front of her when she came back inside, forty-odd pages of entries in the standard format, and what those pages showed was a harbor operating within its own patterns. Nothing short. Nothing disrupted.

She noted this. The way you noted a boat's trim when it was running right — not because you were surprised, but because you kept checking.

The fleet operational. The accounts balanced. The tide log accurate and complete.

She put the ledger on the shelf and went back out to count the morning departures.

---

The news about Galen Fuller came on a Tuesday, mid-morning.

She was at the office with the provisioning log when Henry Cates came in. Robert's father — she placed him by vessel before face, the way she placed everyone: the *Bethia*, dock 7, a steady man who had worked that boat for over twenty years without presenting her with anything she could not solve in a conversation. He stood in the doorway without speaking, and she understood from this that he had not come about the boat.

She waited.

"Bertrand was on Bay Street this morning," he said. "The Fuller house."

She set her pencil down.

He told her the rest of it in the flat, factual manner in which such things were delivered. Galen Fuller. June seventeenth. Normandy — the telegram said Normandy, it did not say where in Normandy, and she did not ask. Two months and a few days between that date and this Tuesday morning in August.

She held the numbers. June seventeenth was eleven days after the landing. Sixty-six days between the seventeenth and this Tuesday morning in August. Both figures presented themselves and she let them sit without deciding what to do with them, the way she sat with a weather forecast that was only probably right.

She had known, since June sixth, that both of those young men could be dead and their families might not know yet. The notification system was not indifferent, only slow — no pattern she had been able to establish in the lag between the fact and the word of it, no correlation with branch of service or theater of operation or any other variable she had tried. Some telegrams came in two weeks. Some took months. She had set this knowledge aside the way you set aside what you cannot act on, and she had watched June go into July and July into August, and she had kept the log and managed the fleet.

Now one of them had resolved.

"The family all right," she said.

"As well as you'd expect." He said it carefully, the words measured, the way Bertrand measured his own words on Bay Street. "Ruth's sister came up from Tenant's Harbor last week. She's still there. Bertrand stayed until nine."

Calvin Fuller had been working the *Helena* alone since the spring of 1943, sixteen months now, since the Army took Galen and Calvin's back gave out the same season. She saw him in the departure log most Tuesdays: *Helena*, dock 3 row, one operator, going out and coming back in without notation beyond the required times.

Robert Cates had been on the same beach. She looked at Henry Cates standing in her doorway and understood that the only thing she could offer him was the absence of bad news, which was not the same as good news, but was what she had. You did not say: *your son has not been killed yet.* You did not say it because the sentence was true and incomplete in equal measure.

"Thank you," she said.

He nodded and went.

She sat with the provisioning log for a moment without working through it. The morning's entries were a sardine supplier's count and two mooring payments.

June seventeenth. She did not know what the front's position had been on that date — whether the worst of the landing's chaos had passed by then or was still present, whether eleven days was enough time for anything she might call a consolidation. It did not change the date. She picked up her pencil and returned to the provisioning log.

---

She saw Ruth Fuller two days later, at the harbor store.

Beal's ran a counter at the harbor end — not the full general store up the hill on Main Street, but the harbor account, closer to the dock: flour, salt, kerosene wicks, tobacco, a few canned goods. She went Thursday mornings. She had not expected to find Ruth Fuller there, and she supposed Ruth had not expected to find her.

Ruth was at the counter when Eira came in, a provisioning slip in her hand, waiting for Myra Beal to come out from the back. The store was not large. The counter was the counter. Eira set her own list down.

She had known Ruth for nine years in the way you knew everyone in a town of eight hundred: by context rather than occasion, by sight at the general store and the Legion hall and the dock, by the accumulated familiarity of years of shared weather and errand. She knew that Ruth ran her dragger herself, on the days the fuel allocation allowed, and had been running it since Galen went to the Army in 1943. She knew that Ruth Fuller was not a woman who came apart in front of the harbor store when she could avoid it.

She was aware, standing two feet from Ruth, of the inventory of things she might say. She ran through it quickly. Something about how sorry she was. Something about what Galen had been part of — about the campaign, its progress, its meaning, the several framings that arranged a man's death in the vocabulary of something large enough to hold it. She knew these framings. She had received versions of all of them after Owen, and she had accepted each one with something that had felt, at the time, like gratitude, and none of them had reached the actual thing, which was that Owen was gone and the harbor was not and she had the work to do.

What she could offer Ruth Fuller was what she knew from the inside of the harbor work. Not the other kind.

She looked up.

She said: "He was a good man with a boat."

Ruth Fuller looked at her. Not grateful, not surprised. She looked at the sentence the way you looked at a measurement that came out right — as if confirming something she had already known.

"He was," she said.

Myra came through from the back with Ruth's order. They moved aside. Eira paid for her flour and her wicks and walked back down to the harbor.

He had been a good man with a boat. She had watched it from the dock log and from the mooring rotation and from the fifteen years of entries in the departure record. That was her authority.

The rest of the afternoon was the ordinary work: the mooring rotation check, the fuel certificate for the *Eda L.* that had been sitting in the district mail tray since the week before, a note to the sardine shed foreman about the truck-pickup window she had moved in July. She dealt with each of them in turn and entered the results in their columns and set the logbooks on their shelves.

---

She did the breakwater walk at four o'clock, as she did each week in the season.

The summer tides ran lower than the spring or winter tides, which pulled back the harbor enough to expose the lower granite courses — the places where winter storm damage showed as cracking or displacement that the high water covered the rest of the year. She went block by block, running the seams with her eye, checking the mortar courses for new fracture, noting the algae line at the waterline and its position against the August low-water prediction. The algae line in August had a different quality than in November: dried pale and brittle on the upper face, the smell less sharp in the heat, the whole surface texture of it different from the slick November version that cost you your footing if you weren't careful.

Nothing to flag. The two blocks on the north-facing run she had marked in May were unchanged — the crack in the lower seam had not progressed. She would note them stable and carry them on the winter watch list.

She walked to the seaward end and stood.

The harbor was behind her. The afternoon light came from the southwest at this hour — flat on the water, turning the surface pewter-gray where it ran in shadow and a thin, particular silver where it caught the sun direct. The chop was easy, the kind that came off the channel in a moderate southwest. A lobster smack on the north approach, hull-down still, making its run in. She watched it until she had the hull line and the approach angle: the *Bethia*, coming in on the north track that Henry Cates always used for dock 7. Expected in the count. She had expected him.

She had been standing at this end of this breakwater for eight years.

The first time had been in November of 1935, a week and a half after Owen's funeral, with the December cold already working its way in from the north and the fleet uncertain who it was taking direction from. She had not stood at the seaward end very long that first time. There was too much to do, and she had been in the part of learning the harbor that was also the part of learning to be someone the harbor would take seriously. She had walked the breakwater for the inspection and she had done the inspection and she had walked back.

At some point in the years since, the harbor had stopped being a thing she held at a slight remove, the way you held something that had belonged to another person. It was not an event she could find in the log.

Galen Fuller was dead in France, his telegram sixty-six days in transit. His wife was going to run the dragger herself and the departure log would show it beginning this fall and probably through the next several years, and Eira was going to enter those departures without annotation because they required none.

The body that came in on the ocean face of this breakwater last October — she was standing at the approximate end where Hector Brann had found him in the lower course on the morning of the twenty-eighth — had been a man named Jan Václav Horak, Czech national, displaced person, last address Halifax in 1942. He had gotten this far. He had not gotten the rest of the way to wherever he had been going. The record had his name now, and the official ruling, and the date.

She was still here. The harbor was still here.

The *Bethia* made the turn at the harbor mouth and came down the line to dock 7, clean and even, the way a man worked a boat he had worked for twenty years and would work until his body stopped letting him.

She turned and walked back to the office.

---

The tide was at three-foot-eight on the ebb, on schedule. She entered the reading in the log and set her pencil on the book.

Through the window: the commercial wharf settling into its evening quiet, the last of the day's work done, the two new boats in their adjusted positions on the inside. The light going long and gold over the water the way it went in August and only in August, already tilting toward the ordinary dark.

She sorted the week's mooring fee receipts in order, the *Halcyon* and the *Eda L.* and the *Nancy Marie* and the *Ida May* in their new positions, everything accounted for. The harbor smell came through the bottom crack of the window — brine, diesel, the last of the processing shed's day.

She had the receipts sorted and the desk cleared by five-thirty.

She closed the ledger. She turned off the lamp. She went out, and the harbor was behind her, and the hill road was ahead, and the August evening was doing what August evenings did in Coldwater Reach — holding its light past the end of the work day, the sky going pale and clear in the west before it finally, gradually, let the dark come in.
