# What Is and Isn't Dangerous

The third period exercises were still on his desk when Hannah Pfeiffer knocked and came in before he had answered.

He had said it at the start of term, as he said it every year: the door open after four o'clock meant questions were permitted. It was not an invitation, merely a statement of availability; occasionally a student appeared. She was not here about Latin.

She did not sit in the third desk on the window side, where she had occupied the same position for three terms. She sat in the desk directly adjacent to his, pulled it slightly forward, and folded her hands on the desktop.

"I need to ask you something," she said.

"Then ask," he said.

---

She was prepared. He could see the structure of it — the way she moved through the categories she had decided on, nothing extraneous, nothing omitted. He had taught her for a year and a half; he knew how she thought when she was ready to think. She was not given to the kind of preparation that performs itself. When she had something to say, she said it.

Since approximately June, she told him, she had been having conversations with Karl Reinmar at the south fence section of the Pfeiffer property. Not every day. The work brought them to the same section two or three times each week, sometimes less, and on those occasions, when Private Reed was occupied with another part of the perimeter, they spoke. The conversations were brief — five minutes, sometimes ten, sometimes less.

What they talked about: the farm. The drainage of the south field, which backed up in wet years and required particular management. The question of what to put in after the corn stubble turned under — both of them favored winter rye, for reasons that had the same agricultural sense behind them and arrived from different directions. His English. In German, when German came up, he spoke a dialect she recognized from her father.

She had not given him anything outside the established program terms. No food beyond the regular mealtimes. No documents. Nothing of military use, in either direction.

She paused.

She said: she had not received anything.

The pause was less than a full breath, and he set his pencil down. He did not comment on it. He asked his first question.

---

"Has Private Reed filed any incident report with the Coastal Patrol that you're aware of? Or has any official — the patrol, the county, anyone — come to your family about the fence section specifically?"

"No," she said.

"Have you passed anything to Karl Reinmar, or received anything from him — food, documents, written communication, any object?"

She held his eyes for a moment. Then she reached into the pocket of her coat and set something on the desk between them.

It was a wooden bird, roughly three inches in length, carved from a single piece of softwood. The grain ran along the body; the tail had been shaped carefully, if not with any particular refinement. Pine, probably, or white cedar — the wood was light. It had been carried: the surface was smooth at the breast and at the base in the way of something handled many times over a period of months.

He picked it up. He turned it once, examining it with the attention he gave to any object he needed to assess correctly — weight, material, what it was and what it was not — and set it back.

"When," he said.

"He left it at the south fence post. In July."

He considered it for a moment longer. Then he pushed it back across the desk toward her.

"That is not contraband," he said.

---

She picked it up without looking at it.

He thought about how to give her the accurate account — not simplified, not reshaped for reassurance, but actually accurate, so that she would know precisely where she stood. He had found, over the past two years, that she received precision better than most people did. She had not come here for comfort.

"The regulations governing prisoner of war labor placements derive from two sources," he said. "The terms of the Geneva Convention, which govern the custody and treatment of prisoners under international law, and the domestic regulations under the Emergency Farm Labor program, which govern the specifics of farm placements and what is required of civilian host communities. The categories of prohibited civilian conduct that carry legal weight are four."

He set them out.

"Assisting an escape attempt — providing any assistance to a prisoner attempting to leave the custody of his escort. Passing military intelligence, or any information that could assist enemy military operations. Providing weapons, tools, or any material with military application." He paused. "The fourth category, which the domestic regulations treat with particular severity, is romantic or sexual relations between civilian women and prisoners of war. That category exists, it is enforced, and the consequences for both parties are not small. I mention it specifically because it is treated differently from the others, and you should know that."

She had not moved.

"None of what you have described falls into any of these categories," he said. "What you have described is a technical violation of the escort arrangement's terms, which specify that civilian interaction with prisoners is supervised and limited to work-related instruction. That is a violation of the arrangement's spirit. It is not a violation of any statute, and it is not a Convention violation. The distinction is meaningful, and the Coastal Patrol knows that it is meaningful."

He had come to know these distinctions carefully. The internment frameworks governing enemy alien status and prisoner status had provisions that overlapped in some areas and diverged sharply in others; he had read the relevant sections when the farm placement program began, and he had read them with the specific attention of someone who had lived under a related but distinct set of provisions for two years, at the Sherbrooke facility and in the administrative proceedings that followed it. The distinctions were not academic to him. They had been practical.

"In practice," he continued, "every farm placement that has been operating for more than a season has some version of what you are describing. The Coastal Patrol is not unaware of this. They manage it by leaving the specific judgment to the escort."

"Lonzo," she said.

"Private Reed has been at your property since September of last year. He knows what happens at that fence section. If he has not reported these conversations, he has made a decision not to. That decision is within his authority." He looked at her. "I think his judgment is probably correct."

---

She was still holding the bird. Not looking at it — looking at the desk surface in front of her, at some middle distance — but she had it in her hand.

"Did I do something wrong," she said.

He had seen it from the moment she sat down, underneath the careful categories of her account.

He thought about it for a moment — not because he was uncertain of the answer but because the answer had two parts that needed to be kept distinct from each other, and collapsing them would not serve her.

"You did something human," he said. "Those are sometimes the same thing. In this case I do not think they are."

She looked at him.

He did not elaborate on this. He said: "But I would stop."

"Because of the risk," she said.

"Because of the risk. Not because the conversations were wrong — I want that distinction to hold. The war is moving toward its end. He will be repatriated when it does, probably within the next year. Between now and that point, neither of you benefits from becoming more visible than you already are." He paused. "What you have described suggests you have been largely invisible. Private Reed has exercised his judgment; your father knows and has not acted on it. I would not test either of those conditions further."

She absorbed this.

"He told me to be careful," she said. "Not to stop."

"I know." And because it was accurate: "I am saying the same thing. The difference between *be careful* and *stop* is the difference between a person who understands what is at stake and a person who does not. Your father understands."

---

She was quiet for a moment. The afternoon light through the east windows had moved to its low October angle, the shadows crossing the floor at length, the room holding its warmth against the cold beginning to come in at the sills. Outside, the school yard was empty.

"I think my father knows more about why I should be careful than he's told me," she said. She said it without emphasis, not quite looking at him, looking instead at the desk between them — the stack of exercises, the pencil lying across the top sheet.

He considered what he knew and what he was going to do with what he knew. He did this the way he did most things that required precision: without rushing to the conclusion before he had located it correctly.

"I think," he said, "that your father is a man who has made some decisions about what he knows and what he does not need to say." He paused. "Like most people."

She looked at him. The light was low and slanted and her face in it had the quality of someone reading something carefully, trying to determine what the text was actually saying. He held her eyes. He did not add anything.

He had said it about Albrecht Pfeiffer, who was, as far as Marcus could read the available evidence, a man carrying a particular knowledge across twenty years — knowledge of a specific kind, the kind that accumulated around certain decisions made in certain years in certain parts of Europe, and that did not dissolve when you crossed an ocean.

After a moment she looked away. She put the bird in her coat pocket. She lifted her bag from the floor and stood.

"Thank you," she said.

"You're welcome," he said.

He listened to her go.

---

The room was quiet after she left. The exercises were in front of him, the pencil on the stack. He sat for a moment without touching either.

He had not told her about Horak. He had not told her the inference that followed from a Franconian dialect and a Czech surname and the known patterns of the displacement networks operating in the North Atlantic corridor in 1942 and 1943. He had not told her about the probable route south from Halifax — the chain of small contacts, the handoffs, the way a person without papers moved through a country that was not permitting him to move. He had not told her that the most probable contact node in this part of Maine for someone coming through those networks was a German-American farm on Route 9, with Bavarian origins in the same Franconian geography where those networks had concentrated in the late 1930s, where a man might have known, twenty years before it mattered, who the reliable people were and how to find them. He had not told her what any of this meant about what her father might have been to Jan Václav Horak, or what Horak had been trying to reach in the hours before the breakwater.

She had not come to ask. She had come to ask whether she had done something wrong at the fence, and he had answered that question as precisely as he knew how.

He thought about the sentence: *a man who has made some decisions about what he knows and what he does not need to say.* He had said it about Albrecht Pfeiffer and he had meant it about Albrecht Pfeiffer. He had also meant it about himself — not as confession, just as fact. He had been making those decisions since Paris, since the particular autumn that had required them, and they had continued to be required. The letter in the right-hand drawer of his desk at the Crows' house was the most recent instance of this. There would be others, there were always others; you arrived somewhere, you assembled what you could, and you made decisions about what you were going to do with the assembling. *Like most people.*

He picked up his pencil. On the first exercise: *dum haec geruntur, Cicero ad senatum scrīpsit.* While these things were being done, Cicero wrote to the senate. The ablative absolute — the construction for two actions occurring simultaneously, neither one subordinate to the other. He had been teaching it for three years. It remained a good construction for what it described: the persistent simultaneity of things, the way the main clause and the absolute clause ran alongside each other without either one subsuming the other.

He marked the page. He worked through the rest of the stack until the light was gone, and then three more by the lamp, and when he was finished he put on his coat and closed the classroom and went down the stairs and out into the October dark, which was the dark of this specific street, this specific town, these three blocks between the school and the Crows' house where the kitchen window would be lit and Lillian would have left something on the stove. His to walk through. His to go home to, which was not the same as home and was also not nothing, and he had made a decision about that too, some time ago, though he had not yet named what the decision had been.

# The Harbor Log

The last of the seasonal boats were gone. The Nancy Marie had cleared for Spruce Head the final week of September; the Ida May had followed on the third of October, Kell running her out on the morning tide in a light northwest wind. The harbor was back to its winter numbers — twelve working moorings, the lobster fleet centered again, the summer berths empty and their cleats washed clean by the equinox blow. The sardine shed had closed its processing run the week prior. This was what October looked like, and it had looked this way for nine years under her management and for a good many years before that.

She was at the chart table by seven. Tide log open, the morning reading copied in at 0715. She set it aside and pulled the annual binder from the lower cabinet.

Log review. Every first full working week of October: twelve months of entries confirmed and closed, mooring registrations checked against the current register, incident notations followed to their official resolution, fuel allocation log balanced against the Portland figures. The accountancy of a year's harbor work — not audit, exactly, more the verification that the record said what had actually happened, entry by entry, so that when the district office asked she could answer for any month. She had done it every October for nine years. The previous harbormaster had done it before her, and she had learned the practice from his version of it and kept the structure without revision.

This year's review covered October 1943 through the present.

She had known, since January, what month it would eventually reach.

She opened to January and started.

---

January: equipment inventory, logged on the third. Chain counts, grapple hooks, the spare bollard hardware ordered in November and received on the 29th. Maintenance checks done. No incidents. She had done the January counts the same morning she found Owen's 1934 ledger in the back of the lower cabinet while tallying the chain. The old ledger was not part of the annual review; she had set it aside. She had come back to it later in the morning. The January log entry was complete.

February: a Coast Guard district letter on the ninth, standard quarterly operations acknowledgment, no action required. Nothing further on the October matter. She had not expected anything. Routine harbor operations. No incidents.

March: the spring opening. The Bethia on the fourth, Henry Cates bringing her down from the Camden haul-out on the morning tide. Mooring assigned to dock seven, as it had been for as long as Eira had been keeping this log and for some years before. Fleet registrations coming in. She checked each against the register. All current.

April: the main registration push. Six boats in, three renewals, two new mooring assignments from boats relocating out of Jonesport. She had processed the paperwork in a single afternoon at the chart table. The Portland fuel allocation confirmed on the 18th. All matched.

May: maintenance week. A corroded ring bolt on dock four's approach fitting, which she had replaced on the 14th with Declan Walsh's help. Materials and hours logged. No incidents. She checked the entry against the maintenance log. It matched.

June sixth: the D-Day notation. She had logged the radio call at 0302 — *Allied landings, Normandy coast; per radio, WLBZ 0300. Harbor routine* — and below it, same date, the dock-three cleat replacement she had done that morning in the window between the call and the fleet departure at 0530. She had also noted Eisenhower's address on WLBZ at 1820 — not harbor business, but she had put it in as context, as she had been in the habit of noting major radio events when the harbor was immediately involved. Fleet out on schedule. No incidents.

She held the June entry for a moment.

Then she turned the page.

July: the Nancy Marie arrived on the twelfth, temporary berth at dock eight, mooring fee paid in advance. The Ida May arrived the nineteenth at dock nine, Kell's double-ended hull needing the longer slip. Both registrations current. Sardine processing shed at capacity through July; harbor boat count and fuel draw elevated accordingly. She confirmed the allocation against the Portland records. They matched.

August: fuel margin held at three hundred gallons above forecast, confirmed on the 15th when the Portland figures came in. Ruth Fuller's dragger registered at dock six with Ruth as sole operator — she had updated the entry in July, Ruth having been running the boat herself on fuel-allocation days since the spring. Three mooring adjustments in August for the high-summer sandbar drift on the north channel approach. All corrected and logged.

September: no incidents. The sardine shed winding toward close. The Nancy Marie's departure logged September 29th, cleared for Spruce Head as anticipated. The Ida May logged October 3rd, Kell out on the morning tide.

She confirmed the departure entries against the register. They matched.

October 1944: current entries. Two and a half weeks of routine operations, tide readings, mooring notations, the weekly fuel draws. An approach-marker adjustment at dock seven on the 9th when Henry Cates came in on the strong northwest chop with the Bethia riding heavy. She had moved the marker eighteen inches north and logged it. The entry was current.

She confirmed the present entries against the register.

Everything matched.

She closed the front section of the binder.

She turned to October 1943.

---

The entries were present.

October 11th, 1943: barometric drop, storm advisory from the Coast Guard district office. Fleet pulled back from the outer moorings per standard protocol. She had confirmed the outer mooring lines herself on the afternoon of the 12th, walking the full dock in the blow. Entry complete.

October 14th, 1943: body found on the seaward face of the breakwater by Hector Brann, crew of the Alicia B., at approximately 0700. She had logged the notification at 0750, the Coast Guard arrival at 0820, the removal of the body from harbor jurisdiction at 0930. Unknown male individual, civilian appearance, no papers found on the person. Entry complete.

The entries following through the month: Lt. Parsons's visit on the 17th, her formal statement, the official ruling received in November. Accidental drowning, unknown individual, case closed to harbor records. Notation dated and signed. Entry complete.

She turned back one day.

October 13th, 1943.

Her entry for the thirteenth: *Mooring check completed, commercial dock, 2300. Fleet secure. No incidents. Tide reading 11.2 ft.*

She read it twice.

The entry was accurate in what it contained. The mooring check had been completed. The fleet had been secure. The tide had read 11.2 feet at 2300 hours. Nothing on the dock that night had required notification to the Coast Guard, or action of any official kind she had been empowered to take.

She had not entered what she had seen at the far bollard.

---

Owen's J.T. entry: January 8th, 1934, with the later addition below the original notation in his handwriting, the slope different from the dated entries above it. *This not entered at time of incident; entering here as complete account.* Then the account. His initials at the bottom.

He had been in Portland when the incident with J.T. happened. His deputy had logged the surface facts. Owen had read the entry when he returned and had made it complete.

She had been thinking about this since January. He had deferred completeness and returned to it; there was a word for what he had done. She had written the tide reading and the mooring check and the words *no incidents* and turned off the lamp and gone home and done it again the next morning and the morning after that, for twelve months.

He had come back to it.

She set her pencil down on the chart table.

---

At 2300 hours on October 13th, 1943, she had completed the mooring check and was walking back along the commercial dock toward the office. The storm had been clearing for the previous two hours, the harbor settling, the boats riding more easily at their lines as the blow moved northeast. She had made the outward pass down the full length of the commercial dock checking each bollard and cleat, and on the return she had seen the man at the far end.

Civilian coat, not oilskins or harbor work wear. Standing at the far bollard with his weight shifted forward, not at his sides in the way of someone working a line. The posture of a person waiting at a specific location rather than passing through. She had not recognized him. Not a registered vessel operator, not a face from the fleet or the dock work or anywhere she could place him.

He had been facing the water when she went past. He had not turned.

She had caught the second figure at the edge of the dock light — a shape in motion, already turning away, already in the first steps of departure. She had heard something: two or three words, spoken low, an exchange between the two of them. Not English. A sound she could not place at the time, consonants she had no frame for. The second figure walked inland before she reached the far bollard end. An ordinary pace, not running.

She had stood at the bollard end for a moment, long enough to see that the first man was still there, that his coat was wet at the shoulders and that he had not turned toward her. She had looked at him for the length of three or four seconds.

She had not approached. She had not called out. She had turned and gone back to the office and logged what the log said now: mooring check complete, fleet secure, no incidents, tide 11.2 feet.

When she turned off the lamp she had told herself there was nothing to enter: a man on a public dock after hours, a second person who had already departed, a few words in a language she did not recognize. No law broken that fell within harbor jurisdiction.

She had known, as she locked the office door behind her, that the log was not complete.

---

She knew things now that she had not known that October night.

Jan Václav Horak: Czech national, displaced person, last known address Halifax, Nova Scotia, 1942. Thirty-eight years old or thereabouts. No papers. The Coast Guard district office had sent her the name in a form letter five months after they closed the case, in April 1944. She had read it twice, noted it in her own log margin, and filed the letter.

She knew the language. In the spring she had gone to Marcus Klein — she had brought him what she could reconstruct of the sounds, the consonants she had been carrying for seven months — and he had given her the answer with the careful precision he gave to answers: Czech. Not German. Czech.

A Czech displaced person, last known Halifax, moving south along the coast through the channels that a man without papers moved through in 1943. Making for Coldwater Reach, for whatever he had been making for here. The second figure at the dock had walked inland. She had not identified that person. She had assembled what she could, from what she had seen and what Marcus Klein had been willing to tell her, and it stopped there.

None of this fell within harbor jurisdiction. None of it changed the official ruling.

What it had changed, slowly, across twelve months: the weight of the blank in the October 13th entry. She had known the blank was different from an ordinary omission since the morning Hector Brann found the body. She had carried that knowledge through the official inquiry, through the case closing, through the winter, through reading Owen's J.T. entry in January, through the spring and summer and this October. She had watched the blank and she had known what it was.

She picked up the pen.

---

She wrote below the original entry, in the space remaining on the dated page. The late notation format was the same regardless of what it corrected; she had used it twice before in nine years, both times for routine administrative matters. She wrote steadily, in the same hand she used for all harbor log entries:

*Late entry, dated October 1944: 2300 hours, 13 October 1943: completed mooring check, commercial dock. One unidentified individual present at the far bollard, civilian appearance, not a known registered vessel operator. Observed in the company of a second party who departed walking inland before I could make identification. No approach made. Not entered at original time. Entering now in accordance with complete record.*

Below that:

*— E. Bowman, Harbormaster, October 1944.*

She set the pen down.

---

She read it.

The entry said what had happened. An unidentified individual at the far bollard. A second party, direction inland, departed before identification. No approach made. Not entered at original time.

It did not say that she had known the next morning, looking at the body in the gray light on the breakwater face, that the man at the bollard and the body were the same. It did not say that she had spent twelve months aware that the Coast Guard's official record rested on the incomplete version. The entry said what she had seen, at the distance and in the light she had seen it, on the night of October 13th, 1943.

The entry did not name Horak. She had not known the man's name on October 13th, 1943. The entry was the night's evidence, and the night's evidence was an unidentified individual. She had not identified him then and could not identify him in this entry now.

The second party was also unidentified. She had not been able to identify them that night and had not been able to identify them since.

She read it a second time.

The record was complete.

---

She closed the binder. The stove was ticking on its steady burn, the morning cold fully pushed back from the desk. Outside the office window the harbor was at its October work: the lobster smacks at their moorings, the northwest chop making the small easy motion the boats were rigged for at this time of year, the channel mouth open and grey under the overcast. The Bethia in dock seven. Ruth Fuller's dragger in dock six, tied up for the morning. The two empty berths where the Nancy Marie and the Ida May had been.

She sat at the chart table for a few minutes with her hands flat on the closed binder.

The entry she had written was in a log that the Coast Guard district office read only in the event of an inquiry. There would be no inquiry.

What the entry changed was not any of this. What it changed was the record. By her hand, in her handwriting, in the log she had kept for nine years. This log, not Owen's — hers. The record now said what had been on the dock on October 13th, 1943. An unidentified individual and a second party and no approach made and not entered at the time.

Whatever she had assembled or suspected or held without saying in the months between then and now — that was not the log's business. The log's business was what she had seen.

---

She opened the current log.

She wrote the noon tide reading. Eleven feet, four inches. Clear. Wind north-northwest, seven to ten. Fleet at moorings.

She closed the log.

She took her coat from the hook by the door and went down the dock to walk the breakwater.

The October tides exposed the lower granite courses on the seaward face; she checked them as she went, working from the shore end out. The seam between the first and second course on the north face had been taking some water since spring; she crouched and ran a hand along the joint. Dry today. The iron pin on the third section was holding, which she had been watching since August. She went all the way out to the end, which was the habit, and stood at the seaward edge looking back at the harbor.

The office at the foot of the wharf. The cedar shingles. The fleet at the inside moorings. The empty summer berths. The harbor at its winter numbers, which were its honest numbers, what it was when the seasonal work cleared off and left the actual work.

She stood there for a moment. Not long.

Then she turned and walked back. There were mooring receipts to sort. There was the fuel report from the Portland office she had not yet opened, which would need to be answered by Thursday. The review was done.

She went inside and latched the door.

# November Weather

The animals were inside by the first week of November, a week earlier than usual, which meant more silage than Hannah had planned for and a barn that never quite emptied of its warmth once the doors were closed. Her father had brought them in on the night the temperature dropped without warning—the 31st of October, the fourth cow already stiff-legged when he found her at supper—and after that it was clear the season was done. The fields the prisoners had spent October picking over for the last of the corn and the last of the squash were bare now under the sky, which had gone the flat white of early winter. The first real snow came the second week of November and stayed.

She did the morning milking at five and the evening milking at six and the late check at nine, which she had taken on in October and not set down. Three times a day into the barn, and between those: the school run, the Latin exercises at the kitchen table, the cooking on the evenings her mother did not come to make it herself.

The prisoners were doing maintenance. The four of them patched the north-facing boards of the barn wall in the mornings, working in pairs with oakum and pitch from the supply shed, their breath making small clouds in the cold air. By afternoon they were in the side yard splitting firewood, and she could hear it from inside the barn: the swing of the maul, the pause, the sound of wood giving. Lonzo sat at his stool near the yard gate with his rifle across his knees and his newspaper, his coat buttoned to the top.

Her father cut the work hours shorter as November went on. By the second week Lonzo was walking the four men into the icehouse by three in the afternoon, and the yard went quiet. The firewood stack grew against the south wall of the icehouse, and the barn wall held its new pitch, and the farm contracted the way it did every year: the fields empty, the animals inside, everything that had been spread out through the working season pulled back into a smaller perimeter.

---

Several evenings, when the late check took her to the barn's far end and she came back up the aisle toward the door, she stopped.

From the barn door she could see the icehouse window.

Karl's lamp was on most nights by that hour—a low warm square in the dark, steady. She could not see him clearly at this distance and did not try; she could see the light and the shadow of the table, and sometimes, if the lamp's angle was right, the small movement of a page turning. She had started noticing this in the first week of November. She had not gone closer.

She had not spoken to him since the first week of October.

The decision had been easy enough to make in Mr. Klein's classroom, with the four categories laid out and repatriation as the word that made the timeframe comprehensible. She had walked home from school that afternoon with it settled, and it had not wavered. Not going to the south fence felt, each time the work took her near it, like something she was doing rather than not doing. She was making a choice in October and she was still making it in November, every time the late check brought her to the barn door and the icehouse window was lit.

He looked different in November than he had in June. Not physically—not thinner or marked by the work in any way she could name. In June he had held himself with a particular watchfulness, the readiness of a person who does not yet know what a place will ask of him. She had seen it in the way he stood at the fence, the careful attention he brought to everything, the alertness of someone who had not yet learned where the fence lines were. By November that was gone. He knew the farm. He knew what it asked. He was reading the newspaper in the icehouse by lamplight with his head bent to the page, and his hands, when the angle of the lamp showed them, were still.

She knew what he was reading. The front page of the Bangor Daily had been running the word counterattack since the middle of December—the German advance in eastern Belgium, the Ardennes, the Allied lines pushed back. She could read the American reports; he could read them too, and could subtract from them what the American papers did not know how to say. What he did with that, when he bent his head to the comics page instead, she could not see from where she stood.

The cold came through the open doorway.

She went back to the Holsteins.

---

Her father turned the radio up in December.

He had been turning it down for two years, since the fall of 1942, when the news began going the direction it went. She had grown used to the low volume—the announcer's voice in the kitchen, available but not quite filling the space. In December he turned it up.

She was at the table doing her Latin exercises when the six o'clock broadcast began, and he turned the volume up before the announcer had finished the date. He sat in his chair—the straight-backed chair he had pulled to the radio in October of last year and kept there—and he did not speak.

The announcer was naming Belgian towns.

She heard them and held them inside her head for the geography book she would look at later, after her father went to the barn. The Ardennes, which the announcer said with a flat American vowel. The German counterattack—that was the phrase the radio used, the phrase the Bangor Daily used, the phrase her father listened to with his hands on his thighs and his face toward the speaker.

He held very still.

The lamp made his shadow long on the kitchen wall. He was not looking at her; he was not looking at anything in the room. She had watched him listen to these broadcasts across the fall, and she had thought at first that it was his way of paying attention, and later she had thought it was grief, and now she thought it was neither of those exactly. He was somewhere else. He was here and also in the country he had left, in the hills and the winter forest that the announcer was describing in flat American syllables. She had not understood this before the last year—not what it meant, not why the radio made the kitchen a room he was only partly in.

The broadcast ended. He turned the volume down. He stood, took his coat, and went out for the last barn check. She put the geography book away without consulting it.

---

Magda's spell came the second week of November.

Four days. The bedroom door closed when Hannah came to the kitchen at five-thirty; breakfast carried to the hall table and left, the coffee half-drunk, the bread gone. Her father went through his work without comment—the barn, the morning feeding, the maintenance work alongside the prisoners—as if this were the farm's normal pattern, which in one sense it was. He had been carrying these days for as long as Hannah could remember. She had seen him do it before the war, when she was twelve and fourteen. He did not speak about it. She had learned not to ask.

She did the cooking. She kept the kitchen warm. She went to school and came home and started supper, and her father came in from the barn and they ate. Three days, four days. The farm ran on fewer conversations and did not stop.

On the fifth morning she came in from the six-thirty milking and her mother was at the stove.

The lamp was on. The smell of coffee already—Magda must have been up a while. She was standing at the stove in her dress and apron, hair down and unbrushed, making the coffee with the care she brought to it: the measuring, the cold tap water, each step in the order it went.

She said: "Es ist heute kalt."

Hannah took off her coat and hung it on the hook. She sat down at the kitchen table.

"Ja, Mutter," she said.

That was all. The most ordinary sentence in the world—not apology, not announcement, not I'm back, just the temperature, the simple fact of November. It was cold today. Magda turned to get the cups, and Hannah set the table, and the kitchen moved through the ordinary morning.

She had stopped expecting this to be the last time. Not this winter—some time before this winter, without being able to say exactly when. She had also stopped believing the returns were fragile, had stopped watching her mother with that particular care as if looking directly at her would send her back. Whatever Magda moved between—whatever the distance was that she traveled when the door stayed closed—it was older than the war and would not end with it. What she could do was be in the kitchen when her mother came back to it.

The coffee came. They sat. Magda drank hers without speaking again and then moved to the icebox for breakfast, and Hannah set out the bread and the plates, and the morning went.

---

On a Tuesday morning in early December she was cutting across the south yard from the barn, going back to the kitchen for the seven o'clock breakfast, and she saw it on the outside sill of the icehouse window: a Bangor Daily, folded open, its corners wind-curled from being outside.

Not inside the window. On the outside ledge, where the cold had been at it overnight.

She stopped when she saw the fold. Even from where she stood she could read the page it was open to: not the front page, not the war news. The comics—the small square panels with their outlined figures and their speech bubbles, the idiom gathered in short lines that sounded nothing like the articles. She knew whose paper this was.

She picked it up. The date in the corner put it two Tuesdays back, not this week's edition. The paper was slightly swollen from the cold, the fold stiffened. She turned it over: the other side was the crossword, worked through in pencil—English words in German-shaped handwriting, the across clues and some of the downs.

She carried it inside and set it on the kitchen table.

She did not mention it. Her father came in at seven-thirty and she had coffee and bread ready, and the newspaper sat where she had put it. Later, when she came home from school, it had been moved to the side of the table where he kept his papers. She did not ask him about it.

---

The nine o'clock check, the last round of the night.

She went stall by stall with the lamp, checking the water and the feed, watching how the animals stood. Number four was eating steadily—good; she had been watching the fourth cow since October. Number twelve was against the back rail, and Hannah stopped and put her hand on the cow's neck until the animal shifted and settled. The barn was the warmest place on the farm at this hour, the twenty-two Holsteins in their stalls generating a warmth that had nothing to do with the stove.

She came back up the aisle and stopped at the barn door.

The icehouse window was lit.

She stood there—the cold on her face from the open doorway and her own lamp in her hand and her breath making small clouds—and looked at the amber square in the dark. No movement she could see, just the steady lamp and the dark around it and the snow between here and there, unmarked except for the boot-print path going to and from the icehouse door.

Behind her the Holsteins shifted in their stalls, the slow sounds of animals settling.

She stood until the cold had come through her coat.

Then she pulled the barn door closed and went back to the house.

# The Names on the Board

Henry was at the table when Marcus came downstairs, the coffee already made and the bread on its board. He set his cup down when Marcus came in.

"Two men from Coldwater," he said. "In the German counteroffensive. I heard it this morning — a parent came to the building before seven." He paused. "The other name is Calvin Wilkes."

Marcus stood at the stove and poured his coffee. He did not say anything yet.

"He was in your Latin class," Henry said. "First year you were here."

"Yes," Marcus said. "I remember him."

He sat down. The kitchen was the same as it was every morning: the lamp over the table, the stove working, the window on the south side fogged where the warmth inside met the cold outside. Henry's cup made a small sound against the wood when he set it down. Neither of them spoke.

The boy's face came without effort. Calvin Wilkes — not a strong student in the grammatical sense, which was to say that his ablative constructions had been uncertain throughout the fall of 1942 and had never quite settled in the spring. But he had had a real facility for the rhythm of the sentences, which was not something Marcus could teach and not something he had expected from a student whose case endings required the kind of repeated correction that tended, in his experience, to indicate that the language was simply not going to come. Most students learned the structure and kept it at a distance, handling it as a formal object rather than working through it from the inside. Calvin had been different. He could recite the Virgil passages with a quality of feeling that Marcus had noticed and not remarked upon — remarking tended to kill it. He had kept marking the ablative errors down all year and had kept hoping the recitation would eventually close the gap.

It had not.

"The other man," Henry said. "Ned Harker's boy. He was on Galen Fuller's dragger before he enlisted. His mother's on Mast Street."

"I do not think I knew him," Marcus said.

Henry stood and took his cup to the stove.

---

The servicemen's board was in the hallway to the right of the main entrance — a framed corkboard, the white cards in rows going back to the spring of 1942. Marcus had walked past it every school day for two years and ten months. He could account for the position of each name.

Calvin Wilkes's card was in the third row. It had gone up in June of 1943, when he enlisted at seventeen. It had been a white card like the others since June of 1943.

It was not white like the others now. There was a black border around it — a thin frame, not theatrical, the standard thing that Bertrand Hatch placed on the card when the telegram arrived. Marcus stopped in the hallway and looked at it.

Fall of 1942, spring of 1943. One complete school year: the ablative absolute in November, the passive periphrastic in February, the Virgil in April. Calvin Wilkes in the second row, right side, the seat he had claimed by the second week of September and held for the year. The way he had set his pen down when Marcus called for the recitation, which was not something most of them did.

Marcus went to his classroom.

---

Third period was his third-year section — eleven students working through Caesar's *De Bello Gallico*, the standard text for the year and the text that came next in order. He wrote the construction on the board: *quo cum consilio convenerant*, explained the relative clause of purpose, and worked through the passage: translate, identify the case, identify the construction, explain the choice.

The passage was not the wrong text only because it was about war. Caesar's *De Bello Gallico* was always about war; that was its nature and its curriculum reason for being there. It was the wrong text because it was about a Roman army moving through a country with the calm procedural vocabulary of completed action — a vocabulary that assumed the events were finished and could now be held at the distance from which patterns became legible. He had taught it for two years in this school and had never entirely resolved what it meant to do so: students with brothers in the Pacific, fathers at the six o'clock radio. He had decided, sometime in the spring of 1943, that the resolution was not his to make. What he could offer was the grammar, and the attention, and the occasional passage that a student might hold for reasons Marcus would not always know.

He did not mention the Ardennes. He did not mention Calvin Wilkes. He taught the lesson, assigned the written exercise for the following morning, and dismissed the class at the bell.

After the last period — the first-year fundamentals section, which was where Calvin Wilkes had been in the fall of 1942, the same room, the same window light in the same mid-afternoon position — he stayed. He had papers to grade and he graded them. The school emptied around him, the hallway voices going, the main door at the far end of the corridor closing and closing again, and then the building going quiet in the way it went quiet at the end of a school day in winter, with the furnace working inside the silence and nothing else.

He graded the papers. He did not hurry.

Calvin Wilkes had sat in the third seat from the window. He had written his exercises in a slightly cramped hand that had improved through the year. By April he had been writing the ablatives correctly most of the time.

By April he had also been able to recite the opening lines of Book Two of the *Aeneid* with a quality of feeling Marcus had not anticipated — in part because Calvin Wilkes was not, technically, supposed to have encountered the passage at all; Marcus had used it as an example of a syntactic construction in February, and Calvin had held it. *Conticuere omnes, intentique ora tenebant.* All fell silent and held their faces intent. The sentence that opens Aeneas's own account of the fall of Troy. Calvin had not known what it was the opening of; they had not gotten there. But something in his reading of it had been right, in the way that some students arrived at a language before they could explain how, and Marcus had marked the ablative down and said nothing about the rest.

He finished the papers. He put on his coat and hat and went out.

---

The walk home was three blocks. He had made it in every weather since March of 1942 and knew it the way he had come to know a small number of things in this town — the exact position of the January ice on the school's side-yard steps, the way the harbor road received the wind off the inlet, the particular sound the Elm Street corner made at night when the cold had been extended for some days. He had not intended to know it so well. He had not intended most of what came from having been in one place for nearly three years, which was longer than he had been anywhere since Vienna.

January in Coldwater Reach was a particular kind of dark — the sun not fully up until after eight, gone before five, the sky between those hours a flat pewter that gave no warmth but gave light enough to work by, which was all the light a working town required.

He had his brother in Vienna, from whom he had had no word since the autumn of 1940. That was more than four years of silence, which had become its own kind of knowledge: not the absence of information but a form of information, indicating that the channels through which word might have come had closed, or that his brother had reasons of his own for not reaching them, or both. He had worked through it from many angles in the early years and had eventually stopped working through it from angles and simply carried it.

He had his colleague from Paris — Kessler, a classicist who had been at the Sorbonne since 1933 and whom Marcus had known for three years of occasional conversation before leaving Paris in 1938. In September of 1942 a second-hand source with the Emergency Committee in Cambridge had sent word that Kessler had been arrested in August. He had received nothing since.

He had the men from Sherbrooke: a handful he had remained in contact with for the first year after his own release, and had then stopped, not because they had ceased to matter but because the contact had become indistinguishable from the carrying, and he had enough to carry.

He had Horak — the dead man who had come to rest on a Coldwater Reach breakwater in October of 1943, whose name and probable history Marcus had assembled and placed in the drawer where he kept the things he held without further examination.

And now he had Calvin Wilkes, who had been alive eight months ago in this town and who was dead now in eastern Belgium in what the radio called a counteroffensive. He had known this boy. He had graded his papers. He had taught him for a year in the classroom at the end of this three-block walk, and Calvin Wilkes was dead in Belgium, and Marcus was walking home in the January dark past the same houses he passed every evening.

This was not the same as the other losses.

He was not certain the distinction held.

He turned the corner onto Elm Street. The Crow house with its kitchen light on — the lamp over the table visible through the window, the yellow square of it in the dark. He had been looking for it when he turned the corner for longer than he had recognized. He had become aware of the looking at some point in the fall and had not done anything about the awareness.

---

Henry was there when Marcus came in, and Lillian was at the stove. She had made soup — the bean soup she made through the winter months, with bread and what remained of the week's butter. They sat down and ate. Henry had the fuller account from Beal's: the two names confirmed, the approximate circumstances, the Battle of the Bulge establishing itself now as the phrase replacing German counteroffensive in the way that phrases settled as an event accumulated its name. Lillian had heard some of it from the church women's group. They covered it between them and then moved on, the way the kitchen moved on: the woodpile question, the Congregational women's event Saturday, whether the coffee at Beal's had improved or whether the November blend was now simply what coffee was going to be.

The kitchen was warm. The stove had been going since afternoon.

After supper Lillian went to her sister's on Birch Street, as she did most Wednesdays. Henry cleared the table and began the dishes. Marcus sat.

"Did you know the Harker boy?" Henry said. He was at the sink, back to the table, running the water.

"Not from the school," Marcus said. "He would have finished before I arrived, or nearly."

Henry washed a bowl and set it in the rack. "He was good with boats. That's what Fuller always said." He paused. "Ned's going to take it hard."

Marcus said: "You knew Calvin Wilkes."

"Since he started at the school. He was a talker in the halls — always had something to say about something. I used to let him keep going while I was doing the floors in the morning." Henry set another bowl in the rack. "That's what you remember. Not the quiet ones."

"He could recite Virgil," Marcus said.

Henry turned slightly from the sink. "Is that something they do in the first year?"

"I used passages as examples — syntactic constructions. He held one. More than most students do." Marcus paused. "He could not explain the grammar behind it. He could do the thing itself."

Henry turned back to the sink.

After a moment Marcus said: "I find I think about my students long after."

"I suppose that's what teaching is," Henry said.

He finished the dishes and dried his hands and put the plates away, the bowls, the cups, each thing where it went. Then he sat down across from Marcus with what remained in his cup.

---

Outside, the cold was at the clapboard — the small sounds a house makes in January when the temperature drops after dark, the contraction of the sills, the occasional shudder in the window glass when the wind came at it. The lamp over the table. Henry with his cup and his own particular quiet; he had his losses too, twenty years' worth of them in this town, and Marcus knew some of them and not others, and they did not, as a practice, place their losses alongside each other's.

Marcus had his hands on the table and nothing in them.

He was thinking about the board in the hallway — not Calvin Wilkes's card specifically but the whole of it: the rows of white cards going back to 1942, the names he had walked past every school day for two years and ten months. He knew those names. He knew which ones had come from the fishing families and which from the inland farms, which had brothers still here, which had been in his classroom and which had not. He had been here long enough to know them.

Nearly three years. The arithmetic of his displacements had recently stopped adding up in the way it once had: Vienna, Paris, London, Sherbrooke, Cambridge, and now here for nearly three years — longer than Paris and London and Cambridge combined. He had arrived in March of 1942 with his document file and his tea and his understanding that this was provisional, and the provisional had extended long enough that he was no longer certain what it was provisionally in the way of.

He could not say exactly when the arithmetic had changed.

He had this kitchen. He had this table, this man across it with his cup, the lamp over them both making the window a dark mirror. He had a classroom at the end of a three-block walk and a board in the hallway with names he had come to know. One of those names had a black border around it now, and he had graded that boy's papers for a year, and the boy was dead in Belgium, and Marcus was sitting at this table in January of 1945 and he had not moved.

He could not yet say what this was.

He was sitting in it.

# What He Left

The mud came up through March the way it always did — not melting exactly but surrendering, the frozen ground releasing one layer at a time, first along the south wall of the barn where the sun hit it earliest, then the path between the house and the milk house, then by the second week the full yard. The Holsteins came in from the morning pasture with it halfway up their legs. Hannah scraped the stalls twice a day now and still the mud came back. It was the season's particular tax.

Her father told her at supper. In German; it was still German at the supper table.

"Lonzo came by this afternoon," he said. He set his bread down and looked at his hands for a moment. "The men are being sent back to the camp. Thursday."

"All four of them?"

"All four." He picked up his bread again. "From Houlton they will go back eventually. To Germany, when the arrangements are made. It takes time, with the war not finished."

She ate the rest of her soup. She heard something in how he said *all four* — a flatness that was not nothing. But she did not ask about it.

After supper she went out to do the late check — water lines, the heat lamp over the new calf, a walk through the stalls with the lantern. The icehouse window was lit at the far edge of the yard. She stopped in the barn doorway and stood looking at it the way she had stood looking at it all winter, from November to now — watching the low amber square of it, the shape of Karl reading at his small table by lamplight.

Four days.

She went inside.

---

She spent those four days in the rhythm of the farm. The 5 a.m. milking, school, the afternoon chores, the 6 p.m. milking, the late check. The prisoners were on their winter schedule: Brunner and Krebs on the wood lot, Fischer running repairs on the east fence, Karl working the strip below the lower field where the dead growth from winter had come down. She could see them from the kitchen window in the mornings and from the barn doorway in the evenings. She kept her distance the way she had been keeping it since October, the choice made once and then remade every day, which was how she knew it was a choice.

She told herself she would not go to the south fence. On the second day she didn't. On the third day she went out with the post bar and the tamping rod, because the south fence needed work — the same corner post on the south section that had heaved in November of 1943 had shifted again over the winter, and she had been putting off the repair since February when the ground was still frozen. The frost heave was real. She had not invented it.

She carried the tools around the barn and set her footing in the mud.

---

He was working the strip between the fence and the lower wood lot, clearing the winter deadfall. When she first came around the corner of the barn, he had his back to her.

She put the bar in and worked the post. Drive, pull, reset — the mud closing back in around the bar each time she pulled out, the cold still in the ground below the first thawed layer. She was thinking about the heel of the post and whether she needed gravel beneath it when she heard him stop.

She looked up. He was at the fence on his side, his hands in his coat pockets, looking at her.

She straightened.

She said: "Guten Morgen."

He said: "Good morning."

She put the bar down.

She had not been this close to him since October. He looked the same and did not look the same — the sun-chapped skin still there, the gray-blue eyes, but something in his bearing that was different. The first year's watchfulness was gone; so was the second year's settled tiredness. He looked like a man who had been somewhere long enough to know it and was now preparing to leave.

She reached into her coat pocket and took out the carved bird. Three inches of birch, the wings folded against the body, the head angled slightly down. The corrected ridge on the breast where the blade had slipped. She had been carrying it for more than a year.

She held it out over the fence toward him.

"You should take this back," she said. In English, because that was what felt right.

He looked at the bird. He looked at her hand. He said: "No."

Just that word.

She kept her hand out a moment longer, then let it drop. She did not put the bird away.

"Will you have somewhere to go," she said. "When you get back. After the war."

He thought about this. She could see him working through it — not making a show of it but actually moving through it, word to word, the way he had all last summer at the fence.

"Back is not a place," he said. He placed each word carefully. "Not anymore."

The fence between them. Three feet of air, the top wire, the mud on both sides the same mud. Behind him the lower wood lot, spruce going dark where the sun had not yet reached. Behind her the barn.

"What will you do," she said.

"I don't know." He shifted his weight slightly. "Start." A pause. "The same thing as everyone."

She looked at the bird in her hand. She turned it once. The grain of the birch, the corrected ridge on the breast, the tail cut to a clean notch.

She had been carrying it for more than a year. In October when staying at a distance was its own kind of heaviness. In December when she stood in the barn doorway watching his lamp. This morning when she loaded the tools and came around the corner.

"I don't know what to do with this," she said.

"Keep it."

She put the bird back in her coat pocket.

Then she became aware of her father at the barn door. He had the pitchfork at his side — he had come out of something in the middle of it, or he had taken up the pitchfork to have something to hold. He was not coming toward them. He was watching. He had warned her to be careful, not stop; he had made his judgment about what was happening at this fence, and the judgment was held in whatever place he kept such things, and he was watching the end of it now without a word.

She had been at the fence perhaps five minutes.

"Good luck," she said.

Karl nodded once. He put his hands back in his coat pockets and turned back to his work.

She picked up the post bar and the tamping rod and walked back across the yard. Her father said nothing when she passed him at the barn door. She went inside and finished what needed to be done.

---

Thursday came in with rain, the fine kind that was mostly mist.

She woke at five and did the morning milking and came back to the house for breakfast. Her father was at the table with his coffee made. Magda was at the stove. Nobody said anything about the truck.

It came at eight. She was in the kitchen and she did not go out.

She watched from the window over the sink.

The four of them came out of the icehouse in order: Brunner first, then Krebs, then Fischer. Karl last. Each carried what he had. Brunner had a bag over his shoulder; the others had bundles or coat pockets that were full. Karl's hands were empty.

The Coastal Patrol truck had a canvas back. The driver stayed in the cab. Lonzo was at the tailgate with the Springfield over his shoulder.

Brunner climbed in first, then Krebs, then Fischer. Lonzo said something to the driver. Karl stood in the mud of the yard for a moment.

He did not look at the house.

He looked at the barn — the long, even look of a man registering what he is leaving. Then he put one foot on the tailgate and climbed up.

Lonzo folded his carrying sling around the Springfield and put it behind the seat in the truck cab. Seventeen months on this farm with that rifle, and now he was putting it away. He turned to where Albrecht had come out of the barn and was standing at the yard's edge.

They had been on this farm together for seventeen months. In that time they had exchanged the morning's schedule and whether the ground was passable and whether the rain was likely to hold, and nothing that needed more than that. Lonzo nodded to him. Albrecht nodded back. Neither said anything.

The truck turned out of the yard and went down Route 9.

She watched it until it passed the willow at the bend and was gone. The willow's branches had gone yellow at the tips, the early yellow that came before the leaves.

---

Her father padlocked the icehouse door himself, not long after. She watched through the window: he crossed the yard without hurrying, fitted the shackle through the hasp, pressed it closed. He stood with his hand on the lock for a moment, not doing anything with it. Then he went back to the barn.

She did the morning work. There was always work to do in a dairy barn in late March — the stalls, the milk lines, the new calf that needed checking twice before noon. The farm had its own schedule and did not care what else had happened in the yard.

Around midday her father came in from the barn, knocked the mud from his boots at the door, and hung his coat. Magda had made the white bean soup — Monday's soup, and this was a Thursday, but the soup was there regardless, on the stove where it always was. The bread was on its board. The lamp was on over the table.

Hannah came in and hung her coat on the hook by the door. She could feel the weight of the bird in the pocket — three inches of birch, lighter than she always expected when she closed her hand around it.

She sat down. Magda set a bowl in front of her and went back to the stove.

Outside, Route 9 ran east toward town and west toward the rest of Maine, and the truck was somewhere on it now, or had long since turned north toward Houlton. The icehouse sat at the edge of the yard with its door locked. Through the window the willow at the bend was yellow-tipped, the tips a little more yellow than they had been in the morning.

The bird was in her coat pocket and she would feel it there in the morning when she went out, and it would still be hers.

Her father reached for his bread.

Magda sat.

The farm went on.

# The Spring Opening

April, and the harbor moving.

The ice had been out of the main channel since the third week of March — long gray pans of it riding the ebb tide south past the breakwater mouth, dissolving in the chop before they reached open water. She had watched from the office window without going out. There was nothing useful to do about ice going out; it went when it went, same as it always had.

The first week of April she had walked all the mooring lines. Three on the east row had ice-chafe bad enough to need ricing; she found one on the main float that had chafed through to the splice entirely, which meant it had been weakening since before the freeze and she had missed it in the fall inspection. She replaced the whole length. She had riced the east row lines herself, kneeling on the dock planking in the early cold with the caulking iron, and entered both repairs in the mooring log. Standard notation. The usual spring assessment of what winter had taken.

Now it was the standard spring inventory, and she worked through it the way she always did: depth soundings off the north pier at low tide, the mooring condition check, the fleet registration review. Ten years of spring openings, and the sequence was her own by now — not Owen's sequence handed down but the order she had settled on in her second year, when she understood what the harbor needed first. Depth soundings before slip assignments; mooring check before registration.

Depth soundings: two days running, the tide gauge and the weighted line, working along the north pier face from the bollard to the end. The year before's sounding log had two shallow readings at the channel's edge, same location both times, which meant winter silting from the January storm surge. She marked the position on the sounding chart and flagged it for the summer dredge schedule; the channel was still inside clearance for the second float's boats, but narrowly. She would watch it through the month.

Fleet registration review: nine boats on the main float, three on the east pier, one at the commercial wharf. She pulled the registration files and went through them against the winter registry.

The fleet was smaller than it had been in 1940. She had taken twenty-three boats through the spring opening of that year; this spring it was thirteen. The difference was in the ledger if you wanted to count it — boats sold, men gone, the war and the fuel allocation together. She did not count it this morning. She went through the files against the registry and noted what had changed.

Two new registrations. The first was a lobster dragger that had come down from Owls Head when the operation there folded — the owner, a man named Severance, had done the Portland transfer and come to her for the slip assignment. She had assigned him the outside berth on the east pier, right for the dragger's draft, and entered him in the Coldwater fleet ledger: vessel name, tonnage, operator's certification, assigned slip. Standard form. The second was Danny Jessup's first boat, a twenty-two-foot trap boat he had worked two seasons to buy. The engine was sound; she had checked the documentation and the certifications and assigned him berth seven on the main float, the small-boat row. She entered both and noted the dates.

Two boats out since last fall.

Haskell's sloop, sold in November to a Rockland man. She had sent the release notice to Knox County in November and heard nothing since, which was how Knox County handled these things; the transfer was complete in the record.

Galen Fuller's dragger. Ruth Fuller had renamed it and reregistered it in her own name, coming in on a Monday morning in February with the completed forms and a check for the registration fee. She had sat across the chart table from Eira and signed where the form required. She said she was thinking about running the lobster route herself come May, if she could find a mate who knew the ground. Eira had said there were a few men who knew it; they had talked through who was available and what the pound was paying. Then Ruth Fuller had stood and shaken Eira's hand and gone out. Eira had entered the registration in the fleet ledger under the new name, Ruth Fuller as registered operator, and filed the original in the back cabinet. Fifteen minutes, start to finish. She had not stopped over it; the paperwork was the same paperwork.

She had processed Robert Cates's spring mooring renewal the day before. Berth 14 — his grandfather's berth and his father's berth before him, the third-generation berth that had sat empty for fourteen months. He had come home from France in February, thirty pounds lighter. She had heard this from his father in March, running into him outside the post office: the old man red-eyed and saying Robert was standing, that he was home. By April, Cates had been out in his boat three times — twice coming in with a decent haul, once with nothing. A normal spring. She wrote the mooring renewal in the ledger: berth 14, April 18, 1945, confirmed and paid.

By mid-morning she had the registration review done and the depth soundings entered. She checked the mooring assignments against the harbor chart. Everything in its place. She set the chart on the drying rack and went to make coffee.

---

At noon she walked to Beal's for flour and two kerosene wicks.

The radio was on. It was always on at Beal's now, had been since November — the Ardennes and then the push east and then the Rhine crossings, Manny Beal keeping WLBZ on the shelf behind the counter where he could reach the dial without putting down what he was doing. She had grown used to the sound of it coming through the store door as she came up the steps.

Today the voice was different. Not the tone; the tone was always measured. What the voice was saying.

Three men at the counter: Harris Vane, Elliot Pease, old Cullen from the lobster pound. Manny had his coffee cup set down and both hands on the counter's edge.

She went to the flour bin and measured what she needed.

Germany. Berlin. The German state radio and then the Allied command's confirmation: April 30th. She listened and tied off the flour bag.

At the counter she waited while Manny tallied her items. Harris Vane and Elliot Pease were talking, low — not the kind of talking that calculated what the news meant for the next push, the next month, the winter holding or breaking. This was the other kind. Old Cullen said nothing and looked at the counter.

Manny made change. She thanked him.

Six blocks to the office. The harbor was opening. The war in Europe was ending. She walked the six blocks in the April air, the breakwater visible at the channel's edge, the water flat and gray-green in the midday light.

---

In the afternoon she went to the breakwater.

Not for any reason the log would record. She went the way she went sometimes — down the wharf, left at the bollard, out along the granite face. Two hundred feet. The blocks cut and laid in the 1890s, rough-faced and gray where they were above the waterline, dark and algae-striped below it, the stripe marking the tidal range exactly: eleven feet, the same it had always been.

Harbor on one side. Open water on the other. The April chop, a foot and a half, the surface running gray-green where the channel went deep. She stood at the end.

She had been standing at this breakwater since 1935. October of that year she had worn Owen's work gloves because her own were still packed and the post was a month old; the gloves were too large for her hands and the tools were Owen's tools, and she had been learning what they were for by using them. She had stood here in January 1944 when the ice came in early and locked the east pier's second float, working through the dredge sequence and what would have to wait. She had stood here on the morning of June 7th, 1944, the harbor quiet before the boats came in, not yet knowing whether Robert Cates or Galen Fuller had been on a Normandy beach the morning before.

Nine winters. The breakwater kept no account of any of it. Granite and seawater and the tidal stripe.

She thought about Horak.

Jan Václav Horak — Czech, displaced, last known Halifax in October 1942. The name had come in a letter from the Coast Guard regional office in Portland in April 1944, six months after the body came in off the blow. It was in the cabinet with the 1944 binders. She had seen him on the commercial dock on the night of October 26th, 1943, moving south from the herring shed toward the lobster landing. She had heard the language, carried it seven months, and Marcus Klein had placed it for her: Czech, the consonant cluster, the first-syllable stress. She had written it all into the late entry in October 1944 — the standard format, her own hand, the record of what she had seen and had not logged at the time. The record was complete.

The second person on the dock. The one who had been there when she came around the corner of the lobster landing and had walked away before she reached them — not running, just walking, back toward the head of the wharf and out of the dock light. Nineteen months since the night of the blow and she had nothing more than she'd had that first morning, when she opened the tide log and read the gap her silence had left.

She didn't know if she needed to.

The harbor log was not a record of everything. It was a record of what a harbormaster could enter in good faith. Owen had known this. His 1934 entry about J.T. — she had found it in January the year before, the deferred notation eventually made whole: what he had seen, in the standard format, when he had what he needed to put it down. He had not entered what he couldn't confirm. Neither had she.

She stood at the breakwater's end another minute. The spray at the south corner where the chop hit the face. The lobster pound at the far side of the harbor, Cullen's truck already back in the lot. The open water south, gray under the April overcast, the horizon gone into the sky.

She turned and walked back.

The wharf, the cedar-shingled office at the foot of it, the window with the tide board visible from ten feet: May figures, her handwriting. The numbers the numbers regardless of what the radio at Beal's was saying.

---

Owen's ledger was in the cabinet. She had not opened it since October's log review, and she would not open it today.

She sat at the chart table.

Her log was open to Wednesday, May 2nd. The day's entry was started but not finished — the six-forty-five tide, the weather notation, the morning fleet status. The spaces below were blank.

She picked up her pen.

The noon notation: wind shift from northwest to west-northwest, gusting ten to twelve. Fleet status unchanged. The Jessup boy had gone out at ten-thirty and come back in at noon; she had noted it in the transit log and she transferred the notation now: departure time, return, no significant events.

The two-o'clock mooring check. All lines good. East pier, second slip — slight fraying at the nip, the same she had noted Tuesday. She entered it formally: slip number, location, description, assessment. *Monitor. No action yet.* Next week she would pull the line and measure what was there.

Hanson brothers: due Thursday to open their season. Three slips reserved on the main float, the same positions every year. She wrote the pending reservation, the dates, the standard mooring-fee condition.

Robert Cates's renewal confirmation. She had entered it yesterday but she added the season notation now in the space reserved for it — *Spring 1945* — and underlined the year the way she always underlined the first confirmed renewal of a new season.

Outside the window the harbor held what it held. The boats on the main float riding the small chop of the afternoon, the light on the water thin and flat in the overcast. A gull on the bollard at the dock's end. The breakwater at the channel's edge, gray in the afternoon, the algae line invisible at this hour of tide but there — she knew where it was.

She turned to the next page.

*May 1945.* She wrote the heading in the top right corner the way she always did, the month and year and nothing else. Below it, the entry for Wednesday was still unfinished — the afternoon's remaining notations waiting, the six o'clock tide still to come, the evening fleet check, whatever else the harbor brought before the day was done.

She kept writing.
